Worked example
Worked example: exposing a C++ object

Sending one piece of data from the server to a window on the client meant four serialization and deserialization parsers, all written by hand, crossing three or four languages. The cost showed in the number of files touched. In autumn 2024 I replaced all of it with one protobuf transport, and a message stopped needing any C++ definition at all.

Raid is the lean case. The packet is declared and encoded in C++ on the server, decoded in the C++ launcher, and pushed to Python. Counted by hand, one raid message touches 10 places: the shared header and structs, the server encode, the client size table, the dispatch switch, the receive function, its declaration, the constants exported to Python, the game window, the interface forwarder and the raid window itself. The request direction, from the player to the server, adds 6 more. Pets are the heavy case. The client-side data lived in C++, so Python could not read it without a hand-written Python C API in front of it. A pet's experience value alone went through about 12 sites: the packet, the server send, the size table, the dispatch, the decode, a setter and getter on the player's pet store, a refresh flag, the C API getter and its method table entry, then three Python files. The pet module has 11 such getters. The launcher stored the data and Python pulled each field back out one call at a time. Every one of those C++ sites meant a rebuild of the server, the launcher, or both. A new field on a window meant a rebuild.

The roulette is the feature I follow end to end. It was a C++ system on the server, with its own packet headers, a command in the chat command table, an input handler and a branch in the launcher's server command parser. The data crossed to the client as a string, and the launcher cut that string apart before Python cut it apart again. This is the launcher side as it was in October 2024: else if ("item_info" == TokenVector[1]) { if (3 != TokenVector.size()) { TraceError("CPythonNetworkStream::ServerCommand(c_szCommand=%s) - Strange Parameter Count : %s", c_szCommand); return; } PyCallClassMemberFunc(m_apoPhaseWnd[PHASE_WINDOW_GAME], "BINARY_Roulette_UpdateInfo", Py_BuildValue("(s)", TokenVector[2].c_str())); } Python then received vnum,count|vnum,count as a plain string and split it on the bars and the commas to fill the prize list.

On 25 October 2024 the roulette was rewritten as a forge, a Lua script that runs on the server. I count it as a new system in Lua, not a port: it was completely different from the C++ one. The commit touched 31 files and deleted 505 lines of C++ for the system itself, plus the launcher parser branch, the four BINARY_Roulette_* methods in the game window and the roulette packet header. What replaced it is a 35-line .proto, a 253-line .forge and the generated Python and Lua stubs. The same message now takes this path. On the old path the launcher parsed the content. On the new one it reads a namespace, a header and a size, and hands the rest through untouched. It does not know what a roulette is. The server side is plain Lua. This is the code today, from another feature, because it shows the whole idea in a few lines: local result = pb_loader.new(messages.GCActivateResult) forge.sys.game.send_client(ch, "activate_result", result:SerializeToString()) local counters = pb_loader.new(messages.GCUpdateCounters) pb_loader.load(counters, { stone_kills = ch:get_quest_flag("casual_mode.stone_kills"), uid_active_count = uid_count + 1, affect_duration = duration, claimed_objectives = claimed, }) forge.sys.game.send_client(ch, "update_counters", counters:SerializeToString()) ch is the player's character. A message is a namespace, a header and a protobuf payload. The .proto compiles to Python and to Lua and never to C++, so nothing in the engine has to know the message exists. There is one Luna header per channel: client to game, game to client, game to game, game to database and database to game.

The list is short. There are no GC, CG, DG or GD packets to declare for a feature. There are no hooks in the input handling. Everything travels from Lua to Python without recompiling anything. For the roulette that is three authored files and none of them C++. A change to the prize list or the window no longer waits for a build of the server or the launcher. The proto compile is still a step, but it rebuilds neither binary.

JSON was too verbose for game traffic. FlatBuffers was not in my knowledge. I had already worked with protobuf, it is compact and fast, and it has a good tooling ecosystem. The same definition compiles for Lua on the server and Python on the client, which is the whole point.

Once the launcher stopped decoding, the hard part moved to the Python side: handler dispatching, with registration and unregistration. The first registry was a little older than the transport. In July 2024 the guild war page subscribed to the same season and ranking data as another window, and the server had to stop duplicating observers for the same player, type and handler. The client registry changed in that commit too, from handing out the first free small id to being keyed by the window's own handle. The Luna registry came on 21 October 2024. Before it, every Luna message went to the game window, which forwarded it by hand. After it, a window registers for a pair of namespace and header: On the Python side a window registers in its constructor and unregisters in __del__, nothing else: def __init__(self): ui.ScriptWindow.__init__(self) self.__Initialize() self.__LoadWindow() luna.RegisterHandler(self.GetWindowHandle(), "ue_curse_manager", "curse_update", ui.__mem_func__(self.__OnCurseUpdate)) def __del__(self): luna.UnregisterHandler(self.GetWindowHandle()) ui.ScriptWindow.__del__(self) The handler receives the raw bytes and parses them with the generated class: utils.Deserialize(curse_gem_pb2.GCCurseGemUpdate(), message) returns the message, or None after logging the decode error. A window rarely listens to one message. The achievements panel registers three of them in its constructor, before its UI script loads, so an early push from the server is never missed. The registry keeps two maps over the same entries. One goes from namespace and header to the list of handlers, for dispatch. The other goes from the window's identifier to everything it registered, so a window being destroyed removes all of its handlers in one call without remembering what it listened to. A third small map turns the window into a number the server can store, which is how a feature asks for its later messages to reach one window and no other.

Dispatch has a fallback. If no registered handler took the message, the launcher passes it to the window named by the target, or to the game window when the target is 0, and that window routes by namespace and header in Python. Several features use that on purpose: a tower window that is created only when the server sends the first floor, for example, or the land data that is not a window at all. The registry decided whether the fallback ran by what Call returned. In October 2024 it ended like this: bool CPythonLuna::Call(uint32_t handler_id, const std::string& ns, const std::string& header, PyObject* py_message, uint64_t receipt) { // Find the namespace in m_handlers auto nsIt = m_handlers.find(ns); if (nsIt == m_handlers.end()) return false; // Find the header in the namespace auto headerIt = nsIt->second.find(header); if (headerIt == nsIt->second.end()) return false; auto& handlerVec = headerIt->second; // Call each handler in the vector for (const auto& lh : handlerVec) { if (handler_id && lh.handler_id != handler_id) continue; // Call the Python function and check for errors PyObject* result = PyObject_CallFunction(lh.callback, (char*)"OK", py_message, receipt); if (result == nullptr) { // If there's an error, print the error to stderr and clear the Python error indicator PyErr_Print(); // Prints the error to stderr PyErr_Clear(); // Clears the Python error indicator } else { // Decrement the reference count if the function call succeeds Py_DECREF(result); } } return handlerVec.size() != 0; } That says "delivered" whenever any handler is registered for the namespace and header, even when the target filter skipped every one of them. With two windows registered and a message aimed at neither, no callback ran, Call returned true, the launcher returned early and the fallback never ran either. Neither window received the data. Nothing was logged and nothing raised. I do not remember which feature showed it. The symptom was always the same: two windows on one message, and neither got it. With a single registrant the bug was invisible, which is why it lived so long. It was there from October 2024 to August 2026, about 22 months. A teammate fixed it in August 2026: the loop now records whether a handler actually ran, and Call returns that. The same change fixed a second bug of the same kind. When the client moved to 64 bits in December 2024, window handles became small ids so the server would no longer hold a memory pointer. The getter that translates a window to that id lacked its return, so every message the client sent with a window handle carried a zero. That too lasted until August 2026. The roulette had its own version of the same pressure. In May 2026 a teammate added one manager that opens the right roulette by its UI type, and in June inline hosts began registering with that manager. One registrant per message, with the routing done in Python. It works around the problem instead of removing it.

Rejoin dungeon and the roulette were the first features on protobuf, in the same week of October 2024 as the season and ranking managers, and both were new systems written for Lua. The first existing system I actually ported was the lobby, a few days later: its logic moved into Lua, while its packets stayed in C++, reshaped to carry strings. Match observer, master hunt, dungeon info, the battle pass and notifications followed through June 2025. When the legacy achievements system was retired in September 2026, seven C++ files went with their database loaders and packet headers, and the new panel talks to its forge directly. The launcher never learned that achievements exist. Today there are 42 protos, 48 forge files and 94 registration calls across 33 Python files. It did not fit everything. In September 2026 the land topology went back to C++, into a client store, and the Luna topology messages were removed. The cost is the other side of the same blindness. Nothing below Python knows what a message means, so nothing below Python can catch a mistake in using it. A forgotten registration is silent, a stale one swallows messages, and for 22 months the registry itself reported success it had not earned. The discipline moved into the window code: register in the constructor, unregister on destroy, by identifier. Once the transport is generic, ownership becomes the protocol. A layer that does not know its payloads has to know exactly who is listening, and "delivered" has to mean that a handler ran.
documents.s: What it cost, what it bought

documents.t: I debugged quests by commenting out one line at a time until the problem went away. The logging that the Metin2 mainline engine gives a quest script could not print a player or a mob, so there was nothing else to try.
documents.s: Debugging Lua like a first-class language

documents.t: The quest log functions were there, but not reachable everywhere and unable to print complex structures like a pc or a mob. This is the Metin2 mainline error function, which is also what my tree had until September 2024: int32_t _syserr(lua_State* L) { if (!lua_isstring(L, 1)) return 0; PC* pc = CQuestManager::instance().GetCurrentPC(); if (!pc) return 0; LPCHARACTER ch = CQuestManager::instance().GetCurrentCharacterPtr(); if (!ch) return 0; sys_err("QUEST: quest: %s player: %s : %s", pc->GetCurrentQuestName().c_str(), ch->GetName(), lua_tostring(L, 1)); ch->ChatPacket(CHAT_TYPE_INFO, "QUEST_SYSERR %s", lua_tostring(L, 1)); return 0; } Read it as a list of ways to log nothing. lua_isstring is true for strings and numbers only, so a table, a nil or a boolean is dropped without a word. With no current player, or no current character, the function returns before it logs. That is any callback that runs without a selected player, a server timer for one. And the output is one string, so a script author could only print scalars fetched one at a time. sys_log is stricter: it wants a numeric level as its first argument, and without one it drops the call. That last rule bit in September 2021. A teammate had added sys_log lines to the kill counter of the Scorpion Desert dungeon. I removed them four days later and added a log to the dungeon rejoin quest instead. The line went in without its level argument, so it printed nothing, and it was fixed half an hour later. Add a log, run the dungeon, look, remove it: in September 2024 that one rejoin line was the only sys_log or sys_err left in any .quest file. Authoring dungeons was a mess. If a stage blocked or did not go as planned, we had to repeat the whole dungeon, placing sys_err prints on flat structures, and go by try. When prints told me nothing I commented single lines until the problem went away. A failing script did not help either. The server reported the quest, the state and the event, not a line. The chunk was named after the quest, and its line numbers counted the compiled snippet, not the .quest file I edited.
documents.s: Logs that could not print the thing I needed

documents.t: The first devtool was the linter, and it was built together with the remote debugger. I started from existing extensions: a remote debugger for Lua and the sumneko language server. I experimented with the two separately, in the same work package, and then folded the linter inside the debugger for convenience. It ships as one VS Code extension. On activation it adds a plugin to the language server's settings, and the plugin rewrites the quest dialect into plain Lua the server can type-check. quest name begin becomes a local table, a define becomes a local, and when <triggers> with <cond> begin becomes if <cond> then. The triggers are blanked with spaces of the same length, so every line and column after them stays where it was. The setup for a script author is one launch.json entry: { "version": "0.2.0", "configurations": [ { "type": "uc-lrdb", "request": "attach", "name": "Metin2 Quest Debug", "host": "localhost", "port": 21110, "sourceRoot": "${workspaceFolder}", "sourceMapPaths": [], "pathMappings": [], "stopOnEntry": true } ] } That entry is the cheap part. Making the debugger understand the engine behind it took three rewrites: the quest compiler, the server's bookkeeping of files and lines, and the way the client loads Python modules. It cost me nothing I would call a price. It was 100% worth it, it was fun, and I learned a lot.
documents.s: One extension, a debugger and a linter

documents.t: Of the three, the compiler hurt the most. It was the hardest for two reasons: edge cases that came out later, and source mapping. The Metin2 mainline compiler does not translate quests, it re-prints them. It walks the token stream and writes every token back out separated by a space, so comments and blank lines vanish and the layout is gone. A line in the output has no arithmetic relation to a line in the source. On top of that my tree ran a Python front end in front of the compiler, which copied each quest into a working folder with the define constants substituted. Errors then named the copy, one more step away from the file I edited. On 20 September 2024 I split the one big compiler file into a compiler, a quest model, a forge part and helpers. Five days later the source-map version landed, in one commit that touched 65 files. It did four things: The Lua lexer was patched to count columns, so every token carries a line and a position. A when body became a slice of the original source text instead of a re-print. Every object the compiler writes records a source map entry: the source file, the compiled file, the start and end line in the source, and the offset inside the compiled file. They are dumped per source file as JSON. A define line is commented out in place, never deleted, so the line count survives preprocessing. The old Python front end and its working copies were deleted. The path from a breakpoint to a running script looks like this. The compiler writes the map next to its output, the debug adapter in the editor loads it, and the adapter translates in both directions: The server never reads the map. The adapter does: it loads every map under sourceMapPaths, builds a forward and an inverse table, and does the arithmetic itself. One editor line can map to several compiled files, because a when body with several triggers is written once per trigger. The edge cases were the long tail, and they kept coming for sixteen months. On 23 September 2024 I fixed or-chained when triggers: the argument was registered before the compiler checked for the or, so the wrong objects came out. That commit also added the first test file for the compiler, 78 lines. Two days later the same test was rewritten so that the triggers and the with condition were split across lines, because a compiler that slices source text, unlike one that re-prints tokens, cares where a condition ends and a body starts. The test file now holds 16 when shapes. On 22 October 2024 state names stopped being converted from a variable to a string, so set_state(__COMPLETE__) had to become set_state("__COMPLETE__") through a regex pass. The old compiler did this on the token; mine no longer re-prints tokens. On 8 November 2024 a quest with two blocks for the same event and no argument kept only the last one. The real case was two take blocks in the Devil Tower quest. The fix merged the blocks into one script, and the source map then needed an offset for where each block starts inside the merged file. On 30 January 2025 a conditioned block lost the return that the Metin2 mainline engine closed it with. Preprocessor substitution was the slowest to show. Defines can use other defines, as in the Wonsui Temple dungeon: define DUNGEON_KEY 11 define D_EASY_MIN_LEVEL forge.game.ue_dungeon_info:get_min_level_access(DUNGEON_KEY) I had kept the defines in an unordered map, so the order of substitution was arbitrary and a redefinition overwrote the first value. On 25 October 2025 they became an ordered list substituted last to first: // Perform the substitution in the entire content in reverse order for (auto it = defines.rbegin(); it != defines.rend(); ++it) { const std::string& identifier = it->first; const std::string& value = it->second; std::regex identifier_regex("\\b" + identifier + "\\b"); new_content = std::regex_replace(new_content, identifier_regex, value); } The last source-map bug I know of is from 23 January 2026. A function inlined into a quest carried an offset that was one line short, because the compiler appends ",\n" after it. Sixteen months after the rewrite, a breakpoint in an inlined function could still land one line off.
documents.s: The compiler was the hardest part

documents.t: The server half was small on paper. On 25 September 2024, the same day as the compiler, I attached LRDB to the quest Lua state behind two config keys, server.lrdb.enabled and server.lrdb.port. Both default to off. Then I made every loaded script remember the compiled file it came from, and passed that name through every call that executes a quest script. The chunk is now named @ plus the file path, which is the Lua convention for a file: stack frames and errors carry the compiled file and line. The adapter strips the @ and looks the file up in its inverse map. That is all the server knows about the whole source-map story. A second pair of path mappings, for the conf/ and locale/ folders, lives in the launch.json, because the machine running the game and the machine running the editor do not share a root.
documents.s: The server keeps a file name per script

documents.t: The client was worse to see. Its Python never runs from files on disk: sys.path is empty and every import is answered by a custom importer that reads the module out of EterPack, the client's packed virtual file system. A debugger maps a frame to a file through __file__, and a module compiled out of a pack has no file a debugger can open. The Metin2 mainline engine pasted the main script into a string and executed it, and its importer handled flat names only. I rewrote how the client manages module loading in May 2024, four months before the Lua half. The launcher runs the main script as a real module, with __file__ set. The importer maps dotted names to paths, supports packages, and compiles each pack module with its absolute path as the filename. The socket and ctypes libraries the debugger needs are linked statically. A build with the debugger compiled in attaches ptvsd on the first free local port from 3000 to 3049. The importer was not finished then. Submodule access and parent linking were reworked in December 2024, with case-insensitive imports a few days later, so that the same module is not instantiated twice. In September 2026 a debugger build began to prefer a .py file beside the executable over the packed one and to re-read it when it changes, executing into the same module object as reload does. A shipped client never sets the flag.
documents.s: The client had no file to open

documents.t: A debugger tells you what went wrong after you run the script. The linter has to tell you before, and it can only do that if it knows what the engine offers. Before 29 September 2024 it knew nothing. A binding was a C function plus a row in a registration table, and the Lua side had no stubs at all. A script author guessed the arguments or read the C++. That day I put the documentation inline, above each binding, as EmmyLua annotations in Doxygen comments, and wrote a Python parser that walks the Doxygen XML and writes one stub file per namespace into the quest meta folder. The first run annotated 28 binding files and produced 37 stub files. Today there are 2,256 inline @lua markers across 93 server source files, and they produce 106 stub files with 15,384 lines. The client got the same treatment in October 2024: 24 .pyi stub files for its C++ Python modules, 27 today. The annotation sits where the function is written: /** * @brief Retrieves the current level of the current character. * * \---\@luadoc pc * * \---**Requires CurrentCharacter** * * \---\@return number # The current level of the character. * \---\@lua pc.get_level = function() end */ and the generated stub is what the linter reads: ---**Requires CurrentCharacter** ---@return number # The current level of the character. pc.get_level = function() end The source of truth stays in one place, so the binding and its documentation change in the same diff. The parser warns loudly when a bare Doxygen command appears inside a block instead of an escaped one. It re-emits the preamble for a second @lua marker with no new documentation, which is how an overload is written. This part is very important. Giving proper support to Lua when you are encouraging people to use Lua is almost mandatory. A language you tell people to write in needs completion, signatures and type checks, not only a debugger for when it breaks.
documents.s: Stubs: the linter needed to know the engine

documents.t: A dungeon stage that does not go as planned no longer means replaying the whole dungeon with prints on flat structures. The breakpoint goes on the line of the .quest file and stops there, with the table open in the editor. The window code on the client is a file I can change while the client runs.

I started Forge because of two things the quest manager would not let me do. The first was to reach two player instances in one block and rely on it. The second was to bind a UI button to an action. The first one the manager could do, in a way so fragile that I stopped trusting it. The second one it could do only if the C++ had foreseen the button, and the price of one foreseen button was 18 files. Why quests were not enough tells what broke. This post is the mechanism, and it hangs on one idea, the quest manager state: how the classic manager works, what it does well, where those two tasks hit its walls, and what the same tasks look like in Forge.
documents.s: How the quest manager works, and what Forge changed

documents.t: The manager is a Lua and C++ integration from the early 2000s, and the Metin2 mainline engine has run its scripting on it for two decades. I do not say that to be polite. It is a good design for what it was built for. The quest compiler turns each when block into one file named after the event it answers. A script for the use of item 71055 lands in object/71055/use/change_name.start, a kill of mob 691 in object/691/kill/..., and an event with no target in object/notarget/<event>/. At boot the game core walks those folders and indexes the chunks by vnum and event. Finding the code for an event is a directory lookup. When the event fires, the manager opens a new Lua thread on the single global state and runs the chunk top to bottom. The thread is short lived. Whatever the script needs to keep goes through the C API into quest flags, and the locals die with the coroutine. Two running scripts share no locals. And yielding is invisible to the author. q.select(...) stops the coroutine, the manager sends the question to the client, and the answer resumes the script on the next line. A scripter writes a conversation as straight-line code. Read the two slots on the left first: CurrentCharacter and CurrentItem are C++ pointers, and the pc. and item. namespaces are bound to them. Each event entry writes them, and every pc.* function reads them. The coroutines on the right are spawned from the one global state and call the namespaces. The dotted line to the client is the yield: the coroutine stops, the client answers, the coroutine resumes. That binding has a name in the engine's own debug dump, "Quest Manager State", and it is the idea the rest of this post reads through. The quest manager state is the snapshot behind the exposed APIs: pc., npc., item., d. and the others. It is set up for one player per event. Its members: the current PC, which holds the quest flags and the name of the running quest, and the current character; the current party member, set by party kill events, and in my engine a target NPC; the current item and the current NPC, which the manager reads through the current character; the selected dungeon, used by d. when there is no current character; the running QuestState, the coroutine being resumed, and the dialog buffer that say appends to; the timer and cron arguments. Every exposed function reads these slots instead of taking an argument. This is the greatest limitation of the quest manager, and one of the reasons Luna was born. The state is built for one PC, and anything that needs a second one has to break it. The binding has a second cost, in writing the API. Every function of every namespace is a C function written by hand, mapped argument by argument, which is slow and easy to get wrong. The engine has 826 such table rows (796 distinct functions) in 32 namespaces plus the globals, 211 of them under pc alone. The Metin2 mainline engine has 649 in 35 namespaces. And since every pc.* function acts on the player the state was set up for, a script cannot work on several players, or several items, as equals.
documents.s: What the quest manager does well

documents.t: The quest manager has two ways to reach a second player, and the author of a script sees them as almost the same thing. pc.select(vid) makes another player the current one and returns the previous VID, so the script can switch back. It substitutes the PC in place and nothing else. The current PC and the current character move to player B. The running QuestState, the dialog buffer and the timer arguments stay set up for player A. item., npc. and d. are read through the current character, so they move too, to whatever B last had: B's last item, the NPC B last talked to, B's dungeon. The state no longer describes one event. It describes a mix of A and B, and pc.select has no stack, no marker of who the root was and no guard. Here is what that does: pc.setqf("x", 1) writes under the quest B last ran, not under the quest whose script is running. B's flag lands in the wrong quest and A's quest never gets it. pc.setf(quest, flag, value) takes the quest name and is immune. q.setstate takes A's running state and looks the state name up in B's last quest. A's state gets another quest's numbering, and B's status for that quest is overwritten. One call corrupts both players. When the script ends with B still selected, the cleanup runs on A's quest but takes the character from the manager. the NPC lock is checked against B, B's quest item is cleared, a pending quest-window update for A goes to B's client, and a state change in A's quest fires its leave, enter and letter events for B. Dialogue written before the switch and flushed after it goes to B. Any nested event, a level up from a script or a unique mob killed by d.kill_all, sets its own PC current and leaves it there. The script resumes with someone else selected, and pc.select cannot notice. The Metin2 mainline engine ships the pattern that never restores. In the Spider Dungeon 3 quest, the kill of the Spider King selects the leader to read the name for the notice, and the script ends there: when "2092".kill begin if pc.get_map_index()>=2320000 and pc.get_map_index()<2330000 then game.drop_item_with_ownership(40072,1) local leader = party.getf("leader_vid") pc.select(leader) local leader_name = pc.get_name() notice_all("Il gruppo di "..leader_name.." ha sconfitto il Re dei Ragni") local map=pc.get_map_index() warp_all_to_village(map, 20) duty.work_on_duty_in_map(special.duty_type.DUTY_DUNGEON, special.duty_dungeon.SPIDER, pc.get_map_index()) end end The killer's script ends with the leader current. If the leader is not on this core, pc.select does nothing and the notice names the killer instead. If the script had changed a quest state, the cleanup would fire it on the leader. This one changes none, so only the NPC and the item of the leader are touched, but the pattern is the hazard. The marriage quest uses the careful form: select the partner, copy the ring and gold checks into locals, select back. That is safe only while nothing between the two selects yields or fires an event, and the script has to know it. My engine did the same: the 2017 dungeon quests looped pc.select over every participant inside a dungeon_kill event without selecting back, and the 2023 thirty-minute dungeon set a cooldown flag with pc.setqf for each player in that loop. I remember this one from the 2014 version. For a long time players there "exchanged" quest state, because a pc.select was used in the dungeon login event to check every participant's inventory and remove forbidden items. Ymir's answer is q.begin_other_pc_block(pid) and q.end_other_pc_block(). I think of it as a stack of quest manager states, and it is the start of one. What the code stacks is only the player id. The begin remembers the first PC as the root, pushes the current PC's id on a vector of ids, and selects pid. The end pops the id and selects it again. So the PC and the character come back, after any depth of nesting, and nothing else is stacked: the running state, the dialog buffer and the timers were never touched, and inside the block the item, the NPC and the quest name are still B's leftovers. My engine's own comment next to the nested-event bug says it plainly: "The correct way to fix this should be to stack questmanager states." The block adds one more rule. A yield inside it would show a dialogue to B while the coroutine belongs to A, so the manager forbids it. In the Metin2 mainline engine the select, wait, input or confirm logs "FATAL ERROR! Yield occur in other_pc_block." and returns without yielding, and the script runs on as if the answer had been nothing. The diagram shows the state as one set of slots. Look at the slot pc.select swaps, at what follows it to player B, at what stays on player A, then at the id stack the block adds beside it. The Metin2 mainline engine uses the block in 38 places, always as a party loop: one for over the member ids with a begin and an end around the body. Read one whole function. It resets a flag on every member of the party: CryptOfCrownless.ResetPartyTimers = function() say_title(string.format("%s:[ENTER]", mob_name(npc.get_race()))) for _, pid in ipairs(party_get_member_pids()) do q.begin_other_pc_block(pid); -- pc.setf(CryptOfCrownless.GetData()["dungeon_name"]["quest"], "entrance_timer", 0); -- q.end_other_pc_block(); end -- for say("Il timer del tuo gruppo è stato reimpostato.[ENTER]") end -- function The flag's quest is named in the call, with pc.setf and not pc.setqf, so the leftover quest name never matters. The dialogue is written before and after the loop and never inside, and nothing in the 38 blocks calls say, select, wait or setstate. A script author who survived the state learned to keep the block to one flag write at a time. That is the block working as intended, and it is also the cost: you switch, do one explicit-name call, switch back, and repeat for the next field. To compare two players you copy every value into a local between switches. In my engine's history no .quest file ever calls the block directly, and the quests that touch a second player use pc.select. The block was still fragile, and the fragility sat in what the manager did not check: If pid has no character on this core, the switch does nothing and the body runs against the previous player. The Metin2 mainline begin returns nothing, so the script cannot tell. A Lua error inside the block skips the end, and the stack stays pushed until the process dies. I fixed these in the engine on 2026-08-10, in one commit with six entries: the depth is restored on every exit from a resume, the begin reports a failed switch so the caller can skip the body, a yield inside a block raises, and d.foreach_participant_safe wraps its body in pcall. All of it is bookkeeping to make a stack of ids behave like a scope. The model is still one state set up for one player, and the script has to remember whose it is.

The second task was to bind a UI button to an action. In the classic manager a button has two homes. The first is a yield that the C++ knows about. The quest calls select_land(), the manager sends a tag to the client, the client opens the land window, and the player's pick comes back as the return value. The button exists only as an answer to a question the script asked, so the player must first talk to an NPC and pass a q.select. And every such yield is written out through the whole stack. For select_land that meant a Lua wrapper, a suspend state, a branch in the resume dispatcher, a handler that resumes the coroutine, a packet header and its handler on the server, and on the client the event type, the network call, the header name, the interface hook and the window itself. 18 files, in Lua, server C++, the shared packet header, client C++ and Python. It was in the repository from the first commit in 2016, and I removed it on 2026-09-05 with the land forge. select_item was the same story on a smaller scale, and questlib.lua still carries a select_alchemy wrapper whose C++ half died with the alchemy system in 2019. A yield is only as good as its branch in C++. The second home is a custom command. The blessing window, added in October 2022, is an example. Its Python sends /blessing_activate as a chat line, the C++ command table maps the name to a handler, and the handler checks the skill and calls the blessing manager. No yield, no quest, but a new row in a table of 289 commands and a C++ function for every button. The client's Python has 76 call sites that send a slash command as a chat line. Both routes end in C++ you must write, compile and deploy for a button.
documents.s: A button needs a foreseen yield

documents.t: A Forge script is a Lua file with one or more environment sections, and each section runs in a named process: game for the game core, db for the database cache. qc writes one file per environment (ue_event_boss_coins.game, ue_event_boss_coins.db), every process loads only the files that carry its name, and whatever a section returns is stored in the global state under forge.<environment>.<name>. The section is a module, loaded once at boot and alive until shutdown. Its locals are its own, its require is isolated, and reads that miss fall back to the globals, so it still sees the quest namespaces, forge and the other forges. The same file can carry a state start begin block, compiled as an ordinary quest under the same name. Quest chunks, which still run in their own coroutines, call into the forge directly through forge.game.<name>. The two scopes share the name and nothing else: the quest block cannot see the environment's locals. The game and the db cache are two processes with two Lua states. Their forge sections never share memory: they talk by protobuf message over the connection the two already had. The client talks to a forge by protobuf too, and the quest manager's current-instance slots are still there, untouched, for the quests that use them. The second change is what a forge receives. The C++ classes are bound straight into Lua: CHARACTER, CItem, CDungeon, CGuild and the rest, 49 usertypes in all, each with its methods. A handler is called with the character itself, not with a slot to read. So the first task, reaching many players, stops being a matter of switching. This is the real boss coins forge from October 2026, paying every player who did at least 10 percent of a boss's damage: function EventBossCoins:pay_boss(contributors, boss_level) for pid, _ in pairs(contributors) do --- Offline contributors are skipped by design: with no character there is --- no level to gate on, and change_* would have nothing to write to. local ch = forge.sys.game.char_manager.find_by_pid(pid) if ch ~= nil and math.abs(ch:get_level() - boss_level) <= EventBossCoins.LEVEL_RANGE then local amount = coins_for_level(ch:get_level()) if self:has_blessing(ch, "mh") then ch:change_mh_coin(amount) ch:chat_packet_v(forge.sys.game.CHAT_TYPE.INFO, locale.events.boss_coins_paid_mh, amount) end if self:has_blessing(ch, "guild") then ch:change_guild_coin(amount) ch:chat_packet_v(forge.sys.game.CHAT_TYPE.INFO, locale.events.boss_coins_paid_guild, amount) end end end end No begin, no end, no copy into locals. Each contributor is an object passed explicitly, and ch:get_level() and ch:change_mh_coin(...) act on that object whoever else is running. There is no snapshot to corrupt: nothing global changes when the loop moves from one player to the next, no quest name is inherited, and a nested event cannot leave someone else selected. The loop asks for as many players as it needs, and the number two has no special place in it. When a script needs a quest namespace on a chosen player, a forge wraps it in ch:with_questmanager(fn), which is the old block with its scope guard. The third change is the button. In Forge a button is a message with a header. The event window of the boss coins event has two HTML buttons, and each one calls a two-line Python function: def DonateBossCoinsMh(self): luna.Message("ue_event_boss_coins", "donate_mh", "") def DonateBossCoinsGuild(self): luna.Message("ue_event_boss_coins", "donate_guild", "") The forge registered a handler for each header when it was created, with set_main_processor("donate_mh", ...). The payload is empty because the header already is the choice. There is no yield to foresee, no packet to declare and no row in the command table: the message goes from the Python window to the server's generic Luna input, which looks up the forge by name and the handler by header, and calls it with the character. The reply goes the other way with send_client, and the window that registered for that forge and header gets it. Registering a window as a handler means send everything about this feature to this window, and the data no longer passes through the C++ launcher. A forge can also hold a conversation with the database without blocking anyone. The vote4buff window, added in June 2026, sends a redeem message. The handler starts a coroutine owned by the player, which yields on a request to the db cache with a 2 second timeout. The db section does the SQL, answers with the receipt, and the coroutine resumes, grants the buff and sends the result to the window. The quest manager could not do that either, since a quest yields only to the client. The dialogue yields, select and input, still belong to the quest state, but a forge runs persistent coroutines of its own that yield on the db and on other cores. The commit that added the feature has 21 files: a protobuf definition, the forge, the window, a SQL table and the web backend and frontend for the votes. No C++ change.
documents.s: The same two tasks in Forge

documents.t: Exposing the instances removes the current-instance globals, and the cost is that nothing guarantees an instance is still there. A player can disconnect between the message and the reply. A forge script must resolve the character by pid when it needs it, and check for nil. The pay_boss above does it with find_by_pid. The vote4buff coroutine resolves the character once, before the yield, and sends the result through that same reference after the resume, which is safe only because the coroutine is owned by the player: when the player disconnects, the manager closes every coroutine the player owns before it drops the player's state. A plain handler, or a reply from another core, has no such cover. Caching a character in a field is the mistake. The rejoin forge did it, and in June 2026 I changed it to hold only the pid and resolve it at each use, with a comment saying why: find_by_pid returns nil for a destroyed player, so every send path heals itself across a disconnect or a channel warp. The quest manager had a different shape of the same hazard. There, a script that forgot a null check read through a stale slot of the manager. Here it holds a stale object of its own.

From June 2022 the arena join closed at 22:00 in the code, and the message told players it was open until 11PM. The message stayed in the source until May 2026, almost four years, and it is a fair summary of how the arena and lobby code behaved before Forge. Arena and lobby were the most used legacy subsystem and the one giving the most problems. Adding a queue or changing a requirement was an engine job, and I was the only one who could do it. It was difficult to customize and very clunky. The code was fragile and a mess.
documents.s: From messy C++ subsystems to Forge

documents.t: The Metin2 mainline engine has no lobby and no matchmaking queue: its arena is a GM-started 1v1 duel. The lobby, the queue and the ranked arena were our own C++ additions, started in November 2017. By the day before the migration they were 12 files and 5,021 lines, plus about 270 lines of lobby handlers in the input code and the MMR manager beside them. The lobby types were a closed C++ enum, the team sizes were picked by a switch, the matchmaking level brackets were if chains, and one arena class served every mode by testing IsRandom() and IsRanked() flags. Lobby type and subtype went over the wire as single bytes, so a new type meant a new enum value on server and client. I once got a request to make the join hour-based. The change took little time. What cost me was finding that somewhere in the input handling code there was already a hardcoded rule and a hardcoded error message deciding when the whole arena lobby was open or closed. The rule itself lived in the lobby manager's enqueue path. A teammate had added it in August 2021 as "random arenas only between 18 and 23". The condition was then edited four times in C++ over the next ten months, and every edit meant a rebuild. This is its last C++ form, from June 2022: if(pkLobby->GetType() == LOBBY_TYPE_PVP_ARENA) { std::time_t t = std::time(0); std::tm* now = std::localtime(&t); if(now->tm_hour < 18 || (now->tm_hour >= 22 && now->tm_min >= 0)) { if(g_bIsTestServer) { pkLobby->SendChatPacketToMembers(CHAT_TYPE_INFO, "<Lobby> TEST SERVER OK! REAL SERVER: Random not open."); } else { return -2; } } } Returning -2 meant "closed". The text the player saw was written in a second file, the packet handler that called the enqueue: <Lobby> Remember it's open only from 6PM to 11PM. When the closing hour moved from midnight to 22:00 in June 2022, the code changed and the message did not. Nobody had a reason to open the second file. Players read a promise the server did not keep. The rule and its message were a pair that had to be edited together and compiled together, and nothing connected the two halves. The lobby was the first existing system I ported to Lua. Rejoin dungeon and the roulette had gone to Lua the week before, but those were completely different systems, and I count them as new. The migration landed in two commits. On October 30, 2024 the lobby manager moved to string type and subtype and a generic Lua lobby processor replaced the C++ switch: 76 files, 5,073 lines added and 4,607 removed, with the old client lobby windows deleted and the packets rewritten to carry strings. On November 5, 2024 the arena followed: the arena class went from 1,400 to 1,062 lines and the arena manager from 698 to 336, and every specialization moved into Lua referees. C++ kept the core of an arena and stopped knowing what kind of arena it was. Lobby properties now come from Lua: forge.sys.game.lobby_manager.set_proto("ARENA_DRAFT", "1V1", { team_count = 2, member_per_team = 1, observer_team_count = 1, flag = forge.sys.game.lobby_manager.LOBBY_FLAG.ENQUEABLE | forge.sys.game.lobby_manager.LOBBY_FLAG.GLOBAL, }) The C++ engine enforces whatever the processor declares. It no longer knows the difference between a ranked match and a custom one. The opening hours moved too. First a cron in the queue script, added on November 6, 2024. Now an availability manager in Lua decides whether a queue is open from the event calendar, the ranked season and manual overrides, and a GM command can force a queue open or closed at runtime. Nobody rebuilds anything to change arena hours. The stale message line stayed in the packet handler long after the rule left C++ and was only commented out in May 2026. The migration moved the rule. It did not clean up the place where the rule had been duplicated.
documents.s: One rule, two files, four years of drift

documents.t: Moving state into Lua gave me a problem C++ never had: the engine holds objects it does not own. A lobby processor or a referee is a Lua table, and C++ keeps a handle to it. The Lua garbage collector decides when a table is dead, and it does not know the engine is still using it. The garbage collector collected the processor and the referee. The system silently stopped. No crash, no error, no stack trace, only arenas that did not start. That is where the pin started. It took me a month to find the cause. What showed it was a log in the destructor of the forge: the object was dying while the server was still running. The cause was in the thread. The processors register themselves from on_boot, which runs in a quest thread with its own Lua state, not in the global one. The reference C++ kept was bound to that short-lived thread. When the thread was gone, the reference went with it, and the GC collected the table while the engine still held its handle. The fix, on January 1, 2025, makes the reference belong to the global state instead of the caller's thread, and the registered processors, the referee factory, event callbacks and their data all got it in the same change. Today the arena manager checks the pinned object and logs instead of crashing: if the referee factory is not valid, creating an arena writes an error and returns nothing. That is the right behavior now, and it is also why the original failure looked like silence. The pin grew with use. In April 2025 the references moved into a registry owned by the bridge, and C++ holds only an id: uint64_t PinObject(sol::object object) { auto id = ++pinned_object_cursor; map_pinned_references[id] = sol::make_reference(GlobalStateView().lua_state(), object); return id; } void UnpinObject(uint64_t id) { map_pinned_references.erase(id); }; template <typename T> T GetPinnedObject(uint64_t id) { auto it = map_pinned_references.find(id); if (it == map_pinned_references.end()) { return T{}; } return it->second.as<T>(); } In July 2026 a handle type bundled the pin with the forge namespace, released when the handle dies, so every arena pins its own referee instance for exactly as long as the arena exists. 23 server files use the pin API today, well outside the arena: guild war, the battle arbiter, player virtualization, traits, land deployment, the REST server. A bug in the arena became the standard way C++ holds a Lua object. What I take from it: when native code keeps a script object, it has to own a reference to it. A borrowed one works until the day the script side decides it is garbage, and it will not tell you.
documents.s: The arena that stopped without a crash

documents.t: The second failure only showed in release builds, where the server crashed outright. I had compiled in release, and the binding library dropped the implicit sol::protected_function to a plain function. A Lua error that a pcall should have caught went through the default panic handler and aborted the process. The calls that did it looked safe. The result was assigned to a sol::protected_function_result, but the call itself was an inline call on the table, and in a release build that inline call goes through lua_call, not lua_pcall. The fix on April 15, 2026 touched 15 files and extracts each method into a named protected function before calling it: sol::protected_function_result result = m_referee[m_methodMapping["on_arena_created"]](m_referee, this); becomes sol::protected_function fn = m_referee[m_methodMapping["on_arena_created"]]; sol::protected_function_result result = fn(m_referee, this); The named type forces lua_pcall in every build, and errors go through the error handler with a stack trace. Today the processor handle does this extraction in one place, so no call site can forget it.
documents.s: Release builds and the pcall that was not one

documents.t: What surprised me in the migration was how much easier gameplay and subsystem authoring became. The first mode I wrote as a forge was the base mode. Then came one without ranking and without MMR. I cannot give a time against the full C++ version, because at the time LLMs did not exist and the two jobs are not comparable. The speedup I felt came when I needed the draft version, which is an extension of the base. Writing it felt like writing a normal child class: no engine change, no new C++ at all, only the new rules and logic. The base referee builds its state and handles the arena lifecycle. Draft takes the base as its __index and overrides what differs, calling up explicitly: local base = require("arena.referees.base") ---@class draft_arena_referee : base_arena_referee local draft_arena_referee = setmetatable({}, {__index = base}) draft_arena_referee.__index = draft_arena_referee ---@return draft_arena_referee function draft_arena_referee:new() return setmetatable(base.new(self), self) end function draft_arena_referee:on_arena_engage(arena) base.on_arena_engage(self, arena) self:start_notice(arena) end Draft adds the guild points, the end-of-match notices, a three-day ban after three desertions, guild coins and battlepass progress. Ranked extends draft and adds MMR on match end. A 5v5 draft is 67 lines: the map positions, the duration, the potion rules and the guild coin payout. The avatar draft layers player virtualization on top, and mayhem, the solo tour and mystery extend that. Ball-Em-Up, the cooperative wave mode, extends the base with its own wave spawning and per-event rankings. The engine at the top knows nothing about this tree. It calls methods by name on whatever the factory returned, and the interface is checked once, when the referee is created. The factory is still a plain chain of branches over type and subtype, one more branch per mode. That is a central file I edit for every new mode, and I did not hide it. A mode is one new file, one branch and a set_proto call in the queue script. In October 2026 a teammate added the 5v5 draft, mystery and Ball-Em-Up as new files extending existing referees. I finally had different lobby and arena logic for different modes, ranked, draft, avatar and mayhem, without changing anything of what existed. We went from needing to touch things that might break existing things, to not caring, because I was building beside what already existed without polluting it. Matchmaking moved the same way. The Lua processor defines the level brackets and the ladder ranges, checks whether a player is banned, has the right arena affect or is stuck in a slow queue, and for a ranked match computes the average ladder of the lobby and compares each candidate against it. A custom match that allows any level difference simply skips the check. I did not measure the cost of this. It works the way the C++ did: it runs a rule against all the characters, level, state and whether they are already in a lobby. The item use policy went through the same migration, replacing scattered restrictions on potions and items with one extensible Lua policy. On the Lua side the arena is now 23 files and 5,395 lines, about the size of the 5,021 lines of C++ it replaced. The difference is who can read it, who can change it, and what breaks when they do.
documents.s: A mode is a child class

documents.t: A quest script can wait for exactly one thing: a player answering a question the C++ asked on its behalf. q.select stops the coroutine, the manager sends the choices to the client, and the next packet from that client resumes the script on the following line. There is no way to write "ask the database and continue when it answers", and no way to write "ask the other core where this dungeon lives". The commit that added it, on 2024-10-09, touched 34 files and added 1,538 lines. The bridge source alone changed by about 500 lines, and a new 299-line header tracks who owns which coroutine. A bug in that header was still being found on 2026-04-08. In between sit a coroutine that restarted from the top, references the garbage collector could take from under the C++, a yield that did not belong in C++, and a disconnect that resumed scripts on a character that was already gone. This post is that mechanism and the three bugs that shaped it. Why quests were not enough told why the short-lived quest coroutine was the biggest flaw, and How the quest manager works, and what Forge changed showed the one global state it runs in. Neither showed what replaced the yield. The quest manager still exists and still runs in parallel with Luna; this is about the coroutine Luna runs next to it.
documents.s: A script that waits on the server

documents.t: The quest yield is a closed set. The C++ knows when a script is about to yield, because the yielding functions are the ones that send a dialogue: select, wait, input, confirm. The manager stores the suspended coroutine on the player's quest state, and the client's answer is routed to that player. A new kind of answer needs a new packet, a new switch case and a new yielding function, written in C++. The limit is not a speed. It is a shape: a script cannot wait for anything the engine did not foresee. A subsystem that needed a database answer therefore did the same thing in C++: send a packet with a header, register a handler for the answer header, and carry the state between the two halves by hand in a table.
documents.s: A yield the C++ must foresee

documents.t: The realistic ways to give a script a wait are three. A per-request callback: the script passes a function, the engine calls it when the answer comes. It works for one wait. It stops working when a feature needs three waits in a row, because the code now nests three functions deep, an error in the second has no way back to the first, and the local variables of the first have to be captured by hand. An explicit state machine: the feature stores a state in a table, and a handler per answer header advances it. This is what the C++ handlers already were. Every feature carries its own table, its own cleanup and its own "what if the player left" branch. Yielding calls: the script is written straight-line, and the wait is a call that does not return until the answer arrives. A quest conversation already reads this way. The first bridge commit says so in its own message: yielding versions of the database and main-core sends exist "to allow the script to wait the answer instead of having to setup another handler". I took the third because the control flow stays in one function, but it moves the problem. A callback is owned by whoever registered it, and the engine forgets it after the call. A suspended coroutine is a piece of script state that the engine holds for an unknown time. Something has to say who can wake it, who can kill it and when it dies if nobody answers.

The bridge keeps a table of coroutine records keyed by an id. A script creates a coroutine with bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner, which runs it immediately up to its first yield. If it ends before yielding, no record survives. If it yields, the record stays. Three things decide how it wakes. A receipt token. A wait asks the bridge for a token that packs the coroutine id, an owner type and an owner id, and sends the token inside the request. The other side answers with the token echoed back. The bridge looks the token up and compares the owner it was issued to with the owner on the answer. A wrong owner finds nothing. An owner. A coroutine can belong to a player or a peer, and one owner can hold many coroutines. When the owner goes away, the bridge closes every coroutine it holds, resuming each one with nil, false. A deadline. A wait can carry a timeout. The bridge keeps the deadlines in a priority queue and cancels lazily: a deadline that has already been answered is marked dead and skipped when it surfaces. The script side is two helpers. This is the code today, from the helper that waits on the database: helper.sys.game.yield_db = function(header, message, desc_handler, ...) local coro_id = bridge.coro.get_current_id() if not coro_id then error("yield_db outside a coroutine") end -- db is the peer 0 local receipt = bridge.coro.generate_receipt_token(coro_id, bridge.coro.COROUTINE_OWNER.PEER, 0) forge.sys.game.send_db(header, message, desc_handler, receipt) return coroutine.yield(...) end The token is made, the packet goes out with it, and the coroutine yields. The game loop is single-threaded, so the answer cannot overtake the yield: it is processed later, on the same loop, after the script is suspended. The database side answers with the same token. One feature end to end shows the shape. The vote buff window sends a redeem message from the client. The handler validates it, then starts a coroutine owned by that player and returns at once. The coroutine claims the vote in the database with a 2 second timeout: local res, ok = forge_helper.coro.with_timeout(2000, forge_helper.sys.game.yield_db, "claim", req:SerializeToString()) if not ok then send_result(ch, false, 0, nil) return end local parsed = pb_loader.parse_string(messages.DGVote4BuffClaim, res) if not parsed.claimed then send_result(ch, false, 0, nil) return end The same function then grants the buff and reports to the client. The database half is a handler that runs SQL and answers with the receipt it was given. There is no registered answer handler on the game side, no table of pending requests and no cleanup branch for a player who left: the owner takes care of that, and ok is false on both a timeout and a close. Read it from the top. The two exits at the bottom are the reason the bridge exists. A wait can end three ways, and the script sees only two shapes of result. Two details keep the picture honest. The token is erased before the script resumes, so a duplicate answer finds nothing and is dropped. And after a failed wait the record is removed even if the script yields again, so a script cannot keep waiting after its owner is gone.
documents.s: A receipt, an owner and a deadline

documents.t: The first version kept the thread and the coroutine handle in the record and nothing else. They were references only C++ held, and the Lua garbage collector does not see a C++ map. A coroutine suspended for a few seconds on a database answer could be collected while the answer was on its way. On 2025-01-20 I tried the obvious pin: put the coroutine and its thread on the global state and use the pinned references in their place. It broke differently. A pinned reference is rebuilt on the global state, so the coroutine handle forgot the thread it came from, and the next resume ran the entry function from its first line instead of continuing. I left a note in the source saying exactly that and fixed it two days later, on 2025-01-22, in a change of 8 added lines. The root cause was not the pin. There were two lifetimes, the C++ record and the Lua garbage collector, and nothing owned the link between them. A pin is how you make the collector respect the record, and the real question is what to pin. The fix pinned the thread and the coroutine, and the pins lived inside the record, so they died with it. After the later cleanup the shape is this: the thread and the entry function are pinned, and the coroutine handle is kept as it is. The code says why: // store the coroutine as it is because if we pin it to global state the coroutine gets basically reconstructed in the // global state losing new_thread's state and therefore we won't be able to get the coro id using the corourine. // This should be safe since we keep the reference in the coda and we are sure the underlying state (new_thread's) won't be collected (it is pinned) The pins are released in one place, where a coroutine dies, whichever way it dies: answered, timed out, closed by its owner or failed. That is the part I would copy into another engine. The pin and the record are one object with one exit.
documents.s: The coroutine that restarted from the top

documents.t: The same bug had a wider form, and I found it from a different side. On 2025-01-01 a commit pinned every long-lived Lua reference that C++ stores: processors, callbacks, guarded calls. A boot-time quest registered the lobby processors from the state the quest manager opens for its scripts. That state is ephemeral, and a reference built on it is eventually collected. When it was, the lobby stopped: no error and no log line, just a lobby that stayed stuck, and every system that went through it stuck with it. "Eventually" is the whole difficulty: the failure depends on when the collector runs, not on what the script did, so no test written around the script reproduces it. Three months later I centralised it. All references and pins live in the bridge, the game asks for them by id, and the bridge cleans up before the global state is killed. An earlier mistake of the same family was a destructor hook on the forge that operated on a Lua state that was already closed and crashed; on 2024-11-20 I commented and documented it. The rule these share is simple: a reference C++ keeps is C++'s to release, and the release has to happen before the state it points into is gone.
documents.s: Everything C++ holds across a call

documents.t: The first yielding sends were C++ functions that sent the packet and called lua_yield themselves. I replaced them on 2025-01-20, the same day as the failed pin. The symptom was a coroutine that started at once, yielded, and could not be resumed by the engine; it finished in a dead state instead of waiting for its answer. The new shape is what is above: token, send and coroutine.yield are three lines of Lua in one visible place, and a script author can read where the script stops. The bridge no longer has a yield function at all. The lesson I take from it is not about Lua. A suspension point should be visible to the code that suspends. When the function that sends also suspends, the call looks like a send and behaves like a goto.

A player-owned wait ends when the player leaves, and ending it means running the script. The close resumes each coroutine with nil, false, and the script runs its failure branch: it logs, it may look up the character, it may roll back. That runs inside the disconnect path. The first order was to erase the player's quest state and then close their coroutines. A failure branch that looked the player up through the quest manager could find nothing. On 2025-05-17 I swapped the two, so the close happens while the character and its state are still there. A continuation never touches a freed character; the character is erased after. The second bug was in the owner table itself. The table is a multimap, because one owner may hold several coroutines, and the close looked up the owner's key with a single find. It closed the first coroutine and left the rest. The header was written on 2024-10-09 and fixed on 2026-04-08: for about eighteen months, a player who left with two waits open had the first one closed. The second stayed suspended with its ownership erased, until its answer or its timeout came. Nobody noticed it in those eighteen months, which is the point: a leaked wait has no symptom until its answer arrives for an owner who is gone. The fix is the range lookup the container needed from the start. Both are the same class, and it is the one the design invites: a missed cleanup is a leak that keeps a script alive, and a late cleanup is a script that wakes in a world that moved on.
documents.s: A disconnect that resumed into a missing character

documents.t: Every wait is a heap record, two pins, entries in the owner table and the token table, and a timeout object when it has a deadline. That is small next to a request to a database, and it is paid on every wait. The costs that matter are the invariants for the next author. Every wait needs an owner or a timeout. Without either, a suspended coroutine stays in the table until the process ends. Code after a wait has two result shapes. A script that reads the answer without checking the flag treats a closed owner as an answer. A failed wait removes the record, so a script cannot wait again after one. It has to return. Closing runs script code during a disconnect, so the order of cleanup in the engine is now part of the script contract. The disconnect fix above exists because of it. Erasing the tokens of a coroutine scans the table of live tokens. It is linear in outstanding waits on every resume and death. It has not mattered at the scale of one server, and a server with far more outstanding waits would index tokens by coroutine. The old quest coroutine had none of these because it could not wait for anything the C++ had not foreseen.

A script can ask any other part of the system and continue when it answers. Rejoin asks another core where a dungeon lives and warps to the answer: the wait resumes on the first reply from the peers. The vote window asks the database and gives the player a buff. Login hands authentication to a background worker and yields until the result comes back, so the game loop does not wait for it. A script can also open a wait that collects replies from several owners for a fixed time and resumes once with all of them. None of these needed a new packet type in the engine, a switch case or a registered answer handler on the game side. A feature is a protobuf message, a forge and a handler on the other end. What a reader can reuse is short: Hand out a receipt that names who may wake the wait, and erase it on the first use. Give every suspension an owner and a deadline, and make failure a different shape of result, not a different call. Pin in the same place you keep the record, and release in the one place the record dies. Make the yield a line of script, not a side effect of a send.

The most typical crash in the quest manager was one line of Lua: d.kill_all(). It killed every monster in a dungeon. If one of those monsters was registered as a unique with a when dungeon_unique_dead block, the kill started that block in the middle of the script that had called d.kill_all. Then the second script started a third, and the stack of when blocks that built up normally ended in a SIGSEGV. Nothing in the script was wrong. The design of the manager was.

The quest manager keeps one set of "current" pointers: the current PC, the current character, the selected dungeon, the running state. Every event entry overwrites them. Scripts read them implicitly, so pc.get_name() does not take a player, it asks the manager who the current one is. For a linear script that is fine. A script runs, yields or ends, the next event starts. The Metin2 mainline engine has the same shape, and the same hole: a kill handler that kills more monsters re-enters the kill path, and every re-entry overwrites the context the outer script is still using. The guard it has is per player, and it only stops a second script on a PC that is already running one. In my engine the hole was wider, because in 2019 I had added a dungeon_unique_dead event (the Metin2 mainline engine only has a polling getter, d.is_unique_dead). Follow one kill through it: A player kills mob 2845. The manager points the current PC and character at that player and resumes a short-lived coroutine for the dungeon_kill block. Call it script A. Script A calls d.kill_all(). That is a C function, still inside A's resume. It walks the map and calls Dead() on every non-player. A mob that players had hit goes through the reward path and fires another dungeon kill event for whoever did the most damage to it: the same player, or a party member. The pointers are set again, and a whole dungeon_kill block runs nested inside A. A registered unique goes through the dungeon's death notification, which fires DungeonUniqueDead. That event runs on a shared fake PC with id 0, sets the current character to NULL, and runs the when dungeon_unique_dead block to completion. Script B, also nested inside A's C call. Nothing restores the previous values. d.kill_all returns and script A continues with the current character NULL, the current PC set to PC 0 and the running state pointing at B. The diagram reads top to bottom, and every arrow into a nested block is a synchronous call. The only thing that ever writes the global slots is the entry of a new event. Nothing writes them back on exit. From there the crash has several doors. The next pc.* call dereferences the current character without a null check: pc.get_name() is one line of C++ that calls GetName() on whatever the manager points at. If script A yields on a select or wait, the manager suspends it on whatever PC is current, which is PC 0. And back in the C++ that launched script A, the kill path read the current character after the script returned, then called GetParty() on it. That order existed from the first commit until May 2026.
documents.s: One C stack, one set of globals

documents.t: My answer in September 2021 was to stop scripters from nesting events, because nesting was bad practice. A flag on the manager, m_bPreventEvents, set around KillAll and checked in the kill, dungeon kill, fire kill, die and unique-dead entries. With the flag on, those entries return at once. The history of that flag is not a clean fix: 2021-09-20, 03:40. I added the flag and the five early returns. It did not compile: a return; in a function returning bool, and a line split in two in the middle of an identifier. 2021-09-20, 14:20. A teammate fixed both compile errors. 2021-09-20, 17:06. In an unrelated master hunt fix touching 10 files, I removed all five early returns. The flag was still set and reset around KillAll. Nothing read it. The record does not say why. 2021-09-24. A separate change took a full snapshot of the manager state whenever a script suspends and restored it on resume. The same class of problem, found from a different side. 2023-10-18, 19:19. Two years after the first attempt, I added the guards back and wrote the comment that describes the bug. Two follow-up commits fixed compile errors again, this time in the return type of the void functions. For two years d.kill_all set a flag that nothing looked at, and the nested unique-dead event was live. The comment I wrote in October 2023 is the most honest piece of the whole fix. It explains that a d.kill_all inside a kill handler triggers DungeonUniqueDead, which resets the current PC, and then says the flag is only a workaround: the correct fix is to stack the quest manager states and reset the top every time a nested event ends. That stack was never built in the quest manager, and the flag is still there. The function that sets it is the same one from 2021: int dungeon_kill_all(lua_State* L) { CQuestManager& q = CQuestManager::instance(); LPDUNGEON pDungeon = q.GetCurrentDungeon(); if(pDungeon) { q.SetPreventEvents(); pDungeon->KillAll(); q.ResetPreventEvents(); } return 0; } The workaround has a price. With the flag on, no mob killed by d.kill_all fires a kill, dungeon_kill, die, eligible_mob_kill or dungeon_unique_dead event, and the dungeon still forgets the unique when it dies. A dungeon_unique_dead handler for a boss killed that way never runs. The scripters pay the rest by discipline: 23 quest files call d.kill_all, 9 of them also use unique-dead, and one of them carries a comment I added in September 2026: nothing may touch pc or npc after kill_all. The flag stopped the crash by deleting events. That is a policy, not a fix. And it protected the manager from its own scripters, which was never the real problem: the real problem was how many places in C++ called back into Lua and met a design that could not take it.

The quest manager was never enough, because its whole purpose was scripting simple quests. Anything more complex than "go there, kill this, drop that, take it" went into the C++ engine. Minigames, battle arenas, guild domains, the guild war: each one brought its own hooks and its own packet handling, and each hook was written in whatever style the developer had that week. The bugs that came from it were rarely in the quest manager's code. New subsystems regressed old ones. There were SIGSEGVs, and design inconsistency everywhere. Many times I created a re-entry bug in the quest manager without touching a line of it, just by adding a C++ hook that called into Lua at the wrong moment. I did try to stretch the boundary first. For the guild domain I exposed the open and close events to a quest script, so scripters could control the times instead of having them hardcoded. For dungeons I did the same. The result was a system with no clear boundary: some logic available to high-level scripters, some hidden in C++. Nobody could say how it really worked, and nobody had an overview of the behavior.
documents.s: The engine as a dumping ground

documents.t: Rejoin lets a player who left a dungeon, by disconnect or by dying out, come back to the same instance. It was the first feature I moved out of the quest manager, and it is the cleanest before and after I have. Before. The rejoinable dungeons were a list in the core's config file, and the doc I wrote in 2019 says to add the base map index on every core that hosts the dungeon, so on every channel. When a player entered a rejoinable dungeon, four places in C++ wrote two quest flags on the player: dungeon.map_index and dungeon.channel. Those four were the member join, the two warp helpers and d.new_jump. Three exit paths cleared them. A 92-line quest script handled the rest: on login it sent a letter, and on click it checked the channel, checked that the core hosted the base map, asked d.can_rejoin, and warped. d.can_rejoin looked the dungeon up on the local core only. A dungeon on another core was "not found", and that read as "battle done". So the script refused unless you were already on the right channel and on a core with the map. Rejoin did not work across cores, and a player could hold exactly one, because there was one map_index flag. Every exit path in the script had to reset the flags by hand, including two that belonged to a different quest: if false == d.can_rejoin(map_index) then sys_log(0, "PG: "..pc.get_player_id().." | map_index: "..map_index.." | channel: "..pc.getf("dungeon", "channel").."") say(locale.dungeon_rejoin.battle_done) clear_letter() pc.setf("dungeon", "map_index", 0) pc.setf("dungeon", "channel", 0) pc.setf("ue_bighunt_2old_villages", "MapIndex", 0) pc.setf("ue_bighunt_dungeon", "MapIndex", 0) return end That four-flag reset appears five times in the script. The patch history says the rest: seven fixes between 2020 and 2022, among them a commit message about removing code "that was supposed to fix the kill event but breaks it even more", a rejoin that closed the letter on any map, and a "third party" rejoin. It was fragile, and it was fragile for a structural reason: the state lived in two quest flags that C++ wrote and a script read. After. On 2024-10-21 I replaced it with a forge: one commit added it (21 files, +2749/-1367 including generated protobuf), and the same day another deleted the old quest, d.rejoin and d.can_rejoin, the flag writes and the config list (13 files, +182/-407). The forge today is 795 lines. A RejoinManager instance lives for the whole server process and holds every open rejoinable: id, map index, hostname, status, and the set of players, several per player. It subscribes to the C++ event bus for dungeon join and destroy, and keeps every core in sync over p2p messages. The rejoin itself, in the forge from October 2024, is a persistent coroutine that may wait on another core. The excerpt is trimmed to the branch that matters: same host warps, other host yields on a p2p request and warps with the channel the owner returns. if r.hostname == get_server_hostname() then local dungeon = forge.sys.game.dungeon_manager.find_by_map_index(r.map_index) if nil == dungeon then sys_err(string.format("PID [%d] requested to join a dungeon without dungeon map_index[%d]", pid, r.map_index)) ch:popup("REJOIN_CANNOT_ERROR") return end local jump_pos = dungeon:get_last_jump_position() ch:warp_set(jump_pos.x, jump_pos.y, dungeon:get_map_index()) else local request = rejoin_messages.GGRejoinCoordsRequest() request.rejoin_id = rejoin_id local response, ok = forge_helper.sys.game.yield_p2p("request_rejoin_coords", request:SerializeToString()) if false == ok then sys_err(string.format("PID [%d] p2p request died dungeon map_index[%d]", pid, r.map_index)) ch:popup("REJOIN_CANNOT_ERROR") return end end What is left in the quest is a shell: when boot starts the manager, when login sends the letter if the player has a rejoinable dungeon, when info or button opens the client window. Before: a 92-line quest, four C++ write sites, two flags, per-core config, one core, one dungeon per player. After: one 795-line forge that holds its state in memory for the lifetime of the process, synced to every core, with rejoin across cores and channels by a coroutine that yields on a request. It did not stay perfect.
