Fixes kept coming: protobuf field order and the ordering of a remove against the p2p sync in September 2025, the state broadcast to the client in October, rejoin enabled for the horse, dragon and spec dungeons, and in June 2026 a change to stop holding a character reference directly.
documents.s: Dungeon rejoin, followed to the end

documents.t: It cost 3 to 4 months of work, and it reached stability after 1 year of development and use. The repository fits that. After a first prototype in February 2024 (the Lua 5.3 move, a first bridge and forge), the Luna work is concentrated between September and November 2024: 25 commits touching Luna paths in October alone. The bridge integrated with all input processors and the quest manager on October 7, in one commit of 93 files. Persistent coroutines, bridge.coro, landed two days later. Rejoin came on October 21, season and ranking on October 23, the roulette on October 25, and the lobby and arena on a new processor on November 5, 57 files. Master Hunt followed in February 2025 (60 files, +8097/-3230), the domain open and close events moved to a forge in May 2025, and the guild war logic went to Lua in June 2026. There are 48 forge files today, 28,632 lines. The year after that was yields and lifetimes. Yields and coroutine continuation were the hardest part, and I broke the execution flow many times. The commit messages say what the breakage was: a __gc operating on a closed Lua state in November 2024, references to Lua tables and functions that needed pinning so the garbage collector would not take them from an ephemeral thread in January 2025, coroutines pinned for the same reason a few days later, the references centralized in the bridge in April, a disconnect that closed coroutines only after the player was erased in May. Adopting a coroutine that the bridge did not create was reimplemented in August 2025, ten months after bridge.coro. AdoptCoroutine is a leftover of that try and break era, and no script under the content folders calls it today. The old problem came back once more, from the new side, which is the part I find most useful. In October 2024 a disconnect left the manager's current PC pointing at a player who was gone. In December 2025 Luna events fired while a quest script was running could still overwrite the global state, so I queued them: they run only when no script is running. In April 2026 I moved that queue into the main loop, because draining it at the end of a script was creating the same nested processing it was meant to prevent. The manager's comment says why: the application is single threaded, so an event fired from inside a running script corrupts the manager. The queue is a bridge to the old manager, not a new design. The new design is below it: // Every resume of a tracked coroutine funnels here. Copies the ns // and coroutine handle out of the map entry first: Lua can mutate // coroutine_map (rehash) during the resume, invalidating references // into it. OnCoroutineDead must run AFTER this returns. template <typename... Args> sol::protected_function_result CallCoroutine(CoroutineData& co, std::string_view detail, Args&&... args) { std::string ns = co.forge_ns; sol::coroutine coro = co.coroutine; dispatch::Scope scope(ns, dispatch::Kind::COROUTINE, detail); return coro(std::forward<Args>(args)...); } Each coroutine carries its own namespace, copied out before it resumes, and a scope that is closed when it returns. Nothing about the call depends on who ran before. An implicit current-instance global does not survive a reentrant event, and a flag that drops the event is not a way out of that. A resumable unit that owns its context is.
Building blocks provide registries and Lua interfaces for gameplay decisions. See Policies for the shared model.

Combat: battle arbiter (behaviour, examples), team manager (behaviour, examples), death manager (behaviour, examples), and spectator (behaviour, examples). Items and skills: item use policy (behaviour, examples), skill use policy, skill policy, and loadout policy with examples. Social: party join policy (behaviour, examples). Visuals: effects and materials and ui.ShaderQuad.

Term Definition Guard A callback that determines whether a registration applies to the characters involved. Verdict The result of a policy decision, such as allow, deny, or pass. Registration A named entry that adds a guard and policy callbacks to a registry. Handle The identifier returned by registration, used to unregister the entry. Forge A Lua module file (forge ... begin) that Luna loads and runs in a named environment; see Forge. Luna and the bridge Luna is a Lua runtime parallel to QuestManager; its bridge connects Lua and engine code. syserr and syslog Engine logs for errors and operational messages, respectively. PK mode A player's selected player-killing mode, used in PvP decisions. Killer The character credited with a death, when one is available. Duel A PvP contest between two players managed by the engine. Session A core-local group of PvP teams bound to a map. Activity lock A core-local marker on a player that signals an active engagement. DUEL_START A client duel state used to mark a pair as enemies. Domain A map-bound gameplay instance that can participate in PvP decisions.

Universal Core is a Metin2-lineage MMORPG engine. The engine owns mechanism: networking, combat resolution, persistence, rendering. Gameplay rules live in Lua and Forge modules on top of a small set of engine registries, so a new mode or system does not need an engine patch. The documentation follows that split in three layers. Read them in order the first time; later, jump straight to the page you need. Layer What it covers Core The runtime everything else stands on: Luna, Forge and its compiler, the headless simulator, the render pipeline, UCHTML, player virtualization, observability Building blocks Subsystems gameplay is assembled from: affects, traits, skills, policies, the battle arbiter, the death manager, teams, rankings, events Gameplay systems Features a player sees, each marked as framework-native, migrated, or legacy

The battle arbiter registry answers combat checks on each game core. A session is a team manager's group of participants; PK mode controls player combat. See the policies glossary for these terms, duel, and killer.

The first Allow or Deny ends the arbiter walk. If all guards are false or all verdicts pass, combat continues through the remaining checks. Registration order is local to one core; across forges it follows forge load order, which is not guaranteed. The path below shows where a verdict can override later checks. Stage Decision Absolute refusals Refuse a dead or observing victim, a mount with a rider, a pet, either character in a no-PvP safe zone, or a stunned, dead, or observing attacker. An arbiter cannot override these. Team sessions For player pairs, refuse if exactly one is in a session, they are in different sessions, their teams are allied, or attacks are disabled. Allow otherwise. Pass non-player pairs, pairs without a session, and same-session pairs with either player off the session map. Same party Refuse. Empire no-attack flag Refuse when the victim's flag for the attacker's empire is set. Empire IDs are 1, 2, and 3. NPC and mob rules Apply NPC skill flags, mob-versus-mob attack-mob requirements, summon target, same-empire NPC, and guard rules. Domain The domain decides when both characters share one in fighting state. PvP rules Refuse warps and portals, and NPC victims except their summoned attack NPC. A rider on a grade-1 horse above level 0 cannot attack. Other NPC or mob pairs are allowed. Protect mode refuses on the player's own empire map and start maps; different empires, killer victims, and Free mode are allowed. Guild mode allows unless both share a guild; Peace mode allows only an active duel. An arbiter's Allow overrides later party, session, empire, and NPC checks; Deny overrides duels and PK modes. A PvP team manager controls client targeting separately.

Check Effect of refusal Character attack and melee hit resolution Attack or hit is stopped. Claimed ranged or arrow blow against a character Blow is dropped. Enemy-only skill target Cast is refused; a test server reports <skill name>: this skill cannot be cast on that target. Ally-only skill and target classification Buff eligibility is checked; classification asks attackability first, then buff eligibility. Buff eligibility An attackable player pair cannot buff each other. Poison, fire, and bleeding ticks Effect ends without damage on a refused tick, while the attacker is online. damage_in_map, damage_in_map_radius, damage_in_map_pct, damage_in_map_pct_radius, drain_sp_in_map, drain_sp_in_map_radius, drain_sp_in_map_pct, drain_sp_in_map_pct_radius The quest operation skips the entity. damage_to_vid, damage_to_vid_pct The quest call does nothing and returns 0. Damage itself does not ask the arbiter. Safe zones, the after-death shield, and an immune-to-all-damage affect can still refuse damage. Guards can run more than once per hit and see pairs on every map on the core, subject to earlier verdicts; keep them cheap.

Deny does not make players allies. Non-player casters can buff only non-players; player casters cannot buff non-players. Allied teams in the same session can buff on the session map; otherwise a session participant cannot buff the other player. Outside that case, attackable players cannot buff each other, and remaining player pairs must share an empire. A killer is a player with the PK flag. After damage passes the safe-zone, shield, and immunity checks, the killer decision uses this order: If either character is not a player or the empires differ, do not flag the attacker. Ask arbiters; Allow prevents the flag, while Deny and Pass continue. An allowing team session or shared fighting domain, an active duel, or a victim who is a killer or has negative alignment prevents the flag. Otherwise flag the attacker.

Condition Result Guard errors or returns anything other than a boolean Treat as false. Verdict errors or returns anything other than a number Treat as Pass. Invalid numeric verdict Treat as Pass without a log. Unknown handle passed to unregister Return false and log to syserr, the server error log. The bridge invokes Lua callbacks and logs type errors and callback errors to syserr. Registration and successful removal go to syslog. A rule lives until explicitly unregistered or the core stops; keep the handle and remove it at event teardown. Each core has its own registry.

The rule does nothing and syserr reports a wrong return type. Guards must return booleans and verdicts must return named verdict constants. Compare objects explicitly and return a verdict on every path. A callback error opens combat to ordinary rules. Guard errors act as false and verdict errors as Pass. Watch syserr and test the failure path when safety depends on a denial. Monsters stop fighting on the map. A map guard also sees non-player pairs. Check is_pc() and pass pairs outside the rule's scope. The cursor remains or cross-empire buffs fail. An arbiter changes the server decision, not client targeting or alliance. Use the team manager when those behaviors are required. A rule persists after its event ends. Duplicate names create separate registrations, and overwriting a handle loses the ability to remove that entry. Store the handle, refuse duplicate registration, and unregister during teardown. A rule works on only one core. Registrations are per core. Register on every core that hosts the affected combat. A new denial ends a running effect. Poison, fire, and bleeding check again on each tick. Account for that when changing a verdict during combat. Next: Battle arbiter examples.

A battle arbiter lets you decide whether an attacker may hit a victim. A guard selects pairs and a verdict allows, denies, or passes the decision to the next rule. See Policies for the shared model and the policies glossary for terms.

This forge, a Lua module loaded by Forge, denies player attacks on one map and passes other pairs to the ordinary rules. forge no_pvp_map begin environment game begin local registry = forge.sys.game.battle_arbiter_registry local verdict = registry.BATTLE_VERDICT local MAP_A = 1 local handle = registry.register("no_pvp_map", function(att, vic) return vic:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(att, vic) if att:is_pc() and vic:is_pc() then return verdict.Deny end return verdict.Pass end) return { handle = handle } end end On that map the server refuses player attacks. The client can still show an attack cursor.

Register in a game forge environment, quest, or callback on each game core that needs the rule. Follow the host's forge setup and restart the game cores after changes; see Forge setup. Registrations are held in memory and must be made again after a restart.

Name Signature Returns Context Effect register register(name, guard, can_attack) Positive number handle Game core, outside a guard or verdict Appends an arbiter. unregister unregister(handle) boolean Game core, outside a guard or verdict Removes the handle; returns false if unknown. BATTLE_VERDICT Table: Allow, Deny, Pass Table Game core Verdict constants. Parameter Type Meaning name string Log label; duplicate names register separate arbiters. guard fun(att, vic): boolean Selects a pair; called before the verdict. can_attack fun(att, vic): number Returns a BATTLE_VERDICT value when the guard is true. Both arguments are character objects, attacker first. Pairs can include players, mobs, NPCs, guards, and buildings. No skill, weapon, or damage type is passed. Callbacks run synchronously on the core's main thread; do not yield or modify the registry inside them. Closures remain alive until removal. Handles start at 1, increase per registration on a core, and are not reused. There is no priority or replace-by-name argument. A non-callable guard or verdict raises battle_arbiter_registry.register: guard is not callable or battle_arbiter_registry.register: can_attack is not callable; an error during forge loading fails the load. Verdict Value Effect Allow 0 Allow immediately. Deny 1 Refuse immediately. Pass 2 Ask the next arbiter, then the remaining combat checks. Use the named constants: 0 means Allow. A number outside 0 to 2 acts as Pass without a log.

Engine code uses the same list: Register(std::string name, GuardFn guard, CanAttackFn can_attack) returns a handle_t (uint64_t), and Unregister(handle_t) returns bool. GuardFn is std::function<bool(LPCHARACTER att, LPCHARACTER vic)>; CanAttackFn is std::function<BattleVerdict(LPCHARACTER att, LPCHARACTER vic)>. Next: Battle arbiter behaviour.
These recipes use the battle arbiter API. Read behaviour for dispatch order and failure handling. A forge is a Lua module loaded by Forge; see the policies glossary.

This forge denies player attacks between empires 1 and 2 on MAP_A. Other pairs pass to the remaining rules. forge friendly_empires begin environment game begin local registry = forge.sys.game.battle_arbiter_registry local verdict = registry.BATTLE_VERDICT local MAP_A = 1 local handle = registry.register("friendly_empires", function(att, vic) return att:get_map_index() == MAP_A and vic:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(att, vic) if not (att:is_pc() and vic:is_pc()) then return verdict.Pass end local a, b = att:get_empire(), vic:get_empire() if (a == 1 and b == 2) or (a == 2 and b == 1) then return verdict.Deny end return verdict.Pass end) return { handle = handle } end end

This module exposes setup and teardown functions. Call them when your event starts and ends; the guard limits the rule to the supplied map. forge event_rule begin environment game begin local registry = forge.sys.game.battle_arbiter_registry local verdict = registry.BATTLE_VERDICT local handle = nil local event = {} function event.start(map_index) if handle ~= nil then return false end handle = registry.register("event_rule", function(att, vic) return att:get_map_index() == map_index and vic:get_map_index() == map_index end, function(att, vic) if att:is_pc() and vic:is_pc() then return verdict.Deny end return verdict.Pass end) return true end function event.stop() if handle == nil then return false end local removed = registry.unregister(handle) handle = nil return removed end return event end end Next: Battle arbiter reference.
documents.s: Register and remove an event rule

documents.t: A block for client-side effect authors: it changes how effects look and needs no server work. An .mse effect keeps its behaviour: spawning, motion, lifetime, texture, blend mode, and animation curves. A material controls how each pixel is shaded, including gradients, emission, erosion, and glow. A group without MaterialFile or Group Material is exactly the plain effect.

Create this material and pack it at the path in the comment. The names are placeholders; use your own folder. // d:/ymir work/effect/my_pack/my_glow.msfvx Group Effect { Family emissive_particle Emission 1.6 Gradient "d:/ymir work/effect/my_pack/ramps/warm.dds" GradientMode replace GradientInput brightness GradientGain 1.2 GradientLifeShift 0.2 Group Glow { Intensity 2.4 Radius 1 Color 1 0.667 0.267 Core 2 Streaks 6 } } In an existing .mse, add this line at the root of a Group Particle: MaterialFile "d:/ymir work/effect/my_pack/my_glow.msfvx" The particle keeps its existing motion, texture, alpha, and blend settings. Its texture brightness selects colours from the warm ramp, and its material adds a glow. Emission above 1 reaches scene bloom when HDR and bloom are enabled; see the render pipeline.

All four use the Metin2 text format: put one key or Group Name header on each line, braces on lines of their own, and a value after each key. Quote paths. Whole-line // comments are allowed; do not put a comment after a key or brace. Relative paths resolve from the file containing them, and absolute pack paths such as d:/ymir work/... also work. File Purpose Contract .msfvx One material. The root group is Effect for particles and effect meshes, Trail for ribbons, or Surface for actor parts. A material of the wrong kind is a load error. .msfvxp A parameterized material template. Group Params declares slots of type float, color, vector, or path, each with a Default. The material body uses $Name; a caller supplies overrides in Group MaterialParams. Missing or unknown slots and values with the wrong token count are errors. .msmask A model’s region-mask sidecar, beside its .gr2. Each Group MaterialNN names a MaterialIndex and regions, each with a texture and an r, g, b, or a channel. A model without a sidecar is unmasked. .msattach A bundle of effects and surface materials. Group Effects contains EffectNN entries with File and optional Bone; Group Materials contains MaterialNN entries with Part, File, optional Intensity, Tint, and Group Params. Optional Group Exit contains one-shot effects. A bundle material file must be an .msfvx or .msfvxp. Its parts are main, weapon, head, weapon_left, hair, and acce. Only MaterialNN groups belong under Group Materials. Mask regions share a vocabulary of at most 16 names. metal, cloth, skin, and accent come first; other names enter the vocabulary as sidecars use them. For example: // d:/ymir work/pc/my_model/my_model.msmask: region masks per Granny material palette index. Group Material00 { MaterialIndex 0 metal "my_model_regions.dds" r cloth "my_model_regions.dds" g skin "my_model_regions.dds" b accent "my_model_regions.dds" a } Group Material01 { MaterialIndex 1 eyes "my_model_eyes.dds" r } Material, sidecar, and bundle paths are normalized, so .. works in them. MSE texture and mesh paths do not resolve ...

Group Effect shades particles and effect meshes. Colours are r g b values from 0 to 1. Key or group Purpose and values Family Required: legacy, emissive_particle, emissive_mesh, or distortion. Emission Brightness multiplier, 0..64; default 1. Gradient Ramp texture path. GradientLifeShift Shifts the gradient input over particle life, 0..1. GradientMode multiply or replace. GradientInput brightness or alpha. GradientGain Scales the gradient input, 0.1..8. SoftDepth Soft depth distance, 0..1e6. Strength, Chromatic, FadeByLife For distortion: strength 0..256, chromatic amount 0..1, and a boolean life fade. Group Erosion Map, Scale, Scroll, Direction, DirectionWeight, In, Start, Softness, EdgeColor, EdgeWidth, EdgeIntensity, EdgeRamp, CharWidth, and CharColor. Group Fresnel Fresnel shading; coloured Fresnel is valid only for emissive_mesh. Group Glow Intensity, Radius (0..1), Color, Core (0..64), Streaks (0 or 4..8), StreakLength (0..1), and StreakRotation (-3600..3600). Group Distort Map, Scale, Scroll, and Amount. Group Ramp Map, Steps (0 or 2..4), Input value, LifeShift (-1..1), Contrast (0.01..16), and Range min max. Group Mask Shape (radial, vertical, horizontal, texture, or none), Softness, and Power. Group Cutoff Value, Softness, and LifeShift. Group Layer00 through Layer02 One to three layers. Each has Map, Scale, Scroll, Rotate, Combine, and Strength. On layer 0, Map texture uses the element’s own texture and Combine is base; other maps are pattern paths and combine with multiply or add. The plain effect’s colour operation runs first. The gradient then uses u = GradientGain × (texel brightness or alpha) − GradientLifeShift × life, clamped to 0..1. GradientMode Colour result before emission multiply The plain colour multiplied by the gradient’s hue at u. replace The gradient colour at u multiplied by texel brightness; MSE colour curves are ignored for colour. The result is multiplied by Emission. Alpha remains texture alpha times particle alpha, also multiplied by erosion coverage when present. Black texels stay black. Group Glow feeds selective glow, which is depth-tested and runs independently of HDR and scene bloom. See the render pipeline for how HDR, bloom, and selective glow differ. Material kind Keys and groups Group Trail Keys include Priority, Core, Tail, Ramp, EdgePower, FadePower, Emission, WidthScale, LifetimeScale, Texture, and Blend. Groups include Ramp, Noise, Dissolve, Flicker, Halo, Glow, Distortion, Distort, Erosion, Mask, Cutoff, and layers. Group Surface Uses Priority and groups Base, Reflection, Techniques (Spec, Rim, Energy, Irid), Erosion, Shell, Envelope, Params, Afterimage, Glow, and PatternNN. Envelope includes FadeInMs, FadeOutMs, and Pulse. Use the world editor’s Material pane and the validator when working with the full Trail and Surface vocabulary.

Put material references at the root of a Particle, Mesh, or Ribbon group. Entry Effect MaterialFile "path" Loads an .msfvx or .msfvxp, relative to the .mse. Particles and meshes need an Effect material; ribbons need a Trail material. Group MaterialParams Supplies template slot values. Requires MaterialFile; nested groups are not allowed. Group Material Defines an Effect material inline. Use it instead of MaterialFile. MaterialProfile Invalid. Use a material file or inline material. EmitterProperty.EmitByDistance With a value greater than 0, emits one particle per that many world units travelled. A stationary emitter emits nothing. TimeEventEmissionCountPerSecond must still be present but is ignored in this mode; 0 disables distance emission. Combining MaterialFile with Group Material, or using MaterialParams without MaterialFile, is a conflict. The client logs has conflicting material references and renders that element as a plain effect. Group Keys and behaviour Ribbon MaterialFile, RibbonType (0 billboard, 1 segment), Width, Lifetime, MinSpeed, SegmentStart, SegmentEnd, List TimeEventWidth, List TextureFiles, TextureMode, TextureTileLength, TextureScrollSpeed, TexAniType, TexAniDelay, Gravity, and JitterAmount, JitterScale, JitterRate. The frame budget is about 900 ribbon segments, retained by Trail Priority and then camera distance. Mesh additions List TimeEventScaleX, TimeEventScaleY, TimeEventScaleZ, TimeEventRotationZ, TimeEventArcHead, TimeEventArcTail, ArcSoftness, and TimeEventStretch. Impact Lifetime, FalloffRadius, Hitstop, HitstopRadius, ImpactFrame (0, 1, or 2), ImpactFrameDuration, TimeEventRadialBlur, TimeEventRadius, TimeEventAmplitude, TimeEventEdgeTint, EdgeTintColor, TimeEventDesaturate, TimeEventShake, LoopEnable, and Width. ScreenImpulse is an alias. At most four impacts are active; reduced-flash mode halves frame strength. Environment Lifetime, LoopEnable, InnerRadius, FalloffRadius, AmbientColor, DiffuseColor, FogColor, FogNear, FogFar, SkyColor, and List TimeEventWeight. TimeBubble A compatibility group. Environment weight at the viewer is the time track multiplied by a smoothstep of XY distance from the camera’s look-at target. Channels absent from the group stay untouched. There are 16 environment slots; a seventeenth does nothing. A render configuration switch can disable the blend. Ribbon, Impact, TimeBubble, and Environment are top-level groups alongside Particle, Mesh, and Light. Unknown group names are skipped, allowing a loader that does not recognize them to draw the remaining groups.

A material lives in the .mse, so anything that plays that effect also plays its materials. Effect paths registered by the engine for equipment and refine looks are outside this page; anything that names an .mse picks up its materials. Place Reference Motion event An .msa effect event uses EffectFileName, AttachingEnable, AttachingBoneName, and EffectPosition; FollowingEnable and IndependentFlag are optional. Fly data AttachFile in an attaching-data group names the travelling effect; BombEffect names the hit effect. Server skill nodes SPECIFIC_EFFECT takes effectPath and bone (default Bip01); AMBIENCE_EFFECT takes effectPath, soundPath, and ttlPoly. These are server-owned and TTL-driven. GROUND_DECAL and IMPACT_EFFECT do not name effect files. Server Lua The effect namespace provides ambience_effect_local, ambience_effect_global, delete_ambience_effect, fly_*, and screen_wave; npc.specific_effect also plays a specific effect. Broadcast affect In the Metin2 mainline client intro script, playerLoad.RegisterEffect(playerLoad.EFFECT_BROADCAST_AFFECT + type, bone, path) associates a broadcastable server affect type with a path. An .msattach attaches as a bundle and ignores bone; an .mse plays on the bone. Item A row of the mainline item_effect.txt contains vnum<TAB>bone<TAB>path. For an .msattach, the bone must be - or empty. Bundles apply to weapon and armour items. Costume shape AttachFile "<path>.msattach" in an .msm ShapeData group attaches a bundle. Map object AttachFile in a .prb or .prd property applies to all instances. An AttachFile in an AreaData.txt object block applies to that instance; "" removes the property’s attachment. Only Part main materials apply, and the bone is optional. RHI-debug client app.AttachBundle(path, vid), app.DetachBundle(vid), and app.CosmeticAttachSurface support inspection. Several MaterialNN entries may name the same part. Each is a separate layer in file order. A part draws at most three surface layers, selecting the highest material Priority first and breaking ties by attach order. The bundle loader warns once about entries that will not draw. Group Exit plays when a broadcast affect actually ends, after the server removes its last affect of that type. Surface layers fade using Envelope FadeOutMs. An actor leaving view, deletion, or a map change is silent; items, costume shapes, and map objects ignore Exit. Each affect type, item, costume, or map object attaches and detaches its own layers.

Tool Availability and use MSE validator validate_mse.py, a Python script that lives in the engine repository; it is not shipped in the client or the packs, so ask whoever holds the engine to run it, or use the world editor. It needs no client. It checks .mse, .msfvx, .msfvxp, .msmask, and .msattach syntax, required tokens, ascending time-event keys, relevant ranges, material conflicts, and distance emission. Given a client folder it also checks referenced files. Errors produce a non-zero exit; warnings do not. F11 Cosmetics panel Available only in an RHI-debug client build (ENABLE_RHI_DEBUG). It can play an effect attached to a bone or at a position, attach surface layers, edit material values, show stats, and toggle enhanced effect materials for comparison. Set a source root and reload from it to see edits without packing. World editor Available only in a world-editor build (ENABLE_WORLD_EDITOR). The Material pane edits .msfvx and .msfvxp; templates have a text editor, Apply button, and parameter defaults. The Bundle pane edits effects, exit effects, and surface materials. The effect editor authors MSE groups, including Ribbon, Impact, TimeBubble, and material references. Debug calls app.CosmeticPlayEffect, CosmeticSetMaterials, CosmeticReloadFrom, CosmeticRoundTrip, CosmeticTextureReport, CosmeticAttachSurface, AttachBundle, DetachBundle, and the related inspection and render switches exist only in RHI-debug client builds. Unattended capture uses the separate scaling-benchmark build option. A player-grade client has none of these tools. Pack the folders you changed, restart the client, and look at the effect in game; check the client log for load errors.

Material keys are strict. An unknown key is a load error naming the key; an invalid value reports the key and its allowed range. A failed material load leaves the element rendering as the plain effect, with an error in the client log. A bundle with more surface layers than a part can draw logs one warning naming the undrawn entries. The client log shows these lines, with the path and key lower-cased: Cosmetic material: d:/ymir work/effect/my_pack/my_glow.msfvx: key 'emision': unknown key Cosmetic material: d:/ymir work/effect/my_pack/my_glow.msfvx: key 'file': resource not found or malformed Cosmetic textures: ramp 'd:/ymir work/effect/my_pack/ramps/warm.dds': missing file; neutral index 0 is used Effect '<mse path>' has conflicting material references There is no C++ registration or Lua namespace for materials: content refers to them by path. Each distinct material and each distinct template value set is interned once into the GPU tables when referenced, with no per-frame parameter cost. Textures take a pool slot on first use: Texture Pool slots Format Patterns 32 256 × 256 BC5, full mip chain Reflections 16 256 × 256 BC1, full mip chain Masks 64 BC3, full mip chain Ramps 64 256 × 1 RGBA8 Slot 0 is neutral. A full pool or wrong texture format logs a load error naming the file, and that texture renders neutral. Judge an effect in LDR first. HDR and scene bloom are off by default, and emission above 1 needs both enabled to show through scene bloom. Selective Group Glow is independent of those settings.

The material does not appear. Check the client log for a missing file, wrong material kind, unknown key, invalid value, or conflicting material references. A failed material falls back to the plain effect. Pack the changed folders and restart the client before checking a player-grade build. A bundle fails to attach to an item. For a bundle row in item_effect.txt, use - or an empty bone. A nonempty bone logs bundle bone must be '-' or empty. Bundle support there applies to weapon and armour items. A second registration for the same affect type changes nothing. The first playerLoad.RegisterEffect call for an anchor and type wins; later calls for the same one are ignored. Edit the one line instead of adding another. A surface layer is missing. A part draws at most three layers. Check the bundle warning and adjust material priorities or remove a layer. A gradient makes the effect flat or floods the sprite. The gradient reads the texture’s own brightness or alpha. A pure-white texture selects one colour; measure the texture’s brightness before choosing the ramp and gain. Use GradientInput alpha for thin shapes, not a sprite whose alpha covers the quad. Smoke becomes an opaque sheet. Keep emission near 1 on alpha-blended groups with DestBlendType 6. Put glow on additive groups with DestBlendType 2. A recolour looks worse than the original. A material is not automatically an improvement to an effect that already looks good. Compare it with the plain effect and keep the original where it reads better. An effect is too large or appears in the wrong place. Size new groups against the surrounding groups. Offsets are relative to the attach bone, so preview using the bone the game uses. Particles stop or move strangely. Keep AirResistance below 1; velocity is multiplied by 1 - r per second. For distance emission, remember that a stationary emitter produces no particles. Erosion looks grainy on large smoke. A fine noise scale can read as grain. Try a scale around 0.6 and an edge around 0.35. An effect mesh renders nearly black. Some meshes need checking before using emissive_mesh. Keep their MSE mesh groups on legacy until the result is verified. A referenced texture or mesh cannot be found. MSE texture and mesh paths do not resolve ... Use a path that does not require it. Material, sidecar, and bundle paths do normalize ... Animation keys behave incorrectly or fail validation. Put keys in every TimeEvent list in ascending order.
Render pipeline ui.ShaderQuad
These recipes use the death manager API and its behaviour. A forge is a script container loaded by Luna; see Forge setup.

Register when an event starts, and retain the handle for teardown. Replace MAP_A with the map index. local MAP_A = 1 local function restore(ch) ch:restart_at_same_pos() ch:revive_invisible(5) ch:point_change(point.HP, ch:get_max_hp() - ch:get_hp()) end local handle = forge.sys.game.death_manager.register( "trial", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, { name = "trial", total_duration = 60, restart_here_available_at = 3, restart_town_available_at = 3, on_restart_here = restore, on_restart_town = restore, on_auto_town = restore, }) When the event ends, remove the registration. Players already dead retain their snapshot and callbacks. forge.sys.game.death_manager.unregister(handle)

Use unreachable timers and empty callbacks when the event settles deaths itself. Hiding the screen alone does not disable restart commands. local MAP_A = 1 local unreachable = 10000 local function no_restart(ch) end local handle = forge.sys.game.death_manager.register( "event", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, { name = "event", restart_window = false, total_duration = unreachable, restart_here_available_at = unreachable, restart_town_available_at = unreachable, on_restart_here = no_restart, on_restart_town = no_restart, on_auto_town = no_restart, }) Unregister handle at event teardown. Arrange a revive separately, after the death path completes. Next: Death manager reference.

The death manager selects a profile for a dying player and controls restart timers and callbacks. Monsters keep their own timers. For the shared policy model, see Policies. A forge supplies Lua code to the game core; Luna is the Lua runtime that runs alongside QuestManager. The bridge calls Lua from the engine and reports callback failures. See the Policies glossary for shared terms.

trial_room.forge makes the trial map a place where a dead player stands up on the spot after 3 seconds of waiting, with full health, instead of walking back from the empire town. Every other map is left to the defaults. forge trial_room begin environment game begin local MAP_A = 1 local function stand_up(ch) ch:restart_at_same_pos() ch:revive_invisible(5) ch:point_change(point.HP, ch:get_max_hp() - ch:get_hp()) end local handle = forge.sys.game.death_manager.register( "trial_room", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, { name = "trial_room", total_duration = 60, restart_here_available_at = 3, restart_town_available_at = 3, on_restart_here = stand_up, on_restart_town = stand_up, on_auto_town = stand_up, }) forge.sys.log(0, "registered, handle " .. handle) return { handle = handle } end end Compile and register the forge, then restart the game cores. The syslog shows [OK] CDeathManager::Register : [trial_room] handle=<n>. A player who dies on the trial map sees the restart screen, can press "restart here" after 3 seconds and is back on their feet where they fell. If they do nothing, the same callback runs when the 60 second timer ends.

Register a profile in a forge, Lua module, or quest on each game core that needs it. A profile has no separate file or config key. Compile and register the forge as required by your host, then restart the game cores after changes. Registrations are local to one core and are not saved across restarts.

Name Signature Returns Context What it does register register(name, guard, profile) number handle, greater than 0 game core, outside any guard or callback Appends a profile to the end of the list. unregister unregister(handle) boolean game core, outside any guard or callback Removes the profile. true when found, false for an unknown handle. register parameters: Parameter Type Meaning name string Labels the guard in the log and the registration line. Never compared: duplicates are allowed and they are two profiles. guard fun(ch: LPCHARACTER): boolean "Is this death mine?" Called with the character that just died. Must return a boolean. profile table The profile fields below. Handles start at 1 and grow by one per registration on that core. They are never reused. There is no priority parameter and no replace-by-name. register either returns a handle or raises an error, so the 0 the stub documents for a failed registration does not occur from Lua.

The profile is strict: seven fields are required and a missing one stops register at once, not at the first death. Field Type Required Meaning name string yes Labels the revive callbacks and on_dead in the log, and appears in the DEAD_EVENT_CREATE line with profile=<name>. Shipped content passes the same string as the register name. total_duration number yes Seconds from the death until the master timer fires on_auto_town. restart_here_available_at number yes Seconds after the death before /restart_here is accepted. restart_town_available_at number yes Seconds after the death before /restart_town is accepted. on_restart_here fun(ch) yes Runs on /restart_here. on_restart_town fun(ch) yes Runs on /restart_town. on_auto_town fun(ch) yes Runs when the master timer expires. restart_window boolean no, default true false closes the stock restart screen right after the death. Only false turns it off. on_dead fun(ch, killer) no Runs once after the death sequence is created. killer is nil when there is none. Errors raised by register: death_manager.register: guard is not callable death_manager.register: profile [<name>] missing field [<key>] death_manager.register: on_dead is not callable <name> in the second line is the register name, not profile.name. The three revive callbacks are fetched without a callable check: a value that is not a function registers fine and fails at the first restart (see the pitfalls).

Slot Called when Return On a Lua error or a returned value guard(ch) the player dies, synchronously inside the death boolean logged, counts as false: the profile does not apply on_dead(ch, killer) at the end of the death sequence, before the dead packet nothing logged only on_restart_here(ch) the player sends /restart_here and the cooldown passed nothing logged, then the stock restart-here runs on_restart_town(ch) the player sends /restart_town and the cooldown passed nothing logged, then the stock restart-town runs on_auto_town(ch) the master timer reaches total_duration nothing logged, then the stock restart-town runs They run synchronously on the core's main thread. Return at once. Do not yield: defer a delayed action with forge.sys.game.event.create and look the character up again by player id when it fires. The three revive callbacks and on_dead must return nothing. A returned value counts as an error. For a restart callback the stock callback then runs after yours; for on_dead it is logged only. guard must return a Lua boolean. Anything else, nothing, or a Lua error counts as false. Failures go to syserr, the server error log, so a broken profile floods the log: Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation lua error: <Lua error message> Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation wrong return: expected [boolean], got nothing Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation wrong return: expected [<type>], got [<type>] [death_manager <name> guard] lua callback error [death_manager <profile.name> on_restart_here] lua callback error Registration and removal are logged to syslog; an unknown handle goes to syserr: [OK] CDeathManager::Register : [<name>] handle=<n> [OK] CDeathManager::Unregister : [<name>] handle=<n> CDeathManager::Unregister : unknown handle=<n>

Engine code shares the registry with Lua. The native API exposes these calls: Call Signature Returns Meaning Register Register(std::string name, GuardFn guard, DeathProfile profile) handle_t (uint64_t) Registers a fixed profile copied onto the player. Register Register(std::string name, GuardFn guard, ProfileFn dynamic_profile) handle_t Resolves a profile per death; Lua cannot call this overload. Unregister Unregister(handle_t) bool Removes the registration; false for an unknown handle. GuardFn is std::function<bool(CHARACTER*)> and ProfileFn is std::function<DeathProfile(CHARACTER*)>. INVALID_HANDLE is 0 for a null guard or profile function. DeathProfile fields are name, totalDuration, restartHereAvailableAt, restartTownAvailableAt, restartWindow, onDead, onRestartHere, onRestartTown, and onAutoTown. restartWindow defaults to true.

Three functions outside the namespace belong to this system. None calls a profile callback. Name Signature What it does pc.revive pc.revive() Revives the current quest character in place. Shield is always 5 seconds. Requires a current character. LPCHARACTER:revive ch:revive(shield_time?) The same for any character. shield_time defaults to 5 and 0 skips the shield and its countdown, while revive invisibility still lasts 5 seconds. pc.enable_revive_event pc.enable_revive_event(enable) Switches the whole death sequence on or off for the current quest character. Default true. Both revive functions close the restart window, stand the character up, apply the optional shield, clear the attackers, count a dungeon revive, cancel the death timer and drop the profile snapshot. Then they set health to a quarter of the maximum and give 5 seconds of revive invisibility, whatever shield_time says. Content that wants more health sets it afterwards. Neither checks that the character is dead. pc.enable_revive_event(false) makes the death skip the whole sequence: no profile is resolved, no timer starts, on_dead does not run, and /restart_here and /restart_town return without a message. A non-boolean argument logs QUEST enable_revive_event call error : wrong argument: bool enable. LPCHARACTER:restart_at_same_pos() is not a revive: it refreshes the view and does not move a dead character out of the dead state. Inside on_restart_* the character is already standing, which is why shipped callbacks use restart_at_same_pos, revive_invisible and point_change there. Next: Death manager behaviour.
Item and potion gates run on the game core that registered them. See the API reference and Policies glossary.

For each kind, the engine walks the list in registration order within one core. Across forges, registration follows forge load order, which is not guaranteed. For every policy it calls the guard; when the guard returns true it calls the policy. The first verdict with allowed = false ends the walk and the item or the recovery is refused. Policies after it are not called. If no guard matched, the engine behaves as if the list were empty. A policy can never answer "yes, over the others": there is no allow that beats a deny. Potion policies add one rule. Each policy receives the amount the previous one returned, and the final amount is what the engine recovers. A global policy that halves and a map policy that halves give a quarter. A refusal drops the amount and stops the chain.

A Lua verdict is decoded field by field, and a field that is missing or has the wrong type keeps its default: allowed true, reason empty, stop true, amount the one you received. So these all allow: {}, { allowed = nil }, { allowed = 0 }, { allowed = "no" }. Only the boolean false refuses. What goes wrong in your own code fails in a fixed direction, and the direction depends on where it goes wrong: What fails Result The guard raises an error or returns anything but a boolean The policy is skipped for that call. Its refusal never applies. The policy raises an error Allowed. For a potion the amount is unchanged. The policy returns anything but a table, or nothing Allowed, as above. A failing call logs to syserr (the server error log) through the bridge, which calls Lua from the engine: Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation lua error: <Lua error message> Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation wrong return: expected [table], got [nil] Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation wrong return: expected [boolean], got nothing [item_use_policy <name>] lua callback error [item_use_policy <name> guard] lua callback error Registration and removal are logged to syslog; an unknown handle goes to syserr: [OK] CItemUsePolicy::RegisterItemUse : [<name>] handle=<n> [OK] CItemUsePolicy::RegisterPotion : [<name>] handle=<n> [OK] CItemUsePolicy::Unregister : [<name>] handle=<n> CItemUsePolicy::Unregister : unknown handle=<n> The reason is chatted as written, so pass a locale string, not a key. Only the empty-reason fallback You can't use this item. is translated by the engine.

The PvP arena is the native arena object, rebuilt from the mainline arena manager. The guard and the policy run synchronously on the core's main thread, inside the item use. Return at once and do not yield. An item use goes through its generic checks first: handling rights, the use delay, trading windows, inventory lock, level limits, class and sex limits. Then it starts the real-time timer of the item if it has one, fires the use_on quest event when the item was dropped onto another item, and only then asks the item gate. Every item type passes the gate, quest items and equipment included, so a refusal also stops the quest use event of that item, and a policy that refuses every item also stops the player wearing or taking off gear by using it (dragging it to a slot is not an item use). Only the use path is gated: an item consumed by a quest or by engine code never reaches it. After the gate the item type switch runs and with it the situational bans of the next section. The item path reaches the policy after generic checks and before the type-specific bans. The potion policies are asked at these places: Place point Notes Instant potion, each recovery component HP or SP An HP absolute, an HP percent, an SP absolute and an SP percent value are four separate asks. A component is asked only when the item has it and the character is not full. The amount includes the potion bonus for the two absolute values and not for the two percent values. Over-time potion, SP component then HP component SP_RECOVERY, HP_RECOVERY Asked after the full-recovery check, so a character who is already full never reaches the policy. The amount includes the potion bonus. Arming an auto-potion HP_RECOVERY or SP_RECOVERY amount is 0, a probe: a refusal here stops the elixir from arming, instead of letting it disable itself on the first tick. stop is not read. The probe runs on every use of an elixir, so a refusal also stops the player from switching an armed elixir off by using it again. Auto-potion tick HP_RECOVERY or SP_RECOVERY Once per second for each armed auto type, and once when the auto-potion is armed. amount is the gap to full and can be 0 or negative; the engine recovers only a positive amount.

Path Refusal with reason Refusal without reason Item consumed Item gate the reason in chat You can't use this item. no Instant potion, every component refused the reason in chat, the use is reported as failed nothing in chat, and the use is reported as done no Instant potion, some components refused nothing nothing yes, one potion for the components that went through Over-time potion, every component refused the reason in chat nothing no Arming an auto-potion the reason in chat You can't use this item. no Auto-potion tick, stop true or missing the reason, and the auto-potion switches off the auto-potion switches off silently the elixir stays, unlocked Auto-potion tick, stop = false the reason, every second nothing, this tick recovers nothing no A switched-off auto-potion has to be armed again by the player. Use stop = false for a temporary refusal (a budget, a phase of a match) and leave it out for a ban.

The Metin2 mainline engine hard-codes these refusals. An allowed verdict cannot override them. A duel is a player-versus-player contest; see the Policies glossary. Condition Applies to Player text PvP arena map fish You can't use this item. PvP arena map items 50107 and 50108 You can't use this item. PvP arena map return scrolls and return memories You can't use this item. Map 200 or map 113 return scrolls and return memories You can not use it here. In a duel: any potion when event flag no_duel_potion is above 0; item vnums 27863 to 27883 always potions, all three kinds You cannot do this in a duel. In a duel auto-potions You cannot do this in a duel. Either spouse on an PvP arena map, on a war map, or in a dungeon marriage rings You can't use this item. Map 113 (the OX event) items 100759 to 100764, firecrackers in the restricted range, item 71013 (silent) You can not use it here. Map 113 or a war map invisibility You can not use it here. In a dungeon return memory, when it is used to mark a position %s cannot be used in a dungeon. Before the gate, the generic checks include the summon-zone rule: summon items are refused where the map does not allow summoning.

The allowlist restricts nothing. A policy that returns { allowed = true } for the listed items and {} for the rest allows everything, because {} allows. Only the boolean false refuses. End the fallthrough with { allowed = false, reason = ... }. A broken policy permits, a broken guard disables its own rule. A policy that raises or returns a non-table allows. A guard that raises or returns a non-boolean (a vnum, 1, an object) is skipped on every call. Both log per call, so a typo shows up in syserr as a flood with your policy name in it. Test with syserr open. You cannot allow what the engine bans. Duel potions, the PvP arena, event maps, war maps, and dungeons can have engine refusals. { allowed = true } is the default, not an override. A silent refusal of an instant potion counts as a use. When every component is refused and the reason is empty, nothing recovers and nothing is consumed, but the engine reports the use as done: the use metric and the use delay run, and so does the item log for an item flagged for it. Always give the refusal of an instant potion a reason. Over-time potions report a failure either way. The budget goes wrong because the policy runs once per component. An instant potion with an HP and an SP value asks twice, once with each point. A counter that decrements in the policy counts per component, not per drink. Key the counter by resource, as the budget example does. The auto-potion drains, or a budget refunds. The tick asks every second, even when the character is full, with an amount that can be 0 or negative. A policy that returns a fixed amount instead of scaling the one it received recovers on every tick and spends the elixir. A budget that adds amount without a guard on amount <= 0 can go down on a negative gap. The player has to arm the auto-potion again. A refusal on a tick without stop switches it off, because stop defaults to true. Say stop = false when the refusal is meant to pass. The reason is chatted every second. With stop = false and a reason, a refused auto-potion tick sends the reason on every tick while the refusal lasts. Leave the reason out there. A refused item still started its timer. The real-time clock of an item with a first-use timer starts, and its use_on quest event fires, before the gate. A refused first use still costs the item that. Every guard runs on every use. Every item use, every potion component and every auto-potion tick calls the guard of every registration. Keep guards to a table lookup or a comparison. A second register adds a second policy. Names are not compared. If you overwrite the stored handle, the first policy is lost for good and only a core restart removes it. Calling register or unregister from inside a guard or a policy. The lists are walked while they call them, and nothing protects that walk. Register from a load, an event or a command. A per-match rule that is never unregistered keeps matching. A guard that captures a match stays on the list, with its closure, until the core stops. Unregister it with the thing it judges, when the match ends. A rule registered on one core does not hold on another. Registrations are per core process. Restart the game cores to pick up a changed forge. Returning fractions. amount is read as a whole number. Return math.floor(amount * 0.5) or amount // 2, never a bare fraction. Next: Item use policy examples.
The death manager reference lists the API. A killer is the character responsible for a death, or nil when there is none; see the Policies glossary.

Read the diagram from the top. The guard is asked in step 3, after the arena and quest hooks of step 1, and with the character already dead. Early hooks: the native death hook for the PvP arena (the native arena object, rebuilt from the mainline arena manager), and the quest Kill and Die events. A revive done here is overwritten by the rest of the death. The character is set to the dead position, affects that do not survive death are removed, and a player is set to the dead phase. A guard cannot test for an affect death removes, such as a buff. If the death event is enabled, the profile is resolved (next section). The hack floor is applied, the profile is copied onto the character with the time of death, and the timer is scheduled for total_duration seconds. The DEAD_EVENT_CREATE line is logged. on_dead(ch, killer) runs. The domain experience malus resolves the profile a second time for any player in a fighting domain, so your guard can run twice for one death. Exchange, skills, poison, fire, bleeding, cube, shop and safebox are cleaned up. The dead packet goes out with the three countdowns (restart here, restart town, auto-town). Then, when restart_window is false, CloseRestartWindow is sent.

Three tiers, from the top: The registry list. Guards are asked in registration order within a core; across forges this follows forge load order, which is not guaranteed. Guards are asked in that order and the first true wins. Guards after it are not called. Engine code and Lua share one list and there is no priority field. The auto-hunt profile, when no registration matched and the character has the active auto-hunt affect: 3 seconds, restart here and town available at once. Restart here and auto-town revive in place at full health; restart town is the stock town warp. The stock profile: 180 seconds total, restart here after 10 seconds, restart town after 7 seconds. Restart here revives in place with a quarter of the maximum health and 5 seconds of revive invisibility. Restart town and auto-town send the player to the empire recall position of the current map, or the empire start, with 50 health. A matching registration beats auto-hunt: an auto-hunting player who dies in your zone gets your profile, not the 3 second revive. No Lua accessor exists for the stock or the auto-hunt callbacks, so a Lua profile cannot call them. The engine also registers raid and domain profiles natively.

/restart_here and /restart_town are ignored without a message while the player cannot warp (within 10 seconds of the warehouse, a trade, their own shop or a refine, or with those windows open) and when there is no death timer. A player who is not dead gets the restart window closed and a recovery event started, nothing more. The cooldown is counted in whole seconds from the death. Before it passes the player gets No new start possible.(<n> seconds left) for restart here, or Still no new start possible in the city. (<n> seconds left) for restart town. When the gate opens, three things happen in order before your callback: The restart window closes, the phase is set to game, the character is set standing, a shield affect starts (5 seconds), the recovery event starts, attackers are cleared and a dungeon revive is counted. Health and SP are not touched. The death timer is cancelled and the profile snapshot is dropped. Your on_restart_here or on_restart_town runs. So in a restart callback the character is already standing, shielded and without a profile. You must set health yourself. Auto-town is shorter. If the character has no connection, the snapshot is dropped and no callback runs. Otherwise the phase is set to game, the character stands, the snapshot is dropped, on_auto_town runs, the recovery event starts and the restart window closes. There is no shield, no attacker clear and no dungeon revive count. The client countdowns are clamped to 255 seconds (the wire field is one byte), so a profile with 10000 shows 255 on the restart screen while the server still refuses.

When the dying player is flagged by the hack check, both restart cooldowns are raised to at least 10 seconds, whichever profile won, Lua ones included. total_duration is untouched. The flag is on within 10 seconds of opening the warehouse, trading, using your own shop or refining, while a trade, shop, warehouse or NPC dialog is open, and during a delayed warp. Some maps are exempt. A profile with restart here at 3 seconds gives 10 seconds to a duelist who traded in the last 10 seconds.

It sends CloseRestartWindow right after the dead packet, so the stock screen vanishes at once. It does not stop the commands: /restart_here and /restart_town still pass the gates above. A zone that settles deaths itself also sets all three times out of reach (the shipped value is 10000) and gives the three callbacks empty bodies. Do not try to close the screen from on_dead: the dead packet goes out after it and undoes it.

A registration lives until unregister or until the core process stops. A forge has no unload hook, so nothing unregisters for you. Tie unregister to the end of the thing the profile belongs to: event teardown. The profile is copied by value onto the dead player. The snapshot lives from the death until a restart, the auto-town, a revive, a new death (which cancels the old timer) or a disconnect at auto-town time. unregister erases the list entry only. A player already dead keeps the snapshot, and its callbacks run later, even after the owner is gone. The Lua functions stay alive for that. What they close over may not. A test server skips both restart gates and sends countdowns of 0. Timers on a test server prove nothing about cooldowns.

A player keeps your callbacks after you unregister. The profile is copied onto the character at death, and unregister only removes the list entry. A player who died under an event keeps its callbacks until a restart, the auto-town or a revive, even after the owner is torn down. In every revive callback fetch what you need from ch again and handle nil, when the event has ended. Never trust an upvalue to still be live. Two profiles overlap and one never runs. The first registered guard that returns true wins and the rest are never asked. Native registrations and forge load order affect precedence. Keep guards disjoint: a map index, an instance identity. The profile never applies and the log says expected [boolean], got [nil]. A guard such as return ch:get_pvp_arena() and ... returns an object or nil. Anything that is not a boolean counts as false, and the death falls to the next registration or the default. End the guard with a comparison, ~= nil or == map_index. A guard with side effects runs twice. A player in a fighting domain resolves the profile a second time for the experience malus. Keep guards pure. Your restart runs and then the player is also sent to town. A restart callback returned a value. Any non-nil return is an error, so the stock callback runs after yours. Return nothing; on_dead must also return nothing, but its failure is logged only. A restart fails at the first press and not at register time. The three revive fields are required, so a missing name is caught as "missing field". A value that exists but is not a function is not checked. It registers, and the first restart fails with a Lua call error and the stock callback runs. Pass functions, and test a restart. restart_window = false and the player still restarts. It hides the screen and nothing else. Also set the three times beyond reach and give the callbacks empty bodies. Anything you send about the restart window from on_dead is undone by the dead packet. A revive on a living character still resets it. Neither pc.revive nor ch:revive tests for death. On a living character they set health to a quarter of the maximum, clear attackers, add a shield and count a dungeon revive. Check ch:is_dead() first. The dead player is stood up but the timer keeps running. Only pc.revive, ch:revive, the two restarts and the auto-town clear the death timer. Other ways of standing a dead player up, such as moving them to a start position, leave it running, and on_auto_town fires later on a living character. Revive with ch:revive(), or make on_auto_town safe on a living character. A reachable on_restart_here leaves the player at the health they died with. The common restart step stands the character up and does not restore health or SP. Set both in every callback a player can reach. Auto-town is not a restart. It skips the shield, the attacker clear and the dungeon revive count, and a disconnected player gets no callback at all. Do that work in on_auto_town if you need it, and do not use it for bookkeeping about players who left. A short cooldown is longer than you wrote. A player who traded or opened the warehouse in the last 10 seconds waits at least 10 seconds, where the hack floor applies. Auto-hunters lose their quick revive in your zone. Any matching profile beats the auto-hunt default. The cooldowns look broken on the test server. Both restart gates are skipped there and the countdowns read 0. A player who died stays dead with no buttons. pc.enable_revive_event(false) disables the whole sequence, on_dead included, and nothing restarts the player until a revive. You expect a callback to wait. Callbacks cannot yield. Schedule the delayed part with forge.sys.game.event.create and look the character up by player id again. Next: Death manager examples.
These examples register policies in a forge, a .forge script loaded by Luna. Replace MAP_A and the example item vnums with values from your game. See the API reference and behaviour.

An allowlist must refuse its fallthrough explicitly: {} allows. Only the listed vnums are usable on the map, and gear cannot be put on or taken off there by using it: add the equipment you want to allow. forge item_allowlist begin environment game begin local MAP_A = 1 local ALLOWED = { [100008] = true, [100009] = true, [100010] = true } local handle = forge.sys.game.item_use_policy.register( "item_allowlist", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(ch, item) if ALLOWED[item:get_vnum()] then return { allowed = true } end return { allowed = false, reason = "You can't use that here." } end) return { handle = handle } end end
documents.s: An allowlist: everything else is refused

documents.t: A potion policy that refuses every potion but one and gives the reason. The reason matters: without it an instant potion refusal is silent and still counts as a use (see the pitfalls). forge one_potion begin environment game begin local ONLY_POTION = 100008 local MAP_A = 1 local handle = forge.sys.game.item_use_policy.register_potion( "one_potion", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(ch, item, point_type, amount) if item ~= nil and item:get_vnum() == ONLY_POTION then return { allowed = true, amount = amount } end return { allowed = false, reason = "Only the selected potion heals here." } end) return { handle = handle } end end

A budget in total HP and SP recovered, shared by instant and over-time potions, with the last drink clamped so the total lands on the cap. The refusal sets stop = false, so an armed auto-potion survives and only skips ticks. The policy leaves non-positive amounts alone, because the tick asks with the gap to full and that gap can be 0 or negative. forge potion_budget begin environment game begin local MAP_A = 1 local CAP = 10000 local spent = {} local handle = forge.sys.game.item_use_policy.register_potion( "potion_budget", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(ch, item, point_type, amount) if amount <= 0 then return { amount = amount } end local is_hp = (point_type == point.HP or point_type == point.HP_RECOVERY) local key = ch:get_player_id() .. (is_hp and ":hp" or ":sp") local used = spent[key] or 0 local remaining = CAP - used if remaining <= 0 then return { allowed = false, stop = false } end local granted = math.min(amount, remaining) spent[key] = used + granted return { allowed = true, amount = granted } end) return { handle = handle } end end Next: Item use policy reference.

A loadout policy selects a plan of skill pages, positions, and levels for a character. For registration, plan fields, and rebuild behavior, see the loadout policy API and the policy model. A guard selects characters; a builder returns their plan. A vnum is a numeric skill identifier. For policy terms, see the Policies glossary. The vnums and map index in these examples are placeholders: use skills and a map available in your content. Register each example on the game cores that need it. See Forge setup for loading a forge.

This rule gives characters on map 1 one skill on ACTIVE. The plan names that page, so it replaces the whole page; unnamed pages keep their ordinary layout. Store the returned handle if the rule must be removed before the core stops. forge example_one_skill begin environment game begin local MAP_A = 1 local handle = forge.sys.game.skill_loadout.register( "example_one_skill", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(ch) return { pages = { { id = "ACTIVE", layout = "flat" } }, skills = { { page = "ACTIVE", slot = 1, vnum = 31, level = 40 } }, } end) return { handle = handle } end end A map change alone does not rebuild the plan. Call forge.sys.game.skill_loadout.refresh(ch) after the map state changes so the guard is sampled again. Registration and removal also rebuild online characters.

plan(preset) copies the supplied table. Each builder call can then change its own plan without changing the shared preset. This example adds a skill to every matching character and another when the character reaches level 100. forge example_preset begin environment game begin local MAP_A = 1 local PRESET = { pages = { { id = "ACTIVE", layout = "flat" } }, skills = { { page = "ACTIVE", slot = 1, vnum = 31, level = 40 } }, } local handle = forge.sys.game.skill_loadout.register( "example_preset", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(ch) local plan = forge.sys.game.skill_loadout.plan(PRESET) plan:grant("ACTIVE", 2, 106, 40) if ch:get_level() >= 100 then plan:page("SPEC", { layout = "flat" }) plan:grant("SPEC", 1, 230, 40) end return plan end) return { handle = handle } end end Refresh after a level or skill group change if the builder reads it; the builder runs only on rebuild.
documents.s: Copy a preset before adding skills

documents.t: A tabbed SPEC page has groups with labels, visible positions, and a gate_slot. A tab appears when the skill at its gate position has a level. This plan fills the gate position of each tab. forge example_tabs begin environment game begin local MAP_A = 1 local handle = forge.sys.game.skill_loadout.register( "example_tabs", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(ch) return { pages = { { id = "SPEC", layout = "tabbed", groups = { { label = "First", gate_slot = 1, slots = { 1, 2, 3 } }, { label = "Second", gate_slot = 4, slots = { 4, 5, 6 } }, }, }, }, skills = { { page = "SPEC", slot = 1, vnum = 230, level = 40 }, { page = "SPEC", slot = 4, vnum = 179, level = 40 }, }, } end) return { handle = handle } end end The positions are relative to SPEC, starting at 1. Check the API page for page capacities and plan fields.

Keep the handle returned by forge.sys.game.skill_loadout.register for a temporary rule. Pass it to forge.sys.game.skill_loadout.unregister(handle) when the rule ends. Removal rebuilds online characters, and another matching rule can take over. Register and unregister outside guards and builders because both operations rebuild online characters.

Granted levels are saved on a real character. The plan writes levels to the live character, and a save writes those levels. The restore values are kept in memory; removing the plan restores them during the running session, but does not prevent a save while the plan is active. Use player virtualization when temporary grants must not be persisted. A builder produces a different plan on each rebuild. Rebuilds compare pages, groups, and skills in order. Use stable input for any choice and sort entries before granting them; otherwise an unchanged set in a different order can cause another update to be sent. A bad entry drops the plan. A page without an id, or a skill with an empty page or vnum 0, makes the Lua builder fail to produce a plan. The character keeps its real skills, and the server logs skill_loadout [<name>]: builder failed for pid <player id>. Check every entry before returning it. A later rule never runs. Rules are tested in registration order within a core. Across forges, the order follows forge load order, which is not guaranteed. The first matching guard owns the character even if its builder fails; later rules are not tried. Make guards exclusive or control the order within one forge. A skill is held but has no visible cell. The server does not enforce client page capacity. Keep positions within the page's visible range and layout; a flat SPEC page draws only its first three positions. The optional grant_next helper checks capacity when the content library provides it. An ordinary page disappears. A plan replaces every page it names, whether through pages or a skill entry. Leave a page unnamed to keep its ordinary bar, or include all the entries you want to retain.

Loadout policy API: plan fields, helpers, resolution, and rebuild behavior. Loadout, use and skill policies: how the policy types fit together. Skill use policy: checks applied when a skill is used. Skill policy: policies for skills. Loadout policy examples: this page. Forge overview and setup: environments and loading.

A party join policy decides the admission rules for a leader and guest. Register one from a forge, a compiled Lua unit, when a map or event needs different party limits. See Policies for the shared model and the Policies glossary for terminology.

This forge allows parties of three on a map, regardless of empire or level difference. forge event_teams begin environment game begin local MAP_A = 1 local handle = forge.sys.game.party_join_policy.register( "event_teams", function(leader, guest) return leader:get_map_index() == MAP_A and guest:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(leader, guest) return { max_members = 3, same_empire = false, level_window = 0 } end) return { handle = handle } end end The registration log includes [OK] party_join_policy [event_teams]: handle=<n>.

Register the policy in a forge on each game core that needs it. Follow Forge setup for the host's compile and registration steps; restart the game cores after changes. For a refusal message, add its locale_key to the client locale.

Name Signature Returns Context Effect register register(name, guard, policy) positive number handle game core Appends a policy. unregister unregister(handle) boolean game core Removes it; returns false for an unknown handle. ERROR table admission codes any Constants for simulator assertions; no live Lua function returns them. Parameter Type Meaning name string Log name; duplicates are allowed and do not replace a policy. guard fun(leader, guest): boolean Selects the pair. policy fun(leader, guest): table Returns a verdict when the guard matches. Both callbacks receive characters and run synchronously on the game thread. Both must be functions; otherwise registration raises party_join_policy.register: guard is not callable or party_join_policy.register: policy is not callable. Handles start at 1, increase per registration, and are not reused.

Each field is optional; missing or wrong-typed fields use the default. The generated Lua stub offers only max_members, same_empire, and level_window. Field Type Default Effect allowed boolean true false refuses admission before stock checks. locale_key string empty Client locale key shown over the character on policy refusal. max_members number 8 Cap including the leader; 0 or a value above 8 becomes 8. same_empire boolean true false skips the empire check. level_window number 30 Maximum level difference; 0 disables the limit. bind_to_map boolean false A newly created party lives on the leader's map and core. guild_group boolean true false prevents a newly created party from becoming a guild group. bind_to_map and guild_group are stored when a party is created; the other fields are resolved for each admission.

forge.sys.game.party_join_policy.ERROR contains PERR_NONE, PERR_SERVER, PERR_DUNGEON, PERR_OBSERVER, PERR_LVBOUNDARY, PERR_LOWLEVEL, PERR_HILEVEL, PERR_ALREADYJOIN, PERR_PARTYISFULL, PERR_POLICY, PERR_DIFFEMPIRE, PERR_PVP_ARENA, and PERR_ENEMY. The admission check does not produce PERR_LOWLEVEL, PERR_HILEVEL, or PERR_PVP_ARENA; a level refusal produces PERR_LVBOUNDARY.

The native singleton CPartyJoinPolicy uses the same list. Keep the handle for teardown. Call Signature Returns Register Register(std::string name, GuardFn guard, PolicyFn policy) handle_t (uint64_t); INVALID_HANDLE (0) if policy is empty Unregister Unregister(handle_t) bool; false for an unknown handle Resolve Resolve(CHARACTER* leader, CHARACTER* guest) const PartyJoinVerdict GuardFn is std::function<bool(CHARACTER*, CHARACTER*)> and PolicyFn is std::function<PartyJoinVerdict(CHARACTER*, CHARACTER*)>. An empty C++ guard matches every pair; Lua requires a guard. PartyJoinVerdict contains allowed, strLocaleKey, max_members, same_empire, level_window, bind_to_map, and guild_group, with the defaults above. Its kStockMaxMembers is 8; strLocaleKey corresponds to Lua's locale_key.

An activity lock marks a player as committed to an activity; see the Policies glossary. It is scoped to a core and does not itself refuse party admission. Name Signature Returns Context Effect set set(pid, locked) nothing game core Adds or removes the player ID. is_set is_set(pid) boolean game core Tests only the explicit lock set. clear clear() nothing game core Removes all explicit locks on the core. is_locked_in_activity character:is_locked_in_activity() boolean character Tests the explicit lock and engine activity participation. Next: Party join policy behaviour.

A loadout rule selects skills and their positions for a character. Its guard selects characters; its builder returns a plan of pages and skills. The ordinary skill bar is the default when no plan is in force. See skill policies and the policy model. The policies glossary defines shared terms.

This .forge file registers a rule for characters on MAP_A, a map index placeholder. Forge loads scripts into Luna, the parallel Lua runtime. A vnum identifies a skill. forge example_loadout begin environment game begin local MAP_A = 1 local handle = forge.sys.game.skill_loadout.register( "example_loadout", function(ch) return ch:get_map_index() == MAP_A end, function(ch) return { pages = { { id = "ACTIVE", layout = "flat" } }, skills = { { page = "ACTIVE", slot = 1, vnum = 31, level = 40 } }, } end) return { handle = handle } end end Save it as example_loadout.forge and load it as described in Forge setup. Matching characters see skill 31 at level 40 in the first active position; other pages retain their ordinary bar. Call refresh(ch) after a map change if the rule must be re-evaluated.

The Lua API exists on game cores. Registrations belong to the core process and are not saved; register them again after a restart. Register from a Forge environment or another game-core callback. Keep the returned handle to unregister the rule. See Forge setup for loading instructions. Load the content library to use its plan helpers. The client skill window must recognize the page IDs and positions used by a plan.

Name Signature Returns Context What it does register register(name, guard, builder) number handle, greater than 0 game core, outside any guard or builder Appends a loadout rule to the end of the list and rebuilds every character online. unregister unregister(handle) boolean game core, outside any guard or builder Removes the rule and rebuilds every character online. true when found, false for an unknown handle. refresh refresh(ch) boolean game core Re-runs the rules for one character and pushes the difference. true when the plan changed. has has(ch) boolean game core Whether a plan is in force on this character. plan plan(preset) PLAN table game core Builds a plan procedurally. With a preset it returns a deep copy of it; without, an empty plan. Parameters of register: Parameter Type Meaning name string Cosmetic. It appears in the log lines of this rule and is never compared: duplicates are two rules. guard fun(ch): boolean "Does this rule own this character?" Required. true makes the rule the loadout of ch. builder fun(ch): PLAN Called when the guard returned true. Returns the plan as a plain table. Required. There is no priority parameter and no replace-by-name. A guard or builder that is not a function stops the call with skill_loadout.register: guard is not callable or skill_loadout.register: builder is not callable, before anything is registered. Inside a forge environment body that error fails the forge load, and then the game core does not start. Handles start at 1, increase per registration, and are never reused. Both callables stay alive until unregister; the handle is required for removal. Lua rejects empty callables, so register never returns 0. plan(preset) returns a table with two extra methods, page and grant. Both return the plan itself, so calls chain. Method Signature What it does PLAN:page page(id, opts) Appends a page to pages. opts is { layout = "flat" or "tabbed", groups = GROUP[] }, copied. PLAN:grant grant(page, slot, vnum, level) Appends a skill to skills. A builder can also return a plain table.

Callable Arguments Notes guard ch The character being rebuilt. Players only: the engine never rebuilds a mob's loadout. builder ch The same character. There is no table of context fields, only the character; anything more is read from it.

What the builder returns. Both fields are optional: a table with neither is an empty plan, which means "no loadout" and puts the character back. Field Type Meaning pages PAGE[] The pages this plan speaks for. skills SKILL[] The skills the character holds, each at a position on a page. A page named in pages or by a skill is replaced whole on the client. Unnamed pages retain their ordinary bar, layout, and levels.
