Call Signature Returns CreateSession CreateSession(int32_t map_index, std::string kind) session_id_t (uint32_t) CloseSession CloseSession(session_id_t) bool AddTeam AddTeam(session_id_t, team_id_t, std::set<team_id_t> initial_allies = {}) bool RemoveTeam RemoveTeam(session_id_t, team_id_t) bool AddAlly, RemoveAlly (session_id_t, team_id_t a, team_id_t b) bool SetAllies SetAllies(session_id_t, team_id_t, std::set<team_id_t>) bool AddMember AddMember(session_id_t, team_id_t, uint32_t pid) bool RemoveMember RemoveMember(session_id_t, uint32_t pid) bool SetAttacksEnabled SetAttacksEnabled(session_id_t, bool) void BroadcastSession BroadcastSession(session_id_t) void IsMember IsMember(uint32_t pid) bool GetSession, GetTeam GetSession(uint32_t pid), GetTeam(session_id_t, uint32_t pid) std::optional AreAllied (session_id_t, team_id_t, team_id_t) or (LPCHARACTER, LPCHARACTER) bool GetAllies GetAllies(session_id_t, team_id_t) std::set<team_id_t> ResolveTeamChatTarget ResolveTeamChatTarget(uint32_t pid) std::optional<TeamChatTarget> CanAttack CanAttack(LPCHARACTER att, LPCHARACTER vic) BattleVerdict OnPlayerConnect, OnPlayerDisconnect (LPCHARACTER) void team_id_t is uint16_t and INVALID_SESSION is 0. The query half (GetSession, GetTeam, GetAllies, CanAttack, the character form of AreAllied, ResolveTeamChatTarget) is C++ only. team_id_t is uint16_t and INVALID_SESSION is 0. The query half (GetSession, GetTeam, GetAllies, CanAttack, the character form of AreAllied, ResolveTeamChatTarget) is C++ only. The PvP arena (the native arena object, rebuilt from the mainline arena manager) opens a session with kind ARENA and exposes LPARENA:set_attacks_enabled(enabled). Next: Team manager behaviour.

A broadcastable server type needs client registration to display a particle or icon. This registers a particle for type 700; use a path in your client pack: playerLoad.RegisterEffect(playerLoad.EFFECT_BROADCAST_AFFECT + 700, "Bip01", "effects/my_buff.mse").

playerLoad.RegisterEffect(effect_type, bone, path) returns None and raises a Python exception for invalid argument types. playerLoad.EFFECT_BROADCAST_AFFECT is 1000000; add the server type to it. playerLoad.EFFECT_AFFECT is the anchor for the separate AFF flag path. Asset Behavior .mse One particle attached to bone; an empty bone uses the character origin. .msattach A bundle whose entries name their own bones, so the bone argument is ignored. Exit effects play when the affect ends. The first successful registration of a key wins. A second registration does nothing. A path that fails to load logs a client error and registers nothing, so a later corrected call can succeed. AFFECT_DATA_DICT maps each type to (title, icon, resize, description, can_be_removed_manually), with an optional sixth element. The owner affect bar and target board use it. A type without an entry has no icon. Keep manual removal False for a script type: the server honors manual cancellation only for a skill whose affect is good. For the same type, the entry is 700: ("My buff", "icons/my_buff.sub", False, "A temporary bonus", False).

Call or event Meaning net.GetBroadcastAffectsByVID(vid) List of (dwType, bApplyOn, lApplyValue, endTime) for the character, or an empty list for an unknown VID. endTime is absolute server time, or 0 for infinite. BINARY_OnBroadcastAffectAdd(vid, dwType, point, value, endTime) A broadcast record arrives. BINARY_OnBroadcastAffectRemove(vid, dwType, point) A broadcast record ends. BINARY_OnBroadcastAffectPurgeVID(vid) All records for the character are dropped. BINARY_OnVidAffectFlag(vid, affectIndex, isSet) An AFF flag changes. chrmgr.HasAffectByVID(vid, index) Tests an AFF flag on the separate flag path. The target board displays remaining time as end time minus client server time, floored at 0. See behavior for delivery and late-viewer replay, and overview for the server side.

Register names and behavior at the top level of a forge game environment or a module it loads. This example allocates a small block and assigns separate rules. local AFFECTS = { MY_BUFF = 700, MY_MARK = 701, MY_GLOW = 702 } for name, id in pairs(AFFECTS) do affect.add_name_definition(name, id) affect.add_no_save(id) end affect.add_no_clear_on_death(AFFECTS.MY_BUFF) affect.add_broadcastable(AFFECTS.MY_MARK) affect.add_broadcastable(AFFECTS.MY_GLOW) Check your allocation first using registration. Each following example is independent and registers its own type.

Default override refreshes the existing record. A nonpositive input removes it instead of adding a zero-duration affect. local MY_STATE = 703 affect.add_name_definition("MY_STATE", MY_STATE) affect.add_broadcastable(MY_STATE) affect.add_no_save(MY_STATE) local function start_state(ch, seconds) if seconds <= 0 then ch:remove_affect(MY_STATE) return end ch:add_affect(MY_STATE, point.NONE, 0, 0, seconds, 0, true) end local function stop_state(ch) ch:remove_affect(MY_STATE) end

match_exact lets each point keep its own record. The guard avoids adding either record again while the type is present. local MY_BONUS = 704 affect.add_name_definition("MY_BONUS", MY_BONUS) local function grant_bonus(ch, move_bonus, attack_bonus) if ch:is_dead() or ch:has_affect(MY_BONUS) then return end ch:add_affect(MY_BONUS, point.MOV_SPEED, move_bonus, 0, affect.INFINITE_AFFECT_DURATION, 0, true, true) ch:add_affect(MY_BONUS, point.ATT_SPEED, attack_bonus, 0, affect.INFINITE_AFFECT_DURATION, 0, true, true) end
documents.s: Keep two points on one type

documents.t: This saved type lasts 90 seconds and refreshes on another add. Flag 0 avoids a second particle through the AFF channel. local MY_VISIBLE_BUFF = 705 affect.add_name_definition("MY_VISIBLE_BUFF", MY_VISIBLE_BUFF) affect.add_broadcastable(MY_VISIBLE_BUFF) local function give_buff(ch, attack_speed) ch:add_affect(MY_VISIBLE_BUFF, point.ATT_SPEED, attack_speed, 0, 90, 0, true) end Register type 705's effect and icon on the client to show them.

This infinite debuff survives death and is saved. Removing it undoes the point change. local MY_DEBUFF = 706 affect.add_name_definition("MY_DEBUFF", MY_DEBUFF) affect.add_no_clear_on_death(MY_DEBUFF) local function apply_debuff(ch) ch:add_affect(MY_DEBUFF, point.MOV_SPEED, -30) end local function lift_debuff(ch) if not ch:has_affect(MY_DEBUFF) then return false end ch:remove_affect(MY_DEBUFF) return true end For the current quest character, affect.remove(affect.name_map.MY_DEBUFF) also removes it. To make remove_bad remove it, register it in IS_CLEANSABLE_AFFECT.

The VID helper accepts players and monsters; find reads the current character. local function slow_target(vid, seconds) if affect.has_specify_vid(vid, affect.name_map.SLOW) then return end affect.add_specify_vid(vid, affect.name_map.SLOW, point.MOV_SPEED, -30, 0, seconds) end local function seconds_left(affect_type) local data = affect.find(affect_type) if data == nil then return 0 end return data.duration end See the Lua API for defaults and the overview for terminology.
documents.s: Inspect another character and a duration

documents.t: An affect applies a point change until it expires or is removed. This call replaces a matching record of type 700, or creates one if none matches. ch:add_affect(700, point.MOV_SPEED, 20, 0, 600, 0, true)

The path below shows the main effects of an add and its eventual removal. A loaded player's add searches for an override match, undoes the old points and tells the owner of the removal before rewriting a match. Otherwise it appends. The engine applies the points, updates the character if a flag or speed changed, broadcasts eligible types, notifies the owner, and saves eligible records. Infinite duration forces real-time off. Every second, the engine charges cost and decrements duration. A positive cost charges SP, or HP when the 1 << 31 flag is set; the affect ends if the character cannot pay. Infinite duration and IS_SPECIAL_BLOCK_CHAT_AFFECT members do not count down. Premium types take remaining time from the premium table. When a type below 400 expires, its skill toggle turns off. Removing an affect undoes its points, informs the owner and viewers, deletes its database row, and updates trait gates. Removing a type through ch:remove_affect removes every record of that type. A duration of 0 logs Character::AddAffect lDuration == 0 type {} and becomes 1 second, except for chat blocks, where it removes the block.

Database records and script adds received before a player is fully loaded enter a queue. Database records enter first; the queue applies in order when the player enters the game. A query immediately after a queued add can return false. Active item affects are then restored, the tick starts, and living players have health and SP refilled. Broadcastable affects are sent to viewers already looking. Real-time duration decreases by the time since logout at login; both kinds tick once per second online. A record that expired offline is still added: a negative remainder expires on its first tick, while exactly 0 becomes 1 second under the duration rule. Death keeps no-clear types, skill tree affects, and privilege types; it removes the rest. Listing AFFECT_QUEST_START_IDX alone does not keep every quest affect: list each actual type. Leaving the game clears in-memory affects without deleting saved rows. The database stores type, point, value, flag, duration, cost, and real-time status. Source VID has no column. A source-bearing affect can be written when added but is skipped on character save, so its old duration and no source can return at login. Make source-bearing types no-save. The supplied table key is player, type, point, and value; identical stacked records replace one row and return as one.

A record is identified by type and point, and by source when a nonzero source is requested. override match_exact Result false Any Always append; records stack. true false Replace the first record of the type on any point; source 0 matches any source. This is the default for affect.add_specify, affect.add_specify_vid, and ch:add_affect. true true Replace only a record on the exact point and, when nonzero, source. ch:add_affect exposes this option; affect.add_specify_map always uses it. An in-place replacement on a different point does not send viewers a removal for the old point. Use exact matching for separate points of a broadcast type, or explicitly remove before changing points.

Broadcast is a state channel for players and monsters. Adds and removals reach the owner and viewers; the packet carries character, type, point, value, source, and absolute end time. Infinite duration uses end time 0. Flag, cost, and real-time status are not sent. State is not periodically resent. The client keys records by type, point, and source, and counts records per type. The first attaches the type's particle and the last removal detaches it. A packet arriving before the character is retained until the character appears. A later viewer receives a replay of broadcastable records with end time computed from remaining duration. Virtual (avatar) characters are replayed like any other. The AFF flag channel travels in character packets and drives its own particles and chrmgr.HasAffectByVID; it is independent of broadcast. See client presentation and the overview.

An affect is a typed record on a character with a point, value, duration, flag, and cost. Use it for a buff, debuff, item blend, or other state that must expire, persist, stack, or appear to viewers. This forge module registers a type and grants a 10 minute movement bonus. affect.add_name_definition("MY_BUFF", 700) affect.add_no_save(affect.name_map.MY_BUFF) local function grant_speed(ch, amount) ch:add_affect(affect.name_map.MY_BUFF, point.MOV_SPEED, amount, 0, 600, 0, true) end local function revoke_speed(ch) ch:remove_affect(affect.name_map.MY_BUFF) end Call grant_speed(ch, 20) with a character to increase movement speed by 20. The engine undoes the bonus on expiry; this type is not saved. Register names at the top level of a forge game environment or a module it loads. Check the id before using it; see registration.

Term Meaning Affect / type A record on a character / its numeric kind. Multiple records can share a type. Point A character property changed by the record, such as movement speed. Apply versus point An apply id is converted to a point by some helpers. Other calls take the point directly; apply_on in returned data holds a point. Flag / AFF bit A bit number in the separate character flag channel. 0 sets no bit. Macro A named set of affect types used for classification. Broadcastable A type whose affect state is sent to characters' viewers as well as the owner. No-save A type excluded from database persistence. No-clear-on-death A type kept when death clears affects. Forge A Lua module environment that runs registration and game scripts; see Forge setup. Avatar / virtual character A character represented as virtual to the engine; its affects reach viewers like any character's and are saved to the session cache. Override An add option that replaces a matching record instead of always appending one. match_exact An override option that requires the same point. Source VID The runtime character identifier associated with the source of an affect. Real-time A duration that also elapses while the player is offline.

Lua registers types and adds or removes records. affect_config.yaml classifies types for persistence, death, broadcast, and macros. The client registers the particle and icon for types that need a visible presentation. A server affect works without a client effect. Material Location or surface Lua registration and use A forge game environment, its modules, or quests; character methods need a character. affect_config.yaml, items_affect.yaml In your locale base folder. affect_class An AFFECT node in a skill file. Client presentation Client Python effect registration and AFFECT_DATA_DICT. File locations vary by codebase. Registrations and configuration load at boot.

Page Contents Registration Id ranges, configuration, macros, item and skill declarations, load order. Lua API Functions, character methods, arguments, constants, and flags. Client Particles, icons, client state, and events. Behaviour Lifetime, saving, override, and broadcast. Examples Working registration and usage patterns. Pitfalls Symptoms, causes, and fixes.

These checks cover common symptoms when registering or using affects. For example, use exact point matching to keep both records here. ch:add_affect(700, point.MOV_SPEED, 10, 0, 60, 0, true, true) ch:add_affect(700, point.ATT_SPEED, 10, 0, 60, 0, true, true)

affect.add stacks on repeated calls. Its duplicate guard checks a different type and id space from the add, so it does not prevent ordinary quest affect duplicates. Use your own type with add_specify or ch:add_affect; identical saved records can return as one after login. Configuration stops the core at boot. A type name defined inside a handler is unknown when YAML loads. Register it at forge top level or use its numeric id; check the detailed configuration log. A skill class does not make a type no-save. Runtime macro memberships do not propagate to lists flattened from YAML. Register the behavior directly or list the id in YAML. Removing a skill class leaves membership behind. Memberships only grow; a skill refresh does not remove them. Correct the declaration before the next boot. A macro typo silently matches nothing. Registration creates unknown names and a query of an unknown name returns false. Copy the exact name from registration. remove_good leaves a buff, or remove_bad leaves a debuff. These use dispellable and cleansable sets, respectively, not good and bad classifications. Add the type to the appropriate macro. For bleeding, use ch:remove_damage_over_time. Two points leave only one record. Default override matches any point. Pass match_exact = true through ch:add_affect; for broadcast types, replacing on a different point can also leave a stale viewer entry and particle. See behavior. A read immediately after login returns false. Adds before the player is loaded are queued. Read after the queue has applied. A source-bearing affect returns with stale time and no source. The source is not persisted and character save skips that record. Make source-bearing types no-save. A particle appears twice. Broadcast and AFF flags draw independently. Use flag 0 for the broadcast type, or omit the type from broadcast. A broadcast type has no particle or icon. Register the effect and AFFECT_DATA_DICT entry in the client. The first successful registration of a key wins; correct that registration rather than adding a duplicate. See client presentation. Duration 0 lasts one second. Except for chat blocks, 0 is an error and becomes 1 second. Use remove_specify or ch:remove_affect to remove it. ch:get_affect_value returns 0. Unknown names, NONE, and a real value of 0 are indistinguishable. Check presence separately; ch:has_affect_flag takes a flag name, not a type name. See the overview and Lua API for terms and signatures.

Use affect.* with the current quest character, an explicit VID, or a map. Character methods use the character held by ch. This call adds a 90 second bonus to a character. ch:add_affect(700, point.ATT_SPEED, 10, 0, 90, 0, true) Registration functions and is_in_macro require no current character. Calls without a VID or map otherwise use the current quest character. Do not call them without one: add, remove, remove_bad, remove_good, add_collect, add_specialization, add_collect_point, add_specialization_point, and get_apply_on dereference it without a check; other calls check and return nothing. affect.add, add_collect, add_specialization, remove_collect, and remove_specialization take an apply id and convert it to a point. Other functions take a point directly. Wrong-typed arguments generally log a diagnostic and return nothing (nil); the find functions raise a Lua error.

Function Returns Behavior affect.add(apply_on, value, duration) Nothing Adds on the converted point with type 1000 plus the current quest index, without override. An apply below 1 or at the limit logs apply is out of range : {}. See pitfalls for its duplicate guard. affect.remove(type?) Nothing Removes all of a type; omitted or 0 selects the current quest type. affect.remove_bad() Nothing Removes poison, fire, and IS_CLEANSABLE_AFFECT members. Bleeding is not a member in the shipped set. affect.remove_good() Nothing Removes IS_DISPELLABLE_AFFECT members. affect.get_apply_on(type) Point or nil Point of the first affect of the type. affect.has_specify(type, point_on?) Boolean Tests type, on any point if omitted. affect.remove_specify(type, point_on) Nothing Removes the first exact type and point match. affect.add_specify(type, point?, value?, flag?, duration?, cost?, override?, is_real_time?) Nothing Adds a record. Only type is required. add_specify and add_specify_vid default to point POINT_NONE, value 0, flag AFF_NONE, infinite duration, cost 0, override = true, and is_real_time = false. See override behavior.

Collect uses type 515 and specialization uses type 537. Each pair below has the same behavior for its respective type. All return nothing. Function Behavior affect.add_collect(apply_on, value, duration) / affect.add_specialization(apply_on, value, duration) Convert apply to point, sum with an existing value there, remove it, and add the sum with the new duration. Reject an out-of-range apply. affect.add_collect_point(point_on, value, duration) / affect.add_specialization_point(point_on, value, duration) Add directly on the point without summing; calls stack. An invalid point logs point is out of range : {}. affect.remove_collect(apply_on, value) / affect.remove_specialization(apply_on, value) Remove the first matching converted point and exact value. affect.remove_all_collect() / affect.remove_all_specialization() Remove every record of the respective type.

Function Returns Behavior affect.has_specify_vid(vid, type, point?) Boolean Tests a player or monster; omitted point means any. affect.remove_specify_vid(vid, type, point?) Nothing Removes the first exact match with a point; omitted or 0 removes all of the type. affect.add_specify_vid(vid, type, point?, value?, flag?, duration?, cost?, override?, is_real_time?) Nothing Adds to a player or monster; a point at or above the limit returns silently. affect.add_specify_map(map_index, type, point?, value?, flag?, duration?, override?, is_real_time?) Nothing Adds to every player on this core's map index. There is no cost argument; override matches the exact point. An invalid VID logs a message containing is not a valid VID. The add_specify variants do not expose match_exact; the map variant always uses exact-point override.

Function Returns Matching affect.find(type, apply_on?, source_vid?) affect.affect_data or nil First match; omitted point and source 0 mean any. affect.find_specific(type, apply_on?, flag?, source_vid?) affect.affect_data or nil First match; omitted point means POINT_NONE. Reserved high bits are masked when comparing flags. affect.find_all(type, apply_on?, flag?, source_vid?) Array of affect.affect_data Every match; omitted point means any. The array can be empty. Each requires a numeric first argument; otherwise it raises, for example, affect.find: expected number as first argument. Data fields are type, apply_on (point), value, flag, duration (remaining seconds or infinite), sp_cost, source_vid, and boolean is_real_time.

Method Returns Behavior ch:add_affect(type, point, value, flag?, duration?, sp_cost?, override?, match_exact?, source_vid?, is_real_time?) Nothing Adds a record. Defaults: flag 0, infinite duration, cost 0, override true, match_exact false, source 0, real-time false. ch:remove_affect(type) Nothing Removes all of the type. ch:remove_damage_over_time(affect_type) Boolean Removes poison, fire, or bleeding and cancels its tick event; returns false for other types. ch:remove_bad_affect(remove_dispel?) Number removed Removes poison, fire, and cleansable types. With false, keeps IS_DISPEL_CURSE_AFFECT; default true. ch:remove_good_affect() Number removed Removes dispellable types. ch:has_affect(type, point?, source_vid?) Boolean Omitted point and source 0 mean any. ch:get_affect_value(name) Number First value for the type name, or 0. ch:has_affect_flag(name) Boolean Tests an AFF_ bit name, not a type name. party.member_has_affect(affect, apply) tests a party member; see the party API for its context.

These functions need no character and only add entries. See registration for load order and merging. Function Returns Behavior affect.add_name_definition(name, value) Nothing Adds a type name and id to the engine and affect.name_map. affect.add_no_save(type) Nothing Excludes the type from saving. affect.add_no_clear_on_death(type) Nothing Keeps the type on death. affect.add_broadcastable(type) Nothing Sends the type to viewers. affect.add_to_macro(macro_name, type) Nothing Adds a member, creating the macro if needed. affect.is_in_macro(macro_name, value) Boolean Tests membership; an unknown macro returns false.

affect.name_map maps built-in and Lua-registered type names to ids. Some engine types are not present, so it is not an exhaustive allocation registry. affect.bit_map maps AFF_ names to bit numbers and is the live list to consult for flag names. The AFF bitfield has 96 bits. Bit 0 is reserved for AFF_NONE, leaving 95 usable; 91 are taken and 92 to 95 are free. Flags at or below 0 or at or above 96 are rejected as bit flags; 0 is the no-flag value for an affect. affect.INFINITE_AFFECT_DURATION is 60 * 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 seconds, defined in the shared quest library wherever it is loaded. The range names are SKILL_START 1, SKILL_END 400, GUILD_SKILL_START 151, and GUILD_SKILL_END 160. See overview for terminology and examples for calls in context.

The client runs Python 2.7 with a process-wide importer that resolves client modules from packed files. Debugger builds can also load loose Python modules from disk. The installed open wrapper prefers a packed file when it can read one: def open(filename, mode = 'rb'): if pack.Exist(filename) and mode in ('r', 'rb'): return pack_file(filename, mode) else: return old_open(filename, mode) For debugger setup and the test window workflow, see Debug client Python.

The ordinary Python search path is empty. The hybrid importer checks the optional rootlib branch when enabled, then the pack importer, and falls back to the original Python importer when the pack importer returns no module. Built-in and frozen Python modules remain available through that fallback. The pack importer lowercases a module name and replaces dots with slashes. It probes <path>.py and <path>/__init__.py; when both packed paths exist, the .py module takes precedence. A loaded package receives a __path__. Import Resolution import a.b.c Loads the dotted module and returns the root module a. The child is attached to its direct parent so it can be reached through the package hierarchy. from a.b import c Returns a.b. If c is already an attribute, it is retained. Otherwise the importer tries the packed module a.b.c, then asks the original importer. from a import * The importer attempts the * item and, on fallback, copies the returned module dictionary into a and sets a "*" guard. from . import x The pack importer does not resolve the relative level against the caller's package. If its empty-name probe misses, the request reaches the original importer. Whether that fallback succeeds depends on package state and what the original importer can access. Use an explicit dotted package import and test it in the target client. The importer creates parent placeholders when needed, registers a child in sys.modules before executing it, and links it to its direct parent. When a packed package replaces a placeholder, its attributes are merged into the loaded package where they do not already exist. Module names are case-insensitive in the pack importer: uiToolTip and uitooltip resolve to the same cached module object. The lowercased name is also used for pack and loose-file probes. This rule does not make Python attributes or arbitrary file paths case-insensitive.

These functions are available as Python builtins after the importer is installed. Signature Behavior open(filename, mode='rb') Returns a pack_file for an existing packed path in r or rb mode. Otherwise delegates to the original open. pack_open(filename, mode='rb') Alias of the installed open; it can also return a disk file. new_open(filename, mode='rb') Alias of the installed open. old_open(...) Original Python open. Use it when you need to bypass the packed-file preference. execfile(fileName, dict) For a text file, reads through the installed open, compiles with an absolute filename, and executes in dict. Returns None. For .pyc and .pyo, it loads the code but does not execute it. old_execfile(...) Original Python 2 execfile. TraceError(*args) Formats each argument and sends it separately to dbg.TraceError. Returns None. sys_err(*args) Alias of TraceError. Tracef(*args) Formats each argument and sends it separately to dbg.Tracen, unless __DEBUG__ is true, when it returns without sending them. LogBox(*args) Formats each argument and sends it separately to dbg.LogBox. Returns None. __import__(name, globals=None, locals=None, fromlist=None, level=-1) The installed hybrid importer.

with pack_open(...) gives you the object returned by the wrapper: a pack_file for an eligible packed path, or an ordinary disk file if the wrapper falls back to old_open. Do not assume both objects have the same file API. pack_file operation Behavior pack_file(filename, mode='rb') Loads the packed content into memory. Accepts only r and rb; text mode converts CRLF to LF. name The requested filename. read(len=None) Consumes up to len bytes, or the remainder when len is omitted. read(0) also consumes the remainder. readline() Consumes through the next LF, or consumes the remainder if there is no LF. readlines() Consumes the remaining lines through the iterator. Iteration Reads one line at a time until no data remains. Context manager __enter__ returns the pack_file; __exit__ does no cleanup and does not suppress exceptions. pack_file does not implement close, seeking, or the full file API. Direct construction for a missing packed path raises IOError('No file or directory'). Packed reads accept .py, .pyc, .json, .yaml, .html, and .txt extensions, case-insensitively. A disallowed extension raises cannot open file. not permitted.

With PYTHON_REMOTE_DEBUGGER enabled, a cache miss probes the lowercased loose path for <path>.py, then <path>/__init__.py, before asking the pack. These paths are relative to the process working directory. Without the debugger option, loose modules are not used. A later import checks the modification time of a cached loose module. If it changed, the importer executes the file again in the same module dictionary. Saving a file alone does not trigger execution. If the file was deleted, the loaded module remains in place. Signature Behavior system.Refresh(names, force=True) Visits names in the supplied order, using case-insensitive module lookups. Skips unloaded and packed modules. With force=True, re-executes eligible loose modules even when their modification times have not changed. Returns the original names it visited. Order dependencies before their consumers. A consumer that uses from dependency import Class must execute again after the dependency to bind the new class. A reference to the module itself continues to point to the same module object. Refresh executes into the existing dictionary without clearing it. A name removed from the source can remain in the module, and existing instances or directly imported class objects do not become instances of a newly defined class. If a loose file has disappeared, its name can still appear in the returned list, so that list alone does not prove the source was re-executed. Compile and execution exceptions propagate to the caller. Do not use import system to reach Refresh. The launcher installs the importer without registering its namespace under that name. An import can compile it a second time and fail when its builtins are a dictionary. The test window obtains Refresh from the installed importer's globals; use the workflow in Debug client Python.

Symptom What happens could not import module c from a.b The original importer returned a false-valued attribute for a non-star from item after the packed submodule lookup. The original importer can raise its own exception first. An exception while executing a packed module The importer re-raises it. Its own import trace is normally disabled, and the module entry is not removed by the shown execution path. IOError: No file or directory Direct pack_file construction did not find the packed path. The open wrapper instead falls back to disk when the packed path is absent. RELOAD: system.Refresh is unreachable -- neither sys.modules nor the builtin importer's namespace has it; nothing was re-read The test window could not find the refresh function. RELOAD failed: The test window caught a refresh exception and logs the traceback after this line. RELOAD: 6 named, none were loaded yet -- the import path will re-read them. __LOOSE__=True Example with 6 requested names: none was an already loaded loose module. This can occur before the first load; __LOOSE__ also shows whether loose imports are enabled.
Registration Description

Use a debugger build to attach your editor to the client's Python process and reload a UI window without restarting the client. The development tools foundation describes the debugger and loose-file mechanism; the client Python imports reference covers the import rules. This attach configuration maps your workspace source to the client directory. Replace both placeholders and set the port to the listener's port. { // Use IntelliSense to learn about possible attributes. // Hover to view descriptions of existing attributes. // For more information, visit: https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?linkid=830387 "version": "0.2.0", "configurations": [ { "name": "Root Debugger", "type": "debugpy", "request": "attach", "connect": { "host": "localhost", "port": 3000 }, "pathMappings": [ { "localRoot": "${workspaceFolder}/[rel_path_to_root]", "remoteRoot": "[abs_path_to_client_folder]" } ], }, ] }
documents.s: Attach a debugger to client Python and hot-reload a window

documents.t: Use a client built with the CMake option PYTHON_REMOTE_DEBUGGER enabled. It defaults to off. The option includes the Python debugger and enables loose Python files; a release client built without it has no debugger and does not load those overrides. The option also disables hardening, so do not ship that build. The client runs Python 2.7; a Python 3 port is not on the roadmap. Start the client with its working directory set to the client directory beside the executable. Put the loose Python files you want to test there, using their module paths. Make them available before their first import: a module already loaded from the pack does not become loose just because a matching file appears later. Restart the client if necessary.

The UI agent skill prescribes a loose uiTest.py in the client directory and test layouts under uiscript/. Give uiTest.py a TestWindow attribute that names the window class to instantiate; the skill's sandbox pattern ends with TestWindow = _Sandbox. In a debugger build, constInfo.IS_TESTING_GUI is enabled. At login, the client enables outlines and opens the test board. Its module field defaults to uiTest; use Load or F10 to load it. The entry file is read from the process working directory, so it must be loose there. Add a RELOAD tuple to the entry file for the loose modules that make up your window. This excerpt shows the ordering pattern: dependencies come first, and the window that consumes them comes last. RELOAD = ( "land.palette", # imports nothing of ours "land.data", # imports palette "land.deployments", # imports data "land.uitowns", # imports deployments, hands out TownDetail "land.uioverview", # imports a NAME from towns, so it comes after it "land.uiguildland", # the window itself, so it comes last ) Replace those names with your own dependency chain. Include a consumer after any module from which it imports a class or other name. The sandbox reloads the named modules in tuple order before it instantiates TestWindow. The previous window is hidden and, if it has Destroy, destroyed before replacement. Implement Destroy to release the handlers and children your window owns.

Start the debugger client, then attach the editor's Python debugger to localhost. The client attempts ports 3000 through 3049. Set connect.port to the actual listener's port; the loop suppresses errors and does not stop after a successful attempt, so do not assume the listener is always on 3000. Set localRoot to your workspace's Python source directory and remoteRoot to the absolute client directory. The mapping translates the client-side filenames into files where your editor can place breakpoints. Startup does not wait for an attachment. For a breakpoint during early startup, the source has a commented wait_for_attach() call that you can enable in a debugger build.

Edit and save the loose subject modules, then press F10 or Load on the test board. The sandbox reloads resources, executes the test entry file, refreshes its RELOAD tuple, and creates and shows a new window. system.Refresh(names, force=True) visits the names in order and re-executes loaded loose modules. Its default forced refresh also re-executes a consumer whose own file has not changed, allowing it to bind names from a refreshed dependency. Unloaded and packed modules are skipped. A returned name means the module was visited; if its loose file has disappeared, it does not prove that the source was re-executed. A later import of a cached loose module also checks its modification time. When it has changed, the client re-reads the file into the same module object. Saving alone does not schedule that check. Names removed from the source can remain in the module dictionary, and existing window instances do not turn into instances of a newly defined class. Use the sandbox to replace the window. The layout loader has a separate rule: it tries the packed layout first and falls back to the loose file on an exception when testing is enabled. A successfully loaded packed layout can therefore shadow a loose layout at the same path. Use a distinct test layout path or avoid that collision.

The client-native Python stubs are in Client-Files/root/stubs/*.pyi. Use them in your editor to discover the C++ modules and their bindings. They are references for typing and completion, and can be incomplete or stale; check the native registration tables when a stub disagrees with behavior. For example, the pack.Reload stub declares an argument, while the sandbox calls it without one. Resource reload is separate from re-executing the Python modules in RELOAD.

A window still uses an old class. from x import Thing binds the class object. Re-executing x creates a new class but does not update that binding in its consumer. Put x before the consumer in RELOAD, refresh both, and instantiate the window again. Importing system to reach Refresh executes a second copy. The launcher executes the module without necessarily registering that execution under sys.modules["system"]. A later import system can execute another copy and fail while accessing builtins. Use the sandbox's existing refresh discovery and RELOAD tuple. An import traceback can surface as an access violation. Check syserr.txt for the Python traceback when a native call fails during an import. The loading worker checks its import result and prints the exception before aborting, but other native import paths need not have the same checks. The sandbox cannot load the entry file. Check that uiTest.py is loose in the client's working directory and that its module field names the file without .py. A missing TestWindow also prevents the sandbox from instantiating the window.
This recipe adds no C++ registration. Registration Purpose

Register names and rules before configuration refers to them. This top-level Lua registration makes a type visible to viewers and keeps it out of the database. affect.add_name_definition("MY_BUFF", 700) affect.add_no_save(affect.name_map.MY_BUFF) affect.add_broadcastable(affect.name_map.MY_BUFF)

Ids Use 1 to 399 Skill vnums; a skill affect uses its skill vnum. 400 to 698, and 999 Engine types, including movement, damage, chat blocks, premium, land, blends, fishing, and item affects. 699 to 998 Free of engine names. 1000 plus quest index Quest affect; AFFECT_QUEST_START_IDX is 1000. 10000 plus privilege id Privilege affect, neither saved nor cleared on death. Choose a block in 699 to 998, or above 1000 plus the highest quest index you use and below 10000. Check affect.name_map and your own forges first. The type is the identity, so two systems using the same id collide silently. The built-in name table is not necessarily exhaustive.

In your locale base folder, affect_config.yaml accepts four optional top-level keys: Key Meaning NO_SAVE_AFFECTS Do not save these types. NO_CLEAR_ON_DEATH_AFFECTS Keep them through death. BROADCASTABLE_AFFECTS Send them to viewers. macros Define named sets for lists and classification. A list or macro entry can be a numeric id, a registered name, another YAML macro, or a range with from and exactly one of to_inclusive and to_exclusive. Bounds may be names. A scalar resolves as a name first, then a macro. NONE resolves to 0, so it falls through to macro lookup and is rejected. This configuration keeps the registered type through death and defines a small range. NO_CLEAR_ON_DEATH_AFFECTS: - MY_BUFF macros: MY_TYPES: - range: from: 700 to_inclusive: 702 A failed configuration load stops the game core at boot and logs cannot load Affect Configuration: <file>. The detailed log identifies the cause: Log text Cause Error loading affect_config Invalid YAML or structure. Circular dependency detected in macros Macros include each other in a loop. Undefined identifier in macro / Undefined identifier in a list Unknown name, id, or macro. Invalid 'from' or invalid upper bound Unknown range bound. Range in macro and must have either 'to_inclusive' or 'to_exclusive' Missing upper bound, including in a list range. Invalid item in macro / Invalid item in affects list Entry is neither scalar nor range.

Macro Purpose IS_SPECIAL_BLOCK_CHAT_AFFECT Special chat-block types do not tick down. The game needs this macro. IS_BLOCK_CHAT_AFFECT Includes BLOCK_CHAT and special blocks; duration 0 removes a block, and duration above 1 announces it. IS_ITEM_AFFECT Item types 671 to 691; used by configuration lists. IS_LAND_AFFECT Land bonus range; used by lists. IS_SKILL_AFFECT Skill range; used by lists. IS_MAP_CURSE Map curse types; used by lists. IS_GOOD_AFFECT Skill-applied buff classification for assist credit, announcements, and immunity. Lua adds do not consult it. IS_BAD_AFFECT Skill-applied debuff classification for assist credit and announcements. Lua adds do not consult it. IS_UNTARGETABLE_AFFECT Hides the holder from target acquisition and prevents attacks. IS_DISPELLABLE_AFFECT Types removed by remove_good. IS_CLEANSABLE_AFFECT Types removed by remove_bad in addition to poison and fire. IS_PARTY_BUFF_AFFECT Label populated by skills; no engine consumer. IS_DISPEL_CURSE_AFFECT Types retained by ch:remove_bad_affect(false). Good and dispellable are separate classifications. Unknown macro names are accepted by registration and match nothing when queried; check spelling.

An AFFECT node can add its type to macros. It uses affectVnum, or the skill vnum when that field is absent. per_use: - type: AFFECT id: my_buff affect_class: - IS_GOOD_AFFECT - IS_DISPELLABLE_AFFECT point: ATT_SPEED amountPoly: 2+14.5*skill_k durationPoly: '1800' collect: source: caster Memberships only grow. A skill refresh adds memberships but does not remove earlier ones. A typo creates a separate macro.

items_affect.yaml maps affect items to types. The entry label is ignored. Field Requirement Meaning vnum Required Item vnum. affect Required Numeric affect type. bonuses Optional, nullable List of type apply names and value numbers. duration Required key, nullable Duration in seconds. stackable Optional Defaults to false. This entry gives a blend one bonus. MY_BLEND: vnum: 50821 affect: 671 bonuses: - type: MAX_HP value: 3000 duration: 600 At creation, the item stores the type in socket 0 and, except for the permanent subtype, the duration in socket 2; 0 there means infinite. Using it removes its own affects, then switches it off if socket 5 is 1. Otherwise, unless stackable, it switches off other active items of the same type and adds one affect per bonus, with item id as flag and no override. Active items restore missing affects at login, so item types belong in the no-save set. No bonuses means no affect is added by this entry. Invalid YAML or a missing duration key raises an exception while loading game tables.

The C++ registration interface supplies the same operations as Lua: Operation C++ registration Lua equivalent Name a type AddAffectStringDefinitions(name, value) affect.add_name_definition Exclude from saves AddNoSaveAffect(int) affect.add_no_save Keep through death AddNoClearOnDeathAffect(int) affect.add_no_clear_on_death Broadcast AddBroadcastableAffect(int) affect.add_broadcastable Add macro member AddToMacro(name, int) affect.add_to_macro Load configuration Load(file) None Query sets IsNoSaveAffect, IsNoClearOnDeathAffect, IsBroadcastableAffect, IsInMacro, GetMacroSet, FromString affect.is_in_macro queries macros. Built-in names populate the initial name table; the skill loader adds affect_class memberships. The diagram shows when YAML can resolve Lua names. Configuration adds to existing sets. YAML macros resolve other YAML macros, and lists copy those YAML members. Members added by Lua or skills join the live macro but do not propagate into already flattened lists or including macros. Register no-save, no-clear, and broadcast behavior directly or list the type in YAML. See the Lua API and overview.

These APIs register processors, send messages, and manage waits across Forge environments. The calling-context rules determine where each operation is legal. Surface What it is Core Use forge.sys Processor registration and logging game and db Handle messages and log. forge.sys.game Game bindings and transport game Send to clients, game cores, or db. forge.sys.db Db bindings and transport db Answer or send to game cores. forge_helper Lua wrapper game and db Bind methods and wait for messages. bridge.coro Coroutine interface game and db Create, own, and close coroutines. Require the helper inside an environment: local forge_helper = require("forge_helper")

Term Meaning Receipt Token routing an answer to a waiting coroutine. Owner Type and ID controlling a coroutine's lifetime. handler_id Handler identifier passed to a db peer processor. client_handler Client window identifier. Processor Function registered to handle a message. Header String identifying a message type.

Available in both environments. Function Signature Description forge.sys.set_main_processor (header: string, processor: function) -> boolean Handle client messages with this header for this forge. Called as processor(ch, message, client_handler). forge.sys.set_peer_processor (header: string, processor: function) -> boolean Game: handle messages from other game cores, called as processor(d, message, receipt). Db: handle requests from game cores, called as processor(peer, message, handler_id, receipt). forge.sys.set_db_processor (header: string, processor: function) -> boolean Game only in practice. Handle replies from the db core, called as processor(d, message). forge.sys.log (verbosity: number, message: string) Log with the prefix [Forge-<name>]. Verbosity 0 to 5. forge.sys.err (message: string) Error log with the same prefix. Registration rules: The call must come from code that carries the forge environment: the environment body, or a function defined in it. Directly from a quest when block it fails with Forge::SetInputHandler called from a non-forge script and returns false. A handler is keyed by input type, forge name and header. Registering the same header twice fails with Forge::SetInputHandler trying to double set input handler and returns false. A when boot block cannot register itself, but it can call a forge method that does. The handler is anchored on the global state, not on the short-lived quest thread. A message with no handler logs Forge::InvokeMainInputHandler no handler registered for forge [<name>] header [<header>] (and the peer and db variants). Processors run on the main thread, not in a coroutine. A processor that has to wait must start a coroutine. The value a processor returns is ignored. An error in a processor is printed to the error log with a stack trace, and the server keeps running.

Messaging functions. They are the transport; each needs a forge environment on the caller, otherwise they log ForgeGame::Send<X>Packet called from a non-forge script and return false. An empty header is refused as well. Function Signature Description forge.sys.game.send_client (ch: LPCHARACTER, header, message, client_handler?: number = 0, receipt?: string) Send to one player's client. Needs a character with a descriptor (null ch or null desc). The packet must fit 65535 bytes (message of N bytes does not fit a packet). client_handler selects the client window that gets the answer. forge.sys.game.send_p2p (header, message, receipt?: string) Send to every other game core. forge.sys.game.send_desc (desc: LPDESC, header, message, receipt?: string) Send to one game core. forge.sys.game.send_db (header, message, desc_handler?: number = 0, receipt?: string) Send to the db core. forge.sys.game.answer_p2p (desc: LPDESC, message, receipt: number) Answer a request that arrived with a receipt. send_client is not a chat line. It delivers a header and a payload to a handler on the client side. To put a line in the player's chat, call ch:chat_packet(type, text) on the character, with a type from forge.sys.game.CHAT_TYPE (INFO for a plain system line). It needs no forge environment, so a hook may call it directly. The enums forge.sys.game.CHAT_TYPE, forge.sys.game.DAMAGE_TYPE and forge.sys.game.WEAR are in the same stub. Receipts go out as strings (send_* parses them as unsigned numbers) and arrive in processors as numbers, which answer_p2p and answer_peer take back as numbers. The namespace on the wire is the sender's forge name, so the receiving forge of the same name gets the message. Everything else under forge.sys.game (for example forge.sys.game.char_manager.find_by_pid, which every login hook uses) is described by its own generated stub.

Db environment only. Function Signature Description forge.sys.db.broadcast_peers (header, message, channel?: number = 0, except?: CPeer, except_channel?: number = 0) Send to all game cores, optionally one channel, optionally skipping one core. forge.sys.db.send_peer (peer: CPeer, header, message, desc_handler?: number = 0) Send to one game core. forge.sys.db.answer_peer (peer: CPeer, message, receipt: number) Answer a request that arrived with a receipt. Answer once: a second answer finds the receipt used and is dropped. forge.sys.db.get_event_flag (flag) -> number Value of an event flag, 0 if unset. forge.sys.db.set_event_flag (flag, value) Persist the flag and broadcast it to all game cores. forge.sys.db.sql, forge.sys.db.log and forge.sys.db.priv have their own stubs.

A Lua module that wraps transport and coroutines. Require it inside the forge environment, never in the main state. If the main state requires it first, every forge gets the cached copy built outside any forge environment, which has no forge name, and every send fails. Processor registration. The helper binds self for you, so a processor can be a method. Function Signature Registers on forge_helper.sys.game.set_main_processor (header, self, processor) forge.sys.set_main_processor. Processor called (self, ch, message, client_handler). forge_helper.sys.game.set_p2p_processor (header, self, processor) forge.sys.set_peer_processor. Processor called (self, d, message, receipt). forge_helper.sys.game.set_db_processor (header, self, processor) forge.sys.set_db_processor. Processor called (self, d, message). forge_helper.sys.db.set_peer_processor (header, self, processor) forge.sys.set_peer_processor on the db core. Processor called (self, peer, message, handler_id, receipt). All four drop the boolean result, so a double registration is not visible to the caller. Waiting. A yielding function sends a message with a receipt that names the coroutine, then yields. It returns when the answer arrives, the timeout fires, or the owner is closed. Function Signature Receipt owner Resumes on forge_helper.sys.game.yield_client (ch, header, message, client_handler?, ...) PLAYER, the character's player id The client's answer. forge_helper.sys.game.yield_db (header, message, desc_handler?, ...) PEER, 0 The db core's answer_peer. forge_helper.sys.game.yield_p2p (header, message, ...) PEER, 1 The first answer from any core. forge_helper.sys.game.yield_desc (desc, header, message, ...) PEER, 1 The answer from that core. forge_helper.sys.game.yield_auth (username, password, hwid, client_ip) none A JSON string with the authentication result. Timeouts wrap a yielding function: Function Signature Returns forge_helper.coro.with_timeout (timeout_ms, yielding, ...) (result, ok) as the yielding function returns them. forge_helper.coro.collect (timeout_ms, yielding, ...) After the full timeout, (results, true) where results is an array of {owner_type, owner_id, args}, one per answer. Without answers, the array is empty. Every yielding function must run inside a bridge coroutine. See calling context.

Owned coroutines. An owner is a pair (owner_type, owner_id). When an owner is closed, every coroutine it holds is resumed with failure and removed. Function Signature Description bridge.coro.create (entry) -> id, thread Create a coroutine and run it right away until its first yield. Returns 0, nil if entry finished without yielding or raised an error. bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner (entry, player_id) -> id, thread Same, owned by the player. It is closed when the player disconnects. bridge.coro.adopt () -> id Register the running non-main thread as a bridge coroutine. Fails on the main thread (trying to adopt main thread). bridge.coro.add_owner (coroutine_id, owner_type, owner_id) Add an owner to a coroutine. bridge.coro.close_by_owner (owner_type, owner_id) Close every coroutine of that owner. The generated stub lists a leading coroutine_id; the binding takes only the two. bridge.coro.close_by_owner_exact (owners: {{owner_type, owner_id}, ...}) Close the coroutines that have exactly this set of owners. bridge.coro.get_current_id () -> number Id of the running bridge coroutine. 0 outside a bridge coroutine, never nil. bridge.coro.generate_receipt_token (coroutine_id, owner_type, owner_id) -> string Token an answer must carry to resume this coroutine. A zero id raises Invalid coroutine_id: cannot be 0. bridge.coro.enable_timout (ms) Arm a timeout on the running coroutine. Outside a coroutine: with_timout outside a coroutine. A second timeout before the resume is ignored with coroutine [id] has already a timeout. bridge.coro.enable_collect (ms) Arm collect mode. Outside a coroutine: collect outside a coroutine. bridge.coro.COROUTINE_OWNER enum PLAYER, QUEST, PEER, AUTH. The generated stub does not list AUTH. The spelling enable_timout (no second e) is the real identifier. What the yielding code sees when it resumes: Cause Values returned An answer with a valid token (message, true) The timeout fired (nil, false) The owner was closed (nil, false) collect, at the timeout (table, true) An answer must come from the owner it was issued for (ValidateCoroReceiptToken checks type and id). A late answer, after a timeout, is dropped and logged as token invalid/expired. After a timeout or a close resume the coroutine is removed, so code that waits a second time after a failed wait is not resumed again. Next: Quest-side events and coroutines.

QuestManager runs login and when blocks; Luna runs parallel to QuestManager. Use hooks to call Forge methods and bridge coroutines to wait for replies. A hook can start a player-owned coroutine: when login begin local pid = pc.get_player_id() bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner( function() forge.game.visit_counter:on_login(pid) end, pid) end

A state block in a .forge file takes any event the quest system fires. The ones a forge uses most: Event Fires Notes when login When the player is in the game phase on a core and the quest data is loaded. Again on every core change. It must run to the end: a block that suspends (a dialog, a wait) is closed and logged as QUEST NOT END RUNNING on Login/Logout. when logout In the disconnect sequence, after the player is saved. The character still exists. Fires when the player leaves a core as well as on a real disconnect. when boot_init When the db core announces boot, before the boot data is processed. Runs before when boot. when boot After the db core has sent its boot data. All forges and all quest states are loaded. when <target>.<event> For example when roster.changed. The target is the part before the dot. There is no local login or logout event on the event bus. The hooks are the when blocks of the forge file.

Keep state in the forge environment; a when thread is collected when the block returns. Wait only in a bridge coroutine. A quest thread and a processor on the main thread cannot wait. Send through a method defined in the forge environment; a hook has no forge environment. Capture pc.* values before yielding. The current player is not preserved after resume. Put conditioned blocks last: matching with blocks return before later blocks for the same event.

Require forge_helper inside the environment. This complete forge sends a request from a player-owned coroutine and collects replies for 1,000 ms: forge headcount begin environment game begin local helper = require("forge_helper") local M = {} function M:collect() local replies, ok = helper.coro.collect(1000, helper.sys.game.yield_p2p, "headcount", "") if ok then sys_log(0, "answers: " .. #replies) end end return M end state start begin when login begin local pid = pc.get_player_id() bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner( function() forge.game.headcount:collect() end, pid) end end end with_timeout returns on the first answer or timeout; collect waits the full timeout. An owner close resumes a pending wait with (nil, false) and removes the coroutine. Set a timeout and tie player waits to that player. bridge.coro.adopt() registers the running non-main thread as a bridge coroutine. Call it only inside a non-main coroutine; on the main thread it raises trying to adopt main thread. On logout, ON_PLAYER_SAVE fires, then when logout runs while the character exists, then player-owned coroutines close. See the API reference for ownership and return values. Next: Creating bindings.
These examples keep state in Forge modules and use quest hooks to enter them. Use the API reference for signatures and the Foundations page for the model.

This local counter records logins. The quick start also counts them across cores. forge visit_counter begin environment game begin local M = { visits = 0 } function M:visit() self.visits = self.visits + 1 end return M end state start begin when login begin forge.game.visit_counter:visit() end end end

This forge stores player IDs and removes them on logout. forge roster begin environment game begin local M = { players = {} } function M:enter(pid) self.players[pid] = true end function M:leave(pid) self.players[pid] = nil end return M end state start begin when login begin forge.game.roster:enter(pc.get_player_id()) end when logout begin forge.game.roster:leave(pc.get_player_id()) end end end

This store asks db for a persisted flag in a player-owned coroutine. forge cooldown_store begin environment game begin local helper = require("forge_helper") local M = {} function M:load(pid) local value, ok = helper.coro.with_timeout(2000, helper.sys.game.yield_db, "load", tostring(pid)) if ok then sys_log(0, "cooldown: " .. value) end end return M end environment db begin local M = {} function M.load(peer, message, handler_id, receipt) local value = forge.sys.db.get_event_flag("cooldown_" .. message) forge.sys.db.answer_peer(peer, tostring(value), receipt) end forge.sys.set_peer_processor("load", M.load) return M end state start begin when login begin local pid = pc.get_player_id() bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner( function() forge.game.cooldown_store:load(pid) end, pid) end end end

This boot hook initializes local state after the forges load. A login collects answers from other cores; each peer answers once with its local count. forge headcount begin environment game begin local helper = require("forge_helper") local M = { count = 0 } function M:reset() self.count = 0 end function M:enter() self.count = self.count + 1 end function M:leave() self.count = self.count - 1 end function M:answer(desc, message, receipt) forge.sys.game.answer_p2p(desc, tostring(self.count), receipt) end function M:collect() local replies, ok = helper.coro.collect(1000, helper.sys.game.yield_p2p, "count", "") if ok then sys_log(0, "cores answered: " .. #replies) end end helper.sys.game.set_p2p_processor("count", M, M.answer) return M end state start begin when boot begin forge.game.headcount:reset() end when login begin local pid = pc.get_player_id() forge.game.headcount:enter() bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner( function() forge.game.headcount:collect() end, pid) end when logout begin forge.game.headcount:leave() end end end

A when block raises with_timout outside a coroutine or Invalid coroutine_id: cannot be 0. The hook runs on a quest thread, not a bridge coroutine. Wrap the waiting call in bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner(function() ... end, pid) and do it there. called from a non-forge script when sending from a hook. The send functions look at the environment of the calling function, and a when block has none. Call a forge method that does the send. A table you built in a when block is gone or invisible. The quest thread is collected when the block returns. Declare the state in the forge environment and let the hook call into it. Every send fails after you required forge_helper in a quest or in the init script. The main state cached the helper without a forge environment. Require it only inside environment blocks. Two forges that require the same module see different tables. Each forge has its own module cache. Anchor shared state on _G, using a shared registry. The core does not start after you changed a forge. An environment body returned nothing, or a body has a syntax error. A load error stops the service. Return a table from every environment, db half included. A forge reads forge.game.<other> at top level and it is nil, sometimes. Load order is the file listing order. Do cross-forge access in methods and in when boot. A stored character pointer crashes the core or reads stale data. Characters are raw engine objects and a forge does not check their validity. Drop them in when logout, check for nil after find_by_pid, and prefer storing the player id. A db answer is lost, or the waiting code never resumes. A late answer after the timeout is dropped (token invalid/expired), a second answer_peer for the same receipt is dropped, and the coroutine is removed after a failed wait. Answer once, and do not wait again in the same coroutine after ok == false. A coroutine that waits on a player outlives the player. bridge.coro.create has no owner. Use create_with_player_owner, or add_owner, so the disconnect closes it. Always set a timeout. The first when login block has a with condition and later blocks stop running. Blocks of the same event are appended into one script, and a conditioned block ends in return. Put conditioned blocks last. Registering the same header twice does nothing and nothing says so. The second set_*_processor returns false and logs once, and forge_helper throws the result away. One header, one registration. A compile error points at the wrong line. For a reserved word used inside an environment body, the line is the end of the environment scan. Search the body for quest, state, with, when, define, begin used as names. A method named set_state gets its argument quoted. The preprocessor rewrites set_state, setstate and newstate in the whole file, environment code included. Pick another name. The wrong table. visit_counter.fn(...) calls a quest function from the quest table; forge.game.visit_counter:method() calls your module. They share a name and nothing else. Next: How Forge works.
A .forge file defines a stateful Lua module for the lifetime of a core and can include quest hooks in the same file. Use it for state and messages across cores; How Forge works explains the model.

One file, one name, a module on the game core, a module on the db core, and the two quest hooks that connect a player to them. visit_counter.forge counts logins across all cores in an event flag stored on the db core. forge visit_counter begin environment game begin local forge_helper = require("forge_helper") local Counter = {} Counter.__index = Counter function Counter:new() return setmetatable({ online = {} }, Counter) end function Counter:on_login(pid) self.online[pid] = true local ch = forge.sys.game.char_manager.find_by_pid(pid) if ch then ch:chat_packet(forge.sys.game.CHAT_TYPE.INFO, "Welcome back") end local res, ok = forge_helper.coro.with_timeout(2000, forge_helper.sys.game.yield_db, "visit", tostring(pid)) if not ok then sys_err("visit_counter: no answer from the db for pid " .. pid) return end sys_log(0, "visit_counter: login number " .. res) end function Counter:on_logout(pid) self.online[pid] = nil end return Counter:new() end environment db begin local _M = {} function _M.on_visit(peer, message, handler_id, receipt) local total = forge.sys.db.get_event_flag("visit_total") + 1 forge.sys.db.set_event_flag("visit_total", total) forge.sys.db.answer_peer(peer, tostring(total), receipt) end forge.sys.set_peer_processor("visit", _M.on_visit) return _M end state start begin when login begin local pid = pc.get_player_id() bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner( function() forge.game.visit_counter:on_login(pid) end, pid ) end when logout begin forge.game.visit_counter:on_logout(pc.get_player_id()) end end end Add the file to your compiler input, compile it, and restart the cores. Every login shows the player a Welcome back line in the chat and writes visit_counter: login number <n> to the game core log, and the number keeps growing across cores and restarts. self.online is the per-player state: it lives in the module, one entry per player id, and the logout hook removes it.

Term Meaning Forge The system that loads and routes forge modules. Environment A core-specific body in a .forge file. Forge name The declared name, used for modules, quest output, and message routing. Quest table The global table of state IDs and quest functions. Forge module The table or instance returned by an environment. Init script A script run before forges load.

A .forge file is a sequence of top-level blocks. Each block starts with quest or forge; any other first word aborts the compile with must start with 'quest' or 'forge'. forge <name> begin environment <env> begin ... end -- any number, any order state <name> begin ... end -- any number, any order end The name is a plain word or a string. It must follow forge directly, and begin must follow the name (need 'begin' after forge name). A forge has no with start condition. The compiler always creates a quest and a forge from the same name token. The forge name is the quest name: every state in the block registers on the quest of that name, the module is published at forge.<env>.<name>, and messages the forge sends carry that name as their routing key. The game half and the db half of one forge find each other through it. The file name plays no role. visit_counter.forge can declare forge visit_counter, and its outputs use visit_counter. forge and environment are not reserved words, they are plain names the parser compares as text. state and environment blocks may come in any order. Inside state the grammar is the classic quest one: when <event> [or <event>...] [with <condition>] begin ... end and function <name>(args) ... end. define NAME value lines are allowed only before the first line that starts with forge or quest . The substitution is applied to the whole file, environment bodies included. Two files that declare the same forge name are compiled independently and the later one silently overwrites the outputs of the earlier, so keep names unique.

One compiler run builds .quest and .forge files together. The diagram shows the outputs of a file with both environments and login and logout hooks: The environment bodies go to the forge side, the state blocks go to the quest side. A forge without an environment db body produces no .db file. Part of the file Output Content environment <env> with a body <out_forge_<env>>/<forge name>.<env> The body text verbatim, without the begin and end lines. environment <env> with an empty body nothing Skipped. Any state (once per quest) object/state/<name> A Lua chunk that assigns the global table <name> with the state ids (["start"]=0) and the quest functions. Written only if the quest has at least one state. when <event> without argument object/<target>/<event>/<name>.<state> The body. Several when blocks for the same event and state are appended into one file. when <target>.<event> object/<target>/<event>/<name>.<state> Target is the part before the dot. An event without a dot gets the target notarget. when <event> with an argument object/<target>/<event>/<name>.<state>.<index>.script, .when, .arg One set per block. function inside state the state table Emitted as <name>.fn, so a quest function is called as <forge name>.fn(...). The quest table visit_counter (global, states and quest functions) and the forge module forge.game.visit_counter (your returned value) are two different tables that share a name. A when block with a with condition compiles to if <condition> then <body> return end. Because blocks for the same event are appended in file order, when the first when login block has a with condition and it holds, the later when login blocks of that forge do not run. Keep conditioned blocks last or put the condition inside the body.

Each environment body needs an output folder for that environment. A core loads files from one folder whose extension matches its environment; the loader does not recurse and skips directories. The init script runs before the forges. Exact folders and flags depend on how your codebase installs Forge. Key or variable Core Points to server.luna.forge.base_directory game Compiled forge folder. server.luna.forge.init_script game Init script. server.luna.bridge.libs_path game Bridge Lua library path. LUNA_FORGE_PATH db Compiled forge folder; required. LUNA_FORGE_INIT db Init script; optional. LUNA_BRIDGE_LIB_PATH db Bridge Lua library path; required. An environment with a body and no output defined aborts compilation with No output defined for forge environment <env>. A missing folder logs Forge::LoadSources Directory does not exist: <dir>. NO FORGE HANDLERS WILL BE REGISTERED; a db core without LUNA_FORGE_PATH exits with LUNA_FORGE_PATH not set. Next: Forge environments and boot.

The functions on forge.sys.game.metrics read and write per-character values. A push supplies a value or key. A declaration defines a named metric, and the catalog contains all declarations. Calls run on the main thread and do not yield. local metrics = forge.sys.game.metrics if metrics.declared("crafts.attempted") then metrics.add(ch, "crafts.attempted", 1) sys_log(0, "attempts = " .. metrics.get(ch, "crafts.attempted")) end Here ch is a character object supplied by the calling context. A seeded metric is one ever written for this character. A block is the per-character record of metric values. A virtual session is described in player virtualization.

Function Returns Use declare(name, decl) ID, or 0 Declares a metric; refusals are logged. add(ch, name, delta?) Boolean Pushes a delta, default 1. add_key(ch, name, key) Boolean Adds an integer key to a distinct metric. get(ch, name) Number Reads the value or set size. is_seeded(ch, name) Boolean Tests whether the metric was ever written. keys(ch, name) Number array Returns distinct keys in ascending order. info(name) Table or nil Returns source, aggregation, virtual option, and key limit. names() String array Returns declared names in ID order. declared(name) Boolean Tests whether the name is declared. flush(ch) Nothing Publishes pending changes for the character now. pending_save(ch) Number Counts metrics awaiting a database save. report() Two numbers Logs declarations and returns queue depth and block count. add and add_key return true only when the stored value or set changes. A repeated key returns false. A virtual session without allow_virtual also returns false silently. Unknown names and wrong aggregation types are logged on pushes. get returns zero for an unknown or unwritten name; validate names with declared. is_seeded distinguishes an unwritten min from a written zero. For a map domain, add_key normalizes private map indexes to their base index. A full set refuses new keys and logs the refusal. pending_save clears on save, independently of event publication. flush is a no-op without pending changes; the engine also flushes on disconnect.

declare accepts the same fields as metrics.yaml. This example declares a signal-derived set: local id = forge.sys.game.metrics.declare("kill.boss", { from = "kill", where = { rank = { "BOSS" } }, agg = "distinct", key = "vnum", domain = { kind = "mob", max_keys = 256 }, }) Prefer metrics.yaml. Lua declaration is safe only at forge load, before the engine reads that file, and only for a name absent from the file. A name in both is a duplicate and fails boot. See declaring metrics for the fields and the outcome of a late declaration.

A consumer is code that reads metrics or subscribes to changes. A dirty queue holds characters with unpublished changes. A heartbeat is the periodic game-core tick; a sweep is the pass that drains the dirty queue each heartbeat and publishes the change event. bridge.e.names.game.ON_METRICS_CHANGED publishes synchronously with a bridge.e.game.metrics_changed payload: Field Type Meaning pids Number array Character IDs in this batch. counts Number array Number of names for each corresponding ID. metrics String array Names concatenated in character order. Subscribe in when boot. This handler walks the names for each character: bridge.e.subscribe(bridge.e.names.game.ON_METRICS_CHANGED, function(ev) local at = 1 for i, pid in ipairs(ev.pids) do for j = at, at + ev.counts[i] - 1 do sys_log(0, "pid " .. pid .. " moved " .. ev.metrics[j]) end at = at + ev.counts[i] end end) The payload has names rather than values. Read values with get when you have the character. The sweep processes the queue in order, with server.player.metrics_drain_size characters per heartbeat, default 100. The queue holds 8192 characters. When full, it logs the dropped ID; another change is needed to enqueue that character again. A subscriber's new push is queued for a later pass. The event does not replay offline changes, so consumers that need a complete view should read at login.

A predicate is a Lua function named in where.predicate that is called last, after integer operand tests pass. Forges register predicates in the global METRIC_PREDICATES table before declarations load. The function receives the subject and, where available, the target: METRIC_PREDICATES.low_health = function(ch, target) return ch:get_hp_pct() < 10 end Only boolean true matches. Predicates must read without mutating state because signal handling can be re-entrant. A predicate is disabled after 16 errors, and its metric stops matching it. Use integer filters first where possible to avoid unnecessary Lua calls.

These /metric implementor commands are registered by a forge. <pg_name> identifies a character, <key> is a metric name, and <value> is a set key. Command Effect /metric get <pg_name> <key> Prints value and seeded state. /metric add <pg_name> <key> <delta> Pushes a delta and prints the result. /metric add_key <pg_name> <key> <value> Adds a key and prints growth and size. /metric list <pg_name> [prefix] Lists matching catalog names and values. /metric pending <pg_name> Prints the number awaiting save. A refused or unchanged push reports the result. There is no set command. See examples and pitfalls for checks.

A declaration names a metric and defines its source and aggregation. The catalog is the collection of declarations. Put declarations in the metrics: map of metrics.yaml and restart the game core after editing it. metrics: kill.stone: { from: kill, where: { type: [STONE] }, agg: count } crafts.attempted: { from: custom, agg: count } A signal is a native event with operands that can feed metrics. A push is a call that supplies a value or key. Signal-derived metrics use native signals; custom metrics receive pushes from either C++ or Lua. See the overview for aggregations.

Names are persistent keys of at most 64 characters. Each value is a map with these fields: Key Values Purpose from kill, damage, skill, item_use, custom Required source. agg count, sum, max, min, distinct Aggregation; defaults to count. where Operand lists and predicate Filters a signal. key Signal operand name Supplies the key for signal-derived distinct. domain.kind map, mob, item, custom Describes distinct keys. domain.max_keys Integer Limits the number of distinct keys. allow_virtual Boolean Allows custom pushes during a virtual session. A virtual session is described in player virtualization. allow_virtual defaults to false and is refused for signals. Enable it only when the value belongs to the session and the code that owns the episode makes the push. A distinct metric without max_keys is unbounded and logs a warning. Custom declarations cannot have where or key; pass the key to add_key instead.

A predicate is a Lua function named in where.predicate that is called last, after integer operand tests. Forges register predicates in the global METRIC_PREDICATES table before the engine reads declarations. See predicates for the function contract. where is a flat map of operand names to lists. Values can be integer operands or supported tokens. Ordinary lists test membership. flags and target_flags are bit words: the list is OR-ed and any matching bit passes. Operand Token vocabulary Kill type Character types such as STONE and PC. Kill or damage rank Ranks from PAWN through KING. Damage type Damage types, including "TRUE". Damage flags Stats flags such as CRITICAL and PENETRATE. Skill grade NORMAL, MASTER, GRAND_MASTER, PERFECT_MASTER. Skill target_flags Shared skill flags. Quote "TRUE" and other YAML boolean-like tokens; bare values may be parsed as booleans and refused. These complete lines show different declaration shapes: kill.stone: { from: kill, where: { type: [STONE] }, agg: count } kill.boss: { from: kill, where: { rank: [BOSS] }, agg: distinct, key: vnum, domain: { kind: mob, max_keys: 256 } } region.visited: { from: custom, agg: distinct, domain: { kind: map, max_keys: 256 } } currency.peak: { from: custom, agg: max } episode.won: { from: custom, agg: count, allow_virtual: true }

Only C++ emits signals. The subject must be a player. Index operands route declarations efficiently; they can also be used as filters or distinct keys. Signal When it fires Operands Index Value kill A qualifying monster or player dies. vnum, type, rank, is_pc, empire, map_index, level_delta vnum 1 damage A qualifying hit resolves. damage, type, skill_vnum, flags, critical, pierce, death_blow, rank skill_vnum Clamped damage. skill A skill is used. vnum, level, grade, type, target_flags vnum 1 item_use An item use succeeds. vnum vnum 1 Damage rank is the target's rank. The monster kill follows the reward path and credits the player who dealt the most damage. The damage signal excludes targets such as fixed training dummies. Quest items do not emit item_use; push a custom metric from their use handler instead.

Six native C++ push sites exist alongside the signals. They include currency-handling sites that push a peak balance, a crafting site, a catch counter, and a pair-forming site. They write custom metrics through the same aggregation and virtual-session rules as Lua. A custom metric can also be pushed by a quest or forge. An unknown name at a native push logs a refusal.

The first declaration of a name wins. A duplicate returns 0 and is logged; a refused YAML entry fails boot. Forges load before metrics.yaml, so Lua declare is safe only at forge load for a name absent from that file. Prefer the file. A name declared in both places is a duplicate and fails boot. A block is the per-character record of metric values. A metric declared after boot returns false from add and add_key for characters already online, with no log, because their block was sized at boot. Restart the core to establish the catalog before characters connect.
