Every refused file entry fails initialization. Check the preceding log for the name and cause. Refusal Fix File unreadable or invalid Fix the file or its YAML syntax. Missing metrics map Add the top-level map. Missing or unknown from Select a signal or custom. Unknown agg Select a supported aggregation. Duplicate name Declare the name once. Unknown operand or token Use an operand and token for that signal. Empty, scalar, or invalid filter list Supply a nonempty list of valid values. Unregistered predicate Register its name before declarations load. where or key on custom Remove the signal-only field. Signal-derived distinct without key Name its key operand. allow_virtual on a signal Use a custom declaration instead. The final initialization failure line can contain a literal %s; use the earlier diagnostic to locate the entry. The Lua API documents declare and push return values.

A metric declaration defines a per-character value. A signal is a native event with operands that can feed a metric; a push supplies a value or key directly. Start with the overview for setup and aggregations. metrics: kill.stone: { from: kill, where: { type: [STONE] }, agg: count } Restart the game core after editing metrics.yaml. This signal-derived counter needs no explicit push. A seeded metric is one ever written for this character; a block is the per-character record of metric values.

With the declaration above, a quest can read the counter for its current character. Put these statements in a quest login handler to print the value in a chat line: local ch = forge.sys.game.char_manager.find_by_pid(pc.get_player_id()) local metrics = forge.sys.game.metrics chat("Stone kills: " .. metrics.get(ch, "kill.stone")) Check the same value with /metric get <pg_name> kill.stone. The implementor commands are registered by a forge. A qualifying kill credits the player who dealt the most damage.

Declare a custom counter and call the function from the code handling an attempt: crafts.attempted: { from: custom, agg: count } local function record_attempt(ch) local metrics = forge.sys.game.metrics if metrics.add(ch, "crafts.attempted", 1) then sys_log(0, "attempts = " .. metrics.get(ch, "crafts.attempted")) end end The return value says whether the value moved. A custom metric may also receive pushes from C++. Validate configuration with declared before writing if the name comes from configuration.

Declare kill.streak.best: { from: custom, agg: max }. Keep the active run in the calling code and push its length whenever it changes: local function record_run(ch, run) return forge.sys.game.metrics.add(ch, "kill.streak.best", run) end The metric keeps the greatest value supplied. A lower value returns false. A zero may be the first written value, so use is_seeded when the distinction between unwritten and zero matters.

Declare a set with room for the expected key range: region.visited: { from: custom, agg: distinct, domain: { kind: map, max_keys: 256 } } This function records a map index and logs the new set size: local function record_region(ch, map_index) local metrics = forge.sys.game.metrics if metrics.add_key(ch, "region.visited", map_index) then sys_log(0, "regions = " .. metrics.get(ch, "region.visited")) end end A duplicate key returns false. keys returns the sorted keys. Private map indexes are normalized to their base map before insertion.

The storage tables start empty. There is no backfill for existing characters, so an unwritten metric reads zero. To seed a history that you can derive from a reliable source, insert scalar rows by SQL into player_stat (pid, metric, value) or set rows into player_stat_set (pid, metric, key). Use the correct database schema for your installation. Do this while the affected characters are offline. Values load into their blocks at login, and a later save can overwrite a direct database edit made while they are online. Verify the source and aggregation before inserting: totals, extremes, and set keys represent different kinds of data.

The core refuses to start. A declaration in metrics.yaml failed validation. Read the earlier diagnostic for the name and cause; the final failure can contain a literal %s. See declaration refusals. A new metric reads zero for existing characters. No history is backfilled. An unwritten metric is not seeded; prepare offline SQL data if a trustworthy source exists. A typo also reads zero. get returns zero for an unknown name. Use declared to validate names rather than treating zero as evidence that a name exists. A minimum of zero looks unwritten. get returns zero for both cases. Check is_seeded before interpreting a minimum. A distinct set stops growing. Once max_keys is reached, new keys are dropped and logged. Size the limit for the expected range and check keys when investigating duplicates. A custom sum looks like a count. Both add the delta supplied by the caller. Choose the delta that represents the quantity you intend to store. A signal filter is refused. Check its operand names and quote YAML boolean-like tokens such as "TRUE". A predicate is a Lua function named in where.predicate that runs last; forges register predicates in the global METRIC_PREDICATES table. A virtual session cannot push. A virtual session is described in player virtualization. Custom declarations default to refusing its pushes; allow_virtual is available only for custom metrics. Use it when the code that owns the episode records that episode. A change event has not arrived. A consumer is code that reads metrics or subscribes to changes. Changes enter the dirty queue, the queue of characters with unpublished changes. A sweep drains that queue each heartbeat, the periodic game-core tick, and publishes the change event. The queue has a budget and can fill; inspect report and the log. See the event details. A Lua declaration is in the wrong place. Prefer metrics.yaml; see declaration order for boot ordering and late declarations.

A player metric is a named number or set of integer keys stored for each character. A declaration specifies how the value is collected and aggregated. The catalog is the collection of declared metrics. A push is a call that supplies a value or key; a signal is a native event carrying operands that can feed declarations.

Declare a signal counter and a custom counter in metrics.yaml: metrics: kill.stone: { from: kill, where: { type: [STONE] }, agg: count } crafts.attempted: { from: custom, agg: count } A forge can push the custom counter and log its value when its code handles an attempt: local function record_attempt(ch) local metrics = forge.sys.game.metrics metrics.add(ch, "crafts.attempted", 1) sys_log(0, "crafts.attempted = " .. metrics.get(ch, "crafts.attempted")) end Call record_attempt from the code handling the attempt. The native kill signal feeds kill.stone; it needs no separate push. Restart the game core after changing declarations, then use /metric get <pg_name> kill.stone to inspect a character.

Term Meaning Declaration A named metric's source, aggregation, and options. Catalog The collection of declared metrics. Signal A native event with operands that can feed metrics. Push A call that supplies a value or key to a metric. Consumer Code that reads metrics or subscribes to changes. Seeded The metric was ever written for this character. Block The per-character record of metric values. Dirty queue The queue of characters with unpublished changes. Heartbeat The periodic game-core tick. Sweep The pass that drains the dirty queue each heartbeat and publishes the change event. Predicate A Lua function named in where.predicate that is called last. Virtual session A session described in player virtualization.

Item Location or purpose Declarations metrics.yaml in the locale folder. Lua API forge.sys.game.metrics in forges and quests. Predicates Forges register functions in global METRIC_PREDICATES. Scalar storage player_stat stores character, metric name, and value. Set storage player_stat_set stores character, metric name, and key. Forges load and register predicates before the engine reads metrics.yaml. Consumers can subscribe to the change event and inspect the catalog in when boot, after declarations load. A predicate is a Lua function named in where.predicate that runs after the integer filters. See declaring metrics for the schema and the Lua API for subscription. The engine reads the file at boot. Restart the game core to apply changes. Metric names are persistent storage keys; renaming one requires a data migration.

agg Result of a matching signal or push count Adds one per signal or the pushed delta. sum Adds the measured signal value or pushed delta. max Keeps the highest value. min Keeps the lowest value. distinct Keeps a set of integer keys. damage supplies its measured damage; other signals supply one. A custom push supplies its delta. For distinct, get returns the set size and keys returns the keys. An unwritten metric reads zero, so check is_seeded before interpreting zero for min. Zero can itself be a written minimum or maximum. The engine ignores a zero delta for sum. A push that leaves the value unchanged returns false and does not enqueue a change. The aggregations retain totals, extremes, or set membership; they do not provide a reset operation.

A block is the per-character record of metric values. The engine saves changed values and newly added keys. A row with an undeclared name is logged and ignored on load. In-memory blocks belong to one game core; database rows provide persistent storage. A virtual session is described in player virtualization. Pushes from one return false unless a custom declaration opts in with allow_virtual. Signal-derived declarations cannot opt in. Use the option only when the value belongs to the virtual session and the code that owns the episode makes the push. A consumer is code that reads metrics or subscribes to their change event. Changed characters enter the dirty queue, the queue of characters with unpublished changes. Each heartbeat, the periodic game-core tick, runs a sweep: the pass that drains the queue and publishes the change event. Publication and database saves have separate schedules. See examples and pitfalls for setup checks and initial data.

A virtual session runs on a cached copy of the character. A processor is the set of hooks registered for a map; a cache entry holds one player and map's session data. A slice is one portion of that data. See the overview, hooks, and the prize commit.

A rate limiter that reads its counters from quest flags reads zero in a virtual session. Pass the pair through transform_quest_load and drop the rest. local processor = {} function processor.transform_quest_load(self, ch, quests, is_account) if is_account then return {} end local kept = {} for _, q in ipairs(quests) do local name, sub = q["name"], q["state"] if name == "session_cap" and (sub == "cursor" or sub == "count") then table.insert(kept, q) end end return kept end return processor kept holds only the records the engine gave you, so they are the right type and survive the read-back.
documents.s: Keep two flags through the boundary

documents.t: on_player_enter runs at every entry. A grant belongs behind the fresh_hydrate flag, or a reconnect grants twice. local processor = {} function processor.on_player_enter(self, ch, fresh_hydrate) if not fresh_hydrate then return end ch:set_quest_flag("practice_room.entered", 1) end return processor The flag is set on the session copy. It stays in the cache and goes away with the session; it is not a commit.

A private map where every player starts at level 1 with nothing, and a win leaves one flag on the real character. The reset is a load transform: it runs once per player and map, and a relog is a cache hit that keeps the session level. local PV = forge.sys.game.player_virtual local SM = forge.sys.game.sectree_manager local processor = {} function processor.transform_player_load(self, ch, player) player.level = 1 player.exp = 0 return player end function processor.transform_item_load(self, ch, items) return {} end local function open_trial(base_map_index) local map_index = SM.create_private_map(base_map_index) if not map_index or map_index == 0 then return nil end if not PV.set_processor(map_index, processor) then SM.destroy_private_map(map_index) return nil end return map_index end local function award(ch) PV.commit_quest_flag(ch, "practice_room.cleared", 1) end items holds the equipped items as well as the inventory, so {} empties both. Call award(ch) from your own event (a kill, an NPC), not from a hook. The flag reaches the real row at once and a quest named practice_room reads it after the player's next load onto a real map.
documents.s: Reset on entry, one flag as the prize

documents.t: Open the map, register the processor, and destroy the map when the match ends. Destroying a private map clears its cache and unregisters its processor. local PV = forge.sys.game.player_virtual local SM = forge.sys.game.sectree_manager local function start(base_map_index, processor) local map_index = SM.create_private_map(base_map_index) if not map_index or map_index == 0 then return nil, "map_failed" end if not PV.set_processor(map_index, processor) then SM.destroy_private_map(map_index) return nil, "processor_failed" end return map_index end local function finish(map_index) SM.destroy_private_map(map_index) end

A hook that errors lets the real data in. A Lua error in any transform hook falls back to passthrough: the untransformed input, real items, real flags and real affects included, is cached and used for the whole session. The only trace is one falling back to passthrough line in syserr. Keep hooks small, test each of them, and watch syserr for that line. A hook that is missing, or whose key is not a function, is a silent passthrough, and so is a non-table return from a vector hook: the input as you left it is used. A transform returns nothing and the slice is empty. Plain Lua tables returned from a vector hook are dropped. Build entries from the records of the input, or filter the input itself. A counter you commit and read in the session reads the old value. A commit writes to the database, not the session copy. Set the session copy too when your code reads it again; see the prize commit. Pending state vanishes on restart. State held only in the memory of one core is lost on restart. A commit has no acknowledgement, so a design cannot wait for it to drain at logout. A commit seems to work and never arrives. A quest name or state of 64 characters or more, an account flag with no descriptor, or an item that already has an owner are logged and dropped. Check syserr. The quest still offers a chat option. questcategory.txt does not gate chat, target, receive-all item use, info and button. A listed quest is dormant on login, kill, click, timers, item use and custom events only. set_processor returns false with players inside. A map that has a processor and active sessions refuses a new one. unset_processor kicks nobody, so the old processor stays with the players in it. Register before the first player loads, or wait until the map is empty. clear with players inside leaves dangling pointers. The stub says it is refused. It is only warned. Clear a map that is empty. A base map you registered stays virtual. The engine cleans only private maps. A base map keeps its cache until clear or a restart, and a player who logs out there keeps a stale session next time. A processor registered after the load does nothing. The player is decided at the load. A processor installed once the player is on the map is seen at the next load. commit_stash_item consumes your item. Reading the item after the call is a use after free in Lua terms. Keep the id the function returns. The char_virtual helpers are permanent on a real character. max_skills, set_specialization, give_blessing_progression and the rest act on the live character. In a virtual session the cache swallows it; on a real one it sticks. For pet caching, see custom transformers.

Virtual session: a character's session on a virtual map. Processor: hooks registered for a map index. Cache entry: cached session data for one player and map. Slice: a portion of character data handled by a hook. Passthrough: using a hook's input without replacing it. Prize commit: an explicit write of a selected result to real data. Stash: item storage for delivery on a later non-virtual load.

A custom transformer handles a slice of player data that is not in the bulk player load. A slice is a group of related player data. Use a custom transformer when a subsystem loads its own data separately; for the bulk-load slices, see processor hooks. Two kinds exist: a native one, where C++ calls a processor method at its own load site (the pet), and a Forge one, where a forge module routes its database load and save through the cache (any subsystem with its own table). For the isolation model, see player virtualization.

Processor: the object whose hooks transform data for a virtual map. Slice: a group of related player data handled together. Virtual session: an isolated player session backed by cached state. Cache entry: the stored virtual state for a player on a virtual map. It can contain several custom records or tables. Native transformer: a processor method called by C++ at a native load site. Forge subsystem: a Forge module that owns data and its database load and save. Forge transformer: a processor hook for a Forge subsystem's decoded table. Key: a stable string that identifies a Forge table for caching and transform dispatch. Pinned table: a Lua table retained by the bridge across coroutine boundaries until its pin is released. Passthrough: using the input without replacing it.
Kind Loaded when Cache holds Hook Registered from Native Native load site Native record transform_pet_load Processor Forge Module load Pinned Lua table transform_forge_load Processor

The pet record is loaded on summon, outside the bulk player load. The cache holds one record per player ID and pet vnum. On a virtual summon, the engine looks for the vnum in the cache entry. On a hit, it summons from the cached record without calling the hook. On a miss, it queries the real database. If the query fails, the summon fails and the player receives a chat message. The processor transforms the record, which is appended to the cache and used for the summon. A Lua hook error is logged and falls back to the untransformed record. A virtual pet save replaces or appends the record in the cache entry. The database save is suppressed. The Lua hook receives and returns a TPetPlayerTable: function processor:transform_pet_load(ch, pet) return pet end The corresponding C++ virtual method has this signature: virtual TPetPlayerTable TransformPetLoad(LPCHARACTER ch, const TPetPlayerTable& in) { return in; } A Lua hook can mutate pet in place or return a TPetPlayerTable; any other return uses the input as left. This hook starts each summoned pet at level 1 with no experience, bonuses or skills, keeping its identity and name: function processor:transform_pet_load(ch, pet) local result = TPetPlayerTable.new(pet.pid, pet.pet_vnum) result.id = pet.id result.name = pet.name result.level = 1 return result end See processor hooks for the record fields and methods.

Use the wrappers for a Forge subsystem that stores its own protobuf table. Choose a stable key, and use the same key for load, save, and the processor hook. For multiple instances, use a key such as name:<id>. Outside a virtual session, with_load_cache calls load_fn and decodes its response; with_save_cache calls save_fn. In a virtual session, a load cache hit returns the pinned table without calling load_fn. On a miss, load_fn obtains the serialized response. If it returns nil, the wrapper returns nil and caches nothing. Otherwise, the wrapper decodes the response, calls transform_forge_load, pins the result, and returns it. A virtual save decodes the serialized message and stores the table in the cache without calling save_fn. There is no save transform. The bridge releases cached tables when the cache is cleared. Replacing a cached table releases its previous pin.

In this example, messages.DGResponseLoad, messages.GDSave, load_request, and save_request belong to the example quest_log module. Supply your module's protobuf types and request messages. The load wrapper returns a decoded table or nil; the save wrapper returns the result of save_fn outside a virtual session and nil inside one. local pv = forge.sys.game.player_virtual local key = "quest_log" local function load_quest_log(ch, messages, load_request) return pv.with_load_cache(ch, key, messages.DGResponseLoad, function() return forge_helper.sys.game.yield_db( "load", load_request:SerializeToString()) end) end local function save_quest_log(ch, messages, save_request) local msg = save_request:SerializeToString() return pv.with_save_cache(ch, key, messages.GDSave, msg, function() return forge.sys.game.send_db("save", msg) end) end The load closure must return the serialized response or nil. The save message type must decode the serialized request passed as msg. See Forge setup for the module environment.
documents.s: Wrap the module's load and save

documents.t: In Lua, branch on the key and return the table. This example clears the example module's entries field on a cache miss: function processor:transform_forge_load(ch, key, data) if key == "quest_log" then data.entries = {} end return data end Return data for keys you do not handle. A non-table return uses the input table as left, including any in-place changes. A hook error is logged and falls back to the input. For a C++ processor, register a handler per key in the constructor of your IPlayerVirtualProcessor subclass, for example RegisterForgeLoadHandler("quest_log", handler) with a handler that returns the table it was given, changed. The default TransformForgeLoad dispatches by key; an unregistered key is passthrough. using ForgeHandler = std::function<sol::table(LPCHARACTER, sol::table)>; void RegisterForgeLoadHandler(std::string key, ForgeHandler handler)

forge.sys.game.player_virtual.get_forge_cache(ch, key) returns the cached table or nil if there is no entry or the character is not virtual. set_forge_cache(ch, key, value) pins and stores a table, replacing any previous table for the key. It has no effect for a non-virtual character. forge.sys.game.player_virtual.transform_forge_load(ch, key, input) dispatches the processor hook directly and returns a table. It returns the input unchanged when the character is not virtual or has no processor. The load wrapper calls it for you on a cache miss.
If a subsystem must not exist in a virtual session, skip both its load and save when ch:is_virtual() is true. This choice does not create a cached form of the subsystem. The battle pass does this.

The pet is a native custom transformer. Character titles are one shipped instance of the cached Forge form; a hunting progression subsystem is the other. The .forge module wraps its database load in with_load_cache and its database save in with_save_cache, both with the stable key char_title: a virtual character reads and writes the cache, a real one goes through the database as before.

A hook change does not affect cached data. The pet hook runs on a miss for each pet vnum, and the Forge hook runs on a miss for each key. A relog that hits the same cache entry does not run either hook again. A processor change takes effect when the core restarts. A Forge transform does not run. Check that the load wrapper and the processor use the same key. A key without a C++ handler, or one the Lua processor passes through, leaves the table as received. There is no save transform. A virtual save stores what the module sent. Filter on the load side, once per cache entry. A load returns nil. The load closure returned nil; nothing was cached, so a later load can try again. A Forge module needs the real database during a virtual session. The C++ with_real_scope facility is not bound as a Lua function. Forge code cannot use it to reach the real database from a virtual session.

Player virtualization runs a character on a cached copy of its data. A virtual session is the character's time on a map registered for virtualization. A processor is the map's set of hooks that can transform that copy. See the foundation for the model.

This module, loaded by a forge, opens a private copy of a map where every player is level 30 with no real items, quest flags or affects. It returns the map index, or nil when the processor is refused. local PV = forge.sys.game.player_virtual local SM = forge.sys.game.sectree_manager local processor = {} function processor.transform_player_load(self, ch, player) player.level = 30 player.exp = 0 player.gold = 100000 return player end function processor.transform_item_load(self, ch, items) return {} end function processor.transform_quest_load(self, ch, quests, is_account) return {} end function processor.transform_affect_load(self, ch, affects) return {} end local function open_room(base_map_index) local map_index = SM.create_private_map(base_map_index) if not map_index or map_index == 0 then return nil end if not PV.set_processor(map_index, processor) then SM.destroy_private_map(map_index) return nil end return map_index end local function close_room(map_index) PV.unset_processor(map_index) SM.destroy_private_map(map_index) end A player who loads onto the returned map index gets a level 30 character with an empty inventory, no quest flags and no affects. Position, exit location, playtime and the UI settings are still the real ones. When the private map is destroyed, the cache of that map is cleared and ordinary session saves stay in the cache.

Use forge.sys.game.player_virtual from Forge Lua. Register a processor for the exact map index before a player loads; a private map has its own registration. See Forge setup. Each map index has one processor slot. A missing hook uses passthrough, meaning the input is kept. Destroying a private map clears its cache. A base map's cache remains until clear or a core restart. A processor change takes effect when the core restarts. What a processor can transform is split into native slices and custom transformers.

A slice is a portion of character data handled by a hook. A cache entry is the cached data for a player and map index. Saves during a virtual session go to that entry, except for the fields in the fixed overlay: the engine copies those fields from the real row over the transformed player table on every load. Always real Location: x, y, z, map_index, and exit location. Session and settings: playtime, inventory lock status and password, and jsettings. Kept in the cache Character data: Level, experience, gold, HP, SP, stats, skills, quickslots, and parts. Currencies and rank state. Other slices: Items and their flags, quest and account flags, affects, and skill trees. Pet records and forge subsystem tables. A forge subsystem is a Forge component with its own stored table. A cache entry lasts until its private map is destroyed, clear runs, or the core restarts. On a cache hit, hooks do not run again and on_player_enter receives fresh_hydrate as false.

The stash holds items delivered by a prize commit, an explicit write of a selected result to real data. Stash rows are removed before transform_item_load; they are delivered on the next item load on a non-virtual map. See the prize commit.

Offline shop, casual mode, matchmaking hub, and safebox are blocked. Drop and PvP eligibility commands are refused. The reward enabler still grants its drop and PvP affects. The Master Hunt hub window is closed on the client; the Master Hunt state itself is cached. The battle pass is never loaded or saved for a virtual character. The client shows the VIRTUAL_SESSION_BLOCKED popup for blocked operations. Guild skill sync is skipped. Logs are marked virtual, and rankings read the real character.

The tab-separated file lists quests; its optional third column is allow_in_virtual. Entry In a virtual session Listed with 0 Dormant on gated events. Listed with another value Allowed. Missing entry or third column Allowed. The quest manager reads the file at startup. The gate covers login, kill, click, timer, item-use, and custom events. It does not cover NPC chat, target, receive-all item use, info, or button.

Virtual sessions drop metrics by default. In metrics.yaml, a custom metric can opt in with allow_virtual: true; a metric derived from a signal cannot. The code that owns the episode must push the opted-in metric. The metric is recorded under the real character's player ID. See player metrics. practice.won: { from: custom, agg: count, allow_virtual: true } practice.entered: { from: custom, agg: count, allow_virtual: true }

Processor: hooks registered for a map index. Slice: a portion of character data handled by a hook. Cache entry: a player and map's cached session data. Passthrough: keeping a hook's input without replacing it. Stash: item storage for delivery on a later non-virtual load. Prize commit: an explicit write of a selected result to real data. Virtual session: a character's session on a virtual map. Fixed overlay: real fields copied over the transformed player table. Forge subsystem: a Forge component with its own stored table. Continue with hooks and records, custom transformers, the prize commit, and examples and pitfalls.
A virtual session runs on cached character data. A prize commit writes a selected result to real data. The stash holds committed items for delivery on a later non-virtual load. See the overview.

Function Result commit_quest_flag(ch, key, value) Writes a real character quest flag. commit_account_flag(ch, key, value) Writes an account quest flag. commit_stash_item(ch, item, why?) Stages an item for later delivery. These functions belong to forge.sys.game.player_virtual. The character helper LPCHARACTER:commit_quest_flag and pc.commit_quest_flag use a commit for a virtual character and set_quest_flag for a real character.

A flag key has the form name.state, split at the first .. Each part is at most 63 characters; longer parts are logged and dropped. A key without a dot has an empty state. Use the quest's name and state so the quest can read it. An account commit needs a character descriptor; without it the write is logged and dropped. Create a stash item with forge.sys.game.item_manager.create_item. The commit consumes the item; do not use its handle afterwards. The item commit returns its item ID, or 0 if the character or item is null, the item has no ID, or it already has an owner. why is recorded in the STASH_COMMIT log.

The commit sends a packet to the database core and does not wait for acknowledgement. A closed database link can drop the write. A commit near a disconnect or database restart can be lost without an error on the game core. Do not rely on an acknowledgement or a logout drain. A stash item keeps its ID and is delivered at the next real item load, after inventory placement. Delivery tries stacking, a free cell, then the ground. The player is notified when the client reaches the game phase. An account flag is visible to characters on that account on their next load.

A flag commit writes to the database, not the live quest state. A read immediately after the commit still sees the old session value. If your code reads it again during the session, also set the session copy with set_quest_flag. That session write stays in the cache; the commit is the write intended to persist. The committed flag becomes visible on a subsequent non-virtual load.
documents.s: Read your own commit in the session

documents.t: Virtual session: a character's session on a virtual map. Prize commit: an explicit write of a selected result to real data. Stash: item storage for delivery on a later non-virtual load. See hooks and records, custom transformers, and examples and pitfalls.

The engine is private; this is a recipe for engine holders and a reading example for everyone else. The rule under test is an arbitrary example, chosen because the Metin2 mainline engine already enforces a same-empire and a level-gap limit on parties. The party join policy tutorial lifts both on one map; the cube proves that, and only that, through the policy API and without a client. Swap in any rule of your own.

The tutorial's forge (a Lua module the server loads at boot) registers a guard that matches when both players are on the chosen map. Its verdict sets same_empire = false and level_window = 0, removing the same-empire requirement and the level-gap limit for that pair. The cube registers the same guard and verdict through forge.sys.game.party_join_policy on the simulator's scratch map. This isolates the policy behavior without staging and booting the tutorial's Forge. It does not test whether that Forge loads or registers successfully.

sim.party_join runs the same policy Resolve (the policy manager's call that matches the registered guards and returns the winning verdict) and the common admission condition (the engine's own party checks) that a direct invite runs, then creates or joins the party directly. It returns a party admission error for the cube to check. It does not use the party finder, replay the invite dialog, or exercise the invite packet and acceptance handlers. Use a test that drives those handlers when the invitation flow itself is what you need to prove.

Save this example as open_party_cube.lua. It is a cube written for this page. -- The open-party cube: the rule of the party join policy tutorial, proved without a client. -- -- O1 stock two same-empire players 50 levels apart are refused: the stock rule is live -- O2 policy with the tutorial's guard and verdict registered, the same pair forms a party -- O3 control the same pair on a map outside the guard is still refused -- O4 empire players of two empires form a party under the verdict -- O5 stock with the policy gone, the same empire pair is refused again -- -- Fixtures: synthetic players from sim.spawn_pc on the scratch map and on a private copy of it. local T = { pass = 0, fail = 0, notes = {} } local MAP = sim.map_index() local SM = forge.sys.game.sectree_manager local POLICY = forge.sys.game.party_join_policy local ERR = POLICY.ERROR local function check(cond, msg) if cond then T.pass = T.pass + 1 else error("CHECK FAILED: " .. msg, 2) end end local function test(name, fn) local ok, err = pcall(fn) if ok then T.notes[#T.notes + 1] = "ok " .. name else T.fail = T.fail + 1 T.notes[#T.notes + 1] = string.format("FAIL %-40s %s", name, tostring(err)) end end local function pc(map, x, level, empire) local vid = sim.spawn_pc({ map = map, x = x, y = 25600, job = "warrior", level = level }) check(vid ~= nil and vid > 0, "spawn_pc must return a live vid") check(sim.set_empire(vid, empire) == empire, "the empire must be set") local ch = forge.sys.game.char_manager.find(vid) check(ch ~= nil, "char_manager.find must resolve the spawned PC") check(ch:get_level() == level, "the PC must have the level the face asks for") return { vid = vid, ch = ch, pid = ch:get_player_id() } end local function pair(map, leader_level, guest_level, leader_empire, guest_empire) return pc(map, 24000, leader_level, leader_empire), pc(map, 24100, guest_level, guest_empire) end local function drop(a, b) check(sim.destroy(a.vid) and sim.destroy(b.vid), "the fixtures must log out") end check(sim.party_enable(true), "PC party admission must be enabled") test("O1 stock refuses a wide level gap", function() local a, b = pair(MAP, 90, 40, 1, 1) local err = sim.party_join(a.vid, b.vid) check(err == ERR.PERR_LVBOUNDARY, "the stock rule must refuse (error " .. tostring(err) .. ")") check(b.ch:get_party_leader_pid() == 0, "a refused guest must not be in a party") drop(a, b) end) local handle = POLICY.register("open_party_cube", function(leader, guest) return leader:get_map_index() == MAP and guest:get_map_index() == MAP end, function() return { same_empire = false, level_window = 0 } end) check(handle > 0, "the policy must register") test("O2 the policy admits the pair", function() local a, b = pair(MAP, 90, 40, 1, 1) local err = sim.party_join(a.vid, b.vid) check(err == ERR.PERR_NONE, "the policy must admit the pair (error " .. tostring(err) .. ")") check(b.ch:get_party_leader_pid() == a.pid, "the guest must see the leader") drop(a, b) end) test("O3 a map outside the guard keeps the stock rule", function() local copy = SM.create_private_map(MAP // 10000) check(copy and copy > 0, "the scratch map must instance") local a, b = pair(copy, 90, 40, 1, 1) local err = sim.party_join(a.vid, b.vid) check(err == ERR.PERR_LVBOUNDARY, "outside the guard the stock rule must refuse (error " .. tostring(err) .. ")") drop(a, b) SM.destroy_private_map(copy) end) test("O4 two empires form a party", function() local a, b = pair(MAP, 60, 60, 1, 2) local err = sim.party_join(a.vid, b.vid) check(err == ERR.PERR_NONE, "the verdict must admit two empires (error " .. tostring(err) .. ")") drop(a, b) end) check(POLICY.unregister(handle), "the policy must unregister") test("O5 without the policy the stock rule is back", function() local a, b = pair(MAP, 60, 60, 1, 2) local err = sim.party_join(a.vid, b.vid) check(err == ERR.PERR_DIFFEMPIRE, "two empires must be refused again (error " .. tostring(err) .. ")") drop(a, b) end) for _, line in ipairs(T.notes) do print(line) end print("") print(string.format(" checks passed: %d tests failed: %d", T.pass, T.fail)) print(T.fail == 0 and " OPEN PARTY FACES O1-O5 SOLVED" or " CUBE INCOMPLETE") print("") sim.destroy(vid) removes the character, which is the simulator's logout; drop() uses it so one face's players do not leak into the next. pc() makes the fixture prove it is live: it checks the VID, resolves the character, reads its level back, and checks the empire returned by sim.set_empire. pair() runs those checks for both players. The cube also checks that party admission is enabled before any face runs. O1 establishes that the stock level rule refuses the wide gap. It checks that the guest has no party leader as well as checking the error: a refusal result alone would not prove the guest remained outside a party. O2 checks that the same levels and empire can form a party under the policy, and that the guest sees the expected leader. O3 is a negative control while the policy is registered: the same level gap on a private map outside the guard must still be refused. O4 checks admission across empires under the verdict. After unregistering the policy, O5 checks that the stock rule refuses the same empire combination again.

Add the cube to the cube runner table and run it by its registered name, or run game_sim --script on the file with the simulator data staged for the run. See the simulator reference for runner options and the verdict rules. Read the verdict and failure lines in the output, not the cube process exit code alone. On the passing path, expect 56 checks passed and 0 tests failed, followed by OPEN PARTY FACES O1-O5 SOLVED. Each pair() contributes 8 checks (4 per player), so the faces count O1 11, O2 11, O3 11 (including the private-map check), O4 10 and O5 10, which is 53; the enabled-admission, register and unregister checks outside the faces add 3. A lower total can mean that assertions did not execute.
documents.s: Run it and read the verdict

documents.t: A failed assertion produces a CHECK FAILED message in its face's FAIL line. test() catches the error so later faces can run, and the final verdict is CUBE INCOMPLETE. Setup checks outside a face can instead stop the driver before it prints a cube verdict. A face that fails before cleanup can leave fixtures or a policy registered. This cube unregisters its policy after O4, even if a face fails, but an error outside the protected faces can stop execution before that point. When adapting the pattern to register policies inside faces, arrange cleanup for the failure path as well. A refused join alone is a weak control. Establish that the stock rule refuses the intended pair, as O1 does, and check the specific error. Otherwise a disabled party system or another admission condition could make a test appear to prove the policy. This cube needs no pulses. For a test that waits on a time-based condition, sim.step drives pulses but does not advance global time. Use sim.advance_time when the condition depends on global time.

A processor is a set of hooks registered for a map. A virtual session uses a cached copy of a character's data; a cache entry holds that copy for one player and map. A slice is one portion of that data. Start with the overview.

These functions are on forge.sys.game.player_virtual. Function Signature Returns What it does set_processor set_processor(map_index, processor) boolean Registers or replaces a map processor. mark_virtual mark_virtual(map_index) boolean Registers a passthrough processor if absent. unset_processor unset_processor(map_index) nothing Removes the registration for later loads. clear clear(map_index, pid?) nothing Clears a map cache or one player entry. is_virtual_map is_virtual_map(map_index) boolean Tests whether a processor is registered. is_player_virtual is_player_virtual(pid) boolean Tests for a session on this core. get_real_player_table get_real_player_table(ch) TPlayerTable or nil Copies the real player row before transformation. commit_quest_flag commit_quest_flag(ch, key, value) nothing Writes one real character flag. commit_account_flag commit_account_flag(ch, key, value) nothing Writes one real account flag. commit_stash_item commit_stash_item(ch, item, why?) number Consumes an item for delivery. get_forge_cache get_forge_cache(ch, key) table or nil Gets a cached subsystem table. set_forge_cache set_forge_cache(ch, key, value) nothing Replaces a cached subsystem table. transform_forge_load transform_forge_load(ch, key, input) table Runs the subsystem load transform. with_load_cache with_load_cache(ch, key, response_type, load_fn) table or nil Loads through the subsystem cache. with_save_cache with_save_cache(ch, key, request_type, msg, save_fn) the result of save_fn(), or nil Saves through the subsystem cache. clear also clears active entries, so use it only when the affected players are gone. unset_processor does not remove the processor from active sessions. See custom transformers for the cache wrappers and the prize commit for commit guarantees. The character exposes LPCHARACTER:is_virtual(); LPCHARACTER:commit_quest_flag(key, value) and pc.commit_quest_flag(key, value) choose the commit for a virtual character and set_quest_flag for a real one.

A Lua processor is a table of optional functions. The engine calls each as fn(processor, ch, ...). Passthrough means keeping the input when a hook is absent or does not replace it. The stash is storage for items awaiting delivery on a non-virtual load. Hook Signature Returns When it runs transform_player_load (self, ch, player: TPlayerTable) TPlayerTable? Once per cache entry, at the first load onto the map. transform_item_load (self, ch, items: TPlayerItemEx[]) TPlayerItemEx[]? Once per cache entry. The stash rows are already stripped. transform_quest_load (self, ch, quests: TQuestTable[], is_account: boolean) TQuestTable[]? Twice per cache entry: is_account false for the character, then true for the account. transform_affect_load (self, ch, affects: TPacketAffectElement[]) TPacketAffectElement[]? Once per cache entry. transform_skill_tree_load (self, ch, trees: TPlayerSkillTree[]) TPlayerSkillTree[]? Once per cache entry. transform_pet_load (self, ch, pet: TPetPlayerTable) TPetPlayerTable? Once per pet vnum, at the first summon. A resummon reuses the cached record. transform_forge_load (self, ch, key: string, data: table) table? Once per key, at the first with_load_cache of that subsystem. on_player_enter (self, ch, fresh_hydrate: boolean) nothing At every entry into the game. fresh_hydrate is true only the first time. on_player_exit (self, ch) nothing At every disconnect, before the saves. What the engine takes from a return value: transform_player_load and transform_pet_load: a returned record of the right type wins. Anything else, nil included, and the engine reads the input you changed in place. The vector hooks: a returned table is read back keeping only the entries that are records of the right type. A plain Lua table such as { name = "x", state = "y", value = 1 } is silently dropped, so a hook that returns only such tables empties the slice. Any other return, nil included, uses the input array as you left it. transform_forge_load: a returned table wins, otherwise the input table as you left it. The hooks pass or filter, in any combination. A hook can keep part of its input (filter the array, leave fields alone) or replace it. The base overlay that follows transform_player_load is fixed, see the boundary.

Hooks work on records bound from the engine. The no-argument constructor form TPlayerTable() exists, and TPlayerSkillTree.new(), TPlayerSkillTree.new(pid, type), TPetPlayerTable.new() and TPetPlayerTable.new(pid, pet_vnum) also exist. Type Fields Methods TPlayerTable id, name, job, voice, level, level_step, st, ht, dx, iq get_skill(vnum), set_skill_level(vnum, level), clear_skills() TPlayerTable exp, gold, x, y, z, map_index, hp, sp, random_hp, random_sp clear_quickslots(), get_part(i), set_part(i, v) TPlayerTable playtime, stat_point, skill_point, sub_skill_point, horse_skill_point, stamina, skill_group, alignment, stat_reset_count, player_new clear_parts(), get_specialization() TPlayerNewTable pid, selected_skill, inventory_status, inventory_psw, seventh_cool_time, eighth_cool_time, guild_coin, raid_prism, mh_coin, mh_level, jsettings get_master_skill(i), set_master_skill(i, v) TPlayerItem id, window, pos, count, vnum, abstract_grade, death_time, physical_value_grade, magic_value_grade, owner get_socket(i), set_socket(i, v), get_attr(i), set_attr(i, v), clear_attrs(), get_real_value(i), set_real_value(i, v) TPlayerItemEx item flag_count(), get_flag(i), set_flag(i, v), add_flag(v), clear_flags() TItemFlagExtended item_id, name, value none TQuestTable pid, name, state, value none TPacketAffectElement type, apply_on, apply_value, flag, duration, sp_cost, source_vid, is_real_time none TPlayerSkillTree pid, type, active, remaining_time get_node_level(i), set_node_level(i, v) TPetPlayerTable id, pid, pet_vnum, exp, level, name get_bonus_level(i), set_bonus_level(i, v), get_skill_level(i), set_skill_level(i, v) set_skill_level on a TPlayerTable clamps to 0 to 40 and sets the master tier at 20, 30 and 40. An out-of-range index on an item getter returns 0 and a setter does nothing. TPetPlayerTable:set_skill_level has no cap despite the stub. gold is a 64-bit value; a Lua number loses precision from 2^53. TPlayerTable:clear_skills_keep_spec() is a Lua extension that ships beside the engine.

The fixed overlay copies real fields over the transformed player table. A forge subsystem is a Forge component with its own stored table. Slice Real to virtual Virtual to real Player table transform_player_load, then fixed overlay Overlay fields only Items and flags transform_item_load commit_stash_item Quest and account flags transform_quest_load Flag commits Affects transform_affect_load None Skill trees transform_skill_tree_load None Pets and forge subsystem tables Custom transformers None Entry grants on_player_enter None Exit on_player_exit May commit Metrics None allow_virtual per metric

Subclass IPlayerVirtualProcessor and override the hooks you need; defaults are passthrough. Register it for the map index with CPlayerVirtualManager::RegisterProcessor before players load. CPlayerVirtualManager::MarkVirtual installs a passthrough processor if none exists. Registration refuses replacement while that map has active sessions. The native fixed overlay always wins over processor changes to its fields. See custom transformers for Forge handlers.

A Lua hook runs in a protected call. A transform error logs the hook name and falling back to passthrough, then uses the untransformed input. Entry and exit errors are logged and the session continues. A missing hook or a value that is not a function silently uses passthrough.

Processor: hooks registered for a map index. Slice: a portion of character data handled by a hook. Cache entry: cached session data for one player and map. Passthrough: using the input without replacing it. Stash: item storage for delivery on a later non-virtual load. Prize commit: an explicit write of a selected result to real data. Virtual session: a character's session on a virtual map. Fixed overlay: real fields copied over the transformed player table. Forge subsystem: a Forge component with its own stored table. See examples and pitfalls.

Use collect to select a node's population and accept to filter it. A seed is the character handed to the node; a trigger subject is the character carried by an event. See the skill file glossary for the cast and node terms used here. This node fragment searches around its seed for up to eight enemies and collects each victim at most once per cast: collect: source: inherit origin: seed search: { radius: 2000, take: 8 } accept: of: ENEMY ledger: { max_per_victim: 1 }

A scalar is shorthand for the source alone, for example collect: caster. A search is optional; without one, the node processes its seed subject to acceptance. The search origin controls geometry, not eligibility. A formula, or poly, in scalePoly can use hit_dist, the distance from the origin. Key Values Behavior collect.source inherit (default), caster, position, trigger_subject Selects the source. caster substitutes the caster and does not search; trigger_subject selects the event's other character. collect.origin seed (default), caster, computation_seed Search center: the node seed, caster, or seed of the current computation. collect.from sectree (default), map Search the local spatial tree, or all characters on the map. map ignores radius. collect.scalePoly Formula using hit_dist Scales non-seed amounts for DAMAGE, HEAL, AFFECT, and PULL. The seed has scale 1.0. collect.search.radius Integer Search radius in world units. collect.search.take Integer Maximum victims; 0 is unbounded. A processed seed counts toward the limit. collect.search.include_caster Boolean Include the caster in the search; otherwise the search excludes the caster. collect.search.order.within distance (default), random Order within each tier. collect.search.order.tiers List of SELF, PC, BOSS, METEOR, STONE, MONSTER, DOOR Search preference in list order. Unlisted kinds sort after listed tiers.

Key Values Behavior accept.of ANY (default), ENEMY, ALLY, PARTY, TEAM, SELF Relation to the caster. ENEMY and ALLY use the owner's decision; SELF admits only the caster. TEAM behaves like ANY. accept.kind ANY (default), PLAYER, NON_PLAYER Filter player characters or all non-player characters. accept.seed Boolean, default true Set false to skip the seed and process only search results. accept.seed_may_be_caster Boolean, default true Set false to skip the seed when it is the caster. accept.ledger.max_per_victim Integer, default 0 Maximum collections of one victim by this node in a cast; 0 imposes no limit. accept.ledger.cooldown_per_victim Seconds, default 0 Minimum time before this node can collect the same victim again. PARTY admits the main target and characters sharing a party with both the caster and main target, subject to map restrictions. A strict NPC is collectable only if the skill has NPC_BUFF and the NPC's AI accepts buffs. targets: accepts the same collect and accept clauses for the second population of AUTO_SHOOT and CONCATENATED_ATTACK. The mechanic supplies its origin. The collection ledger belongs to a node, identified by id or its position. It is separate from the cast's entry-point ledger: resolve.bound limits client claims, while accept.ledger limits collections by that node. The entry-point ledger is recorded but its bound is not enforced for server-resolved casts. Formula references use.victims and node.<id>.victims read the respective ledgers.

A trigger runs a skill when an event occurs on its holder. This fragment turns on a passive skill when its mounted holder has at most half HP, and turns it off on dismount: type: PASSIVE triggersOn: - event: RIDE conditions: - { type: HP_BELOW, arg: 50 } triggersOff: - event: UNRIDE Each entry has an event and an optional conditions list. An entry without an event is logged and skipped. Event When it fires Carried subject RIDE, UNRIDE Holder mounts or dismounts None HP_CHANGED Holder's HP changes New HP, not a character DEAL_BUFF, DEAL_DEBUFF, DEAL_HEAL Holder gives a buff, debuff, or heal Receiver RECEIVE_BUFF, RECEIVE_DEBUFF, RECEIVE_HEAL Holder receives one Giver Use collect: { source: trigger_subject } to select the carried character. The skill flag TARGET_TRIGGER_SUBJECT instead seeds the cast on that character; the cast is skipped if the subject is absent, dead, observing, or on another map.

All conditions in a list must pass. For a condition with multiple arguments, match selects ANY (default) or ALL within that condition. type arg Passes when the holder has HP_BELOW Percent HP above 0 and at most the given percentage of maximum HP. HP_ABOVE Percent HP above the given percentage of maximum HP. SP_BELOW Percent SP at most the given percentage of maximum SP. SP_ABOVE Percent SP above the given percentage of maximum SP. HAS_AFFECT Affect type or list of types The specified affect, or the types selected by match. An affect is a state applied to a character. IS_MOUNTED None A mount. LEVEL_ABOVE Level A level at least equal to arg. LEVEL_BELOW Level A level below arg. triggersOn is retained only for type: PASSIVE. The holder must have a level in the skill and the skill must be off cooldown; a charge arrival can pass the cooldown check. triggersOff is registered for every skill type and requires the skill to have been used. A triggered cast pays no cost, runs per_use and per_compute once, and does not run post_preflight. Triggers can chain up to depth 8. Without a cooldown, each matching event can trigger another cast. Event names and condition types are not validated at load. An event that is never fired cannot trigger the skill. An unknown condition logs Unknown trigger condition type: <type> when evaluated and fails.

The simulator runs game engine behavior headlessly under a Lua driver, with a staged world and observable infrastructure boundaries. Use it to test scenarios, compare behavior, and calibrate outcomes; the simulator foundations describe its design.

Driver: the Lua script that stages a world and acts on it. Cube: a driver script of faces that assert a specification and end in a verdict. Face: one scenario inside a cube; a failing face does not stop the others. Forge: a Lua module the server loads at boot and keeps for the whole process; see How Forge modules work. Its tables are reached through forge.sys.game.*. Differential gate: a comparison of two recorded runs, classified against declared expectations. Boundary: the simulated edge to network, database, disk and clock. The engine is private.

Use the cube runner with cube names to select runs. With no names, it runs the cubes in its table. --jobs N sets the number of parallel jobs; --kill-orphans requests termination of existing simulator processes. Identify those processes before using the flag: it kills them forcefully. The runner returns: Exit code Meaning 0 At least one cube passed, and none failed or lacked a verdict. 1 A cube failed. 2 A name is unknown, a cube is missing or has no verdict, no work was selected, or staging failed. 3 Existing simulator processes were found, or survived the requested orphan kill. Read each cube's verdict and failure lines from its output. The runner records the process exit code, but classifies the cube by its output. A driver error also produces a process-level exit code of 1; that is distinct from the runner's aggregate exit code.

A cube groups assertions into faces. Each face runs under pcall, so a failure is recorded and the remaining faces can run. Prove that the setup is live before checking its result, and include a negative control. A cube is one Lua file with four parts: a header that lists the faces, the fixtures and the run line; two helpers, check (raises on a false condition) and test (runs a face under pcall and records it); the faces; and the verdict lines. Nothing in the engine asserts for you, the cube carries its own helpers. local T = { pass = 0, fail = 0, notes = {} } local function check(cond, msg) if cond then T.pass = T.pass + 1 else error("CHECK FAILED: " .. msg, 2) end end local function test(name, fn) local ok, err = pcall(fn) if ok then T.notes[#T.notes + 1] = "ok " .. name else T.fail = T.fail + 1 T.notes[#T.notes + 1] = string.format("FAIL %-56s %s", name, tostring(err)) end end test("A1 the setup is live", function() local vid = sim.spawn_pc({ job = "warrior", level = 30, x = 24000, y = 25600 }) check(vid ~= nil and vid > 0, "spawn_pc must return a live vid") end) for _, line in ipairs(T.notes) do print(line) end print("") print(string.format(" checks passed: %d tests failed: %d", T.pass, T.fail)) print(T.fail == 0 and " SKELETON FACES A1-A1 SOLVED" or " CUBE INCOMPLETE") Start the file with a comment that lists each face on one line, the fixtures it loads, and the command that runs it. A binding that returns nothing is read back through its getter; never wrap it in check.

Who prints what: Source Final line A cube <NAME> FACES a-b SOLVED, or CUBE INCOMPLETE A unit script <NAME>_OK or <NAME>_FAILED Either checks passed: N tests failed: N, and one FAIL line per failed face The runner reads the output and applies these rules in order; the first match wins. The process exit code is not part of the verdict, because each face runs under pcall. Order Condition Verdict 1 Last token is CUBE INCOMPLETE or _FAILED, or tests failed: N with N not 0, or any FAIL line FAIL 2 Last token is SOLVED or _OK, or tests failed: 0 PASS 3 None of the above NO VERDICT Failure beats success: a cube that prints SOLVED after a FAIL line still fails. Compare the check count with the last run. A passing verdict with fewer checks may mean that a face or assertion no longer runs.

The simulator registers more than 200 bindings under sim. This table is an index of areas and names. Area Names World and lifecycle seed, step, reset, fork_scenario, child_exit, timeline, report, bench, pulse, log, map_index, leak_check, kill, destroy (removes the PC, the logout), sync, set_event_flag, set_quest_flag, quest_flag PC and party spawn_pc, pc_pos, pc_place, pc_hp, pc_att, set_empire, party_enable, party_join, party_link, party_guild_group, party_alive Combat and observation attack, cast_skill, use_skill, client_hit, mob_skill, mob_skill_info, shoot, affects, points, point, flags, skill_state, can_target Guild and empire guild_create, guild_join, guild_set_name, guild_set_skill, guild_gold, guild_war, empire_gold, intracore_deliver Footprint, land, and deployment footprint_new, footprint_apply, footprint_cells, land_register, land_grid, land_apply_cell, land_apply_land, land_land, deploy_proto_load, deploy_apply, deploy_get, deploy_process, unit_apply, unit_get Map, movement, and assets map_block_of, map_watch, map_request, input_split_probe, asset_png, asset_upload, client_move, route_search, route_stats Gates and passage gate_open, gate_close, gate_state; passage also provides canvas and survey functions Spectator spectator_camera, spectator_cycle, spectator_invalidate, spectator_state, spectator_metrics Wire and DB capture, packets, client_message, peer_deliver, peer_message, db_on, db_insert, db_put, db_delete, db_get, db_rows, db_forward, db_deliver, db_log, db_stats Codec struct_define, struct_size, struct_encode, struct_decode Forge and quest quest_boot, quest_login, forge_has_processor, quest_info Real links db_linked, db_link_stats, db_link_pump, db_link_drop, db_send, peer_count, p2p_send, p2p_stats Records and time bg_open, bg_close, bg_probe, bg_note, data_dir, advance_time Selected contracts: Binding Behavior sim.step([pulses = 1]) Drives pulses and returns no Lua values. It does not advance global time. sim.advance_time(seconds) Advances global time and drives each second's pulses. Negative input raises an error. sim.spawn_pc{ x=, y=, job= \| player_file=, ... } Spawns a PC and returns its VID. Options include map, immortal, bonuses, items, skill, buff, and hp. sim.destroy(vid) Removes the PC, which is the simulator's logout. Returns false when the VID is unknown. sim.set_empire(vid, empire) Sets and returns the resulting empire integer. sim.party_enable(boolean) Sets and returns whether party admission is enabled. sim.party_join(leader_vid, guest_vid) Resolves the party join policy and the common admission condition, then admits directly. Returns a numeric party admission error. It does not replay the invite dialog or acceptance path. sim.quest_boot() Returns boot_init_ok, boot_ok. A false boot-event return can mean no quest handled the event. sim.quest_login(vid) Establishes the quest-loaded state required for PC quest events. sim.forge_has_processor(ns, header[, kind]) Checks for a registered processor. Kind 1 selects peer processors. sim.fork_scenario() Returns true in the child, allowing a scenario to run in an isolated process. sim.child_exit() Flushes output and exits the child. sim.client_message(vid, ns, header[, payload[, client_handler]]) -> bool Delivers a Luna client message. It does not carry the legacy party invite packet. sim.peer_message(peer, ns, header, payload, receipt) Invokes the peer processor path. sim.packets Reads captured packets; the DB capture cannot be drained while the in-process DB is open. sim.capture Controls packet capture at the simulated boundary.

Area Real behavior Simulated or selected boundary Game Engine managers, rules, quest VM, and game entry points A Lua driver stages the world and drives the scenario. Time Engine events and character updates The driver advances pulses and global time separately. Network Packet handling and engine writes Captured buffers are the default; real DB and peer links are optional. Database Gameplay issues serialized requests An in-process DB supplies configured answers, or a real headless DB link can be used. Content Forge artifacts, quest objects, and protos The driver chooses and stages the data. A staged world proves behavior under that setup. It does not by itself prove that the setup represents a live world.

A differential gate starts with a manifest; the probe runner resets and stages each probe and emits records that a diff classifies. Keep fixture identity, build flavor and manifest order consistent across comparable runs, because the pulse count accumulates across resets. A cube states expected behavior as assertions and prints a verdict; see Write and run a cube. Calibration tunes toward an objective rather than comparing two records. The foundations explain why each exists.

The bindings are registered natively in C++. A cube uses the registered table; it does not register these bindings in Lua. Registrar Area Main simulator table World, lifecycle, characters, combat, time, and other simulator operations Wire Packet capture and message delivery Database Simulated DB operations Codec Structure definition and encoding Passage Passage, canvas, and survey operations

A probe passes without measuring the behavior. Missing SP, an uncast buff, the wrong skill class, an untriggered condition, or a damage floor can produce plausible observations. Assert the preconditions and use the probe's liveness check. PC quest events never reach Lua. A spawned PC needs quest-loaded state. Call sim.quest_login(vid) before testing its quest events. A Forge table exists but its processor is absent. A forge can have a game artifact and a quest object, and some processors register only through the quest object at boot. Stage both the compiled Forge artifact and quest object, call sim.quest_boot(), and check sim.forge_has_processor. A cooldown never expires. sim.step drives pulses without moving global time. Use sim.advance_time for a gate based on global time. An affect-duration assertion has an unexpected result. Affect durations tick once per second through the engine's own affect event as live; keep a control probe that reads the rate beside anything that depends on a duration. A successful land update fails its check. sim.land_apply_land returns no value. Read the applied state back with sim.land_land and assert on that. DB packet capture refuses to drain. The in-process DB needs the captured messages to answer requests. Inspect DB statistics and logs instead. A real DB link fails while the DB double is enabled. Capturing an armed DB descriptor can swallow the socket handshake. Use the in-process DB or the real DB link, not both. A linked DB does not respond after stepping pulses. Pulses do not wait for real socket I/O. Use sim.db_link_pump(ms) to pump the linked DB. An observation uses a stale character. A character can be destroyed after death. Resolve it by VID each time you need it. Point traversal stops early. The points table omits zero entries, so gaps can truncate array traversal. Use the named point accessor or deliberate numeric indices. A received-message count passes for the wrong message. An unrelated DB or peer message can increment the generic count. Check the expected header in by_header. A party admission test claims to cover an invite. sim.party_join exercises direct admission and its policy checks, but bypasses the invite and acceptance handlers. Drive and observe those handlers when the full invite path is the behavior under test.
Simulator foundations Write a simulator cube

A skill description combines localized text with values read from the skill configuration. The client renders the text; the server validates the variables and supplies values that require server state. See the Skills glossary for terms used here and Skill descriptions for the model.

In the skill config conf/skill/100.ucskill.yaml, add a description variable that refers to a node with ID hit and an amountPoly field: desc: vars: damage: { ref: node.hit.amountPoly } In the client locale sentence file skill_desc/100.ucskilldesc.yaml, use that variable: name: Example strike description: |- Deals $damage damage. The tooltip replaces $damage with the evaluated number. A poly is a formula expression; the formula reference explains its vocabulary.

File Side Purpose conf/skill/<vnum>.ucskill.yaml Server and client Skill configuration, including desc.vars. Keep the client copy in sync with the server. skill_desc/<vnum>.ucskilldesc.yaml Client locale Skill name, description and optional policy-specific text. skill_desc/policies.ucskilldesc.yaml Client locale Display labels for policy IDs. conf/skill/policies.yaml Server and client Declares policy IDs. locale_game.txt Client locale Formula-name and tooltip labels. The client loads configs before descriptions. It looks for sentence files numbered 1 through 1000 and skips missing files. A sentence file with no matching config is skipped. Loading fails if no configs or no description files load. No description compilation step is required.

A sentence file accepts these keys; other keys are ignored. A policy is a named configuration variant; see Skill policies. Key Meaning name Player-facing name. An empty value keeps the config name. description Player-facing text. An empty value leaves no text. A block scalar preserves line breaks. policies.<id>.name Name for a variant; absent means the base name. policies.<id>.description Text for a variant; absent means the base text, evaluated against the variant config.

Text Result $name Value of desc.vars.name. A name starts with a letter or _ and continues with letters, digits or _. ` cAARRGGBB... % A literal percent sign, including after a variable. Replacement uses declared names longest first. Text immediately following a name can be consumed as part of a replacement: $costs with a declared cost prints the cost followed by s. An undeclared token remains visible and is logged.

The label file maps each policy ID to a name: example_policy: name: Example configuration The switcher uses SKILL_POLICY_BASE for the base configuration. A missing label falls back to the policy ID. A policy-specific sentence needs a corresponding declared policy and a variant in the skill config.

desc.vars maps each token name to a source and optional transformations. Each variable has exactly one of ref or value. Key Value Meaning ref Path to a scalar poly Read a formula from the skill config. value Plain number State a constant; expressions that read names are refused. with Map of name to number Pin names read by a referenced poly. Requires ref. delta_at Map of name to number Evaluate the referenced poly at the given value and at zero, then subtract. Requires ref. as Poly Transform the result after the source values are evaluated. A constant duplicates a number rather than tracking another source. Keep it synchronized when that source changes.

Shape Target node.<id>.<field> Field of a node identified by id. node.<id>.nodes.<child>.<field> Field of a child node. node.<id>.traits.<trait>.formulas.<name> Formula attached to a node; see the traits reference. resolve.bound.targets, resolve.bound.hitsPerTarget Resolve bounds. cooldownPoly Example of a skill-level field. Segments after the node ID are YAML keys. A path must end at a scalar that parses as a poly. Trait constants are substituted before the formula is evaluated.

with and delta_at must name a value the referenced poly actually reads. The same name cannot appear in both maps. A pin applies to the displayed value and formula. delta_at gives a rate only if the poly is linear in that name; choose a unit large enough that truncation does not erase the result. For a poly that reads victim_point_MAX_HP, these variables describe its value at zero and its change per 100 points: desc: vars: base: { ref: node.heal.amountPoly, with: { victim_point_MAX_HP: 0 } } per100: { ref: node.heal.amountPoly, delta_at: { victim_point_MAX_HP: 100 } }

as runs once after all source values are evaluated. value means the variable's own source result; a sibling name reads that sibling's source result, before its own as. An expression cannot name its own variable or read another as result. desc: vars: drop: { ref: node.drain.amountPoly, as: '0-value' } This displays a negative amount as a positive drop.

Name Client Server Description rule skill_level, skill_k, skill_power, skill_spec Yes Yes No pin needed. calc_missing_hp, calc_missing_sp, calc_precision_rate, calc_raw_phys_att, calc_raw_magic_att, calc_raw_adaptive_att, calc_total_adaptive_att Yes Yes No pin needed. point_<NAME> Yes Yes No pin needed for character points. quest_flag.<flag> No Yes Unpinned flags make the variable server-resolved; a pin keeps it local. subject_level, subject_member_count, subject_gold, subject_flag.<flag> No Yes Pin unless the variable is server-resolved. calc_horse_level, calc_hp_without_defensor, calc_def_penetration, is_mental, is_archer, is_assassin No Yes Pin unless the variable is server-resolved. victim_is_self, victim_calc_*, victim_point_<NAME> No Yes Pin unless the variable is server-resolved. node.*, self.*, use.* No Cast state Pin for a description. Unresolved names No No Pin or use delta_at. A pin or delta_at supplies its name to both evaluators. Unknown names are rejected even in server-resolved variables.

The client evaluates source polys with pins, applies each as, then substitutes tokens longest first. Displayed numbers are signed whole numbers, truncated toward zero. A negative value retains its sign. Python call Result or behavior skill.GetDescription(vnum, level, power[, mode]) Rendered string. power is the tooltip efficiency as a float. An unknown skill raises an exception. Requests server values on each call when needed. skill.HasFormulas(vnum) 1 if a variable has as or a poly that reads a name, otherwise 0. skill.GetSkillName(vnum) Player-facing skill name. skill.GetPolicyCount(vnum) Number of configurations, including the base. skill.GetPolicyInfo(vnum, index) (id, label); index 0 is the base with empty strings. An out-of-range index raises an exception. skill.GetActivePolicyIndex(vnum) Index of the first active policy in server registration order, or 0 for the base. skill.SetPreviewPolicy(vnum, index) Preview the indexed configuration. skill.ClearPreviewPolicy() Clear the preview. The optional rendering mode controls each token: Mode Output skill.DESC_PLAIN Number; the default. skill.DESC_EXPANDED Number and, where applicable, (= formula). skill.DESC_SYMBOLIC Formula alone. Expanded mode omits the formula for a constant poly and for a delta_at variable. Pinned names print as numbers. Formula output uses {p:<pointType>} for points and {s:<name>} for other names; * prints as x. LocalizeSkillFormula turns these markers into display words. For a string marker it looks up SKILLVAR_<NAME> in locale_game.txt, uppercasing the name and replacing dots with underscores. An unknown name displays as itself. The tooltip displays plain values by default and expanded values while SHIFT is held. SHIFT+TAB cycles configurations when more than one is available. The tooltip opens on the active configuration; a preview selects another until cleared.

A variable is server-resolved when its poly reads an unpinned quest_flag.<flag>. The client requests values with the skill vnum and level on each description call for a skill with such variables. The server clamps the level to the skill maximum and evaluates the variables for the caster under the active policy. The exchange follows this order: The client renders with unread flags at zero while it waits. The server sends values multiplied by 1000 as 32-bit integers. Both sides sort server-resolved variables by name, so the reply is positional. The client drops a reply with an unexpected value count. When accepted values change, it calls BINARY_SkillDescValuesUpdated on the game window to redraw the tooltip. Keep client and server configs synchronized: a count mismatch drops the reply. A pin on the flag prevents that flag from requiring a server value.

The server validates every base configuration and policy variant. A bad variable fails the skill table load. At boot this stops the game core; on reload the previous table remains live. Server messages identify the skill and variable. Problem Fix Both or neither of ref and value Supply exactly one source. with without ref, or a nonconstant value Pin a reference, or use a plain numeric value. Reference does not resolve to a scalar poly Check the node ID, path and target value. Unknown or client-unavailable name Pin it, use delta_at, or use a server-resolved variable where applicable. Pin or rate name is absent from the poly Match the name read by the referenced poly. Same name is pinned and used in delta_at Use one operation for that name. Invalid as, self-reference or unknown sibling Correct the expression; use value for its own source. The client logs missing or unused sentence variables, missing configs, unresolved references, undeclared policies, missing labels, unknown active policies, mismatched server value counts and invalid sentence YAML. Missing variables remain literal in the text; unused variables are still evaluated. An unresolved client reference is dropped. A missing policy label displays its ID.
Skill file and glossary: config keys and terminology. Skill policies: variants and policy selection. Skill formulas: formula vocabulary and evaluation.

A skill file that fails validation prevents the new skill table from loading. Use the log to locate the fault, then check the examples and pitfalls below. A node is one effect in a skill, and a poly is a formula string. See the skill file glossary for these and other terms. This server-resolved skill deals magic damage to one selected enemy: name: example_bolt type: CLASS maxLevel: 20 cooldownPoly: '10' costType: SP costPoly: '20' range: 1200 useTimeout: 2500 flags: [ENEMYONLY, ATTACK_SKILL, LEVEL_UP_BY_POINT, NEED_TARGET] client: job: SHAMAN icon: skill/shaman/jeongeop motionIndex: 19 resolve: by: server bound: { targets: '1', hitsPerTarget: '1' } per_compute: - type: DAMAGE id: bolt amountPoly: '100+60*skill_k' damageType: MAGIC Place it in conf/skill/<vnum>.ucskill.yaml, substituting a numeric skill vnum (identifier). The selected target seeds per_compute; ENEMYONLY rejects a friendly target, and NEED_TARGET makes the client request one. Configure the icon and motion for your client.

The loader reads the files in one pass and reports broken files. If any fail, it logs There were errors when loading skill table from YAML and discards the new table. At boot the core exits; on a proto reload the old table remains in force. Inspect the log after a reload even if the core stays up. Skill diagnostics use Skill[<vnum>] <name>:; node diagnostics add node[<n>] <TYPE>:. The tables show representative log text. For required keys by type, see Skill nodes. Fault Log text or cause Skill directory missing Skill YAML directory does not exist Invalid YAML Skill YAML: cannot parse file Filename stem is not numeric cannot parse vnum from filename Missing resolve: or invalid resolve.by no resolve: block, or resolve.by must be server or client Invalid cooldown, cost, or bound formula syntax error cooldownPoly, syntax error costPoly, or syntax error in resolve.bound Unknown range_bonus or subject unknown range_bonus point, or unknown subject Charge declaration and dash affect disagree charge: true requires an AFFECT node that raises TANHWAN_DASH; the affect also requires charge: true Client-evaluated formula reads a server-only name which only the server can resolve Unknown or retired node type unrecognized node type Invalid node formula cannot analyze amountPoly, or the corresponding ...Poly key Required node key missing For example, amountPoly empty, delayPoly empty, or ttlPoly is mandatory Affect has no required duration affect inside a non-toggable cast skil with no duration, or affect not in root node without douration Timed node lacks required children or targets a ticker with no children ticks nothing, should have at least one inner node, or a timed node must declare targets Ticker affect lacks attachment an affect on a ticker needs attach: affect Unknown node point or invalid CUT_POINT point unknown point, or point has to be an instant point; CUT_POINT accepts HP or SP Invalid upkeep, counters, attach, or traits The diagnostic identifies the invalid field, event, or missing trait id Trait constant uses a name outside the skill formula vocabulary which the skill poly vocabulary does not resolve Duplicate node id duplicate node id Invalid desc.vars See Skill descriptions for validation rules Policy id is absent from policies.yaml policy [<id>] is not declared by policies.yaml Policy restates a node's traits or counters without its own affectVnum restates traits at ... without giving that node its own affectVnum

Fault Log text or result Unknown flag unknown flag Unknown or non-list weaponLimitation unknown weaponLimitation, or weaponLimitation must be a list Unknown skill type unknown type string Unknown collect: or accept: token For example, unknown collect.source or unknown accept.of search.radius with collect.from other than sectree The radius is ignored Handler has no Lua file declares a handler but ... is missing; the node stays inert Trait id cannot be resolved resolves to no native, Lua or colocated trait An unknown client.job is a separate client-side failure: the client discards that skill and logs names an unknown type.
