These methods belong to the mob object. They manage data for non-player characters identified by a vnum.

Constant Description mob.MOB_TYPE_NPC Identifies an NPC mob mob.MOB_TYPE_MONSTER Identifies a monster mob mob.MOB_TYPE_STONE Identifies a stone or ore mob.MOB_TYPE_METEOR Identifies a meteor object mob.MOB_TYPE_BOSS Identifies a boss mob

Name: mob.get_drops Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries representing drop data. Return Dictionary Schema (each element of the list): { "vnum": 72701, "vnums": [72701, 72702], // optional "count": 1, "rarity": 10, "type": "drop|limit|quest|stone|kill|common|belt|thiefgloves|dungeon", "requirements": { "level_limit_min": 1, "level_limit_max": 120, "days": [], "time_from": 0, "time_to": 0, "max_drop": 0, "during_event": "", "during_quest": "" } } Call Example: {% set drop_list = mob.get_drops(101) %}
Name: mob.appears_in_quests Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of strings indicating the quests where the mob appears. Call Example: {% set quest_ids = mob.appears_in_quests(101) %}
Name: mob.appears_in_dungeons Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dungeon identifiers (strings). Call Example: {% set dungeon_list = mob.appears_in_dungeons(101) %}
Name: mob.appears_in_raids Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of strings, each representing a raid zone. Call Example: {% set raid_ids = mob.appears_in_raids(101) %}
Name: mob.appears_in_maps Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of map indexes (integers). Call Example: {% set maps = mob.appears_in_maps(101) %}

Name: mob.sells Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries describing items sold by the mob. Return Dictionary Schema (each element of the list): { "item_vnum": 30100, "count": 1 } Call Example: {% set vendor_items = mob.sells(9003) %}
Name: mob.crafts Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of cube crafts ids (integers). Call Example: {% set craft_list = mob.crafts(9003) %}

Name: mob.spawn_data Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A dictionary containing spawn details or None if no data is available. Return Dictionary Schema: { "map_index": { "random": false|false, "points": [ { "x": xcoord, "y": ycoord, "time": seconds_to_respawn }, ] } } Call Example: {% set spawn_info = mob.spawn_data(101) %}
Name: mob.get_mob_origin Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A localized string describing the mob’s origin, or None if none is defined. Call Example: {% set origin = mob.get_mob_origin(101) %}

Name: mob.is_any_of_type Parameters: vnum (int) *args: any combination of mob-type constants (e.g. mob.MOB_TYPE_BOSS, mob.MOB_TYPE_NPC) Return: A boolean indicating if the mob matches any of the provided types. Call Example: {% if mob.is_any_of_type(101, mob.MOB_TYPE_NPC, mob.MOB_TYPE_MONSTER) %} <!-- do something --> {% endif %}
Name: mob.mob_name Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A UTF-8 decoded string with the mob’s localized name. Call Example: {% set name = mob.mob_name(101) %}

This documentation explains how the Wiki configuration file and the localization file work together. Each section includes detailed explanations and complete examples to help you understand how to customize and maintain your Wiki.

YAML is a human-friendly data serialization language commonly used for configuration files. Its are readability and ease of editing lead the choice of using it as gonfiguration language instead of json, but it has some pitfalls: Indentation Matters: YAML relies on correct indentation using spaces. Mixing tabs and spaces or using inconsistent indentation can lead to parsing errors. Data Structure Sensitivity: The structure (lists and dictionaries) depends entirely on indentation. A small mistake can change the hierarchy of your data. Quotes and Special Characters: Use quotes when needed, but be consistent. Improper quoting may cause errors or misinterpretation of values. Example of correct YAML syntax: PACKED_QUERY: NEW_FILTER: [101, 102, 103, 104] Ensure every nested level is indented equally (usually 2 spaces) and avoid tabs.
documents.s: What is YAML and Common Pitfalls

documents.t: The configuration file (config.yaml) uses keys that map directly to entries in the localization file (locale.json). The keys use dot notation to indicate hierarchy. For example, the locale key "items.origin.fishing" in the configuration corresponds to a nested entry in the localization file Example: For example "items.origin.fishing" key will select the string associated to the below locale tree { "items": { "origin": { "fishing": "Obtanable fishing" } } }

All configuration and localization files are located within the locale directory for each supported language: Configuration File: locale/[localization]/wiki/config.yaml Whitelists File: locale/[localization]/wiki/whitelists.yaml Localization File: locale/[localization]/wiki/locale.json These files are essential for the Wiki's operation and should be maintained carefully.

To keep configuration files concise, ranges can be specified instead of listing every individual number. This is supported in several sections: config.yaml - PACKED_QUERY config.yaml - ITEM_ORIGIN_LOCALE_MAPPING config.yaml - MOB_ORIGIN_LOCALE_MAPPING whitelists.yaml - ITEM_WHITELIST whitelists.yaml - MOB_WHITELIST A range is defined with a range key, for example: - range: [10, 19] This instructs the system to expand the range into all integers from 10 to 19. This method reduces repetition and minimizes errors when listing many sequential values. Ranges can be combined with normal numbers: MOB_WHITELIST: - 501 - 502 - 504 - 101 - range: [102, 115] - 10001
Below the sections of config.yaml are explained.

What It Is and Its Purpose: PACKED_QUERY defines groups of item or filter identifiers (vnums) used to set filter target values and URL parameters. When a template uses a value like "packed_query:HELMETS_WARRIOR", the fun.var function recognizes it and replaces it with a comma-separated list of numbers from the PACKED_QUERY section. CAUTION Since PACKED_QUERY are expected to be lists, it is important to pass an empty array as second parameter of fun.getv("query:vnums", []), to force UCHTML engine to return a list. Example to Creating a New Packed Query and using it as filger: Configuration (in config.yaml): PACKED_QUERY: NEW_FILTER: [101, 102, 103, 104] Usage in a Template:
{% for value in fun.getv("query:race", []) %} {% endfor %}
When one of the buttons (filter) is clicked, the page puts packed_query:NEW_FILTER or packed_query:OLD_FILTER in the variable query:race. Then using fun.getv("query:race", []) we can unpack and use the single values to iterate over them and, for example, place an for each vnum. Example to Using PACKED_QUERY as a Category/Hyperlink Parameter: Configuration (in config.yaml): PACKED_QUERY: SPECIAL_ITEMS: [201, 202, 203] Usage in a Category Link: Special Items NOTE The hyperling will carry the information that vnums is the shothand for [201, 202, 203] and whe can later use it in a page (in this case items/special.html) Usage in items/special.html: {% set new_filter = fun.getv("query:vnums", []) %} {% for value in new_filter %} {% endfor %} The for loop will iterate over all values defined in config.yaml (201, 202, 203)

What Is It and How It Works: The Mob/Item Origin sections (ITEM_ORIGIN_LOCALE_MAPPING and MOB_ORIGIN_LOCALE_MAPPING) map specific vnums to locale keys. This means that any mob or item whose vnum is listed in these mappings will have its "origin" automatically set to the corresponding localized string when using functions like mob.get_mob_origin(vnum) or item.get_item_origin(vnum). Tags such as <monster-card> and <chest-card> will display this origin information. Example to Creating a New Origin Group: Configuration (in config.yaml): ITEM_ORIGIN_LOCALE_MAPPING: "items.origin.mystic": [50001, 50002, 50003] MOB_ORIGIN_LOCALE_MAPPING: "mobs.origin.forest": - range: [600, 610] Localization (in locale.json): { "items": { "origin": { "mystic": "Mystic Lands" } }, "mobs": { "origin": { "forest": "Brave Forest" } } } Expected Behavior: When item.get_item_origin(50002) is called, it will find the locale key "items.origin.mystic" and display the corresponding localized string Mystic Lands. Similarly, mob.get_mob_origin(605) will return the localized string for "mobs.origin.forest" Brave Forest.

These configuration sections associate identifiers with locale keys (and in the case of MAP_INFO, additional properties) to be used in hyperlink tags. QUEST_NAMES​ QUEST_NAMES Associates quest IDs with locale keys. Example: QUEST_NAMES: example_quest_lv10: "quest_names.example_quest_lv10" example_quest_lv25: "quest_names.example_quest_lv25" example_quest_lv40: "quest_names.example_quest_lv40" RAID_NAMES​ RAID_NAMES Maps raid IDs to locale keys. Example: RAID_NAMES: example_raid_a: "raid_names.example_raid_a" example_raid_b: "raid_names.example_raid_b" DUNGEON_NAMES​ DUNGEON_NAMES Associates dungeon IDs with locale keys. Example: DUNGEON_NAMES: example_dungeon_a: dungeon_names.example_dungeon_a example_dungeon_b: dungeon_names.example_dungeon_b MAP_INFO​ MAP_INFO Contains map IDs, each mapping to an object with a name (locale key) and a path. The path is used by tags like <atlas-info> and <monster-spawn> to load atlas images. Example: MAP_INFO: "61": name: "maps.snow" path: map_n_snowm_01 "63": name: "maps.desert" path: metin2_map_n_desert_01 Localization (in locale.json) for above entries: { "quest_names": { "example_quest_lv10": "Main Quest Level 10", "example_quest_lv25": "Main Quest Level 25", "example_quest_lv40": "Main Quest Level 40" }, "raid_names": { "example_raid_a": "Example Raid A", "example_raid_b": "Example Raid B" }, "dungeon_names": { "example_dungeon_a": "Example Dungeon A", "example_dungeon_b": "Example Dungeon B" }, "maps": { "snow": "Snow Map", "desert": "Desert Map" } }

What It Does: WIKI_CATEGORIES defines the navigational structure of the Wiki by creating a category-subcategory tree. Each category can have multiple subcategories, each linking to a Wiki page. Example to Creating a New Category-Subcategory: Configuration (in config.yaml): WIKI_CATEGORIES: - category: "categories.equipment" subcategories: - name: "subcategories.equipment.new_weapons" url: "wiki://p/items/new_weapons" - name: "subcategories.equipment.new_armor" url: "wiki://p/items/new_armors" Locale Example (in locale.json): { "categories": { "equipment": "Equipment" }, "subcategories": { "equipment": { "new_weapons": "New Weapons", "new_armor": "New Armor" } } } This configuration creates a new category called "Equipment" with subcategories "New Weapons" and "New Armor", linking to their respective Wiki pages.

What It Does: INDEXED_PAGES lists the Wiki pages that are indexed by the search engine. Each entry specifies a category, a title, and a URL. Mobs and Items are indexed automatically (following Whitelists rules). All other custom pages like dungeons, systems, guides need to be manually indexed. CAUTION Page not indexed are not returned from the search bar. Example to Adding a Document to the Search Engine: Configuration (in config.yaml): INDEXED_PAGES: - category: dungeon title: dungeon_names.new_dungeon url: "wiki://p/dungeons/new_dungeon" This entry makes the new dungeon page searchable and categorizes it under "dungeon". Locale Example (in locale.json): { "dungeon_names": { "new_dungeon": "A Fresh new Dungeon" }, }

What It Does: SEARCH_RESULT_CATEGORY configures how search results are grouped and displayed. Each category has a defined color and a display name used in the search result visualization. The category defined in INDEXED_PAGES refers to this section. When a page with a given category is returned, the name of category is appended in front of the page name in the search result list. Example to Creating a New Search Result Category: Configuration (in config.yaml): SEARCH_RESULT_CATEGORY: item: color: fffa4834 name: results_category.item dungeon: color: fffa4834 name: results_category.dungeon new_category: color: ffaabbcc name: results_category.new_category This configuration adds a new search result category called "new_category" with the specified color. Locale Example (in locale.json): { "results_category": { "item": "Items", "dungeon": "Dungeon", "new_category": "New Sparkly Category", }, } Using the above INDEXED_PAGES example, the page indexed will return as: [Dungeon] A Fresh new Dungeon

What They Are: Whitelists control which item and mob vnums are enabled for search and Wiki build. Example to Modifying Whitelists: ITEM_WHITELIST (in whitelists.yaml): ITEM_WHITELIST: - 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 5 - 6 - 7 - 8 - 9 - range: [10, 19] - 100 MOB_WHITELIST (in whitelists.yaml): MOB_WHITELIST: - 107 - 109 - 113 - 115 - 401 - 402 - 501 - 502 - 504 - 101 - range: [102, 115] - 404 - 405 - range: [191, 194] - range: [493, 496] To add a new mob, simply add its vnum (or a range) to the corresponding list. To remove one, delete it from the list.
These methods belong to the item object and allow you to query item data by vnum.

Constant Description ITEM_TYPE_WEAPON Weapon-type item ITEM_TYPE_ARMOR Armor item (body, depending on subtype) ITEM_TYPE_HELMET Helmet-type item ITEM_TYPE_SHIELD Shield-type item ITEM_TYPE_EARINGS Earring-type item ITEM_TYPE_NECK Necklace-type item ITEM_TYPE_BRACELET Bracelet-type item ITEM_TYPE_BOOTS Boots-type item ITEM_TYPE_BELT Belt-type item ITEM_TYPE_ARTIFACT Artifact item ITEM_TYPE_SHINING Shining-type item ITEM_TYPE_COSTUME Costume item ITEM_TYPE_COSTUME_PET Pet costume item ITEM_TYPE_COSTUME_MOUNT Mount costume item ITEM_TYPE_CHEST Chest/box item
Name: item.get_base_vnum Parameters: vnum (int) Return: An integer representing the base vnum of the item. Returns 0 if none is found. Call Example: {% set base_id = item.get_base_vnum(72701) %}
Name: item.get_refine_count Parameters: vnum (int) Return: An integer indicating how many times the item has been refined. Call Example: {% set refine_times = item.get_refine_count(72701) %}
Name: item.get_in_chest Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of chest vnums (integers) that may contain this item. Call Example: {% set chest_list = item.get_in_chest(30100) %}

Name: item.get_chest_content Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A dictionary describing the chest content, or None if the item is not a chest. Return Dictionary Schema (example): { "multidrop": "all" | false | number, "items": [ { "vnum": 72702, "count": 1, "rarity": 5 } ] } Call Example: {% set chest_data = item.get_chest_content(30100) %}

Name: item.get_item_drop_by Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries detailing which mobs drop this item. Return Dictionary Schema (each element of the list): { "mob_rank": "BOSS", "mob_vnum": 101, "quest": "quest_name", "type": "drop|limit|quest|stone|kill|common|belt|thiefgloves|dungeon", "rarity": 10 } Call Example: {% set drop_data = item.get_item_drop_by(72701) %}

Name: item.get_item_sold_by Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries specifying which NPCs sell this item. Return Dictionary Schema (each element): { "npc_vnum": 9003 } Call Example: {% set vendor_list = item.get_item_sold_by(72701) %}
Name: item.get_item_drop_by_mobs Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of mob vnums (integers) that can drop the specified item. Call Example: {% set mob_list = item.get_item_drop_by_mobs(72701) %}

Name: item.get_in_quests Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries indicating quests, dungeons, or raids in which this item appears. Return Dictionary Schema (each element): { "type": "quest|dungeon|raid", "identifier": "quest_or_dungeon_name" } Call Example: {% set quest_info = item.get_in_quests(72701) %}

Name: item.get_reward_of Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries indicating which quests or activities reward this item. Return Dictionary Schema (each element): same as item.get_in_quests. Call Example: {% set reward_data = item.get_reward_of(72701) %}

Name: item.is_upgrade_material_for Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of item vnums (integers) that can be upgraded using the specified item as a material. Call Example: {% set upgrade_targets = item.is_upgrade_material_for(30090) %}

Name: item.get_cubes_as_material Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of cube definitions describing how this item is used as a material in crafting. Each definition may include fields such as "npc", "reward", "gold", "percent", and "materials". Call Example: {% set material_cubes = item.get_cubes_as_material(72701) %}

Name: item.get_cubes_as_result Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of cube definitions indicating how this item is produced as a result of crafting. Call Example: {% set result_cubes = item.get_cubes_as_result(72701) %}

Name: item.has_upgrade Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A boolean indicating if the item is part of an upgrade chain (returns True) or not (returns False). Call Example: {% if item.has_upgrade(72701) %} <!-- This item has an upgrade path --> {% endif %}

Name: item.get_upgrade_level Parameters: vnum (int) Return: An integer denoting the item’s upgrade level (e.g., +0, +1, +2...). Returns -1 if the item cannot be upgraded. Call Example: {% set level = item.get_upgrade_level(72701) %}

Name: item.can_show_stats Parameters: vnum (int) Return: Either an integer (the item’s base vnum) if the item can display stats, or False if it cannot. Call Example: {% set stats_base_vnum = item.can_show_stats(72701) %}

Name: item.get_item_origin Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A localized string describing the item’s origin, or None if none is defined. Call Example: {% set origin_string = item.get_item_origin(72701) %}

Name: item.is_any_of_type Parameters: vnum (int) *args: any combination of item-type constants (e.g. item.ITEM_TYPE_COSTUME) Return: A boolean indicating if the item matches any of the specified types. Call Example: {% if item.is_any_of_type(72701, item.ITEM_TYPE_COSTUME, item.ITEM_TYPE_SHIELD) %} <!-- It's either a costume or a shield --> {% endif %}
Name: item.item_name Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A UTF-8 decoded string with the item’s localized name. Call Example: {% set name = item.item_name(72701) %}

Name: item.item_desc Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A UTF-8 decoded string representing the item’s full description (with | replaced by newlines). Call Example: {% set description = item.item_desc(72701) %}

Name: item.item_summary Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A UTF-8 decoded summary string for the item (often a shortened form of the description). Call Example: {% set summary_text = item.item_summary(72701) %}

The world object provides advanced game data handling. It integrates items, mobs, and cube or refine logic to give you higher-level methods that retrieve upgrade paths, refine sets, grouped drop info, and more. Each method is outlined below, with its parameters, return values, and expected data schemas for developers.

Name: world.item_has_epic_upgrade Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A boolean indicating whether the item or any of its upgrades has an epic refinement path. Call Example: {% if world.item_has_epic_upgrade(189) %} <!-- Item has epic refine path --> {% endif %}

Name: world.item_get_last_refine_vnum Parameters: vnum (int) Return: An integer representing the final item vnum in the item’s upgrade sequence. Returns 0 if none is found. Call Example: {% set final_vnum = world.item_get_last_refine_vnum(189) %}

Name: world.item_get_dropby_grouped Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A dictionary grouping drop entries by their "type" field. Keys are drop types, values are lists of drop data dictionaries. If the item has multiple upgrades, entries are appended with "item_vnum" to indicate which upgrade stage the drop pertains to. Return Dictionary Schema (example): { "drop": [ { "mob_rank": "BOSS", "mob_vnum": 101, "quest": "quest_name", "type": "drop", "rarity": 10, "item_vnum": 189 }, { "mob_rank": "BOSS", "mob_vnum": 101, "quest": "quest_name", "type": "drop", "rarity": 10, "item_vnum": 190 } ], "quest": [], "stone": [] } Call Example: {% set drop_groups = world.item_get_dropby_grouped(189) %}

Name: world.item_get_sold_by_all_upgrades Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries describing which NPCs sell the item or any of its upgrades. Each dictionary may include an "npc_vnum" field. Call Example: {% set all_vendors = world.item_get_sold_by_all_upgrades(189) %}

Name: world.item_get_in_chests_all_upgrades Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of chest vnums (integers). Combines all chests that contain any upgrade level of the specified item. Call Example: {% set chests = world.item_get_in_chests_all_upgrades(189) %}

Name: world.item_get_in_quests_all_upgrades Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries describing the quests, dungeons, or raids in which this item (or any of its upgrades) appears. Duplicate entries are filtered out. Return Dictionary Schema (each element): { "type": "quest|dungeon|raid", "identifier": "name_of_quest_or_dungeon" } Call Example: {% set quest_data = world.item_get_in_quests_all_upgrades(189) %}

Name: world.item_get_reward_of_all_upgrades Parameters: vnum (int) Return: A list of dictionaries indicating which quests or activities reward the item or any of its upgrades. The returned list is sorted by "type" and "identifier". Return Dictionary Schema (each element): { "type": "quest|dungeon|raid", "identifier": "quest_or_dungeon_name", "vnum": 189 } Call Example: {% set rewards = world.item_get_reward_of_all_upgrades(189) %}

Name: world.item_is_chest Parameters: vnum (int) Return: Chest content data (dictionary) if the item is indeed a chest, or None otherwise. Equivalent to item.item_data.get_chest_content(vnum). Call Example: {% if world.item_is_chest(30100) %} <!-- It's a chest or box --> {% endif %}

Name: world.item_get_cube_as_material Parameters: vnum (int) group_by_npc (bool, default=False) Return: If group_by_npc == False: A list of cube definitions. If group_by_npc == True: A dictionary grouped by the "npc" field. Return Schema (Ungrouped): [ { "npc": 20018, "reward": { "vnum": 50821, "count": 1 }, "gold": 10000, "percent": 100, "materials": [ { "vnum": 102505, "count": 10 }, { "vnum": 27995, "count": 5 } ] }, ... ] Return Schema (Grouped by NPC): { "20018": [ { "npc": 20018, "reward": { "vnum": 50821, "count": 1 }, "gold": 10000, "percent": 100, "materials": [ { "vnum": 102505, "count": 10 }, { "vnum": 27995, "count": 5 } ] }, ... ], "20019": [ { ... } ] } Call Example: {% set cubes = world.item_get_cube_as_material(72701, True) %}

Name: world.item_get_cube_as_result Parameters: vnum (int) group_by_npc (bool, default=False) Return: If group_by_npc == False: A list of cube definitions (same schema as item_get_cube_as_material). If group_by_npc == True: A dictionary grouped by "npc". Return Schema (Ungrouped and Grouped by NPC): same as world.item_get_cube_as_material. Call Example: {% set cubes_result = world.item_get_cube_as_result(72701) %}

Name: world.mob_get_crafts Parameters: vnum (int): The mob’s vnum. Return: A list (or map object in Python) containing cube definitions for crafts associated with the specified mob. The cube definition follows the same structure used by cube.json. Call Example: {% set mob_crafts = world.mob_get_crafts(9003) %}
This quickstart guide will help you create and deploy a new wiki page in the game’s wiki system,.

A wiki page is the file locale/[localization]/wiki/p/<pagePath>.html (default localization is universal). The client looks for it in this order: The pack file, at locale/[localization]/wiki/p/<pagePath>.html. The client-folder, at [client-folder]/locale/[localization]/wiki/p/<pagePath>.html. The pack always wins: a page that exists in the pack is never read from the folder. During development, keep the page out of the pack and place it in the client-folder; for release, pack the files in a .hpa pack. The same order applies to the other wiki files, including configuration and localization. Example With an URL like wiki://p/items/details?vnum=2000 the engine reads locale/[localization]/wiki/p/items/details.html from the pack, and from [client-folder]/locale/[localization]/wiki/p/items/details.html when the pack has no such file.

We encurage you to use a debug launcher to speed up development and to place all your page and config files in [client-folder]/locale/[localization]/wiki/.... Before starting we strongly suggest to follow some steps to setup a profiecient working environment: Download VScode. Install beautiful-jinja VScode Extension. Create a folder in your workspace ([client-folder]/locale/[localization]/wiki) folder named .vscode. Create a file name settings.json inside .vscode with the following content. { "html.customData": [ "uchtml.json" ], "files.associations": { "*.html": "jinja-html" }, } Download uchtml.json and place it in workspace ([client-folder]/locale/[localization]/wiki`) folder. This ensures suggestion and linting while writing html pages. This quickstart guide will help you create and deploy a new wiki page in the game’s wiki system,.

In your client-folder, create the following folder tree named /locale/[localization]/wiki/p (default localization is universal). The Client folder is the folder where the launcher (metin2client.exe/bin) is. Then a new .html file inside the p folder: [client-folder]/locale/[localization]/wiki/p/example.html And write a simple html page <main> Hello from example page. <txt align=center>We can show some fancy stuff like</txt> <item-card vnum="{{ fun.getv('query:vnum') }}"/> </main>

The wiki window opens a page by URL. To reach your page, link to it from another page of the wiki (see URL): <txt><hyperlink url="wiki://p/example?vnum=10">Open the example</hyperlink></txt> p/example matches your example.html file. ?vnum=10 sets the query:vnum variable to 10 inside the page. More info in the URL page. Testing changes Navigating to a page reads its file again, so with the page in the client-folder and not in the pack, save the .html file and navigate to the page again to see the change. The developer buttons (Navigate, Refresh, Copy URL) are disabled in the wiki window. CAUTION A client that is not a debug client still opens the .html file, but renders from the page's compiled module. A page with no compiled module does not render, and one without its .html fails to load: compile the pages with the compiler tab of the Wiki Manager and ship both, or test in a debug client. See compiled templates. CAUTION Changes to configuration, locale files, or files containing wiki data do not refresh until client restart.

There are some predefined jinja templates in the wiki. These templates are "lego blocks" you can reuse everywhere in the Wiki. For example a very common include is an h1 which already has the right font name, font size, text color and text position and an optional id for anchoring. You can fin the templates in /locale/[localization]/wiki/templates. By using this import we can ensure consistency of the H1 around all wiki. Marcro (template) file templates/headers.html {% macro h1(title, id=None) %}

{{ title }}

{% endmacro %} Usage in your file (continuing from 1.) {% import "templates/headers.html" as header %}
{{ header.h1("Hello from example page", "title") }} We can show some fancy stuff like

Once you’re satisfied with the page: Move the .html file to the production environment folder: locale/[localization]/wiki/p/<pagePath>.html For example: locale/universal/wiki/p/example.html Repack the client files and restart the game client for the changes to apply in production mode.

Now you can enrich your page using templating, functions, the data namespaces and the UCHTML tags with the wiki tags. We also suggest you to read about the grid system which manages component placement in the page following the same logic as plain HTML and CSS.
item-shop-card and ranking-window are data-bound tags that belong to the item shop and ranking clients rather than to the wiki.

Attribute Requirement Default Constraints/Notes id Required none Item shop item ID (integer). Must match an item loaded in ItemShopStore. Base Attributes Optional none Inherits all common base attributes. Renders a full ItemShopDisplayItem widget (200×145) with icon, name, price, quantity selector, and purchase button. The item data is pulled from ItemShopStore by id. The purchase button calls into the host window's interface module. CAUTION Should not contain any child elements. The item shop must be loaded (store populated) before this element renders correctly. Code Example <item-shop-card id="7" />

Attribute Requirement Default Constraints/Notes ranking-type Required none The ranking to subscribe to. width Required none Window width, or auto. height Required none Window height. rows Optional 10 Number of rows shown. show-pagination Optional true false hides the pagination controls. more-info Optional false true adds a "more info" button at the bottom. more-info-text Optional More Info Text of that button. Base Attributes Optional none Inherits all common base attributes. A self-contained ranking ladder: it subscribes to the ranking data when it is created and unsubscribes when the element is destroyed or rebuilt. CAUTION Should not contain any child elements. Code Example <ranking-window align="center" ranking-type="example_ranking" rows="2" width="auto" height="200" show-pagination="false" more-info="true"/>

An environment body runs on its core and returns the module that scripts call. Boot order and calling context determine which operations are safe; see How Forge works for the model. The smallest body returns a table: return {}

Environment Loaded by Lua state Notes game every game core Shared with the quest manager Sees forge.game.*, forge.sys.game.*. db the db core Its own Sees forge.db.*, forge.sys.db.*. forge.game.* does not exist there. The halves talk only through messages. auth nobody none The compiler accepts --out_forge_auth, no core loads these files. Not supported. Any other environment name compiles if you give it an --out_forge_<name> flag, and is never loaded.

Each environment body is a chunk. It must return a table or a class instance. The value is stored as forge.<env>.<forge name>, with no copy and no wrapper. If the name contains dots, the loader nests the tables (a.b becomes forge.game.a.b). The body runs with its own environment: reads fall through to the globals, writes to undeclared names land in the forge's own table and are invisible to quests and other forges. Three keys are set on it: __forge_ns (the forge name), __forge_id and __forge_file. The engine uses __forge_ns to know which forge a call comes from.

The game core loads forges before QuestManager loads quest states and runs boot hooks. Read it top to bottom: every forge has run before any quest state table exists and before any when fires. A when boot block can call any forge. The init script runs first, then the forges, then the quest states, then when boot. The load order among forges is the order the file system lists the compiled files. It is not sorted and not guaranteed. A forge must not touch forge.<env>.<other> while its environment body runs. Cross-forge calls belong in methods called later, or in when boot. If one environment fails to load, the load of the whole folder stops. On the game core initialization returns false and the core exits. On the db core the process returns 1. A load error takes the service down. A body that returns nothing compiles and fails at boot with Forge::ExcecuteSources result is nil for forge[<name>]. Each environment should return a table or a class instance. Always return a table, even if it is {}: a failed db half stops the db core. A syntax or runtime error in the body fails with Bridge::LoadCode Error loading code [<path>]: <error>. Changing a forge means restarting the core. There is also no per-forge teardown hook.

Each forge gets its own require. Its module cache starts as a copy of whatever the global package.loaded held when that forge loaded, and every module first required inside a forge is loaded once per forge. Two forges that require the same module get two tables. Top-level globals of that module go into the requiring forge. Modules the main state loaded before the forges (the Penlight modules pl.dir, pl.path, the protobuf runtime) are the same table everywhere. Shared state across forges goes through _G. Reads fall through to the real globals, so a table anchored on _G is one physical table for everyone: _G.registry = _G.registry or {} local M = {} M.registry = _G.registry return M A plain global assignment inside a forge (function example(...)) lands in that forge's environment. Quests and other forges do not see it. forge_helper must be required inside the forge, for the reason given in its section.

A forge file runs code in three kinds of place, and what you can do depends on which. Where your code runs Thread get_current_id() May wait (yield) May send (forge.sys.game.send_*) May register processors Environment body, at load Main thread 0 No Only through a method Yes A processor or an event-bus callback Main thread 0 No Yes Only if the function was defined in the forge A quest when block Short-lived quest thread, not a bridge coroutine 0 No No, call a forge method Not directly; a forge method it calls can A coroutine from bridge.coro.create* Its own bridge coroutine Its id Yes Yes, through a forge method Yes The rules behind the table: A when block runs on a quest thread that is collected as soon as the block returns. Do not create tables, caches or any long-lived state in it. State lives in the environment body, the hook only calls in. The quest thread is not a bridge coroutine, because nothing adopts it. bridge.coro.get_current_id() returns 0 there, so the helper yields cannot wait. with_timeout fails first with with_timout outside a coroutine; a bare yield_db passes its guard (0 is truthy) and fails in generate_receipt_token with Invalid coroutine_id: cannot be 0. To wait from a hook, start a coroutine and do the waiting inside it. create_with_player_owner runs the function right away until its first yield, then returns, and the hook ends while the coroutine waits. To send from a hook, call a method of the forge that sends. The send_* functions check the environment of the calling function. The hook has none; a method defined in the environment block carries it, so the call works. Capture what you need from pc.* before the coroutine yields. After a resume, the code runs from an input handler where the quest "current player" is not the hook's player. A processor or the environment body is on the main thread and cannot wait either. Start a coroutine with bridge.coro.create, add an owner with bridge.coro.add_owner, or use create_with_player_owner. Owners decide what dies when. A coroutine owned by a player is closed by the disconnect sequence, and its pending wait resumes with (nil, false). Tie every coroutine that waits on a player to that player, and always set a timeout.

When a player disconnects, in this order: The save event fires on the event bus (ON_PLAYER_SAVE). when logout runs, while the character still exists. The player's owned coroutines are closed. A wait still pending resumes with (nil, false). forge.sys.game.char_manager.find_by_pid(pid) returns the live character or nil. A forge does not check that a stored pointer is still valid. A forge that keeps characters (a table characters[pid] = ch) must drop them in when logout.

Situation Result Error while a forge loads The service stops. Error in a processor, a callback or a hook at runtime Printed to the error log with a stack trace, the server continues. Compile: two environments with the same name in a forge Aborts: duplicate environment <env>. Compile: set_state(x) to a state that does not exist Aborts: state name not found : <name>. Compile: a reserved word (quest, state, with, when, define, begin) used as a name anywhere, environment code included Aborts with syntax error : <message>. The reported line is the end of the environment, not the offending line. Compile: set_state, setstate or newstate anywhere in the file The preprocessor rewrites the call in the whole file and quotes a non-string argument. Do not use these names for your own methods. Next: forge.sys API reference.

How the systems Universal Core stands on work, why they are built the way they are, and what they replaced. Each foundation also has a reference page in the docs with its API and usage. Luna: the framework that moves whole gameplay systems into Lua and Python, in seven pages. Policies: the decisions the engine stopped hardcoding, one registry per decision, and what is still in the engine. Affects: state on a character, its lifecycle, and broadcast as the channel that shows it to everyone else. Traits: mechanics instead of hardcoded bonuses, with the bump point that makes a bonus depend on the moment. Skills: one file per skill that the server and the client both read, the nodes a cast runs, who owns it, and how one cast reaches a map or every core, in nine pages. Player metrics: one catalog of named per-character counters that C++ and Lua both feed, and the change event achievements and the codex listen to. Virtual players: a temporary character on a map that never writes back, and the prize commit as its only road to the real one. The headless simulator: the whole game engine driven from Lua with no client, no socket and no database, and the two kinds of harness built on it. UCHTML: the client's markup engine: Jinja templates rendered into native UI, and reactive zones. Render pipeline: the client's frame as a graph of passes over one device interface, typed handles, a DirectX 11 backend, and the shader cache.

The Lua bridge owns the Lua VM used by Luna and provides a boundary between C++ and Lua. In the Metin2 mainline engine, quest execution centers on quest threads. The bridge adds tracked coroutines, persistent references, and dispatch context for work that crosses into Lua. Luna runs parallel to QuestManager. QuestManager owns quest state, drives login and logout quest events, and dispatches when blocks. C++ obtains the bridge through QuestManager, and both use the Lua state and native bindings. That connection does not give the bridge responsibility for quest state. QuestManager does not automatically adopt its quest threads. bridge.coro.adopt registers the non-main thread that calls it with the bridge; it rejects the main thread. A quest action is therefore not a tracked bridge coroutine merely because QuestManager dispatched it. The Forge setup and API reference cover the script-facing interface.

The bridge keeps a table of coroutine records, keyed by an ID, and a mapping from Lua threads back to those IDs. A record holds the thread and the information needed to manage its lifetime, including owners and timeout state. A running thread can ask for its bridge identity; an untracked thread has ID zero. This distinction lets the bridge find a suspended thread when an answer arrives without treating every Lua thread as a managed wait. Creating a bridge coroutine starts it immediately. The call runs the entry function synchronously until its first yield, return, or error. If it returns or fails before yielding, there is no suspended work to keep in the table. If it yields, control returns to the creator and the bridge retains the record for a later resume. Starting a coroutine therefore does not defer all of its work: side effects before the first yield happen before creation returns. An adopted thread gets a bridge record for the thread already running. Adoption and creation both establish identity, but adoption does not start a new entry function. The calling rules explain which contexts can wait.

An owner identifies a lifetime by type and ID. A coroutine may have owners, and closing an owner finds and closes its associated coroutines. A player-owned wait can consequently end when that player disconnects, even if the remote answer never arrives. A timeout gives an unanswered wait a separate time limit. Without either a suitable owner or a timeout, a suspended coroutine can remain in the table indefinitely. The flow shows the values delivered at the wait boundary. A normal resume gives waiting code (message, true). A timeout or owner close gives (nil, false): the flag is the second value. After a failed wait the bridge removes the coroutine, even if the resumed code yields again. A second wait after failure cannot be resumed. A receipt token connects a response to the wait without exposing the coroutine itself. The bridge stores the token with a coroutine ID and an owner type and ID. On an answer it checks the token and owner together before resuming the coroutine. A foreign owner cannot use the token to resume that wait. Tokens are removed when used or when their coroutine is removed, so a late or duplicate answer is dropped. This is a routing and lifetime check, not a promise that a remote peer will answer. The API reference describes the wait and timeout operations.

Each forge has a private environment in the shared VM. Reads can fall through to the global environment, while assignments belong to the forge. Functions retain their defining environment even when a different thread calls them. The Forge model explains the module cache and load order. The environment also carries the forge namespace. A callback or bridge coroutine can carry that namespace into a dispatch scope, so a log or error can be attributed to the forge whose code is running. The namespace is significant for routing as well: code that lacks a Forge environment cannot supply the same attribution as a method defined inside one. A quest action can call such a method without acquiring its own Forge environment.

C++ may retain a Lua callback after the thread that registered it has finished. A reference tied only to that short-lived thread is not a safe basis for a later call. The bridge pins the Lua object on the global state, then retrieves it there when the callback runs. Pinning keeps the Lua object reachable; it does not extend the lifetime of a native object captured by that callback. The following invariant ties the pin to the lifetime of the C++ handle: its deleter releases the pinned object. std::shared_ptr<uint64_t> PinScoped(const sol::object& obj) { auto id = PinObject(obj); return std::shared_ptr<uint64_t>( new uint64_t(id), [this](uint64_t* p) { UnpinObject(*p); delete p; }); } The shared handle keeps the pin until its last owner releases it. A long-lived callback can therefore survive the registering quest thread, while destroying the callback also releases its reference to Lua. Subscriptions use this distinction: their lifetime must be managed explicitly, as the event bus explains.

A dispatch scope surrounds a C++ call into Lua. It carries the forge namespace, dispatch kind, detail, and player ID on a thread-local stack. A nested call pushes another scope; returning restores the previous one. An observer can attach ambient state to the active scope, letting logs and diagnostics identify the Lua work responsible for the call. The scope has a precise boundary. C++ work performed after the callback returns no longer has that callback's scope. Protected calls capture Lua errors and can return a fallback to C++ rather than letting the error cross the boundary unchecked. The context makes a failure attributable to a forge and dispatch, while the protected call controls how the caller continues. See creating bindings for the binding interface and error handling.

An affect is a timed state on a character: a buff, poison, stun, or quest bonus. In the Metin2 mainline engine, behavior depends on server macros and switches, while visibility depends on an AFF bit and separate client tables. A visible state crosses several representations, and the fixed-size bitfield is finite. The affect manager classifies types as data. Broadcast sends affect elements to viewers, so a client can show a state and its duration without allocating another AFF bit. The overview covers the representation and setup; this page explains the decisions behind it.

Term Meaning Affect type The identifier for a kind of state. Several elements of the same type can coexist. Affect element One entry on a character, with a type, point change, duration, optional source, and optional AFF flag. Point The character property changed by an element. An apply identifies a change that resolves to a point. AFF flag A bit used for status checks and some client effects. It is separate from the affect type. Virtual character An avatar represented by a character on the server; its affects reach viewers like any character's and are saved to the session cache.

The server keeps affect elements in the character's list. The owner receives the elements directly. Viewers receive the AFF bitfield with character data and, for broadcastable types, receive affect elements tagged with the character's VID. AFF bitfield Broadcast affect element Carries Flags, without duration or source Type, point, value, end time, and source Reaches viewers With character insertion and updates On changes and on replay to a later viewer Drives Status checks and flag-based particles Per-type particles or bundles and target information Recovers from a missed change A subsequent character update carries the bitfield again A later replay or relevant change can restore state; ordinary updates do not resend the list A character update is sent when an affect changes a flag or movement speed. The two channels can describe the same state, but neither substitutes for the other: a flag supports engine checks, while an element carries the detail needed to show a duration and distinguish sources. The flow below follows an element from the server list to the two client representations.

The server sends an absolute end time. The client compares it with its estimate of server time, so changing targets does not restart a countdown. An end time of zero means infinite duration. Additions, removals, expiry, and bulk clears send changes as they happen. At the end of login, broadcastable affects are sent to viewers who may have seen the character before its list was ready. A viewer who arrives later receives a replay of the whole broadcastable list. Between replays, broadcast is a delta channel. If a change packet is lost, an already present viewer can hold the wrong state until a relevant change or replay corrects it. The bitfield instead rides character updates, so a subsequent update can repair a missed flag change. A replay is useful synchronization, but it does not turn every update into a full affect snapshot. The client stores elements per VID, keyed by type, point, and source. It counts elements per type: the first attaches the type's particle or bundle, and the last removal detaches it. An actor created after its affects arrive attaches the stored types; when the actor leaves, its entry is purged. Target information reads the same store. The client reference describes the registrations and interfaces. AFF flags have no equivalent count. If two live elements carry the same flag, removing either clears that bit even while the other element remains. The broadcast count avoids that particular problem for the visual attached to a type.

The affect manager holds sets for no-save, no-clear-on-death, and broadcastable types, as well as named sets used for classification and removal. This puts decisions about a type in registrations instead of scattering each decision across a switch. The sets are independent: a state that must survive death and remain absent from the database needs both properties. Classification and removal answer different questions. A good affect can survive a dispel, and a dispellable state need not count as a buff. Keeping those sets separate lets the engine ask the question it actually needs instead of treating every beneficial state as removable by the same operation. Registrations from Lua and the skill loader can exist before the configuration loads. The load merges them into the manager's sets rather than replacing them. Named sets used by the no-save or no-clear lists are expanded when configuration loads: adding a member to the named set later does not update the list that already copied it. A missing name or circular definition stops the load rather than leaving a partially understood classification. See registration for the configuration and registration interfaces.

A player can receive an affect while its database list is still loading. The manager queues that addition until loading and entry into the game are both ready. A caller adding an affect during that interval must handle a null return; it cannot assume the element is already in the character's list. Once loading finishes, pending additions are replayed, the affect event starts, and viewers receive the broadcastable state. The server counts durations down in relative time, while the client sees an absolute end time. Real-time affects also count time spent offline: loading subtracts the interval since logout, and an element whose time has run out expires on the next tick. Removal and expiry update the list and notify viewers. Some affect types also have engine-owned side effects on expiry, so removing an entry is more than deleting a row. Override makes identity important. The lookup considers type and, when present, source; the point can also be required to match. Without an exact point match, an override can replace the first element of that type on a different point. That matters when a single type contains both a marker and a point change. The behavior reference describes matching, loading, death, and expiry in detail. Source identity has a persistence limit. Logout saving skips sourced affects, while an affect saved when added can reach the database without its source: the stored row has no source field. On reload that source is zero. Do not depend on source identity surviving a save and load cycle.

A broadcastable type with an AFF flag can drive both a broadcast particle and a flag-based particle. There is no runtime guard against drawing both. Use a zero flag for a broadcast visual unless the flag is also needed for its status meaning, and check the client registrations for both paths. A missing affect-data entry can leave the target icon absent; a missing effect registration leaves the particle absent. The pitfalls and examples show the checks, and the Lua API covers script operations.
documents.s: The two channels can draw twice

documents.t: Luna lets a whole system (state, synchronisation between cores, a client interface) be written in Lua on the server and Python on the client, without engine changes. Luna runs parallel to QuestManager, which retains quest state and dispatches login, logout, and when blocks. The bridge runs alongside it. It is several pieces that work together; each page explains one. Page What it explains The Lua bridge and the dispatch boundary The single boundary every script call crosses, and the coroutines it owns Luna transport and protobuf One message layer for every channel, client to game to database How Forge modules work Stateful modules loaded at boot, written in the same file as their quest hooks The event bus Engine events delivered to Lua subscribers Luna on the Python client Windows registered as handlers for server messages Quest compiler, source maps and the Lua debugger Source maps and the embedded debugger Lua annotations and the generated stubs How the engine's Lua API is documented for the editor

The luna Python extension connects Python handlers to the network stream. It routes server messages by namespace and header, with a handler ID identifying a particular recipient. Python code interprets the serialized payload and controls the interface; the C++ network layer carries the bytes. The transport page explains the server side, and the Forge API describes the server messaging surface. Luna runs parallel to QuestManager on the server. QuestManager owns quest state, login and logout quest events, and dispatch of when blocks; the bridge runs alongside it. Client messages enter a Forge processor through the transport rather than changing who owns quest dispatch.

The sequence separates a window's handler ID from the receipt used to answer a waiting server coroutine. The handler ID selects a Python recipient; the receipt identifies a pending server wait. A message need not be a request waiting for an answer. When it is, returning from the Python callback does not itself send the response: the response must travel through the network stream with the receipt. A normal answer resumes the waiting server code with (message, true). Timeout or owner close resumes it with (nil, false). The second value is the success flag. A delayed client response can arrive after that wait has expired, so a client action and a server wait do not have identical lifetimes. The extension stores registrations by namespace and header, with a list of IDs and callbacks for each key. The callback receives the payload and receipt; it parses the payload as the expected message type before acting. An outgoing message supplies routing keys and bytes, while a response uses the receipt to address the waiting request. Handlers are registered under namespace and header, with an ID to distinguish recipients. The names have to match the sender's routing keys. A window handle is available during window initialization and can serve as the ID; a windowless object can use its own stable ID. The ID used for removal must match the one used for registration.

Registration holds a Python reference to the callback. This lets the network layer call it when a message arrives, but it also means that ordinary loss of a Python reference does not necessarily release the registered callback. Explicit unregistration removes the network layer's reference and prevents later delivery to an object being torn down. Window teardown can have a Python-side Destroy phase before the window handle itself is destroyed. Remove registrations at teardown as well as final cleanup, using the same ID in each case. Otherwise a callback may reach a window whose children or other state have already been cleared. Registration should happen once the handle exists and before the window depends on receiving messages. A window handle already exists during window initialization. Register at that point, before loading the UI script, to avoid a gap in which messages can arrive before the handler exists. Callback wrappers matter for both network handlers and UI buttons: button event setters store the callable directly, so instance methods need the UI method wrapper at the call site. A windowless recipient has no window handle. Its identity and lifetime still need to be stable for as long as it is registered. A catch-all client dispatch can also route messages to a non-window object; that path has its own lifetime and routing responsibilities.

The sender and receiver agree on a protobuf schema independently of the transport's routing keys. The Python side receives bytes and decodes them into the expected message type. A header that routes correctly does not prove that the bytes parse, or that the sender used the expected schema. Luna message schemas use proto2 field rules, and generated bindings supply the message classes for Python and Lua. Python imports the feature's generated module and the serialization utilities explicitly; the package alone does not expose the utility functions. The sender and receiver must use corresponding generated types. The serialization and deserialization helpers return None on failure after logging the error. Check the result before sending or reading fields. Passing a failed serialization result to an operation expecting bytes raises an exception; reading fields from a failed parse cannot produce a valid response. Empty payloads remain distinct from failed serialization. The network stream drops messages queued during the connection-in-progress phase. This applies to both messages and responses; the client cannot use that interval as a reliable queue. The interface should wait until it can communicate and handle a request that never receives an answer. Server waits also need a timeout and an appropriate owner, as explained in the events guide.

QC turns quest and Forge source into the Lua chunks the game loads. A single source can contain Forge environments and quest states; the compiler separates their output. QuestManager loads quest states and dispatches their when blocks. Luna runs parallel to QuestManager: it does not take over quest state, login or logout quest events, or quest dispatch. The bridge runs alongside it. The quest grammar includes a define preprocessor that replaces identifiers globally, so a definition can affect every matching use rather than a single Lua scope. QC can check input without writing output, accept several inputs, and target selected Forge environments; the setup guide covers the Forge compilation workflow. The compiler also produces source maps that connect generated code to the original source. This matters because the debugger sees the chunks that run, while you place breakpoints in the source you edit. The Forge setup guide covers compilation and installation; the environment guide covers boot order. The flow shows where the map is used. The server runs the generated chunks. The editor extension reads the maps and translates locations between those chunks and the original source; the server does not use the maps to execute the code. A map is meaningful only for the compiled output from the same source revision.
documents.s: From quest source to running Lua

documents.t: A breakpoint starts as a location in the original source. The extension translates it to a generated location before it communicates with the debug server. When execution stops, the reverse translation lets the editor display the corresponding source line. The mapping is necessary because compiler output does not have the same layout as the source. Paths are a separate part of the problem. The server reports the path by which it loaded a chunk, while the editor opens a local workspace. Path mappings connect those two views. If they do not describe the same files, a valid line mapping cannot identify the correct local source. Remote and local roots can differ without changing the code, but the debugger must know the relationship. QC writes a JSON map per script when source-map output is enabled. Its source-map working directory establishes the original-source base for the debugger's workspace; a separate remote working directory describes execution paths when deployment differs. The extension's map search location must point to the maps produced by that compilation, and its path mappings must match the roots reported by the server. A pre-launch compile task can keep maps and generated chunks aligned before attaching. It must produce and deploy the same output the server runs; regenerating a map alone cannot make old running code match edited source. Source, compiled chunks, and maps must stay together. Editing source without compiling leaves the server running the prior chunks and the debugger using the prior map. Inserting lines above a breakpoint shifts the source location without shifting the running instruction. Recompile and deploy matching output and maps before attaching again; merely reconnecting cannot repair a stale map.

The game and database servers embed LRDB listeners. An editor debugger attaches to the listener for the process being inspected. Each process needs a distinct reachable port; a listener assigned an ephemeral port cannot be attached using port zero as though it were the assigned port. The Universal Core editor extension adds source-map translation to the LRDB connection. The server initializes its configured listener at boot. The editor's uc-lrdb configuration attaches to the matching host and nonzero port, and its source-map and path settings tell the extension where to find and translate the maps. The extension also supplies its language-server integration for quest files. The client Python debug build starts a debugger listener at boot on the first available local port from 3000 through 3049. The debugger attaches to that listener; application scripts do not need to start it themselves. The listener exposes a running process to a remote debugger. Enable it only in an environment intended for debugging, not on a production server. The client Python debugger likewise belongs in a debug build: that build disables client process hardening and must not ship. A debug client also resolves Python modules differently. Loose modules beside the executable can override packed modules and be reread when their modification time changes. A regular client uses packed files instead. This distinction explains why an edit visible in a debug session may not be present in a packaged client.

QC parses the quest grammar and emits the pieces that QuestManager and Forge load. A successful compile establishes that the compiler accepted the source; it does not prove that a runtime event reaches the intended block or that a remote process answers a request. A breakpoint in a QuestManager-dispatched when block tests that path at runtime. The Forge examples provide a neutral visit counter for such a flow. The compiler stops at the first critical error, so a later error may only become visible after the earlier one is fixed. State names are assigned CRC32-based indices. Identical names are deduplicated, while distinct names with the same hash require a different available index. On a collision, the compiler increments the hash until it finds an unused index and emits a warning. A collision can therefore make an index depend on the other names compiled with it; the state name is the meaningful identity in source. For editor completion and type information, the language server reads generated Lua stubs. They describe bindings rather than executing them. Lua annotations and the generated stubs explains that boundary.
documents.s: What compilation can and cannot tell you

documents.t: Each page in the wiki is addressed by a URL following the pattern: wiki://p/[pagePath]?param1=value1&param2=value2#location p/[pagePath]: The logical path of the page inside the wiki’s structure. This represents where the corresponding .html file for that page is located inside the game client in the folder locale/[localization]/wiki. For example, if [pagePath] is items/details, the wiki tries to load locale/[localization]/wiki/p/items/details.html.

Query parameters are the part of the url after ?. In the page url wiki://p/items/belt?vnum=100 ?vnum=100 is the query parameter and allows you to dynamically select data to be displayed. These parameter are enbedded in the document using jinja2-context and cane be retrieved inside page using fun.getv(query:vnum) or fun.getvi(query:vnum).

Location is the string after #. It tells the wiki window, through UCHTML's main tag, where to scroll the target page after load. It works together with Grid System's id attribute: you can create an anchor using id attribute in any html tag you want, and it becomes a possible "target" for location. Example items/belt.html
Some data on top
wiki://p/items/belt#foo When the page load, it will automatically scroll to the .

The event bus lets C++ and Lua react to events within one server process. In the Metin2 mainline engine, a native event needs explicit paths to its consumers; the bus provides a local subscription boundary. Each game or database process has its own bus. Publishing on one core does not deliver to subscribers on another core. Luna runs parallel to QuestManager. QuestManager owns quest state, drives login and logout quest events, and dispatches when blocks. The event bus is a separate local subscription mechanism, not a replacement for those actions. The events guide covers subscriptions, available events, and usage.

A subscription associates an event name with a callback and receives an ID. The bus keeps subscribers under that name and calls them synchronously when the event is published. IDs increase as subscriptions are added, and the bus walks subscribers in ID order. Native and Lua listeners participate in that same order; the bus does not group all native listeners ahead of Lua listeners. The publisher continues after dispatch returns. A listener therefore observes the event at the point where the publisher raises it, not at an independent scheduled time. A slow listener delays the publisher and the listeners after it. Ordering between subscribers follows registration order, but that does not establish a cross-process order or make a local event into a message to another core. The flow shows the representations delivered during one local dispatch. A guard runs before its own callback and sees the same Lua payload. A false result suppresses that callback, not the event's other subscribers. The guard itself is Lua code, so the payload has already crossed the boundary before it can filter anything.

A native publisher provides typed event data. If there are no subscribers, the bus returns before converting it. If there are native subscribers but no Lua subscribers, it passes the native data without constructing a Lua table. Once at least one Lua subscriber exists, the bus serializes the data and builds a table for Lua listeners. The same table is passed through the Lua side of that dispatch. A Lua publisher supplies its table directly to Lua listeners. The bus also converts it into native event data for native listeners, using a known event's data type or a generic representation for other names. This lets the two kinds of listener receive the form they understand, but conversion is a real boundary: native fields must use supported types to appear in the Lua representation. The events guide and binding guide describe the supported interface. The cost follows subscription, not whether a guard accepts a particular occurrence. A Lua subscriber to a frequent native event causes table construction for each occurrence before its guard runs. Filtering in C++ before publishing a lower-frequency event avoids crossing the boundary for every discarded occurrence. Payload shape matters too: conversion probes field types, and nested structures require more shape work than flat data.

During a player disconnect, the game core publishes the player-save event before asking QuestManager to run logout quest actions. The save subscriber therefore runs while that disconnect sequence is still before when logout. The core avoids publishing the same save event again from the subsequent standard save path in that sequence. This order matters when a save listener and a logout action touch related state. The listener sees the state at the save event; it cannot observe changes that the later logout action has not made yet. A save event can also occur outside logout, so receiving one alone does not mean the player is leaving. QuestManager's logout action remains the place for quest logout behavior; the bus does not dispatch it.

The bus retains a subscription until it is removed. For Lua listeners the callback is pinned so it can survive the thread that registered it. The optional guard is retained with the callback. Returning from a quest action does not remove the subscription, and losing the subscription ID does not remove it either. Any Lua values captured by the callback can remain reachable for the same period. Removing a subscription releases its callback and reduces the count of Lua listeners for that event. When the last Lua listener is removed, native publishes no longer need a Lua table for that event unless another Lua listener is registered. A forgotten listener thus has two costs: retained state and repeated conversion on every publish. Pinning preserves a Lua callback, but it does not keep a native object referenced by that callback alive. The events guide shows how to retain the ID and unsubscribe. Cross-process communication uses Forge messaging instead; see the API reference.

Lua scripts call functions exposed by C++ bindings, but the language server cannot infer their Lua signatures from the running server. Generated EmmyLua stubs describe those functions, types, parameters, and return values in a form the editor can read. They provide completion, documentation, and type checking while you write a script. A stub is a description of an API, not its implementation. It does not register a function or run on the server. A binding can work at runtime without appearing in editor completion if its documentation is missing or the stubs are out of date. Conversely, a stale stub can describe a function that has changed. When the editor and runtime disagree, check that the generated stubs match the bindings installed with the server. The editor extension supplies the generated quest metadata to the Lua language server. The stubs cover the Lua surface available to scripts, including QuestManager's quest API and Luna bindings. Luna runs parallel to QuestManager: QuestManager retains quest state, login and logout quest events, and dispatch of when blocks; the bridge runs alongside it.

Every binding carries a documentation comment describing its Lua surface. The generation process turns those comments into stubs grouped by namespace, and the language server reads the result. The path from implementation to editor is shown below. Extraction has two stages: Doxygen turns binding comments into XML, then a parser finds the Lua documentation markers, removes escaping, and groups blocks into one metadata stub per namespace. Ordinary namespaces receive a class declaration and table initialization. The global namespace instead describes global functions and supplies the generic array type, so it must have a documentation block even when no other global binding needs one. The extraction filter controls which binding sources Doxygen sees. A new binding in a source that matches no configured pattern is omitted even if its annotation is correct; the filter must include it before regeneration can produce its stub. Regenerate after changing or removing bindings so the editor does not retain obsolete declarations. The comment records the signature and the meaning of its values close to the binding. This lets the editor show more than a name: it can distinguish parameters, return values, and documented types. Multiple return values are especially sensitive to order because Lua assigns them by position. A description that reverses them may look plausible in completion while leading the script to interpret a payload as a flag. Doxygen escaping is part of the pipeline. Unescaped commands can become structured XML instead of flat text; the parser recovers child text and warns, but properly escaped annotations avoid ambiguous output. Its line splitting also treats triple dashes specially, so literal triple dashes use the dedicated escape directive. For overloads, consecutive emitted signatures share the preceding documentation. That works only when the documented parameter names match each signature; different names need separate documentation. A new class or field block before a signature has its own documentation and does not inherit the earlier preamble. A dummy class can describe the keys of a returned table or the individual indices of a fixed array. When such a class has no emitted Lua declaration, a line-break directive closes the block so later annotations do not run into it. The binding guide gives the annotation form. Stubs also describe objects and enums exposed to Lua. Their declarations help the language server understand members and accepted values; they do not extend the lifetime of the underlying C++ objects or validate runtime state. The binding and its runtime contract remain authoritative. For the comment form and how to document a binding, see Creating bindings. The Forge API documents the callable surface and its return values.

Forge gives Lua process-lived modules alongside quest hooks. In the Metin2 mainline engine, a when block runs as a quest action. Forge adds an environment that can retain state and expose behavior across actions, without making that state part of a quest thread. Luna runs parallel to QuestManager. QuestManager owns quest state, drives login and logout quest events, and dispatches when blocks. A hook can call a Forge module; the module does not take over the quest or its dispatch. The Forge docs describe how to write and load one.

Forge environment: the private global table and module cache for one forge on one core. Quest thread: the thread on which QuestManager runs a quest action. Bridge coroutine: a thread tracked by the bridge for its lifetime and waits.

A .forge file can contain a module and quest hooks under the same forge name. The module defines the persistent behavior; the hooks give QuestManager actions that can call it. This keeps the point where a quest event enters the module close to the behavior it invokes, while each part still runs in its own calling context. The module returns a value to expose its behavior. A quest hook can call that value after loading is complete. The setup guide owns the file grammar and compilation steps. A forge can have game and database environments. They run in separate processes, with separate Lua states and separate instances. A shared name routes messages between them; it does not make their tables or local variables shared memory. See the API reference for the message interface.

The defining environment and the executing thread answer different questions. A Forge method retains the environment in which it was defined, but runs on its caller's thread. Calling it from a quest action does not move execution onto a persistent Forge thread. The sequence shows a login hook starting work that can wait while QuestManager's action finishes. The quest action ends independently of the waiting coroutine. A normal resume supplies (message, true); a timeout or owner close supplies (nil, false). The flag is the second value. The bridge explains ownership and receipts.

On a game core, initialization prepares bindings and runs the init script, then loads Forge environments. QuestManager registers and runs quest states after those environments. It dispatches when boot later, once boot data arrives. The database core also runs its init script before loading its Forge environments, without the game quest-state phase. The sequence shows the dependency boundary between loading modules and QuestManager's boot actions. A successful environment returns the value placed under its forge name. The loader stores that value directly, so calls through the exposed name reach the same object rather than a copy. A nil result or an error during environment loading fails the load and stops core initialization. A missing directory is handled separately; the environment guide describes the load rules. The order among forge environments is not guaranteed. One environment cannot rely on another having already returned its value while its own body runs. A later call or QuestManager's boot action happens after all successful loads. Forges have no per-forge teardown hook; their process-lived state ends with the process.

Each forge gets a private environment table. Assignments to globals in that environment land in its table; reads that are absent there fall through to the shared global environment. Native bindings and shared tables remain visible, but an accidental global assignment in counter does not become a global in roster. Functions keep their defining environment even when called from another thread. That is why a Forge method called by a quest can access its module's state and namespace, though the call itself still executes on the quest thread. The returned module is an explicit way to share behavior and state with other scripts on the same core. Each environment also gets its own module cache. When a module is first required inside each of two forges, its loader runs in each environment and returns two separately cached tables. A later require in the same forge gets its cached table. The cache starts with entries copied from the main state's already loaded modules, however, so a module loaded there first can be shared by all forges. This distinction matters for modules whose functions need a forge namespace. A forge can deliberately share a table through _G: the environment's lookup of _G reaches the shared global table, so each forge reads and writes the same object there. This bypasses per-forge cache isolation and makes changes visible to all users of that object on the core. It does not share data across processes. The environment guide covers module loading and the practical rules.

Code Execution and consequence Environment body Main Lua thread during load; it cannot wait on a bridge coroutine. Message processor Main Lua thread when a message arrives; work that waits needs a bridge coroutine. QuestManager's when action A short-lived quest thread; values held only by the action do not persist after it finishes. Bridge coroutine A tracked thread that can suspend and resume while its owner and timeout govern its lifetime. A when block can call a Forge method, but that call alone does not turn the quest thread into a bridge coroutine. QuestManager does not automatically adopt its quest threads. bridge.coro.adopt instead registers the non-main thread that calls it; it rejects the main thread. Adoption is explicit, not a request made by QuestManager. Login and logout actions must still finish, so a separate owned coroutine is the appropriate place for a wait. See quest events and coroutines. A long-lived module also does not extend the life of a native character or item. Keeping a reference past the native object's lifetime can leave a dangling reference. Store a stable identifier and resolve the object when needed; use QuestManager's logout action to clear any state that depends on the live character.

Symptom Cause by design Guidance A wait from a hook or processor fails Neither the ordinary quest thread nor the main thread is a tracked bridge coroutine. Calling context A direct send from a quest hook fails The hook does not carry the Forge environment and namespace needed for routing. API reference Another forge is absent during load Environment load order is unspecified. Environments and boot Two users of a module see different tables Each forge caches a module first loaded in its own environment. Module isolation A retained character reference becomes invalid The module can outlive the native character. Quest events A wait never finishes An unanswered wait without an owner or timeout has no automatic completion. Coroutine API

Luna routes messages between the client, game cores, and database core through one transport model. A message carries a namespace and a header alongside its payload. The namespace identifies the Forge; the header identifies the kind of message within it. Together with the input channel, they select the receiving processor. This keeps two forges free to use the same header without sharing a handler. The transport moves serialized bytes. Protobuf provides a schema that both ends can use to encode and decode those bytes, but routing does not depend on the contents of the schema. Sender and receiver must agree on the message type: a successful route does not establish that the payload has the meaning the receiver expects. Luna runs parallel to QuestManager. QuestManager owns quest state, login and logout quest events, and dispatch of when blocks. The bridge manages its own coroutines (a script thread joins them only by calling bridge.coro.adopt); the transport uses those coroutines for waits without taking over quest dispatch.
