For processor registration, send functions, and signatures, see the Forge API. A complete request is in the Forge setup.

Term Meaning Namespace Forge name carried with a message to select its recipient. Header Message kind within a namespace and input channel. Processor Lua function registered to receive a routed message. Receipt Token that associates an answer with a waiting coroutine and its expected owner. Handler ID Identifier that directs a client response to a particular registered handler.

The path below separates packet routing from the payload's interpretation. The lookup selects a processor before Lua decodes the payload. The sender object and routing identifiers accompany the bytes, so the receiver can identify the connection or character involved and, when appropriate, answer a request. Game-to-game, game-to-database, and client-to-game messages enter through different input channels; the same namespace and header on different channels do not identify the same registration. The sender differs by input channel: client input supplies a character, game peer and database input supply a descriptor, and database peer input supplies a peer. A database response may also carry a descriptor handler to identify the client connection that initiated the round trip; that identifier is distinct from both the client window handler and the receipt. The API reference lists the values available on each channel. Game-to-game sending broadcasts to connected game cores, while game-to-database sending targets the database core. The database can address one game peer or broadcast, optionally limiting the channel or excluding a peer. These choices determine which processes receive a message; the header still selects a processor at each recipient. The database transport reads its packet using a different framing convention from the other channels: its input starts after the packet header. The transport handles that difference, so feature code passes serialized payloads rather than constructing network packets. A processor runs on the main thread. It can handle a message immediately or start a bridge coroutine for work that must wait. Its return value does not itself travel back across the network. An answer is a separate message, and a request that expects one needs a way to connect the two. Forge supplies the namespace from the calling environment. That context matters: a quest hook does not itself carry a Forge environment, so a transport operation belongs in a method defined by the Forge. QuestManager dispatches the hook, and that method crosses into the transport. The environment guide describes the calling contexts.

A receipt makes an asynchronous exchange look like a wait to a coroutine without holding up the main thread. The sequence shows the roles of the processor and the waiting coroutine. The diagram shows a successful answer. The receipt identifies the wait and the expected owner of the answer. Validation prevents an unrelated sender from completing it. Once a wait expires or its owner closes, a late answer cannot resume that coroutine. An answer is not a guarantee that the remote operation did or did not happen before the timeout; application state must account for that uncertainty. A normal resume returns (message, true) to the waiting code. A timeout or owner close returns (nil, false): the success flag is the second value. Collection is different from a single-answer wait: it gathers replies until its timeout and returns a table of answers. See the API reference for the precise return values and the events guide for owned waits. Ownership ties a coroutine's lifetime to an entity such as a player or peer. A player-owned wait can finish when the player disconnects instead of retaining work indefinitely. A timeout also bounds a wait when a remote process never answers. After a failed wait the coroutine is removed, so it cannot rely on a second wait being resumed in the same coroutine.

A server response can carry a client handler ID in addition to its namespace and header. The client uses it to choose a registered Python recipient. A receipt serves a different purpose: it connects a reply to a server coroutine waiting for it. Confusing the two can deliver a message to a window without completing the wait, or complete a wait without addressing the intended window. A player save also has a lifetime boundary. Virtual players can represent offline state without writing it to the real database. The virtual-player save cache intercepts such saves and retains their state instead of executing the database send; if the character cannot be resolved, the save must be skipped. See player virtualization for that contract. The helper module must be loaded inside a Forge environment. Loading it in the main state caches functions without the Forge namespace, so later sends lack the context needed for routing. The environment guide explains the module boundary. The Python client page explains handler lifetime and decoding. The same payload contract applies on both sides: serialization can fail, a received payload can be malformed, and a compatible routing key alone does not validate its contents. A receiver must handle decoding failure before using the result.

Player metrics give per-character measurements shared names. In the Metin2 mainline engine, separate counters need separate storage and read paths. Here a declaration defines how a metric is collected, and a catalog holds the declarations. A consumer can read a value or subscribe to changes without giving the counting machinery its own vocabulary.

Term Meaning Declaration A named metric's source, aggregation, and options. Catalog The collection of declarations. Seeded The metric was ever written for this character. Block The per-character record of metric values. Dirty queue The queue of characters with unpublished changes. Heartbeat The periodic game-core tick. Sweep The pass that drains the dirty queue each heartbeat and publishes the change event. Virtual session A session described in player virtualization. Predicate A Lua function named in where.predicate that is called last. Signal A native event with operands that can feed metrics. Push A call that supplies a value or key to a metric. Consumer Code that reads metrics or subscribes to changes.

The engine reads and validates metrics.yaml at boot. Forges load first and register predicates in the global METRIC_PREDICATES table, so the validator can resolve them. A refused file declaration fails boot rather than leaving a partially loaded catalog that counts incorrectly. These declarations show the difference between filtering a signal and supplying keys through custom pushes: metrics: kill.stone: { from: kill, where: { type: [STONE] }, agg: count } region.visited: { from: custom, agg: distinct, domain: { kind: map, max_keys: 256 } } A metric stores a scalar or a set of integer keys. Aggregations retain counts, sums, extremes, or distinct membership; they provide no reset operation. The seeded state distinguishes an unwritten value from a written zero, which matters for a minimum. A bad push cannot be undone through the metrics API. The YAML and Lua declaration paths share a validator. Custom metrics can be pushed from either C++ or Lua; signals come only from C++. Predicates and every consumer are Lua. Moving a custom push between languages does not change the metric's declaration. The declaration reference and API cover the available fields and calls.
documents.s: Declarations fix the meaning of a name

documents.t: The native sites provide signals and direct pushes. A signal lets several declarations filter the same event; a push names the custom metric directly. Registration Native site kill A qualifying death. damage A qualifying hit. skill A skill use. item_use A successful item use. Three push sites Currency handling pushes peak balances. One push site A crafting site records an attempt. One push site A catch counter records a catch. One push site A pair-forming site records a pair. The kill signal follows the reward path for non-player targets, so its exclusions affect the resulting counts. The damage signal excludes targets such as fixed training dummies. Quest items do not emit item_use. The signal reference describes their operands.

The route eliminates work before entering Lua; the diagram follows a signal from its native site to a changed block. A signal mask skips dispatch when no declaration uses that signal. An inverted index routes indexed operands to matching declarations, alongside a list that always runs. Integer tests precede predicates, avoiding Lua calls for events already rejected by a filter. A predicate error is a non-match; after 16 errors that predicate is disabled for the process. Only damage supplies a measured signal value. Other signals supply one. A custom push supplies its own delta, so its sum and count both add that delta.

The manager owns blocks by player ID, not by character pointer. Each block tracks values, seeded state, changes to publish, and changes to persist. Publication and saving are independent. Saving sends changed values and newly added distinct keys; loading restores rows without marking them dirty. Dense IDs index the in-memory arrays, but the persistent key is the metric name. Renaming a declaration leaves its old rows under the old name. Undeclared rows are logged and ignored on load, while remaining in storage. A new metric has no automatic backfill, so an unwritten value reads zero. Blocks live on one game core; database rows provide persistent storage.

A changed value marks its block dirty and queues the character once. Each sweep drains characters in order up to a budget and publishes one synchronous ON_METRICS_CHANGED batch containing player IDs and changed metric names. A consumer subscribes to ON_METRICS_CHANGED and re-evaluates only what the batch touched; its own config naming an undeclared metric is that consumer's error, not the core's. The sweep clears the queued flag and dirty bits before publishing. A consumer can push during the synchronous event, so clearing afterward would erase the new change and prevent it from being queued correctly. Disconnect and flush publish pending changes for a character; the event does not replay offline changes. The event reference describes the payload and queue limits.

Signals observe the character as it is during a virtual session. Counting those events as ordinary lifetime measurements would retain values produced under the session's temporary conditions. The default gate therefore refuses virtual subjects. Only a custom metric can opt in with allow_virtual: true. Use it when the value describes the virtual episode itself and the code that owns the episode makes the push. A refused virtual push returns false without a log.

A metric declared after boot returns false from add and add_key for characters already online, with no log, because their block was sized at boot. See declaration order. Prefer metrics.yaml. Lua declare is safe only from a forge at load, before the engine reads that file, and only for a name absent from it. A name in both is a duplicate and fails boot. get returns zero for an unknown name as well as an unwritten value. Use declared to validate names and is_seeded to distinguish an unwritten value. A predicate must not mutate state. Errors disable it after 16 failures, leaving its metric unable to match it. A distinct set at max_keys drops further keys and logs the refusal. Size the domain for the expected keys. The dirty queue has a finite capacity. If it fills, the engine logs the dropped character; another change is needed to enqueue that character again.

In the Metin2 mainline engine, a character loads from persistent rows and normal saves write its state back. Player virtualization lets you change a character for a mode without writing that temporary progression over the real rows. A processor is a set of hooks registered for a map index that transforms loaded data. A virtual session is a character's session on a map with a processor. A prize commit is an explicit write of a selected result to real data; a small set of fields also stays real throughout the session. Start with the overview for setup.
documents.s: A temporary character on a map

documents.t: The load path checks the exact map index for a processor. A private map has its own index, so register its processor before a player loads there. A cache entry holds the virtual state for one player and map index in memory. A slice is a portion of that state, such as items or quest flags. On the first load of a slice, the processor can transform the real input and the result is cached. On a cache hit, the stored state is restored without another transform. Reconnecting to the same map while the entry lives resumes that state. The real player row is also retained for fields that must remain real. The diagram follows the load and save paths across the cache boundary; the prize commit is a separate explicit write. The entry hook runs when the client reaches the game phase; the exit hook runs on disconnect before the save chain. Entry runs again on reconnect, so one-time grants need the hook's fresh-hydration signal. Destroying a private map clears its cache; explicit clearing and a core restart also clear entries. A base map keeps its entries until explicitly cleared or the core restarts. Unregistering a processor does not end active sessions, which retain their reference to it.
documents.s: A processor on a map index

documents.t: The bulk player load carries the player table, items, quest flags, affects, and skill trees. Their virtual changes go to the cache. The quest data has separate character and account slices; the quest hook runs once for each slice per cache entry. On save, the engine copies live virtual state into the cache. It builds the database player row from the retained real row and copies only the passthrough fields from the live character. Passthrough means keeping data unchanged across a boundary; here those fields continue to follow the real character. The other slices have their own save redirections. There is no save transform: a processor shapes the input on load, and later saves preserve the resulting session state.

A processor cannot transform data the bulk load never hands it. A pet is loaded lazily at summon, per pet vnum, through a native C++ load hook. A forge subsystem is a Forge module that owns its own state and database table; it loads through a key-routed wrapper instead of the bulk player load. For a forge subsystem, with_load_cache calls transform_forge_load on a cache miss. A C++ processor can route a key to a handler with RegisterForgeLoadHandler. The cache holds a pet record per vnum and a forge table per key. Pet saves and forge saves through with_save_cache are redirected to the cache, with no save transform. A subsystem can instead opt out by skipping its load and save when the character is virtual; the battle pass does this. The shipped cached Forge instances are character titles and a hunting progression subsystem. The wrapper path shows why a subsystem's own storage still needs a door into the cache. See custom transformers for the wrappers and load hooks, and Forge setup for the runtime.
documents.s: Custom transformers: data that is not in the player load

documents.t: The fixed overlay is the set of real player fields copied over the transformed player table on load. On save, those fields are copied from the live character onto the retained real row. They include position, exit location, play time, inventory lock and password, and UI settings. A processor cannot override this boundary. Other player fields, including balances, can remain virtual. A stash holds items committed for delivery on a later non-virtual load. Stash rows are removed from virtual item loads. Safebox loads are refused and its saves are dropped. The reward enabler remains available and grants its drop and PvP affects; the corresponding eligibility commands are refused. The client shows the VIRTUAL_SESSION_BLOCKED popup for blocked client features. Isolation also needs gates at integrations with shared or external state. Quest dispatch can be restricted by configuration. Metrics are dropped by default, though a custom metric can opt in; the code that owns the episode must push it. Logs mark virtual activity, and rankings read the real character. See player metrics and the overview for the boundary details.

Each processor hook receives a slice and can keep, filter, or replace its contents. A missing hook uses passthrough. The fixed overlay still applies after the player transform. Processors compose through Lua inheritance. Slice Load hook Player table transform_player_load Items transform_item_load Character and account quest flags transform_quest_load Affects transform_affect_load Skill trees transform_skill_tree_load A C++ processor can override the same hooks; Lua processors use an adapter. There is one registration slot per map index, and replacement is refused while sessions are active. See hooks and records for signatures and return rules.

Writing a whole virtual slice to the real character would also persist temporary levels, items, and flags. A prize commit writes only a selected quest flag, account flag, or item. Items go to the stash for delivery on the next non-virtual item load. The commit is not a merge of the session state. A flag commit writes to the database rather than the live session copy. If the session must read the new value, it must update its own copy too. Commits are unacknowledged: a closed database connection can lose the write. See prize commit for ownership and delivery rules.
documents.s: The prize commit is a narrow path back

documents.t: A failed hook can admit real data. The adapter falls back to passthrough and caches the input. Check errors and test the boundary of each transform. Registration after load is too late. Virtuality is decided at load, so register the exact map index before players enter. Clearing a live cache breaks its lifetime assumption. Clear entries after the affected players leave; unregistering alone does not disconnect them. A new external store needs its own gate or redirection. The cache only isolates integrations that participate in it. See examples and pitfalls for recipes and failure cases.

Processor: hooks registered for a map index that shape virtual loads. Virtual session: a character's session on a map with a processor. Slice: a portion of character data handled as a unit. Cache entry: the in-memory virtual state for one player and map index. Passthrough: keeping data unchanged across a boundary. Fixed overlay: real fields copied over the transformed player table on load. Stash: storage for committed items awaiting a non-virtual load. Prize commit: an explicit write of a selected result to real data. Forge subsystem: a Forge module that owns state and its database storage.

A policy lets the engine ask an ordered list of registrations for a decision. In the Metin2 mainline engine, decisions like these are branches in C++. A registry lets you put a rule beside the system that owns it and remove the registration when that system ends. Each registration has a name, a guard, and a payload. The guard selects the cases the rule owns; the payload supplies an answer. If no rule decides, the call site applies its fallback. The Policies glossary defines terms shared by the registries.

Eight registries share this shape: battle arbiter, death manager, item use policy, spectator, party join policy, skill use policy, skill policy, and loadout policy. C++ and Lua registrations enter the same list for each registry. A registration returns a handle that its owner can use to unregister it. The name identifies the rule in logs; it does not determine priority. Payloads and fallback answers differ by registry. The path below shows where a decision crosses from the engine to a registered rule and back. A forge is a script package, Luna is the Lua runtime beside QuestManager, and the bridge connects Lua calls to C++; see Luna. A registry owns its native list without depending on Lua. The binding checks and pins Lua callbacks before registering them, so the engine can call them through the same interface as C++ callbacks. This keeps the call site independent of the rule's origin, but callback failures need an explicit fallback.

A registry walks its list in registration order within one core. Across forges, registration follows forge load order, which is not guaranteed. There is no separate priority field. Do not rely on one forge loading before another to settle overlapping rules. The dispatch rule differs by axis: a battle arbiter can pass to the next registration, death, spectator, and party join use the first matching guard, and item use and skill use stop at the first denial. Potion amounts can pass through multiple matching policies. Consult each behaviour page for its exact resolution rules. Scope guards to the cases their owners control. A broad guard can capture another rule's cases, and the registry does not resolve that conflict for you. Spectator and party join accept a native registration without a guard, which matches every case; battle and death require one, as do Lua registrations. Unregister a rule when its owner ends so that it cannot keep answering for a case it no longer owns.

A Lua guard that errors returns false: its registration does not vote. A payload error uses the axis's default, which may permit or refuse the action. A C++ payload has no Lua error path. These differences matter when a rule is intended to enforce a restriction. Registry Failure direction and call-site limits Reference Battle arbiter Lua payload errors pass. Absolute refusals run first; if the arbiter passes, the team session fallback runs before stock rules. A session groups participants for team decisions. API, behaviour Death manager A profile is validated at registration; the first match precedes the auto-hunt and normal fallbacks. API, behaviour Item use policy Lua payload errors allow use. Engine refusals still apply after a policy permits it. In a duel, the Metin2 mainline engine refuses any potion when no_duel_potion is above 0, and always refuses vnums 27863 to 27883. API, behaviour Spectator Lua payload errors refuse. With no registration, the default permits GMs only. API, behaviour Party join policy Lua payload errors use stock rules. Policy refusal precedes the remaining admission checks; hard checks still apply. API, behaviour Skill use policy Lua payload errors allow use. Config limiters can still forbid use on paths that would otherwise allow it. reference Skill policy Skill decisions use their own resolution rules. reference Loadout policy Lua payload errors yield no plan. reference A permission from a policy is not necessarily the last word. For example, battle's absolute vetoes cannot be overridden, and item use retains map and other hard refusals. The PvP arena is the native arena object, rebuilt from the mainline arena manager; it has its own spectator rule and restrictions at relevant call sites.

Policies expose selected decisions, not every engine gate. CanWarp, for example, checks conditions including an open exchange, shop, or pending warp. Lua can read its answer but cannot change it. When a policy appears to permit an action that still fails, check the call-site order and hard refusals in that registry's behaviour page.
documents.s: Decisions that remain in the engine

documents.t: Universal Core’s render pipeline separates the scene’s rendering work from the graphics device. Specialized renderers prepare draws and compute dispatches, the render graph organizes passes and their resources, and the rendering hardware interface (RHI) carries commands to the DirectX 11 backend. In the Metin2 mainline engine, a caching state manager and direct device calls share responsibility for graphics state, while particles draw one at a time. The RHI gives resource creation and submission a common interface; batching and compute paths let renderers submit work in groups. The normal forward frame runs through the graph. This overview follows its main outputs; conditional passes and dependencies determine the compiled order. The server is untouched by all of this. It is a client subsystem with no Lua surface, and work on it is optional: you only need it if you ship your own shaders or materials. Python reaches rendering through graphics options and ui.ShaderQuad; effect authors use effects and materials.
documents.s: The render pipeline: three layers between a scene and the GPU

documents.t: RHI: the rendering hardware interface, a device-neutral layer for creating GPU resources and recording commands. Render graph: the per-frame list of passes, each declaring the resources it reads and writes. Blackboard: a type-keyed store where graph-building code publishes handles for later passes to find. Transient and persistent resources: a transient resource lives for one frame and comes from a pool; a persistent one is named and kept across frames. G-buffer: the textures a deferred renderer fills with surface data before lighting. SSR, SSGI: screen-space reflections and screen-space global illumination, computed from the rendered frame.

Before graph construction, the application renders model previews and the map overlay. It then prepares the frame, builds either the forward or deferred graph, compiles it, and executes it on the frame’s command buffer if compilation succeeds. The normal path is forward lighting. Its graph imports an output texture or the swapchain backbuffer and obtains persistent scene color and depth textures. With the forward HDR target disabled, scene color is RGBA8_UNORM; enabling it selects RGBA16_FLOAT and activates tone mapping. The forward builder declares the following work. Declaration order describes the intended sequence; the graph compiler determines which passes survive and their execution order from their resource declarations. Cascaded shadows, when enabled and a map is ready, render the shadow maps used by the scene. Forward scene writes scene color and depth. It renders the sky, lens-flare preparation, clouds, map, actors, water, snow, and map effects in that order. Effect writer targets are set around this work. Ground decals and transparent map areas draw against the scene targets. Ground decals load the existing color and depth rather than clearing them. Forward effects render effects with distortion and selective-glow writer targets available. Forward post effects, terrain overlays, and optional scene overlays add their contributions. Scene overlays can include debug primitives. Resolve passes, when needed, resolve multisampled color and depth for later consumers. Screen-space passes produce enabled results such as god rays and volumetric scattering. Post-processing reads the scene and the available effect outputs, then writes the output. The deferred path separates material collection from lighting. It declares shadow work and a terrain composite, then writes albedo, normal, material, emissive, and depth to a G-buffer. A lighting compute pass reads those textures, visible point and spot lights, and available shadow and screen-space inputs, and writes a floating-point accumulation texture. Transparent objects, effects, and overlays still have forward passes after lighting. Deferred lighting is off by default and is subject to a compile-time guard.
documents.s: A frame, pass by pass: forward by default, deferred behind a switch

documents.t: A graph pass combines an execution function with declarations of the resources it reads and writes. Those declarations tell the compiler what must exist before the pass and which results later work depends on. A ground-decal pass, for instance, loads the scene color and depth and writes back to them. Compilation builds dependencies from reads and writes, propagates references from outputs and passes with side effects, culls unreferenced work, sorts the remaining passes, calculates resource lifetimes, and validates the result. A pass that has an externally visible effect needs that fact declared: a function that executes a draw does not by itself tell the graph why the pass must survive. If compilation fails, the application skips graph execution and finishes the frame. It does not execute a fallback graph. Diagnose the compilation error before assuming that any of the declared passes ran. The graph uses three resource lifetimes: Imported resources wrap physical resources owned elsewhere, such as the swapchain backbuffer. Persistent resources are named and retained across graph resets. A persistent texture is recreated when relevant descriptor properties, such as dimensions, format, usage, mip count, layers, or samples, change. Transient resources come from a pool. The compiler calculates first and last use, but execution acquires referenced transients before the pass loop and returns them after it. The pool can reuse a matching texture or buffer on a later acquisition; that lifetime calculation does not by itself imply aliasing between passes in the same frame. The shipped client creates no transient resource: every scene target is persistent. A type-keyed blackboard shares data between graph-building code and passes. For example, deferred construction publishes G-buffer handles and dimensions for screen-space consumers. Putting a handle on the blackboard shares it; the pass must still declare its resource access for dependency tracking.
documents.s: The render graph: declared reads and writes decide what runs

documents.t: The RHI device creates resources including buffers, textures, samplers, shaders, pipelines, render passes, and framebuffers. Descriptors specify the properties the backend needs: a texture’s extent, format, samples, and uses, for example, or a buffer’s size, memory access, and structured-element stride. Pipeline descriptions bring shaders, vertex input, topology, and rasterizer, depth, and blend state together. The interface names several backend types, but the device factory creates a DirectX 11 device. An enum value for another API does not establish a working backend. Resources use typed handles that carry an ID and a generation, so a stale handle never resolves to the resource that reused its slot. IsValid() only tests for the invalid sentinel; it does not prove the resource is alive.
documents.s: The RHI and its DirectX 11 backend: typed handles over one device

documents.t: A renderer receives a command buffer and data for its pass. The base renderer stores them, uploads pass constants, binds them, and calls the specialized renderer’s pass hook. The common graphics convention places frame context at constant-buffer slot b0 and pass context at b1. The 2D shader quad uses b13 for its own constants. These are conventions for their respective workloads, not a claim that every shader stage reserves the slots globally: particle compute uses its own constants at compute b1. The path from a graph pass to a draw crosses these boundaries: For a model batch, the renderer binds its textures, vertex buffer, and index buffer, then submits an indexed draw with an instance count and first-instance offset. The backend selects an instanced draw when either there is more than one instance or the first-instance offset is nonzero. The latter matters even for a single instance: it selects the correct position in the instance stream. The command buffer caches bindings to avoid redundant device calls. It also unbinds shader inputs that conflict with a resource becoming a render target, depth target, or unordered-access output. Resetting its shader-resource cache clears the corresponding device slots as well as the cached records. A direct device-context call can change state without updating that record. The next RHI bind may then be filtered as redundant even though the device no longer has the expected state. Route bindings through the command buffer and use its invalidation mechanisms when a direct path changes tracked state.
documents.s: Renderers, frame context and pass context: how a draw reaches the device

documents.t: The shader manager reads HLSL through the virtual file system, compiles it, and reflects the result. Shader content can live under client content paths such as shaders/ui/. A cached compilation is identified by the source bytes, entry point, profile, define names and values, and debug and optimization flags. Included dependencies have recorded hashes and are validated separately: a missing or changed include causes recompilation. The cache path also includes the entry point, so distinct entry points in one source have distinct cache files. Cache reading and cache saving are separate controls. Turning off cache reads forces compilation but does not, by itself, stop a successful result from being saved. When checking an edit to loose shader content, make sure the client is reading that content rather than a packed copy, and check cache behavior as well as the top-level source. A stale compiled result or a different source selected by the virtual file system can make an edit appear to have no effect.
documents.s: Shaders and the shader cache: what invalidates a compiled result

documents.t: Cascaded shadow mapping has capacity for three cascades; the default active count and the application’s configured shadow-map count are two. The two active maps hold disjoint caster sets: The character map holds nearby characters at finer resolution. The world map holds terrain, buildings, and trees over a larger area. The separation gives small character shadows useful resolution while keeping large world casters together. A caster belongs to one set, so it is not rasterized into both maps and combined with a coarser duplicate. A model shadow pass can collect instance data once for multiple views. Each view gets its own draw list indexing that shared instance buffer, because the instance data is the same while view membership differs.
documents.s: Shadows: two maps with disjoint casters

documents.t: Model rendering groups compatible instances into batches. A skeleton’s bone palette remains at a fixed GPU-buffer offset for its lifetime and is rewritten when its pose advances. Single-material rigid meshes can be concatenated at load, reducing the number of separate mesh entries submitted for those models. The effect renderer can keep particle simulation state resident on the GPU and use compute to generate billboard vertices. The CPU still handles birth, death, and texture-frame bookkeeping. A particle born in the frame supplies its initial state without being integrated immediately, preserving its birth-frame position. The resident chain dispatches simulation first. It then dispatches billboard generation over both resident-produced state and any CPU-uploaded particle state. GPU billboarding therefore does not require resident simulation. Before graphics consumes the generated buffers, the command buffer unbinds compute resources; the renderer then draws the generated geometry in batches. If the required GPU billboard resources are unavailable, the effect renderer uses CPU billboarding.
documents.s: Effects, models and the GPU: resident state and compute

documents.t: Forward lighting is the default. Deferred lighting, screen-space reflections (SSR), and screen-space global illumination (SSGI) ship off. Ordinary graphics options do not switch them on; only a debug build exposes a runtime control. Declaration defaults are not the whole settings story. Client settings apply volumetric scattering, volumetric rays, SSAO, and bloom after the initial render configuration. The loader’s fallback enables volumetric scattering and SSAO, while bloom’s fallback is off. Volumetric rays additionally require shadows; the unshadowed haze is a separate part of the effect. Bloom enable and intensity are separate ambience controls. Post-processing executes HDR-stage effects, tone mapping, and then LDR-stage effects. Scene bloom reads the full-resolution scene into a quarter-resolution bright target, then applies horizontal and vertical blur using two targets. Each additional blur iteration adds another pair of quarter-resolution passes. Selective glow is a separate, writer-fed effect: scene and effect rendering can write its contribution to a target for later post-processing. Its six-level down-and-up chain is distinct from scene bloom’s quarter-resolution bright pass and blur.
documents.s: Settings and what ships on: declaration defaults versus the client settings

documents.t: The minimum accepted DirectX feature level is 11_0. The client rejects a device below it because its shaders require shader model 5; a device reporting only 10_x is refused at creation, before any effect fallback runs.

Start with the graph: confirm that compilation succeeds, the pass survives culling, and its declared reads and writes match the resources its execution function uses. Check whether the input is imported, persistent, or transient, and whether a persistent target was recreated after its descriptor changed. For a draw that reaches the backend but produces the wrong result, inspect the bound pipeline, vertex input, buffers, textures, and constant-buffer slots. For compute-produced geometry, also check the transition from compute outputs to graphics inputs and the unbinding of conflicting views. The DirectX 11 debug layer reports binding and pipeline problems in client log messages marked [D3D11]. For a depth-only pass, omit the pixel shader when no clipping is needed, or use a shader with no color output when clipping is required. In-app RenderDoc loading is opt-in through UE_RENDERDOC=1. Its hook replaces the debug layer, so use a run without that hook when you need the normal validation queue. You can also launch the client from RenderDoc for capture.
documents.s: Diagnosing a frame: graph first, then bindings, then the debug layer

documents.t: A fullscreen draw uses the previous vertex input. A pipeline with no vertex input needs a null input layout. Leaving the preceding layout bound can retain its referenced vertex buffers and make the draw depend on unrelated earlier state. A buffer looks valid but compute has no usable view. A nonzero handle alone does not prove that the required shader-resource or unordered-access view exists. Failed view creation must return an invalid resource handle rather than let a dispatch proceed with a null view. A depth texture cannot also be sampled. The underlying depth resource must use a typeless format so the backend can create compatible depth and shader-resource views. A pass never executes. A pass whose writes are not referenced can be culled. Declare the resources its consumers read, and mark genuine side effects so the compiler can retain the work.
documents.s: Common traps: the failures that log nothing

documents.t: A skill in Universal Core has one YAML definition, read by the game server and the client. In the Metin2 mainline engine, separate records can give the two sides different values. A shared definition keeps the values together, while each side reads the parts it needs. The server runs a skill's effect tree during a cast; the client uses the file for presentation and its own checks. Sharing a file does not mean both sides have the same state. Deploy the same skill files to both, and account for values the client cannot compute when writing descriptions.

One file per skill: how the server and client load the definition and what each reads. Nodes and phases: how a cast runs effects and selects targets. Beyond the formula: formulas and the ways a skill can extend its behavior. Owners and cores: who owns a cast and how its effects reach across game processes. Policies: rules for skill variants, use, and loadouts. For the keys and examples, see the skill file reference.

Term Meaning Definition and binding A definition describes a skill or a named rule. A binding connects that definition to where it applies, such as a trigger event or a policy registration. vnum The numeric identifier of a skill; its YAML filename uses this number. Node One typed effect or operation in a skill's tree. A node can have children that run for targets it reaches. Phase A stage of a cast that runs a list of nodes: once per use, once per computation, or after the cast's victims are known. Poly A formula expression evaluated to a number, using variables supplied by the evaluation context. skill_k A formula variable for the skill's power, expressed on a fractional scale. use.victims A formula variable counting distinct victims recorded by the cast's entrypoint ledger. hit_dist The distance from the search center to a candidate, available when a node evaluates distance scaling. Anchor A position at which a timed effect stays and from which its position-seeded searches run. Sector tree The spatial partition used to find nearby entities; a normal search takes candidates from the performer's sector and neighboring sectors. Subject The character, guild, or empire that owns the skill's cast and supplies its owner-specific state. The performer is the character executing it. Core A running game server process that hosts part of the game world. Mesh The network connecting game cores so they can exchange server-to-server messages. Intracore A skill mode that authorizes a cast on one core and executes it on each core without a performer. Policy A registered rule that selects a skill variant, restricts use, or supplies a loadout. Resolution follows registration order. Forge The system for loading and managing Lua modules; skill policies can register through it. See Forge. Luna A Lua runtime alongside QuestManager, with engine bindings available to scripts. See Luna.

The headless simulator lets you exercise server behaviour through Lua without running a client or connecting a live server. It supports unit, integration and regression tests, as well as calibration against a measurable objective, such as a target damage range. game_sim is the game server built a second time from the same sources, with a different entry point. It boots without a socket, a database or a disk map. A Lua driver stages a world and calls real engine entry points, including combat and skill execution. The Metin2 mainline engine has a test server for testing gameplay in a server environment. The simulator adds a headless level where a driver can construct and observe a scenario directly. The engine is private, so you cannot run the simulator as a reader. The simulator reference describes its interface, and Write a cube describes the test harness.
documents.s: The simulator runs the game engine without a client

documents.t: Driver: the Lua script that stages a world, acts on it and reads the result. Boundary: a place where the engine meets infrastructure it does not own: network, database, disk, clock. Forge: a Lua module the server loads at boot and keeps alive for the whole process; see How Forge modules work. Cube: a driver script that asserts a specification and ends in a verdict. Face: one independent scenario inside a cube. Differential gate: a comparison of two recorded runs, not a pass or fail against fixed values.

The driver loads after simulator boot. It stages the actors and prerequisites, invokes engine behaviour, observes the result and decides whether the scenario passes. The engine executes its own rules; the driver supplies the world those rules act on. The call path crosses from the Lua driver into the engine and back through observations. The simulator substitutes infrastructure around the game, while keeping the gameplay path real. Area Runs for real Supplied or controlled by the simulator Gameplay Game sources, managers, combat and skill entry points Actors, fixtures and scenario state Lua and content Quest VM, forges, bridge and loaded prototypes Staged artifacts and boot prerequisites Network Packet construction and engine handlers Captured buffers by default; real links are opt-in Database Game-side requests and response handlers An in-process database supplies configured answers by default Time Event queue and character updates The driver advances pulses and global time World Engine logic acting on the staged world A scratch world rather than a disk map
documents.s: The driver calls the real engine through Lua

documents.t: The simulator stands on the same Forge and bridge machinery that exposes engine managers to Lua. The driver uses native simulator bindings alongside the ordinary Lua-facing manager and processor interfaces, delivers messages through engine handlers and inspects the state they change. Each forge has its own package.loaded, so a module required by the driver and the same module required by a forge are separate tables. Set up a condition through the engine and assert the state the engine actually holds. The reference lists the processor trap that follows from this.
documents.s: Forge and bridge carry the scenario into the engine

documents.t: More than 200 native bindings expose the simulator to Lua. They cover world lifecycle, characters and parties, combat and observation, maps and movement, wire and database operations, forge and quest boot, time, and other engine areas. The registrations are native engine bindings; a cube does not register them. The driver calls them to construct a scenario and inspect its effects. Their signatures belong in the simulator reference.
documents.s: Native registrations expose the simulator by area

documents.t: By default, the in-process database answers configured game requests and records messages that no handler claims. You can instead opt into a real link to a headless database core. That core runs the DB-side handlers, while a simulated SQL and store layer supplies the database beneath it. The database core's SQL wall asks a Lua scenario to claim and answer each statement. A statement no rule claims is refused with its own text, rather than receiving an empty result. This makes missing database behaviour visible instead of allowing the core to continue against an invented empty world. A real peer link is also opt-in. It lets a scenario exercise communication across a peer connection rather than only delivering a message to a handler inside one process. Captured packets and in-process delivery remain useful for inspecting the boundary, but they do not by themselves demonstrate interaction between separate cores.
documents.s: Database and peer links can cross a real boundary

documents.t: sim.step drives engine pulses, including the event queue and character updates. It does not advance get_global_time. A cooldown that reads global time can therefore remain in force even after many pulses. sim.advance_time advances global time one second at a time and drives the corresponding pulses after each increment. Use the clock that the behaviour under test reads: pulses for pulse-driven work, and global time for a deadline based on global time.
documents.s: Pulses and global time are separate

documents.t: A differential gate records observations from probes and compares two records. It has no expected value for each measurement: the question is what moved between the records and whether the declared expectations permit that change. A manifest defines actors, preconditions, actions and observations. The runner resets and stages each probe, observes before and after the action, checks liveness and emits canonical records. A diff classifies the changed keys against declared expectations. Comparable records need the same fixtures and build flavor. Scenario order matters too: a reset clears the scenario world but does not reset the process's pulse counter. A record must also avoid incidental identities and uncontrolled randomness that can change without a change in the behaviour being measured.

A cube uses assertions as its oracle. Its faces stage scenarios and check the behaviour the specification requires. Each face can fail independently, and the harness collects the checks into a verdict. A cube can exercise gameplay through the same forge and processor paths as the engine. Its assertions need to cover both the intended effect and the prerequisites that make that effect meaningful. A cube decides pass or fail from its own checks, but the runner, not the cube, applies the final verdict; the reference tabulates the rules. The cube guide shows how to write one.

A calibration pipeline uses an objective rather than a reference record. It runs scenarios and adjusts inputs until measurements reach a target range. The engine still supplies the behaviour being measured, and the scenario still has to establish that the measurement is meaningful.

A result is trustworthy because the engine is real. The risk is that the driver sets up the world by hand: the real engine can run over a state nobody plays and produce a plausible result. A differential probe needs a liveness assertion that fails if its action did not do the work being measured. For example, a skill probe must establish that the cast succeeded and the expected effect landed. A learned buff is not necessarily a cast buff; a character without enough resource may never cast at all. A negative control checks the other side of the claim. If a conditional multiplier is under test, run a scenario with the condition absent as well as one with it present. If both produce the same observation, the test has reason to suspect that the condition never took effect. Assert setup through engine-held state before asserting the outcome. A clean diff or a passing negative assertion over an empty world is not evidence that the intended behaviour ran.
documents.s: A probe must prove that it measured something

documents.t: The test server and its branches remain in the engine. The simulator adds a separate way to drive server logic; it does not cover a client. Client rendering, interaction and other client-side behaviour need their own tests.
documents.s: The test server remains in the engine

documents.t: A skill needs numbers, but a formula alone cannot express every decision made during a cast. The Metin2 mainline engine puts skill-specific interactions in C++ branches. Universal Core combines shared formulas with node data and optional handlers, so a skill can describe its numbers and make decisions at the point where they matter. A node is an operation in a skill's execution; a poly is an expression evaluated to a number. See the Skills glossary for these and related terms. Nodes and phases explains when nodes run. The skill extension reference covers the handler API and configuration.

A skill file stores an expression once. The server evaluates it for gameplay, while the client can evaluate the same expression for a tooltip. A description variable can refer to a node's expression instead of copying it. Sharing the expression removes one source of drift; it does not guarantee that both sides have the same inputs. The evaluator parses arithmetic and functions, then asks for the names the expression uses. Each side supplies values from its own state. The server can read the caster, a victim, and state accumulated during the cast. The client reads the player's available state and cannot know the outcome of a hit that has not happened. The paths share an expression but resolve its inputs independently: The server resolves caster and victim names in separate passes. Node and cast state are supplied between them. A reference to a node that has not run yet gives zero; an unknown node name remains unresolved. Cost and cooldown have no victim at evaluation time, so a victim value cannot supply a meaningful input there. A description can pin an input to a chosen value when the client cannot know it, for example to show both outcomes of a target-dependent formula. Some inputs, such as cost and cooldown, are evaluated by the client itself and cannot use server-only names. Validation rejects those expressions and checks description variables for unresolved or unpinned server-only names. See skill descriptions for the syntax.

The server and client resolve their values separately. Even a name available to both can differ if their state or accessor differs. Some point names read a server point map while the client receives a value from a separate accessor. For example, point_STAMINA can read zero on the server while the client displays stamina. A valid name is not proof of equivalent values. The expression evaluator also has failure behavior worth designing around: An unknown name in a node formula can read as zero. Description validation does not cover every node formula. Division or modulo by zero, an invalid root or logarithm, and a parse error return zero for the whole expression. Guard a divisor when zero is possible. The evaluator retains variable values. Skill evaluation uses a fresh copy so an unset name does not inherit a value from a previous evaluation. The shared vocabulary and its implementations are native code. Adding a derived name requires an implementation on each side that can answer it. A startup check compares the declared names with the client implementation, but it does not compare their results. Test displayed values against server results with representative inputs.
documents.s: Shared syntax does not guarantee equal results

documents.t: A formula computes a number from named inputs. A node selects an operation and its data. Ability scaling is data on a damage node: the engine adjusts damage using an attacker point and a target resistance point. This needs no script because the operation and its inputs are already defined. A handler is a Lua function attached to a node. Use it when a decision needs context or behavior the formula and node data do not express. A gate decides whether a node runs for a target; a damage handler shapes the hit before defense; an applied handler runs after an affect is added. An affect is a status applied to a character. The pre-defense position matters: increasing attack before defense produces a different result from multiplying damage after defense. A handler is called per node and target, synchronously within the cast. It does not define a new node type. Node types are native engine behavior: there are 24 live types, with four retired slots retained separately. Adding a type requires engine changes, while a handler extends an existing operation. The node reference lists the available types. For behavior that remains active with an affect after the cast, a node can bind a trait to that affect. The affect controls its lifetime. See Traits for that model.
documents.s: Choose the boundary for the behavior

documents.t: A node names a handler in the skill's configuration. At load time the engine loads the Lua module for that skill, finds the named handler, and records which supported functions it provides. During a cast it looks up and calls the function for the appropriate stage. The engine does not retain a Lua function reference across the lifetime of the Lua state. The gate runs before a node for each target. The damage handler runs only on a damage node, after the formula and ability scaling and before the damage resolver. The applied handler runs only after an affect actually lands. A stronger existing affect can prevent that addition, so an attempted application is not enough to trigger the handler. A gate sees the caster, victim, and skill, but not a computed damage value. A damage handler can change the pending attack and related damage properties; later defense and modifiers consume those values. These boundaries let a handler change a decision without taking over the whole cast.

A malformed skill configuration can refuse the skill load and stop the game core. A missing or invalid handler instead produces a log entry and leaves the affected node without the handler. Check the log after loading changes; a successful boot does not prove the handler was found. A gate error is logged and fails open, allowing the node to continue. A gate that returns no value is different: its result is false and the node is skipped. A handler function on the wrong node type is also ineffective: a damage handler is called only during damage processing, and an applied handler only during affect processing. A damage handler receives mutable state. If it changes that state and then errors, its earlier changes can remain. Calculate first and write the result only after the operations that can fail. An intracore cast runs on every core and may have no caster, so its skills cannot declare handlers that require one; see owners and cores.

A skill combines effects as a tree of nodes. Each node says what it does and can select who it reaches; a child runs from each recipient of its parent. Universal Core has 24 live node types, including effects, population and timing controls, and visuals. The Metin2 mainline engine expresses a skill with a small set of point changes and flags; effects beyond those need skill-specific C++. Nodes separate the effect from its population and timing, so a skill can compose behavior without a separate branch for every combination. See the node reference for types and keys, and the Skills glossary for shared terms.

A cast, or use, is one execution of a skill. A computation is a traversal of nodes from a starting point, called its seed. The seed can be a character or, for some traversals, a position. The phase determines when a root node runs and what seed it receives: per_use runs once for a cast, starting with the caster. A node can still search for others from that seed. per_compute runs for each computation. A server-resolved player cast has one; a client-resolved cast can have one per accepted attack packet. post_preflight runs once at the end of an ordinary cast, when the server's record of victims is available. It starts with the caster. Each phase starts a fresh computation. Otherwise a node could retain a seed from the preceding traversal and fail to run for the next one. Node identifiers are shared across the phases of a skill, so a later phase can refer to an earlier node's records. The end of a cast depends on its resolution. A server-resolved player cast finishes after its computation. A client-resolved cast waits for the client to report the end of the hit window; the server uses its own victim record, not the count in that report. If the report never arrives, there is no timeout that runs post_preflight. A mob cast finishes at its last scheduled splash. Put work that must happen when a player uses the skill in per_use, rather than relying on the final phase. The diagram follows the ordinary player path and the shorter event-triggered path.

A node's population is the set of characters it reaches in one computation. collect determines where candidates come from and whether to search around a center. accept filters candidates by rules such as their relationship to the caster and character kind. The collect and trigger reference lists the fields and defaults. The seed is the starting point, not necessarily the final population. A node can act on the seed, search around it, or use another source. A search can also choose a different center. For example, a child can be seeded by its parent's recipient while measuring distance from the caster or the computation's original seed. For an ordinary character-seeded collection, the order matters: A caster source selects the caster directly. Otherwise, the seed is considered first. If the seed is enabled and fails the acceptance test, the node stops; its search does not rescue it. An accepted seed is collected before search results and consumes a slot in the search limit. The search filters and orders candidates, then takes up to the remaining limit. If the seed should only be the center for a search, disable its acceptance with accept.seed: false. With no search, that leaves nobody to collect. The caster is excluded from searches by default; including the caster in a search is a separate choice from allowing the caster as the seed. Search reach has two parts. The center sets where distance is measured, but the default character-seeded sweep draws candidates from the performer's sector tree, the spatial index for nearby characters, and neighboring sectors. A map-wide collection uses a different sweep. Moving the center far away does not move that sweep, so a distant center can find few or no candidates. A position-seeded traversal sweeps around its position. For wider reach, see Every core.
documents.s: A node collects before it acts

documents.t: The dispatcher collects a node's population, then processes each recipient. A gate or a supported success roll can stop the node for that recipient. The node's effect runs next; only a successful result allows its children to run. Each child gets the parent's recipient as its seed and collects its own population. A child without a separate search can act on that recipient. A child with a search can instead find a new population around each parent recipient. The latter can multiply work and reach the same character through more than one parent recipient. The traversal is depth-first for ordinary nodes. A child's collection state is reset for each parent recipient, so a per-victim collection limit on the child does not impose a single shared limit across all of those child traversals. Nesting describes population as well as order. This flow shows the distinction between an ordinary child traversal and a timed node that schedules its children.
documents.s: Children run once per parent recipient

documents.t: A timed node hands its children to a run that executes later. Each collected recipient can carry a separate run. The run retains the cast that created it, including the state needed by its nodes, even when the skill instance points at a newer cast. The skill definition itself is shared and read-only. Some timed nodes need two populations. Their own collect and accept select the carriers; targets defines the population a timed attack searches for as it fires or chains. Those timed attacks require a target search. A carrier is therefore not automatically the character that receives every later effect. A skill can have several live runs. Ending one does not turn the skill off while others remain. Turning the skill off cancels its live runs and removes its associated caster affect; caster death stops only runs configured to stop on death. An affect is a timed state on a character; see affects for its lifecycle.
documents.s: Timed nodes keep a cast alive

documents.t: The cast keeps an entrypoint ledger for victims claimed through the client attack path. resolve.bound limits those claims and hits per victim at that entrypoint. For a server-resolved cast, that bound does not limit the node's search population. Use the search limit when the collection itself must stop at a given number. A separate collection ledger records what a node collects. Its per-victim count and cooldown can limit repeat collections by that node. A zero count limit expresses no cap from that rule; it does not mean one. The scopes matter: a packet bound, a node's collection limit, and the reset of a child's state per parent recipient answer different questions.

A trigger connects a native game event to a skill. A passive skill can declare conditions for starting a cast, and an off trigger can end an active skill. The event provides context, which can include the other character involved, called the trigger subject. A node can collect that subject, or a triggered cast can use it as its computation seed where configured. The trigger path checks the learned skill, conditions, instance, and cooldown. It does not take the ordinary player-use path, so it does not pay that path's cost or consult its use policy. A triggered cast runs per_use and one per_compute, but does not run post_preflight. An invalid trigger subject can prevent a subject-seeded cast from computing. A frequently fired event needs an appropriate cooldown if repeated execution is unwanted. Triggered effects can themselves cause events and start other triggers; nesting is capped at 8. An unknown event name can be accepted into the trigger map yet never fire, while an unknown condition fails when evaluated. The reference lists supported events and conditions.
documents.s: Triggers enter without a player press

documents.t: A node type is part of the engine's closed set. An unknown or retired type prevents the new skill table from building. At boot, a failed build stops the core; on reload, the previous table remains in place. This keeps a malformed replacement from leaving a partially loaded table, but it also means one invalid skill can block the whole update.
documents.s: Load failures protect the skill table

documents.t: One skill file gives the server and the client a shared definition. The Metin2 mainline engine keeps skill data in separate server and client records, so values such as cost and range can disagree. A shared file puts those values in one place while leaving each side responsible for its own decisions. A vnum is the numeric identifier of a skill. Its definition lives in conf/skill/<vnum>.ucskill.yaml. The Skills index has a glossary of the terms used throughout this series. For the keys and authoring details, use the skill file reference.
documents.s: One file per skill, read by the server and the client

documents.t: The file describes the skill's rules and the work it performs. Its root holds shared values such as range, cost, and cooldown. The client: block holds presentation information such as the icon and motion. The server does not read that block, so a rule placed only there cannot govern a cast. A node is an operation in the skill's execution tree. The server builds the tree and runs it during a cast; the client does not execute it. The file also describes how targets are resolved. Nodes and phases explains how the tree runs. The same definition crosses a deployment boundary: the game core loads it from its configuration, and the client reads a copy in its pack. Shared formula and flag handling give both readers a common vocabulary, but they do not make the copies update together. A server-only deployment can leave the client displaying and checking old values. The diagram follows the definition to its two readers and the separate words used by the tooltip.

A prerequisite is a skill and level required before another skill can be learned. The server reads the root prerequisite: {vnum, level} and enforces that requirement. The client does not read prerequisite: it reads the flat root keys preSkill and preSkillLevel to set its requirement UI. When the requirement must appear in the client UI, write both forms with matching skill and level values. Writing only the client keys can display a requirement that the server does not enforce; writing only prerequisite enforces it without setting that client UI.

Each game core loads the skill directory and builds a replacement table. If a file fails validation, the replacement is rejected as a whole. At boot, failure stops the core. On reload, the previous table remains in use and the error is logged. A reload that appears to have no effect may therefore have failed; check the log before assuming the edited values are active. The client loads its own copy and reads only the parts it needs. A malformed client entry can be dropped even when the server accepts the file, because the two readers do not consume identical fields. A valid server load is not proof that the client's icon, requirements, or checks are correct. The client searches for skill files by vnum within a fixed range, while the character's skill storage has its own limit. A definition that the server can load is not necessarily discoverable by the client or grantable to a character. The file reference gives the limits and loader errors.
documents.s: Loading keeps the server table whole

documents.t: A poly is a formula evaluated using skill and character values. A tooltip can show a number derived from a poly in the skill file instead of carrying a second copy of the formula. The localized description supplies the words; named description variables connect those words to values in the definition. This lets a formula change without requiring the same change in each translation. The server validates description variables when it builds the skill, including whether a reference resolves and whether the client can evaluate the needed inputs. The client uses the variables to render the tooltip. Some values require server-held state and are resolved by the server for display. The descriptions reference covers the authoring and delivery details. The connection prevents a copied formula from drifting, but it does not prove that the sentence describes the number correctly. A literal value still needs manual maintenance, and a mismatch between a sentence's variable names and the definition can leave text or values unused. Check the tooltip and client log after changing either side.

A policy selects a variant of a skill definition for a context. The selected variant can change values while retaining the same localized description; its description variables resolve against that variant. When more than one policy is active, selection follows registration order. See skill policies for how variants are selected. Sharing a definition removes copies of the rules, not the need to verify each reader. Keep the server and client copies aligned, author both prerequisite forms when the UI needs them, and inspect the rendered description as well as the server load result.

The engine should be solid, lean and tested. Gameplay should be free, easy to author and driven by what players actually do. Everything in Universal Core follows from keeping those two apart. My rule is blunt. If a piece of code is not a fundamental ground truth, it leaves the engine and comes back as a pluggable policy or hook. Whether a player may join a party, whether someone can warp, how a damage modifier stacks, how a skill is authored, what a bonus does: none of these belong in the Metin2 mainline engine. The engine defines how people author and express those concepts. It does not decide them. I am writing this for three readers. My team, so we share one picture. Other server operators, who may find something to borrow. And engine authors, who may want to see where the line between engine and gameplay can sit.

The Metin2 mainline engine ships a fixed set of subsystems, and every new feature becomes another C++ subsystem next to them. Each one is a small project: write it, test it by hand, debug it in production. Nothing can be isolated or built as a module. When a feature is retired, pieces of it stay behind and rot in the tree. A new subsystem breaks an old one, and the symptom is usually a crash far from the cause. The quest system does not help. It is made for simple quests: go there, kill this, drop that. Anything more stateful, more collaborative, more server-wide, or with a real interface, has to become C++. The scripting layer also leaks into the engine: guards so scripters cannot nest events into a crash, flags around calls that are harmless in one place and fatal in another. The engine fills with hooks shaped like the last feature that needed them. Each hook is reasonable alone. Attack rules are open to every code path, so a seasonal event can break normal combat. Character state lives in a fixed set of flags that only a source edit can widen. Together the hooks make a system with no clear boundary: some logic is visible to the people writing content, some is hidden in C++, and nobody has an overview of how it really behaves. Better hooks do not repair that. What has to change is what the engine is for.
documents.s: What goes wrong in the engine

documents.t: Quest scripting is short-lived by design. A script runs, yields, and is gone, all inside one shared state. A subsystem with memory, several cores and a client to talk to does not fit that shape. So gameplay moves up from the engine to a structured and deliberately limited language. Luna is the layer that lets whole gameplay systems live in Lua on the server and Python on the client. Forge is how those systems are written: a subsystem with its own state, its own lifetime and its own boundary. The engine is left with mechanisms such as registries, dispatch and transport. The quest system did not go away. It still runs, in parallel, and it is still the right tool when a script is tied to one player. A Forge system is the right tool for a subsystem with state, several cores and a client interface. C++ is for hot paths, and for the moments when the engine itself has to learn something new. Three tools, each with a reason. The depth is in Luna.

A scripting language does not help if every feature still needs C++ glue. In the mainline engine each new message means a struct, a packet header, a handler on the server and a parser on the client. Universal Core hides the transport. Lua and Python exchange protobuf messages directly. The launcher routes an incoming message to the Python window that registered for it, and the server never reads a packet by header. A new feature needs a namespace, a header and a message definition. The transport is no longer something a feature author writes. That is what lets gameplay live outside the engine in practice and not only in principle. The blog post on the transport layer walks through it.

On that foundation the question is no longer how to move one subsystem out. It is what shared mechanisms a whole family of features needs, built once. Policies. An engine decision, such as whether an attack is allowed, is asked of a registry. C++ and Lua register answers, scoped to what they apply to. The engine keeps its own refusals, and everything contextual belongs to a policy. See Policies. Affects. State a player can see, such as a buff, a stance or a mark, has a lifecycle and a broadcast. It does not depend on a small, fixed set of flags. See Affects. Traits. In the mainline engine a bonus is a branch inside a function, driven by a point type. Traits are a mechanics layer gated by affects, so a bonus is a rule that applies while a condition holds. See Traits. Skills. A skill is a tree of nodes in one file that both the server and the client read. The server runs the effect. The client presents it. See Skills. None of these is a feature. They are the places where an engine decision became a thing a content author can reach.

Some systems need a character to exist without being real: a practice room, a preview, a simulation. Virtual players isolate temporary state and commit only the results I choose into real data. A player can fight, try a build or rehearse a dungeon, and the database never notices. Player metrics follow the same instinct. A measurement is declared once, counted once and persisted once, and anything that cares can read it. An achievement is then data on top of a counter, not a subsystem of its own. Neither is a goal in itself. Each answers features that should be written without a new engine change, with a mechanism the engine offers to all of them.

When the logic lives in Lua, a deterministic test can drive it. The simulator is an agent's entry point to the whole server: it drives the real engine from Lua, controls the world and its boundaries, and produces unit, integration and regression tests. An AI coding agent does the work end to end. It writes the feature and the scenarios that test it. That works because Forge isolates the logic, makes it deterministic and leaves fewer edge cases. The alternative is a heavy, clunky C++ test that rarely gets written.

The same idea reached the client. UCHTML renders templates into panels, supplies them with game data and updates reactive zones. A template language embeds functions and logic in the markup, and that is the part a panel needs. The render pipeline applies the same idea at the lowest level: a render graph over a hardware interface, for performance, quality and extensibility. In the engine, a foundation is worth rebuilding when everything above it keeps asking for more.

Moving logic across the boundary adds risks. When C++ calls into Lua, a dead instance or a missing method can crash the server. So interfaces are validated strictly, and calls into Lua go through protected paths. The garbage collector can also collect something a system still depends on, and the system stops without a crash. That is why objects are pinned. Some things do not move at all. A mechanic built on a spatial grid with storage and broadcast needs C++ to own the cells, their persistence and what is sent to clients. Only then can Lua own the rules. The approach fails when the engine lacks the mechanism, and that is the signal to extend the engine.

A C++ subsystem is built one at a time, and testing and debugging dominate. A new system beside what exists, instead of inside it, takes a fraction of that. A queue with its own rules, or a mode that extends another, feels like writing a child class. The engine is rarely touched for quests, interfaces, upgrades or progression. Gameplay becomes a fast, disposable layer that a team can rewrite without fear, and the core stays a stable foundation instead of a bottleneck. The posts that show the work are From messy C++ subsystems to Forge and Hiding the transport layer. The foundations explain how each system works, and why.

A skill cast needs a body to perform it and an owner to answer for it. For an ordinary character skill these are the same character. A guild or empire skill belongs to a shared owner even when a member presses the button. The Metin2 mainline engine ties the cast to the character; the subject model lets shared skills use shared level, authority, cost, cooldown, and target relations. The Skills glossary defines the terms used throughout this series. The skill file reference covers the keys and their exact rules.

The performer is the character who starts a cast. The subject, or owner, holds the skill and supplies the rules that belong to it. The performer supplies a position and a body when the cast needs them. A subject can be a character, a guild, or an empire. The skill's subject selects the owner kind. If it is absent, a guild skill defaults to a guild subject and other skills to a character subject. The client uses the subject kind to select the store from which it displays the skill level; the server uses it to construct the owner for the cast. A shared skill's level is the owner's level in that skill, not the performer's character skill level. The owner answers whether the performer may cast, which level applies, where the cooldown is stored, how the cost is paid, and whether a candidate is an ally or an enemy. A guild cast also requires the performer's guild skill authority. An empire cast requires membership and a positive skill level. Shared skills skip character-specific checks such as weapon and skill group, but use policies can still refuse the cast. A shared purse is not the performer's purse. Guild and empire subjects pay a shared gold cost; they cannot pay character HP or SP. A character subject cannot use the shared gold cost. Choose a cost compatible with the owner, or the cast is refused.
documents.s: The performer and the owner answer different questions

documents.t: Target relation is an owner's answer, not a universal definition of combat permission. A character subject uses the ordinary attack and buff checks. A guild subject treats its members as allies and a guild at war with it as an enemy. An empire subject treats characters of its empire as allies and those of another empire as enemies.
