A candidate without the relevant affiliation is neutral. For guild and empire subjects, enemy relation does not apply the ordinary character attack checks. A skill that selects enemies by owner relation therefore needs its use restrictions considered separately. See skill policies. A character's skill instance holds its level and cooldown. Guild skill levels and deadlines belong to the guild and are distributed to game cores. Empire skill levels and deadlines use shared server flags forwarded to the cores. Shared cooldowns use whole-second deadlines, rounded up, and do not vary with the performer's casting speed. Otherwise two members could disagree about one owner's next usable time. Shared state also has a cost. Guild gold changes are requested through the database core. An empire skill's purse deduction changes the local core's in-memory balance without propagating that deduction to the other cores or the database. Do not assume that this payment is a synchronized server-wide transaction.
documents.s: Relations and state belong to the owner

documents.t: A game core hosts part of the running world. A map-wide collector searches a map on its hosting core; it does not send the cast to other cores. It changes where a node finds candidates, not which candidates pass its filters. A child node performs its own collection, so a map-wide parent does not automatically give the child map-wide reach. See nodes and phases for collection and filtering. An intracore skill instead executes on every game core reached by the server's core-to-core mesh, including the core where it started. It requires a guild or empire subject whose state is available across cores. The authorizing core makes the use decision once; each executing core works with its own local population. The diagram separates the single authorization from the execution on each core. The resolved skill level travels with the cast. Each core uses that level even if its copy of the owner's level has not caught up. The origin stamps the shared cooldown once; receivers do not stamp it again. Each core enumerates its local players, so the combined roster covers the shared owner without applying the cast twice to a player who is online on one core.
documents.s: Map reach and core reach are separate

documents.t: Every executing core, including the origin, runs an intracore cast without the performer. This keeps the origin from using character data unavailable to the other cores. The subject can enumerate its local allies or enemies; a top-level node must use that roster rather than a position around the performer. A child can use a local target as its new seed, including its position. The loader checks that an intracore skill can run under those conditions. It rejects performer-dependent formulas, handlers and actions that require a performer's body, as well as invalid top-level collection. It also rejects a per_use phase, which normally starts with the caster, and requires per_compute nodes. Local victim data and subject data remain available. The skill file reference lists the authoring rules. An invalid skill prevents the skill table from loading at boot. A failed live reload leaves the previously installed table in place. A successful reload therefore matters separately from a successful boot. Damage without a performer has no attacker stats or killer attribution. The victim's defense still applies, but attacker-side penetration and pierce do not. This is a material choice when deciding whether an effect should run on every core or remain with a performer on one core. A performerless cast is held by the skill manager while it has live delayed runs. A delayed effect can therefore continue after the initial execution returns. Each core owns only its local execution; the broadcast does not move a character or a running effect between cores.
documents.s: Execution without a performer has limits

documents.t: A skill needs more than a formula: a character must hold it, be allowed to cast it, and use the appropriate version. The Metin2 mainline engine makes many of these decisions in fixed tables and native checks. Universal Core adds three registries so rules can select a loadout, restrict use, or choose a skill variant without placing every condition in the cast path. Each registry follows the policies model: a rule has a name, a guard that decides where it applies, and a payload that supplies the decision. A registration returns a handle used to remove the rule. Registration order determines resolution order. For skill terms, including vnum and character, see the Skills glossary.
documents.s: Skills: loadout, use and skill policies

documents.t: A loadout is a plan for the skills a player holds and their client slots. A use policy can refuse a cast. A skill policy selects a named variant of a skill for a character. These decisions have different lifetimes. The diagram shows the cast decision separately from the edges that update state shared with the client. The use policy is a predicate: the engine asks it when a cast is considered. The other two produce state that the client must also see. Their guards are sampled at specific edges, and the result is kept on the character. A condition that changes between edges cannot update that state by itself.

Native cast checks run before the use policy. If a native check refuses a cast, the registry is not asked; an allowing policy cannot reverse that refusal. The engine walks applicable use rules in registration order. The first denial stops the walk, while an allowing answer leaves later rules free to deny. The rule can filter by skill vnum before its guard runs. This keeps a rule for a small set of skills from calling its guard for every other skill. The same registry also receives mob skill decisions, so a guard must account for the kind of character it accepts. The decision carries a message key back to the caller instead of sending a message itself. Cast eligibility can be queried without a cast actually taking place; sending from the predicate would make those queries visible to the player. A failing guard skips its rule, and a failing Lua policy leaves the cast allowed by that rule. These failure directions matter when a restriction is required. The skill use policy reference covers registration, filters, and verdicts.
documents.s: A use policy can only deny

documents.t: A skill can define named variants as changes to its base definition. The server builds each variant when the skill table loads. At a sampling edge, it evaluates the registered guards and keeps the matching policy IDs on the character. The client receives those IDs and uses the same skill definitions to select the corresponding variant. The one-file model explains the shared definition. If several active policies override the same skill, they do not merge. The first applicable override in registration order wins; if none applies, the base skill is used. Multiple rules that activate the same ID leave it active only once. If two changes must apply together, define a variant containing both changes. Sampling happens on map changes, registration, removal, explicit refresh, and entry into the game. It includes mobs as well as players. When a guard reads state that changes without one of those edges, refresh the character after changing that state. Otherwise the server and client keep the previous selection even though the guard would now answer differently. Sampling avoids calling every guard on each skill lookup, but registration and removal re-sample characters on the core. Keep guards inexpensive and avoid registering rules for each individual cast. See the skill policy reference for the registration and refresh interface.
documents.s: A skill policy selects a variant

documents.t: A loadout rule builds a plan for a player. The first matching guard in registration order owns the decision; later matching rules do not contribute to the plan. The plan replaces the client pages it names, leaving other pages alone. With no matching plan, the ordinary client bar remains. The distinction between a slot and a held skill matters. The server tracks skill levels by vnum and receives a vnum in a cast request; slots are client presentation. Applying a plan changes live skill levels on the server and sends the slot layout to the client before the levels, so the client can place them. The engine keeps the previous levels for restoration when the plan is removed. An active loadout also lifts the skill group and specialization membership checks, while other cast checks still apply. Loadouts are sampled for players on registration, removal, explicit refresh, and entry into the game. A map change alone does not rebuild one. Refresh after changing any state a guard or builder uses if no sampling edge follows. A failing builder does not hand control to the next matching rule. The builder is called again at each rebuild, so it should produce a stable plan for the same state. Loadout levels are live character state: a normal save can persist them while the plan is active, and the restoration record is kept in memory. Use an appropriate player virtualization arrangement when temporary levels must not be saved. The loadout policy reference describes plans and their lifecycle.
documents.s: A loadout changes held skills and slots

documents.t: UCHTML is the client's markup engine for content-shaped panels. It renders HTML-like templates against a context a host supplies and turns the result into client UI elements. In the Metin2 mainline engine, a window takes three hand-written artifacts: a layout, client logic, and the data interface that connects it to the game. The quest letter has a fixed set of markup tokens. The data a window shows must be copied by hand or carried through shared C++ structures and packets. UCHTML gives content a template and a data context, so changing a page does not require a new hardcoded window for every arrangement of that content.

A host creates an HTMLLayoutLoader, gives it a template path and optional variables, and loads the page. The loader reads the source through pack_open, assembles the context, renders the template, and builds a tree of UI elements. The context holds the loader's fun and bonus namespaces, whatever data namespaces the client registers, and the variables the host passes. Injected variables are merged last, so a host can replace a standard entry. The template context reference lists the names. After Jinja renders the template, BeautifulSoup parses the resulting HTML. The loader turns that structure into its own UIElement tree. Measurement creates real UI objects for leaves when their size is needed; layout then assigns positions and sizes, and finalization completes the UI.

Jinja provides control flow, includes, macros, expressions, and function embedding. A page can share a fragment, select content from data, and call functions supplied through its context. A home-made markup language needs its own parser and conditional syntax, and a strict, narrowly supported one leaves authors without the linters and tooling an established template language has. Jinja supplies those without making every content decision a new markup rule. The Jinja reference covers the syntax, and the grid and tag references cover layout and elements.

A reactive zone limits which part of the UI tree an update rebuilds. A div or body with a parent, an id and a reactive attribute listing variable names is a zone. When SetVar changes a value, the loader renders the whole template again, finds each watching zone by ID in the new result, destroys that zone's children and builds new ones. The engine has a tree differ and stores virtual trees, but this path never calls the differ. The saving is in not rebuilding the rest of the UI tree; template rendering still happens, so the cost scales with the template, not with the change. A variable no zone watches, or a failed zone update, falls back to a full reload. The reactive zones reference has the rules and the batching behaviour.

A debug client builds a fresh Jinja environment and parses the source on every render, so edits reload. A production client with a template name uses a cached environment and a precompiled module looked up by the SHA-1 of the template name, so the source text is not parsed. The loader still opens the original template path first, so the module does not replace the file: both ship. See compiled templates. The source validator runs when ENABLE_WIKI_DEV is set. It strips Jinja directives and expressions, checks the remaining HTML, and stops the load on errors before any UI exists. It checks the source, not every result of rendering.
pack_open checks the pack and falls back to the filesystem. A disk edit can appear to do nothing when a packed copy of the same path exists.

A client embeds the loader in a window, configures its path resolver, and loads a template with variables. The host owns the surrounding window and the state the panel needs; UCHTML owns the rendering and the tree inside the loader. The in-game wiki, which feeds templates with generated game data, is one such client. The existing UI script loader can also construct an html_loader element.
UCHTML exposes its surface through Python and templates. It has no native registrations. Native registration Purpose

Hand-built uiscript windows remain the default for general client windows. UCHTML is the path for panels whose structure follows content: a description, a list of events, state shown to the player. A hand-built window can contain a UCHTML loader without giving up the rest of its UI.

The client runs Python 2.7 and carries vendored libraries for template and HTML parsing. Those must stay compatible with that runtime, and rendering a template and building UI elements costs client time. A Python 3 port is not on the roadmap.

A point holds a number. It has no condition, state, or moment at which it applies. In the Metin2 mainline engine, conditional bonuses require branches in the damage path or additional points. Traits add a gate that says when a rule is active, hooks that say where it runs, and state for values that change over its lifetime. A trait can reduce damage while an affect is active, count damage for a later action, or add a conditional bonus to a point for one calculation.

The affect is the attachment. When it is gained, the trait attaches to the holder. When the last affect of that type ends, the trait detaches. The affect system supplies cleanup, persistence, dispel interaction, and stacking. A trait does not remove its own affect by hand: end_self removes the gating affect and the gate closes as a consequence. See Affects for the affect lifecycle. A trait definition is the behaviour. It carries no gate and no numbers. A binding combines a definition, an affect type, and formulas with their numbers. One definition can be gated by several affects, each with its own values. Two things create a binding: the skill loader, for a skill node that lists traits, and the Lua bind call. Nothing else does. Anything that adds a bound affect opens the gate, whether a skill, a mode, or a consumable item. Equipping gear cannot: equipment applies points, not affects. When an affect is added, the engine asks a reverse index from affect type to bindings. If nothing is gated on that type, it makes one hash miss and does nothing else. The gate closes through one path on removal, expiry, bulk clear at death, and direct unlinking. Each holder keeps a trigger mask, the OR of the hooks of its active traits. A call site performs a bitwise AND against it, and the engine crosses into Lua only when the mask and the node's active flag agree. Every Lua call goes through one dispatch point. An error is logged as [traits] <hook> [<id>]: <what>, and the other traits still fire.

A trait can add a delta to a point for one damage calculation. A transient overlay accumulates the delta and the point read folds it in without changing the stored points, so a recompute never writes a temporary bonus into them. A nestable guard unwinds the overlay; bumps on the same point compose additively, so +40 and -20 both apply and both unwind. A bump is legal only inside a guard. The melee hit, the shot, and each skill damage node open one, and each fires the attacker's on_damage_dealt_pre and the victim's on_damage_taken_pre with the settled damage type. Outside a guard the call is refused and logged. The condition is read at hit time. There is no trigger for a changing value such as health, so the pre hook asks when it matters instead of a toggle that could drift out of sync: forge.sys.game.traits["define"]{ id = "wounded_edge", gate = { affect = affect.name_map.EXAMPLE_EDGE }, hooks = { on_damage_dealt_pre = function(ch, victim, dam_type, ctx) if ch:get_hp_pct() < 80 then ctx.bump_point(point.ATTBONUS_HUMAN, 15) end end, }, }

A definition subscribes by naming hooks; each is a trigger bit in the mask. The 24 hooks fall into groups: gate changes, the two point-bump hooks, transforms inside the formula, observers of a resolved hit, targeting, time, and events such as skill casts, buffs, debuffs, and heals. The full list and signatures are in the Traits reference. A transform receives the number in ctx.damage, or ctx.amount for a heal, and writes back the value that continues down the formula. An error or a non-number leaves it unchanged, and a negative result is clamped to 0 so it cannot heal. A hit meets the damage hooks in this order:

Several traits can occupy one formula position. stage orders them ascending, with 0 as the default. With three invented traits at the same position: Stage Trait 0 ward_a 10 ward_b 20 bonus_c Native and Lua traits share one list and one walk in stage order. Each transform sees the number the previous one left, so a ward that cuts damage before a later one changes what the later one works on.

A trait is defined in C++ or Lua. Both reach the same formula positions and interleave by stage. C++ Lua Define a class with an id, a stage and a hook macro per hook, registered at start-up forge.sys.game.traits.define{...} State none in the object: a stateless singleton, every hook const ctx.state per (character, binding), plus counters, cooldowns and schedules Only here the point limit none Adding a native trait never edits a central switch: the hook macro defines the override and its trigger bit together, because a hook declared without its bit would silently never be dispatched. A native id wins; a Lua define with an id a native already owns is refused. The point limit is native only: it is asked on every capped point read, too often for a script call.

A constant is a number the gate resolves and freezes when the affect lands. A formula is evaluated per call with the constants, the gate's amount, the damage, and whatever the call site passes. A formula that names something nobody supplies is logged once per binding and returns its fallback. Pass live values as variables, because a constant keeps the value it had when the affect landed.

A persistent gate has no constants after a login: an affect restored from the database at login has no applier to prime them, so the fallback answers. Gate such a trait on a no-save affect, or take one scaled number from gate_value(), which persists with the affect. A binding is keyed by trait and affect type for the whole process. Sources that raise the same affect cannot carry different traits or formulas. Only a bump from a pre hook changes the hit. A bump lasts for one calculation, so an affect is still needed for an icon, a visible flag, or a lifetime between attacks. More traps and worked examples are in Examples and pitfalls.

You build a Forge module named friendly_empires. A GM types /friendly on 1 2 and from then on, on the map the GM stands on, a player of empire 1 cannot hurt a player of empire 2, and the other way round. /friendly off takes the rule away again. Everyone else fights as before. The rule is one battle arbiter: a guard that says which attacks it cares about, and a verdict that says yes, no or no opinion. Then you break it twice on purpose, once with a wrong return value and once with a stale handle, and read what the server logs.

The finished module of Your first Forge module, and the way you compile, register and restart from that page. This module uses the same loop. The battle arbiter reference open beside you. It lists the dispatch order and the verdicts; this page uses them without repeating them. The Forge API reference for the forge file layout. A GM account, and two test characters of two different empires. Empire ids are 1, 2 and 3. Put both characters on the same map, and keep a third character of the remaining empire if you want to see the rule leave it alone. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files; you create the real one in share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/.

An arbiter is a (name, guard, can_attack) triple. forge.sys.game.battle_arbiter_registry.register takes the three and returns a handle, a number greater than 0. The registry asks every arbiter in registration order. If the guard returns true, it calls the verdict; the first Allow or Deny wins, and Pass hands the question to the next one. This guard owns the pair when both characters stand on the map the GM chose. The verdict denies the attack only if both are players and their empires are exactly the two the GM named, in either order. Everything else is Pass: mobs, NPCs, the third empire, a player on another map. Openshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge The guard and the verdict are closures over map_index, empire_a and empire_b, so one arbiter carries its own rule. The module keeps the handle in self.handle; you need it later to remove the arbiter. The switch is a GM command. cmd.register_router adds /friendly, and cmd.new_implementor_route adds the on route with two number arguments. The callback receives the GM as ch first. new_implementor_route fixes the permission level: only implementor-level GMs can run the route. Create share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge with exactly this content, then register it. Add one line to share/locale/italy/quest/qc/quest_list: ../system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge Then compile it alone, from the runtime root: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge Check. The compiler prints no error, and share/locale/italy/quest/forge/friendly_empires.game exists. There is no state block, so nothing is created under object/. Restart the game cores and search the log: grep friendly logs/syslog You should see: [OK] cmd.register_router : [friendly] [Forge-friendly_empires]: loaded
documents.s: Step 1: register an arbiter from a command

documents.t: Before the command, put your two characters of empires 1 and 2 next to each other on one map and hit one with the other. The hit lands. Two players of different empires are attackable on any map unless one of them is in Protect mode on its own empire's map or on a start map, so use a map where neither is. Log in with the GM account on that map and type: /friendly on 1 2 Check. The GM gets the chat line Empires 1 and 2 are friendly on this map, and the log shows the registration. The handle number varies, because other arbiters registered earlier take the lower ones: [OK] CBattleArbiterRegistry::Register : [friendly:<map_index>] handle=<n> [Forge-friendly_empires]: on for map <map_index>, handle <n> Now hit again, in both directions. What you see: No damage. The victim's HP does not move. Deny beats every PK mode. The verdict is asked before the PK rules, so a duel, a PK mode switch or a killer flag changes nothing. The client still shows the attack cursor and the swing. The arbiter sends nothing to the client, and the client only knows that a player of another empire is a valid target. A team session would broadcast a message that hides the cursor; an arbiter does not. A targeted skill that is for enemies only is refused. On a test server the caster also gets the chat line <skill name>: this skill cannot be cast on that target. The two empires still cannot buff each other. The buff check asks the arbiter too, but Deny only means "not attackable"; it then falls back to "same empire", which is false for these two, so no buff. "Friendly" here means "cannot hurt", not "allied". The third empire fights both of them, and mobs fight everyone, because the verdict answered Pass. Poison, fire and bleeding already running between the two characters also stop on their next tick. Now the flaw. Type /friendly on 1 2 a second time: the log gets a second Register line with a new handle, and the first handle is lost, because self.handle was overwritten. Nothing can remove that first arbiter any more except a core restart. A forge has no unload hook and no hot reload, so the rule would live until the core stops. Step 3 fixes both.

A registered arbiter stays until you drop it, and its handle is the only way to do that. Handles are never reused, and names are not compared, so enable has to refuse a second registration and disable has to give the handle back to the registry. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge Replace the whole file with this version. enable returns false when self.handle is already set. disable calls registry.unregister, which returns true when it found and removed the arbiter, logs only on success, then clears the handle. The off route reports the result in chat. Compile and restart as before. Check. Type /friendly on 1 2, then /friendly off. The chat shows Empires fight again, and the log shows: [OK] CBattleArbiterRegistry::Unregister : [friendly:<map_index>] handle=<n> [Forge-friendly_empires]: off for map <map_index>, handle <n> Hits land again at once. The registry is asked on every attack, so nothing needs a restart. Type /friendly off once more: the chat shows Nothing to turn off and logs/syserr stays empty. Type /friendly on 1 2 twice: the second time the chat shows Already on for map <map_index>, use /friendly off first and the log has one Register line.

The verdict must return one of the three BATTLE_VERDICT numbers. This version returns the boolean false where it denies. It compiles, it loads, and it does not work. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge Replace return VERDICT.Deny with return false (the button does it), compile, restart, and type /friendly on 1 2. Then hit. Check. The hits land. The wrong type makes the call count as Pass, so the two empires fight under the ordinary rules, and logs/syserr fills on every check that reaches the verdict: Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation wrong return: expected [number], got [boolean] [battle_arbiter_registry friendly:<map_index> can_attack] lua callback error A verdict that falls off the end without a return gives got nothing in the same place. A guard that returns something other than a boolean is logged the same way, with guard in the second line, and counts as false, so the arbiter never applies. Do not use return 0 or return 1 either: the numbers are Allow = 0, Deny = 1, Pass = 2, and the names are the only safe way to write them. Put VERDICT.Deny back with the next button, compile and restart.
documents.s: Step 4: break the verdict on purpose

documents.t: A handle that the registry no longer knows is not an exception. This version of disable forgets to clear self.handle after the unregister, so the second /friendly off presents a stale handle. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge Compile, restart, type /friendly on 1 2, then /friendly off twice. Check. The first off behaves as in step 3. The second one returns false and writes to logs/syserr: CBattleArbiterRegistry::Unregister : unknown handle=<n> The chat shows Nothing to turn off, and no off for map line appears, because the function logs only on success. After the first off, /friendly on 1 2 answers Already on, because the module still believes it holds a handle. Nothing is damaged, but the module no longer knows what it has registered. Restore the clean version with the last button: friendly_empires-2.forge is also what the Solve view shows. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge
documents.s: Step 5: break the handle on purpose

documents.t: The loop is the same after every change: Compile: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/friendly_empires.forge. Restart the game cores: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. Read logs/syslog for the Register, Unregister and [Forge-friendly_empires] lines, and logs/syserr for the errors above. The command needs implementor level. A player gets silence, and so does a lower-level GM who types a valid route. Anyone above player level who types it wrong gets usage in chat, with the routes in key order: wrong sub command. Usage: /friendly off /friendly on <empire> <empire> /friendly on 1 prints wrong arguments. Usage: and the usage line, and a non-number prints need a number as 1 parameter. got <arg>. If another forge already owns /friendly, logs/syserr shows cmd.register_router : [friendly] already registered; keeping the first.

A forge has no unload hook, so nothing unregisters your arbiter for you. Tie unregister to the end of the thing being judged: a command here, an event teardown, a war end. The registry lives as long as the core, and on restart the rule is gone. Keep the handle. Without it the arbiter can never be removed, and a second register without an unregister adds a second arbiter instead of replacing the first. Guard and verdict must return what they promise: a boolean from the guard, a BATTLE_VERDICT number from the verdict. A wrong type is logged on every check and fails safe, and the log floods. Keep the guard cheap. It runs for every attack check on the core, and each arbiter is asked in registration order. Never register or unregister from inside a guard or a verdict. The registry walks its list while it calls them, and nothing protects that walk. The rule is per core. A /friendly on lands on the core that hosts the GM's map; other cores are untouched. The command does not validate empire ids. /friendly on 1 1 registers a rule that denies attacks between two players of empire 1. The arbiter changes the server's answer only. Players of the two empires still see each other as targets, and every swing is wasted.

Battle arbiter reference: dispatch order, verdicts and the rest of the chain. Forge API reference: files, environments, boot order and the full surface. Your first Forge module: the module loop this page reuses. Previous Send a message from the server to a client window Next Lift the party rules on one map

You build skill 360, Imperial Stride. It belongs to an empire, not to a character. One cast gives every player of your empire on your map a movement speed buff for 60 seconds, and the cost comes out of the monarch purse. The skill is three pieces: a skill file, a description file for the client, and a forge that puts the skill on your support page with an on/off command. You set its level with eskill, press it, and read the purse, the cooldown and the affect list to see that it worked.

The client reads two files for the skill: a copy of the skill file in the locale pack's skill/ folder and the description in skill_desc/, side by side (locale/universal/skill/360.ucskill.yaml and locale/universal/skill_desc/360.ucskilldesc.yaml). After you write either file, repack the client locale and restart the client. Without them the support page shows a dead cell. The loadout replaces your support page while it is on. The skills you keep there leave the bar until you type /istride off. The finished module of Your first Forge module and its loop to compile, register and restart, and the router pattern of A bonus that only counts when. A test server, where every character can use GM commands, and one character whose empire you know, 1 to 3. Off a test server eskill needs the high wizard GM level and /istride the low one. Optional, for the last check: a second client with a second character of the same empire.

The client has no slot for a new vnum. Its guild and empire slots are a fixed list compiled into the client: 150 to 158, and a new vnum is in none of them. The server has no idea of a slot at all. The one door from the server is the skill loadout: a rule that sends the client (page, position, vnum) and the client installs it. So the tutorial puts 360 on the SUPPORT page. It is server Lua and needs no client build.

The shape is a map-wide empire skill: the AFFECT of the skill file reference with collect.from: map and accept.of: ALLY. The affect is a movement speed point, 5+3*skill_level, for 60 seconds. The model is 156, a shipped map-wide empire skill. Its top node sweeps the caster's map and its affect lands on every player it accepts: OpenLocale/conf/skill/156.ucskill.yaml Four lines carry the idea: subject: empire makes the empire the owner. Its level is a number the empire holds, not one a character learns, and any player of an empire that holds the skill at level 1 or more may cast it. costType: SUBJECT_GOLD takes the cost from the monarch purse of the caster's empire. The cost is a constant, '100000', and the reason is in Pitfalls. collect.from: map sweeps every player of the caster's map on this core, not the neighbourhood of the caster. search: { take: 0 } must stay: with no search block the sweep collects nobody. accept takes of: ALLY, kind: PLAYER. Players of your own empire are allies. The cast is seeded with the caster, who is his own ally, so he is buffed too and no seed: false is needed. The vnum is 360, in the band for skills nothing grants and clear of the guild war list. The file name is the vnum. CreateLocale/conf/skill/360.ucskill.yaml Create Locale/conf/skill/360.ucskill.yaml with exactly this content. Restart the game cores: skill files load at boot. Check. Search the log: grep "vnum 360" logs/syslog You should see: [SkillBuild]: Building Imperial Stride (vnum 360) logs/syserr says nothing starting with Skill[360]. A file that fails to build stops the boot, and the game core does not start.

The client builds the skill tooltip from a description file. The $speed in it is the speed variable of the skill file: it reads the node's amountPoly at the empire's level, so the tooltip always shows the real number. The colour codes are the client's |c...|r form. See Skill descriptions. CreateClient-Files/locale/locale/universal/skill_desc/360.ucskilldesc.yaml Create Client-Files/locale/locale/universal/skill_desc/360.ucskilldesc.yaml with this content. Repack the client locale, with a copy of the skill file from step 1 in the pack's skill/ folder, and restart the client. Check. The client log has no line about skill 360. A description without its skill file is skipped with the message CPythonSkill: skill 360 has a description but no config.

The level is the empire's. No loadout and no character table row holds it. Use your empire number for <e>: /eskill <e> set 360 1 /eskill <e> show 360 /eskill <e> gold 1000000 /eskill <e> gold Check. The replies, in order: Empire 1 skill 360 set to level 1. Empire 1 skill 360: level 1, cooldown 0s. Empire 1 gold: 0. Empire 1 gold: 1000000. The number after the add is the balance before it, so the first gold line shows what the purse held. The second one shows the balance after. The numbers are an example. The level and the purse are written through the database core and come back to the cores a moment later, so a show or gold typed in the same breath can still print the old value. Wait a moment before you cast. eskill set checks nothing: not that a skill file exists, and not that the level is within maxLevel. This file takes 1 to 7. /eskill 1 set 361 1 succeeds and writes a flag nothing reads.
documents.s: Step 3: give it to the empire and fill the purse

documents.t: The forge registers one loadout rule. Its guard answers "did this character ask for it": a table filled by the command. The builder returns a plan with the SUPPORT page and one entry: vnum 360 in slot 1, with level = 0. The level in an entry is written to the character's own record for that vnum, and 360 is not the character's. So the entry says 0, and the empire's level from step 3 is what the server casts with and what the client draws on the slot. That a level-0 entry for an owned skill casts is what the code does: the character level is never asked for an empire skill. No loadout that ships carries an owned skill. The router is the one from the first trait: /istride on records the wish and refreshes the loadout, /istride off clears it and refreshes again, which brings back the page the loadout displaced. Createshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/imperial_stride.forge Create share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/imperial_stride.forge with this content, then register it. Add one line to share/locale/italy/quest/qc/quest_list: ../system/tutorial/imperial_stride.forge Compile it alone, from the runtime root: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/imperial_stride.forge Restart the game cores. The wanted table is in memory, so every restart forgets who asked: type /istride on again. Check. The log shows: [OK] cmd.register_router : [istride] [Forge-imperial_stride]: loaded, skill 360 Type /istride on. The chat says imperial stride on the support page, and the first cell of the support page in the character window shows the Imperial Stride icon at level 1. The tooltip shows the cost, 100000 Yang of the empire.
documents.s: Step 4: put it on the support page

documents.t: Press the cell. Your character plays the motion, the effect of the speed buff appears and you run faster. Then read three things. /affect_remove <your name> /eskill <e> gold /eskill <e> show 360 Check. The affect list has a row that starts with type 360, point 19, value 8 (5+3*1) and a duration counting down from 60. The purse reads 900000: 100000 lower. show 360 reports a cooldown of about 30 seconds. Press the cell again before it runs out: the press is refused and nothing is paid (a test server prints Cooltime not finished Imperial Stride). To see "every ally on the map" and not "around me", cast with the second client logged in anywhere on the same map, far outside view range. /affect_remove <second name> shows the same 360 row. A character of another empire on that map gets none.

The loop after each server change: Compile the forge: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/imperial_stride.forge. A skill file change needs no qc. Restart the game cores: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. Read logs/syslog for the [SkillBuild] and [Forge-imperial_stride] lines and logs/syserr for errors. After a change to the skill file or the description, repack the client locale and restart the client. A forge that fails to load makes the quest manager initialisation fail, and the game core does not start.

Take a vnum from 151 to 157 and the war-only rule refuses the cast off a war map: the player sees "Puoi abilitare questa abilità solo in guerra." above the character, nothing is paid and no cooldown starts. That is the rule the shipped empire skills 154 to 157 live under today. Those vnums are also shipped skill files, so you would overwrite one. 360 is outside the list. A cost that reads skill_level is priced at a stale level. The cost is charged before the cast takes its level from the empire, so the first cast after a restart prices at level 0 and the later ones at the level of the previous cast. A constant is exact. This is read from the call order, not observed. The purse is debited on one core only. The cast takes the money from the memory of the core that ran it. /eskill <e> gold on that core shows the drop, other cores do not, and a restart brings back the value of the database. For this tutorial, on one core, the check holds. Do not read it as the empire's treasury being charged for good. collect.from: map with no search: collects nobody. You get your own buff and no one else's. The seed, the caster, is still processed, so the cast looks fine on one client. search.radius does nothing on a map sweep. The skill still loads and syserr says `search.radius` is ignored when `collect.from` is not sectree. A misspelled from: value is logged and falls back to the neighbourhood of the caster. Read logs/syserr after every restart. A skill with no level shows level 0 and the client refuses the press itself. Run /eskill <e> set 360 1. An empty purse is not checked by the client. The press goes out and the server refuses it; on a test server the chat says Imperial Stride: You can't cast the skill because the costs aren't redeemable. A client without the skill file fails when it draws the page: skill.GetSkillType - Failed to find skill by 360, and the cell is dead. A server without it casts nothing. The loadout empties the whole support page. /istride off puts the page back. The vnum must stay under 400. At 400 and above the server logs vnum overflow (vnum <n>) to logs/syserr and the character never gets the slot's level.

Skill file reference: every key, collect.from, accept and the loader errors. Loadout policy: the pages, the rule order and what a loadout saves. Skills: owned by a character, a guild or an empire: the subject, the purse and eskill. Previous A back hit that lands 30% harder Next Count something, reward it

You build a Forge module named wounded_fury. A GM command /wfury on adds an affect, type 3910, to you. While you have it, every melee hit you land on an ordinary monster does 15 points of monster attack bonus more, but only when your HP is under 80%. Above 80% the trait does nothing. /wfury off takes it away. The trait is one hook and one if. It does not undo anything: the bonus exists only while one hit is being worked out, and the engine takes it back by itself.
documents.s: A bonus that only counts when

documents.t: The finished module of Your first Forge module, and the loop you use there to compile, register and restart. The visible buff tutorial. This module registers an affect type and a /cmd on|off router the same way and does not explain them again. The traits reference open beside you, and Traits for why the engine ties a trait's life to an affect. This page uses both without repeating them. A test server, where every character can use GM commands, and one character. On a server that is not a test server, /wfury needs the low wizard GM level. The battle_hit: readout in step 3 exists only when the core config has server.type.test_server set. An ordinary monster near you that hits back. Not a boss, a metin stone or a meteor: they take only 4/5 of the monster bonus, and a monster that is immune to bonuses takes none. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files.

A trait is a set of hooks that the engine calls at fixed points of a character's life. It is attached to a character by an affect: its gate. While the character has the affect, the trait is attached. When the last affect of that type goes, the trait goes with it. There is no call to grant or revoke a trait. The affect here changes no stat. It is a switch, so the add uses point.NONE and a value of 0. The type is 3910, clear of the 3900 of the visible buff. add_no_save keeps it out of the saved affects, so a warp or a relog drops the trait too, and you type /wfury on again. The hook is on_damage_dealt_pre. The engine calls it on the attacker just before the damage formula reads the attack points, with the victim and the damage type. It has no damage argument, because the damage is not computed yet. ctx.bump_point(point, delta) adds delta to a point for the length of that one hit. Here the condition is the attacker's own HP: ch:get_hp_pct() is an integer percentage, so < 80 is true at 79% and below. ATTBONUS_MONSTER counts against any ordinary monster, so one character fighting one monster is enough. The model for this trait, cold_blood, bumps ATTBONUS_HUMAN, which counts only against players. Swap the point to try it with two clients. Openshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/wounded_fury.forge define is a reserved word in a .forge file, like state, quest, with, when and begin. The quest compiler adds those six to Lua, so traits.define{...} does not compile in a forge. The bracket form traits["define"]{...} is the same call, and the compiler never sees the word. In a plain .lua module the dot form is fine. The rest of the file is the router from the visible buff: /wfury on adds the affect with override true, so a second on replaces it instead of stacking a second copy, and /wfury off removes it. Create share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/wounded_fury.forge with exactly this content, then register it. Add one line to share/locale/italy/quest/qc/quest_list: ../system/tutorial/wounded_fury.forge Compile it alone, from the runtime root: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/wounded_fury.forge Restart the game cores. Check. Search the log: grep wounded_fury logs/syslog You should see these lines. The numbers after id= and binding= depend on how many traits loaded before yours. [OK] [traits] define [wounded_fury] id=<n> affect_gate=3910 binding=<m> hook_mask=0x1 [OK] cmd.register_router : [wfury] [Forge-wounded_fury]: loaded, affect 3910 affect_gate=3910 is your gate. hook_mask=0x1 says the trait subscribed to one trigger, on_damage_dealt_pre. logs/syserr says nothing about wounded_fury. In game, type /wfury on. The chat says wounded fury on, and /affect_remove followed by your character name lists a row that starts with 3910. Open the character window: no stat changed. Nothing will, outside a hit.
documents.s: Step 1: define the trait and gate it on an affect

documents.t: The log says the trait is attached. It does not say the hook runs. Make the hook talk: one chat line to the holder on every hit it bumps. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/wounded_fury.forge Replace the file's content with this version, compile again and restart the game cores. Type /wfury on. Check. Hit your monster while your HP is full. No fury line appears. Now let the monster hit you until your HP is under 80% and keep hitting back. Each of your hits now prints a line before anything else: wounded fury +15 (hp 71%) Drink a potion until you are above 80% and hit again: the line stops. The condition is read again on every hit, and you undid nothing by hand.

The chat line only proves that the hook ran. On a test server the engine also prints how each melee hit was worked out, and that shows the 15 itself. In the chat window, one hit prints the fury line, then a line like this: battle_hit: [You] attack to [Wild Dog]: pure -> 120 | base (after def) -> 100 | % bonus 135 | 2nd type modifiers -> 135 (The numbers here are an example, a hit at full HP with a 35 points total attack bonus. Yours depend on your character and the monster.) The same monster hit under 80% with the trait on would read % bonus 150: the same base 100, 15 points more. base (after def) is the damage after the monster's defense. % bonus is the damage after the attack bonuses: despite the name it is a damage number, not a percentage. So % bonus divided by base is the attack multiplier, 1.35 in the example. The last number, 2nd type modifiers, also folds in the weapon resist and your attack multiplier, so it can differ from % bonus; read the ratio from % bonus. Write down that ratio from a hit at full HP and from a hit under 80%. The second is higher by 0.15: the 15 points of ATTBONUS_MONSTER, as a fraction of base. Rounding to whole damage moves it a little, so compare the ratios and not the raw numbers. A pierce roll or a fully absorbed hit also breaks the match, so look at several hits. Then type /wfury off and hit again under 80%. The fury line is gone and the ratio is back to what it was at full HP. You wrote nothing that takes the 15 away. The bonus was added to the point for this one hit, and the engine removed it when the hit was done. That is also why the character window never showed it. Check. Three readings agree: the fury line appears only under 80% with the trait on, the ratio rises by 0.15 on exactly those hits, and both disappear after /wfury off.

The loop is the same after every server change: Compile: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/wounded_fury.forge. Restart the game cores: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. Read logs/syslog for the [Forge-wounded_fury] line and logs/syserr for errors. A forge that fails to load makes the quest manager initialisation fail, and the game core does not start. If you write traits.define{ in the forge, the compiler stops with a syntax error and no .game file is written.

Bump in the two pre hooks, on_damage_dealt_pre and on_damage_taken_pre: that is where a bump changes the hit. A hook that runs later in the same hit accepts the bump, but the formula has already read the points. A hook that runs with no hit in progress refuses it and logs one line per call: [traits] bump_point outside a damage-pre guard (point=51, delta=15) ignored A misspelled hook name is ignored without a word. The hook_mask= in the define line is how you see it: 0x1 for on_damage_dealt_pre, 0x0 for a typo. The pre hook takes (ch, victim, dam_type, ctx). The post hooks take a dam before dam_type. Copy a post signature and ctx is nil, so the hook raises a Lua error. The error is logged as [traits] on_damage_dealt_pre [wounded_fury]: ... and the hit goes on without the bonus. Trait ids are global. cold_blood is taken, and so are about a hundred others. A repeated id logs [traits] define: duplicate id [cold_blood] to logs/syserr and the trait is not registered. The forge still loads. A gate whose affect name is misspelled gives gate.affect nil. The engine logs [traits] define [wounded_fury]: gate is present but gate.affect is 0 and registers nothing. The hook fires for the melee hit, for arrows and magic shots, and for every skill damage node. This trait reads only your own HP, so that is safe. If you change the condition to read victim, check dam_type first: a splash skill computes its amount once and reuses it for every victim, so a bonus that depends on the victim would leak to the others. Do not read the bonus back. ch:get_point(point.ATTBONUS_MONSTER) from a command returns the stat without it. Without add_no_clear_on_death the affect is cleared when you die, and the trait detaches with it. Run /wfury on again.

Traits reference: every hook, the context, counters and the gate in full. Traits: why the engine keeps a trait's life in an affect and how a hit reaches the hooks. A buff other players can see: the affect half of this module, with the client side. Previous A buff other players can see Next A back hit that lands 30% harder

You build a small panel that sits beside the game window while you are in a dungeon. It shows a line of text and a progress bar, "Defeated: 0/5". A chat command moves the bar one step, and the bar redraws on your client at once, with no reload of the page. Two files make it: an HTML template that lives in the client pack, and a Forge that opens the panel and sets the counters the template reads. The shipped progress.html on the right is the macro library the template uses; read it first.

The finished module of Your first Forge module, and its compile and restart loop. The UCHTML reference open beside you, and UCHTML for why a page is a template and not a hand-built window. A debug client. A release client still opens the .html file but renders from the compiled module, so your new page shows nothing there until you compile it with the Compiler tab of the Wiki Manager. In a debug client the .html is read as it is. A test character that can use GM commands and can stand inside any dungeon. The panel is bound to a dungeon instance, so outside one the Forge refuses.

The panel does not draw the bar itself. progress.html defines three macros. progress(text, count, max) draws a label and a <progress> element beside it. progress_block puts the bar under the label. rprogress(done_var, need_var, ...) wraps whatever you hand it in a <div> with an id and a reactive attribute that names the variables it reads. Openpack/locale/universal/dungeon_states/templates/progress.html The reactive attribute is the whole trick. When a counter named in it changes, the client re-renders only that zone and patches it into the window. The rest of the page stays as it is. Check. You can name the two counters the zone below will watch: done and need.

A page is a Jinja template. It imports the macros with with context, so the macros see the counters, and it calls rprogress with a call block. The block receives the current done and need as arguments, and everything inside it is the part that redraws. Createpack/locale/universal/dungeon_states/panel_demo.html Put the file in the client pack under locale/universal/dungeon_states/, next to the folder templates/. The import path is relative to that folder. Check. Every tag you used is a tag of the template engine: main, spacer, progress, div. The page has one reactive zone, progress-done-need.

The shipped dungeon state module exposes open(map_index, template, title) and set_counters(map_index, counters). open binds a state to the dungeon on that map and sends the template name to every player inside. set_counters stores each value as a string and sends only the keys you pass. A key set to nil is removed. Create the Forge and register a /panel_demo open command with it. Createshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/panel_demo.forge Add ../system/tutorial/panel_demo.forge to share/locale/italy/quest/qc/quest_list and compile it: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/panel_demo.forge Check. The compiler prints no error and share/locale/italy/quest/forge/panel_demo.game exists. Restart the game cores.
documents.s: Step 2: open the panel from a Forge

documents.t: A counter that changes is the only thing that has to cross the wire. Add step and close commands. step reads the stored done back as a string, adds one, caps it at NEED, and sends only done. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/panel_demo.forge Compile and restart again. Check. The file has three routes, open, step and close, and returns a table at the end of the environment, because a forge that returns nothing fails to load.

Log in to a debug client, step into any dungeon and type /panel_demo open. A window titled "Yard drill" appears with the line "Defeat the dummies in the yard." and the bar "Defeated: 0/5". Type /panel_demo step five times: the label and the bar advance each time and stop at 5/5. /panel_demo close closes the window. If the window appears with nothing in it, the client could not render the template: you are on a release client without a compiled page, or the file is not under locale/universal/dungeon_states/. If the chat says "Stand inside a dungeon first.", the map you are on is not a dungeon instance.

UCHTML: the pipeline from template to native widgets, and the reactive zones. Wiki Manager and data generation: the Compiler tab. Luna Forge: the Forge module format used here. Previous A practice room that pays out Next A shader in a window

You build a Forge module named login_counter, one piece at a time. At the end, every login is counted, the player gets a chat line and the game core log gets one too, and a logout drops the reference to the character. The count itself stays in the module until the core stops. The tutorial has six steps. Each one changes one file, ends with a check you make in the compiler output, the log or the game, and has its own solution. If a step does not behave, press Check in the workbench to compare your files with the solution of the current step, or Solve to see it. The Start step button at the top of each step sets the workbench to what the previous step left, so you can begin from a known state at any point. It overwrites your edits. Step You add You see 1 the module file the compiler writes login_counter.game 2 the quest_list line [Forge-login_counter]: loaded in the log 3 the counter and the when login hook a login line in the log 4 the chat line Login 1 in the game 5 the when logout hook a logout line that still says online 1 6 the cleanup the logout line says online 0

A runtime you can compile and restart: the folder that holds share/, qc.sh, run.sh and shutdown.sh, and a game core you can log in to. About twenty minutes. A rough idea of what a Forge is: the Forge API reference lists the API, and How Forge modules work explains what happens underneath. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files; you create the real ones in share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/ and share/locale/italy/quest/qc/. The quest_list file in the workbench is the one the game ships, shown as it is.

A forge file is a forge <name> begin block. Inside it, environment game begin holds Lua that runs once, when the game core boots, and it must return a table or an object. That return value is what the rest of the server sees as forge.game.login_counter. The module here is a small class with two tables keyed by player id: logins for the counts and online for the live characters. Nothing uses them yet. Createshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/login_counter.forge Create share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/login_counter.forge with exactly this content. Then compile it alone, from the runtime root: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/login_counter.forge The path is relative to the quest folder, the same form quest_list uses. Check. The compiler prints no error, and share/locale/italy/quest/forge/login_counter.game exists. There is nothing under object/ for this forge, because the file has no state block.

Start step 2 Without an entry in quest_list, --f compiles the file, but the next full compile deletes the result and does not rebuild it. The workbench shows the shipped quest_list; it ends with the forges of the game. Add one line at the end: Updateshare/locale/italy/quest/qc/quest_list Compile again, then restart the game cores so the forge loads (see Run it below). Check. Search the log: grep login_counter logs/syslog You should see: [Forge-login_counter]: loaded If the line is missing, logs/syserr tells you why; the most likely cause is the missing quest_list line or a path that is not relative to the quest folder.
documents.s: Step 2 of 6: register it and see it load

documents.t: Start step 3 A hook is a when block in a state block. It runs as a quest, with the player who triggered it as the current player, so pc.get_player_id() works there. Keep the hook short: read the player id, find the character, call into the module, return. The module keeps the state, the hook does not. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/login_counter.forge Replace the whole file with this version. Three things to notice: Counter:on_login is called with :, because the environment returned an instance and the method needs self. The module logs with forge.sys.log(0, ...). Level 0 always prints, and the line always carries the [Forge-login_counter]: prefix. The hook never waits. A when login block must run to the end. Check. Compile again: share/locale/italy/quest/object/notarget/login/login_counter.start and object/state/login_counter now exist. Restart, log in, and the log shows a line like this one (your name will differ): [Forge-login_counter]: Alice login 1, online 1
documents.s: Step 3 of 6: count logins from a when login hook

documents.t: Start step 4 The count is only in the log so far. One more line in on_login writes it to the player. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/login_counter.forge chat_packet takes a chat type from forge.sys.game.CHAT_TYPE and the text. Check. Compile, restart, log in. The chat shows: Login 1 on this core since it started Log out and in again without restarting: the chat says Login 2. The count survives a logout because it lives in the module, not in the character.

Start step 5 A when logout hook mirrors the login one. Pass the player id, not the character: the character may already be on its way out, and a plain number needs no nil check. This version only logs, on purpose. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/login_counter.forge Check. Compile, restart, log in and out. The log shows: [Forge-login_counter]: pid 1234 logout, online 1 [QUEST_LOGOUT][INFO][1234] Logout PC OK! online 1 after a logout is the problem. The entry for your player id is still in the table and points at a character the engine has already destroyed. Log in again and the entry is only replaced because it has the same player id; for the whole time you were out it pointed at freed memory. It is harmless here because count_online never touches the stored character, but any code that used it would be reading freed memory.
documents.s: Step 5 of 6: log the logout and see the stale entry

documents.t: Start step 6 A character pointer that outlives the character is the classic trap in a forge. Remove the entry in on_logout. Leave logins alone, so the count survives a logout. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/login_counter.forge Check. Compile, restart, log in and out. The log shows: [Forge-login_counter]: pid 1234 logout, online 0 [QUEST_LOGOUT][INFO][1234] Logout PC OK! Log in again: the chat says Login 2 and the log says login 2, online 1. The module name appears in three roles in this file: the quest name behind object/state/login_counter, the module you reach as forge.game.login_counter, and the output file name. The quest table and the module are different tables. You have built the whole module: a loaded environment, a counter fed by a hook, a message to the player and a clean logout. Press Solve to compare it with the final file.
documents.s: Step 6 of 6: drop the reference on logout

documents.t: The loop is the same after every change: Compile the file: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/login_counter.forge. A syntax error aborts with <file>:<line>:syntax error : ... on stderr. For an error inside the environment body the reported line is where the environment ends, not where the mistake is. Restart the game cores: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. The db does not need a restart for a game-only forge. In the local docker runtime, restart the containers. Read logs/syslog of a game core. At boot the forge prints [Forge-login_counter]: loaded; at login and logout it prints the lines above. logs/syserr should have nothing about login_counter. There is no hot reload for forges. A changed forge is picked up only at the next core start, and a core restarts with its counts back at zero. A player who warps to another core starts at Login 1 there, because each game core has its own copy of the module. If the module returns nothing, the file compiles, and the core refuses to start. The error is in logs/syserr: Forge::ExcecuteSources result is nil for forge[login_counter]. Each environment should return a table or a class instance could not load Forge: [./locale/italy/quest/forge] Every forge after it in the load order is not loaded either. Put return Counter:new() back.

state and with are reserved words in .forge files, as are quest, when, define and begin. The compiler rejects them as names, even after a dot. local state = {} or self.with fails the compile with syntax error : and the word. Rename the field, or write t["state"] for a field you do not own. Global sys_log(1, ...) prints nothing on a live server: any level of 1 or more is dropped unless the server is a test server. Use forge.sys.log(0, ...) in a module. Do not wait inside a hook. wait(), select(...) or input() in when login ends with QUEST NOT END RUNNING on Login/Logout in logs/syserr, and the block is closed. A module that has to wait starts a coroutine owned by the player. A typo in forge.game.login_countr:on_login(ch) compiles, because the compiler does not check calls. It fails at the first login with attempt to index a nil value (field 'login_countr'), and the server keeps running. forge.game.login_counter.on_login(ch) with a dot instead of a colon passes the character as self, and the first access to self.logins fails. Do not read another forge's module in the body of environment game. Forges load in directory order, which is not guaranteed, so it works on one machine and kills the core on another.

Forge overview and setup: files, environments, boot order and the full surface. How Forge modules work: how a forge is loaded, why state lives in the environment and how it differs from a quest. Make the counter survive a restart: it needs a db or a quest flag, which this module deliberately avoids. Next Send a message from the server to a client window

You add one line to metrics.yaml and two entries to achievements.yaml. The line counts every bear a character kills, for the whole life of the character. The first achievement is earned at 100 bears, the second at 1000 and follows the first in the achievement window. There is no C++ and no Lua to write.

The player metrics reference open beside you. It has the full list of fields and operands; this page uses three of them. A test server, a character you can give GM commands to, and a client. Both /metric and /achievement are implementor commands, and <pg_name> below is the name of your character. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files; you edit the real ones in the locale folder. They are shown here as short excerpts of the shipped files, and you can leave the rest of each file as it is.

A metric is a named number the engine keeps per character and saves under its name. This one reads the kill signal, keeps the kills whose monster is one of four vnums, and counts one per kill. kill.dog above it in the file is the same shape. OpenLocale/italy/metrics.yaml Add the line below kill.dog in Locale/italy/metrics.yaml. UpdateLocale/italy/metrics.yaml 110 to 113 are the four bears in the mob list: Orso, Orso Grizzly, Orso Nero and Orso Bruno. where takes a list for each operand, and a kill matches when its vnum is any of them. agg: count adds 1 per matching kill. Two things are easy to get wrong in this file. A typo stops the game core. The engine reads metrics.yaml itself, once, at boot, and it refuses the whole boot if one line is bad. Write form: instead of from: and the log says: [metrics] declare [kill.bear]: no from: A misspelled operand or a token the engine does not know is refused the same way, each with its own line that names the metric. The last line of the failure is cannot initialize metrics from %s, with a literal %s instead of the path: look at the line above it, which names the metric. The game core does not start until the line is fixed. A metric added late starts at zero. A character has a stored value only for the metrics it has moved. A metric that is new has no stored value for anybody, so every character that already exists begins at 0, whatever it killed before. Nothing backfills it. Bears killed before the restart in this step do not count. Restart the game core: the file is read at boot and there is no reload for it. Check. Search the log for the declaration pass: grep "\[metrics\]" logs/syslog You should see the declared count one higher than it was before your edit, and no refusal. The number is an example: [OK] [metrics] 53 declared from [Locale/italy/metrics.yaml], 0 refused The path in brackets is the one your core read. Further down, the pass prints one line for each metric, and yours is among them: [metrics] 53 kill.bear from=kill agg=count operands=1 predicates=0 max_keys=0 The number on the left is the dense id of the metric, set by the order of the file. Any number is right.

An achievement is a row in achievements.yaml that names a metric and a threshold. It owns no counter: it reads the one you declared. The shipped stone_hunter is the model. OpenLocale/italy/achievements.yaml Add bear_hunter with the other combat entries, under stone_breaker. The order of the file does not matter; the category and subtype fields decide where it shows. UpdateLocale/italy/achievements.yaml category and subtype place it in the window: combat and monsters already exist, so no new rail entry is needed. The task names the metric and the count. A threshold is a lifetime total, not an increment: 100 means a hundred bears in all. name, description and the task label are not text but keys. They resolve against the client locale file, Client-Files/locale/locale/universal/locale_it.json, under achievement.names, achievement.desc and achievement.tasks. Add the keys bear_hunter under names and desc, and kill_bear under tasks, with the text you want players to read. A key that does not resolve is drawn as the key itself, so nothing breaks if you skip it for now; the window shows achievement.names.bear_hunter. The icon is a client path and this one reuses an existing icon. A typo in an achievement is gentler than one in a metric. A task that names a metric nobody declared, say kill.bare, does not stop the boot. The entry is dropped, the other achievements load, and the log says: [achievement] bear_hunter: task names undeclared metric 'kill.bare' — ignored The achievement is simply missing from the window. Search for ignored in the log after every edit. Restart the game core. Check. The achievement forge prints one line when it has read the file. The totals are those of your file, and the line must be there: [OK] [achievement] N achievements, M categories

A step that deserves its own name, icon and description is its own achievement. supersedes names the one this follows. It is presentation: the window keeps a link out of sight until the one it follows is earned, and then lists both. Add bear_slayer after bear_hunter. UpdateLocale/italy/achievements.yaml It reads the same metric with a higher threshold: 1000 bears in all, not 900 more. Add bear_slayer under achievement.names and achievement.desc in the locale file. The task label is the same key as the first one, because both bars count the same bears. supersedes never decides whether an achievement is earned. Each entry is evaluated against the metric by itself, so a character that is already above both thresholds earns both together. A supersedes that names an id that does not exist logs [achievement] bear_slayer supersedes unknown '...' followed by link dropped: the link goes and the entry stays. Restart the game core once more.
documents.s: Step 3: add the one that follows it

documents.t: Killing a thousand bears is slow. The /metric command moves the counter for you and shows what the engine holds. Log in with your GM character and type: /metric get <pg_name> kill.bear The reply is the value and whether it was ever written: metric kill.bear = 0 (seeded: false) Zero and not seeded: you have killed no bear since the restart. Kill one bear and ask again. The reply is metric kill.bear = 1 (seeded: true). Now push the counter to 100: /metric add <pg_name> kill.bear 99 metric kill.bear += 99 -> 100 Within a few heartbeats the achievement forge hears the change and evaluates only the achievements that read this metric. The log says: [achievement] pid 1234 unlocked bear_hunter (The number is the player id of your character.) In game, the plaque of the new achievement appears. Open the achievement window from the achievement button of the taskbar. Under Combat, in the Monsters list, bear_hunter is shown as earned, and bear_slayer has appeared below it with a bar at 100 out of 1000. Before bear_hunter was earned, the window showed only that one. Ask the server the same thing: /achievement inspect <pg_name> bear_slayer bear_slayer [combat] follows bear_hunter kill.bear: 100/1000 (count) /achievement simulate <pg_name> bear_slayer answers that the achievement is not yet earned and names kill.bear as the unmet task, and it grants nothing. Then push the rest: /metric add <pg_name> kill.bear 900 bear_slayer is earned, and both cards are shown as earned. The Completati filter of the window lists them. When it does not work, look first for the line you expect: No [OK] [metrics] line, and the core is gone: a metric line was refused. Read the [metrics] declare [...] line above the failure. metric kill.bear = 0 right after a restart even though you killed bears: the metric is new, and the old kills were never counted (step 1). no metric named 'kill.bear' from /metric add: the core runs a metrics.yaml without your line. You edited a file the core does not read, or you did not restart. /achievement inspect answers no achievement 'bear_slayer': the entry was dropped. Search the log for ignored and link dropped. The window shows achievement.names.bear_slayer in place of a name: the locale key is missing or the client was not repacked.

Player metrics reference: every aggregation, the filter operands, predicates and the full /metric list. Player metrics: why the engine keeps the numbers itself and lets achievements only read them. A skill damage handler in Lua: another reward path that needs no C++. Previous A map-wide empire skill Next A practice room that pays out
You give the green visible buff particle gold tones from a gradient ramp. The material reads the brightness of the existing texture, so the particle keeps its soft shape.
documents.s: A colour gradient on a particle

documents.t: Finish A buff other players can see, or have another .mse effect that you can make appear in game. Open the effects and materials reference beside you. Have a client pack you can edit and rebuild. Use a text editor. The workbench shows both .mse and .msfvx files as plain text.

Open the particle's ParticleProperty group. Its red, green, and blue curves give it one color: 0.2 red, 1.0 green, and 0.4 blue. SrcBlendType 5 and DestBlendType 6 make it alpha blended. TextureFiles names universalled.dds, beside the effect in the locale pack. Openlocale/universal/effect/visible_buff.mse Check. Find the three color curves, the blend values, and the texture name.

Create the material beside the effect. It selects a shared ramp and tells the particle how to sample it. Createlocale/universal/effect/visible_buff.msfvx Family emissive_particle selects the particle material family. Family is required. Emission 1.0 leaves the sampled color at its original intensity. Keep it at 1.0 for this alpha blended particle: a higher value can turn it into an opaque glowing sheet. Gradient names the shared gilded.dds ramp. GradientMode replace uses the ramp color in place of the .mse color curves. GradientInput brightness samples the ramp using the texture's brightness. A pure white texture would give one flat color. GradientGain 1.2 scales the brightness used to choose a point on the ramp. GradientLifeShift 0.2 shifts that point as the particle ages. The ramp position is GradientGain times texel brightness, minus GradientLifeShift times particle life, clamped from 0 to 1. The sampled color is multiplied by texel brightness and Emission; black texels stay black. Alpha still comes from the texture and the particle's alpha curve. Check. The material has all seven keys inside Group Effect, and Gradient points to gilded.dds.

Add MaterialFile immediately after StartTime in the root of Group Particle. The relative path resolves beside the .mse. The affect still names the same effect; the effect now names the material. Updatelocale/universal/effect/visible_buff.mse Check. The marked line reads MaterialFile "visible_buff.msfvx", and both files are in locale/universal/effect/.
documents.s: Step 2: name the material from the effect

documents.t: The affect is not the only place that plays an effect. Each row of locale/universal/item_effect.txt gives an item an effect, and a row that names an .msattach bundle attaches everything the bundle lists. The bundle below plays visible_buff.mse, and with it the material you just added. Createlocale/universal/effect/visible_buff.msattach File is resolved beside the bundle, like MaterialFile. Bone is optional and left out here. Now open locale/universal/item_effect.txt. Each row has three columns separated by tabs: the item vnum, a bone, and the effect path. A bundle row must leave the bone as - (or empty); any other bone is refused with bundle bone must be '-' or empty. Add one row at the end of the file, using real tab characters between the columns: Updatelocale/universal/item_effect.txt 447<TAB>-<TAB>locale/universal/effect/visible_buff.msattach Vnum 447 is a weapon that already has rows in the file. Bundle rows attach only for weapon, rage weapon and armour items, and the vnum must exist in the item prototype table. A row with fewer or more than three columns is skipped without a message, so a row typed with spaces does nothing. Check. The new row has exactly two tab characters, the middle column is -, and the last column ends in .msattach.
documents.s: Step 3: put the effect on a weapon

documents.t: If you have an engine repository checkout, run its MSE validator on the three effect files. It is agent tooling in that repository and is not shipped with a client. It runs without a client and returns a nonzero exit code on an error: python validate_mse.py locale/universal/effect/visible_buff.mse locale/universal/effect/visible_buff.msfvx locale/universal/effect/visible_buff.msattach A debug client build can also have an F11 Cosmetics panel for playing effects and comparing materials. The panel exists only in builds configured for it. A normal client has neither the validator nor the F11 panel. Pack the locale folder with your client pack step, restart the client, look at the effect in game, and read the client log.

Pack the locale folder and restart both clients. On the character with the visible buff, type /vbuff on. You should see gold tones from the ramp instead of the flat green, with the same soft shape. Equip a character with a vnum 447 weapon and look at it. The same effect now plays from the weapon as well as from the affect. For an A/B comparison, delete the MaterialFile line, repack, and restart both clients. The plain green effect returns, on the affect and on the weapon. Add the line back, repack, and restart to restore the material. Materials are read when the effect loads, so restart after each change. If the result is still plain, read the client log. A misspelled material key produces a line like this: Cosmetic material: locale/universal/effect/visible_buff.msfvx: key 'emision': unknown key A material missing from the pack produces: Cosmetic material: locale/universal/effect/visible_buff.msfvx: key 'file': resource not found or malformed A missing ramp produces: Cosmetic textures: ramp 'd:/ymir work/special/cosmetics/ramps/gilded.dds': missing file; neutral index 0 is used Conflicting material references produce: Effect '<mse path>' has conflicting material references Fix the named file or reference, repack, and restart both clients. A bad or missing material leaves the plain effect; a missing ramp uses the neutral ramp.

Effects and materials reference: material keys, paths, and gradient behavior. A buff other players can see: build the effect used here and make it visible to nearby players. Previous A shader in a window

You build a Forge module named practice_room. A player talks to an NPC, and the server opens a private copy of the map and warps them into it. Inside, their character is a level 30 with no gold, no items, no quest flags and no affects, whatever the real one is. A wild dog stands three meters away. Killing it commits one prize to the real character, 20 red potions, and sends the player back. The point is the line between the two. Everything the player does in the room happens on a copy that is thrown away. The prize is the one thing you send back on purpose. You check that on the real character, after a real re-login.
documents.s: A practice room that pays out

documents.t: The finished module of Your first Forge module, and the loop you use there to compile, register and restart. This module uses the same loop.
