The player virtualization reference open beside you, and Player virtualization for why the engine keeps a copy instead of the real rows. This page uses both without repeating them. A test server and one character with GM rights, with a level above 30, some gold and something in the bag, so the reset is visible. The NPC with vnum 9006 (Vecchietta) standing on a map your game core hosts. She stays on the real map. If you have none, add a line to that map's npc.txt (m cx cy 0 0 0 0 1m 100 1 9006, in map cells). The room is a copy of the map you talk to her on, and the dog is spawned inside the copy by the module, so nothing is placed by hand in the room. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files; you create the real ones in share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/. The workbench opens on the avatar arena processor, a processor that ships with the server. You model yours on it in step 2.

A player cannot be virtual on a map that does not exist yet, so build the room first. forge.sys.game.dungeon_manager.create takes a base map index and returns a dungeon: a private copy of that map, addressed by its own index, 10000 or more. The engine frees it when it empties, once you call set_delete_when_empty(true). The copy keeps the base map's world coordinates, so warping to the player's own x and y with the new index lands them on the same spot in the copy. warp_set is a reconnect, not a move inside the process: the client drops, and comes back on the new map. Save the exit location first, so there is a place to return to. Do not close anything from a logout handler for this reason, because logout fires on the way in as well. The module has two parts. The environment game block holds the class and runs once at boot. The state start block holds the NPC talk, which calls into it. The class tags the dungeon with a flag so leave only sends people out of a room it made. The /practice leave command is the way out until the prize does it for you. Create share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/practice_room.forge with exactly this content, then register it. Add one line to share/locale/italy/quest/qc/quest_list: Createshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/practice_room.forge ../system/tutorial/practice_room.forge Do not add the quest to questcategory.txt. A quest listed there with 0 is dormant in a virtual session, and the kill handler of step 3 has to run inside the room. A quest that is not listed is allowed. Compile it alone, from the runtime root: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/practice_room.forge Check. The compiler prints no error and share/locale/italy/quest/forge/practice_room.game exists. Restart the game cores and search the log: grep practice_room logs/syslog You should see: [Forge-practice_room]: loaded Talk to the NPC and choose "Enter". The client reloads and you stand where you were, on a copy of the map. Other players on the base map are gone. A wild dog waits three meters to your right. You are still yourself: your level, your gold, your bag. There is no processor yet. Type /practice leave to go back to where you stood.
documents.s: Step 1: a private map and the way in

documents.t: A map is virtual when a processor is registered for its exact index. The shipped avatar processor is a plain table of hooks: transform_* functions that change the character as it loads, and on_player_enter. A hook you leave out is a passthrough. Yours needs four transforms and one greeting. Openshare/locale/italy/system/arena/avatar/virtual_processor.lua transform_player_load runs once, when the character first loads onto the room. {} from the item hook empties the bag and the equipped items, since both are in the list. {} from the quest hook drops every quest flag, the character's and the account's. on_player_enter runs at every entry, so keep the greeting behind fresh. Createshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/practice_processor.lua Then register it on the room. The processor has to be set before the player warps in, because the player is decided at load. It goes between creating the dungeon and the warp. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/practice_room.forge Compile, restart and talk to the NPC again. Check. The greeting [Practice room] Level 30, no gold, no items. Hunt the dog. arrives in the chat. Your level is 30, your gold is 0, the bag is empty and no buff is on you. Your position is the same: the engine keeps the position, the exit location, the play time and the UI settings real. Walk around and kill the dog if you like; nothing it gives you is saved. In step 3 the kill handler does not exist yet, so nothing happens on the kill. Type /practice leave. On the way out, look at your real character: level, gold and bag are back as they were. The room never touched them.
documents.s: Step 2: a processor on the shape of the shipped one

documents.t: A virtual session cannot write to the real rows, so a result that has to outlive it goes through the prize commit. commit_stash_item hands an item to the real character. Create the item with item_manager.create_item, commit it, and do not touch it again: the engine consumes it. The call returns the item id, or 0 when it refuses. Commit at an event the player triggers. A kill is one. on_player_exit runs at every disconnect before the saves, and a commit made there can be lost when the link to the database core is gone, so no shipped mode commits from it. The quest kill event runs for the player who made the kill. Guard it with is_virtual(), so a real player who kills a dog elsewhere gets nothing. After the commit, wait a few seconds so the player sees the message, then send them back with the same leave as the command. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/practice_room.forge Compile, restart and talk to the NPC. Check. Kill the dog. The chat says [Practice room] Prize committed. You are sent back in 5 seconds. Five seconds later you are back on the base map. The game core log has the commit line, with the vnum 27001 and the reason you gave: grep STASH_COMMIT logs/syslog PlayerVirtualRewards: STASH_COMMIT pid <pid> id <item id> vnum 27001 count 20 flags <n> why='practice_room' logs/syserr says nothing about practice_room.
documents.s: Step 3: one prize at the kill

documents.t: A commit is fire and forget. The write goes to the database core as one packet, and the running session is not updated. The only proof is the real character, loaded fresh. Log out of the game, close the client, log in again. Open the bag. Check. Your level, your gold and your own items are what they were before you started, and 20 red potions (Pozione Rossa) are in the bag. The potions are the only thing from the room that reached the real character. The level 30, the zero gold and the dog's drops stayed in the copy, which was freed when you left. If the potions are missing, the commit did not reach the database. Look in logs/syserr for practice_room: prize refused and for the engine's lines about an item bound to an owner.
documents.s: Step 4: check it after a real re-login

documents.t: The loop is the same after every change: Compile: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/practice_room.forge. The processor is a plain Lua file the forge requires, so it needs no compile. Restart the game cores: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. A forge is not reloaded while the core runs. Read logs/syslog for [Forge-practice_room]: loaded, and logs/syserr for the errors below. If the NPC does nothing and logs/syserr has practice_room: no private copy of map, the base map is not loaded by this core. A core loads only the maps in its own maps_allowed, so the base map has to be on the same core as the NPC.

The player is decided at load. Register the processor before the warp, never after. Logging out inside the room ends it. The dungeon deletes itself when empty, and the copy goes with it. The committed prize does not. The flag a commit writes is not visible in the running session. get_quest_flag right after commit_quest_flag returns the old value; the real character sees it on the next load onto a real map. The stash is delivered by the next real load. A player who warps out of the room gets it as the real character loads, and a player who logs out inside gets it at the next login. Keep the quest out of questcategory.txt. Listed with 0, its kill handler does not run in the room. A processor error does not stop the load. The engine falls back to the real data and logs PlayerVirtualLuaProcessor::TransformPlayerLoad Lua error: in logs/syserr; that is how a typo shows a level 30 that is not.

Player virtualization reference: the 15 functions, the 9 hooks and what the boundary keeps real. Player virtualization: why the only road back is a commit. Write a battle arbiter rule: another Forge registered rule, on the combat side. Previous Count something, reward it Next A live dungeon panel

You extend the login_counter Forge from the first tutorial. On every login it sends the player's login count to that player's client as a protobuf message, and a small Python window shows it: Login 2, online 1. Then you break the match between server and window on purpose and see that the message disappears without a single error. Three files make the trip: a .proto both sides compile, the forge that sends, and the window that receives.
documents.s: Send a message from the server to a client window

documents.t: The finished module of Your first Forge module, compiled and registered in quest_list, and the way you restart the game cores from that page. Docker, to run the protobuf generator, and a client whose root folder you can edit and repack with your packing tool. The Forge API reference for send_client. How messages travel and How the client receives them explain what happens underneath. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files; you create the real ones in your server tree and in the client root.

Server and client must agree on the bytes of a message. A .proto file is that agreement: field names, types and, above all, field numbers. The folder under protobuf/ becomes the import path on both sides, so protobuf/ue/login_counter.proto is require("ue.login_counter_pb") in Lua and from luna.protobuf.ue import login_counter_pb2 in Python. Createprotobuf/ue/login_counter.proto Create protobuf/ue/login_counter.proto with exactly this content. File and folder names may only use letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. required fields must be set before the message serializes; the numbers 1 and 2 are what travels on the wire. Run the generator from the folder that holds protobuf_config.yaml. The protobuf/ folder with your .proto files sits next to it, and both scripts read the config and resolve paths relative to it. Its python_path and lua_path keys say where the two outputs land. Build the image once, then generate: sh protobuf_build_image.sh sh protoc.sh On Windows use protobuf_build_image.bat and protoc.bat. Run protoc again after every .proto change. The generator wipes and rebuilds. It deletes both output folders first and regenerates every .proto in the tree, so a file you placed by hand in root/luna/protobuf/ or share/locale/protobuf/ is gone after the next run. Check. Two outputs exist: root/luna/protobuf/ue/login_counter_pb2.py for the client, and share/locale/protobuf/ue/login_counter_pb.lua for the server. The Lua file defines GCLoginCount: grep GCLoginCount share/locale/protobuf/ue/login_counter_pb.lua The server reads the Lua file at boot, so it must sit in the share/locale/protobuf/ folder your game core runs with. If your protobuf_config.yaml writes somewhere else, copy the folder across.
documents.s: Step 1: define the message and generate the bindings

documents.t: The send call is forge.sys.game.send_client(ch, header, message). The message is the serialized protobuf, the header is a string of your choice, and the namespace is not an argument at all: it is the name of the forge that makes the call. For forge login_counter begin, the namespace on the wire is login_counter. It is not the proto package (LoginCounter), not the file name and not game. The call must be made from a function defined inside the forge's environment, so it goes into Counter:on_login, not into the when login hook. A call made straight from the hook fails with ForgeGame::SendClientPacket called from a non-forge script. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/login_counter.forge Replace the whole file with this version. Two lines at the top load the generated module, and the end of on_login builds a GCLoginCount, fills both required fields and sends it under the header count. A required field left unset makes SerializeToString raise Message is missing required fields, and a misspelled field name raises <name> not found. Both are logged with a stack trace and the core keeps running. Check. Compile and restart as in the first tutorial: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/login_counter.forge Log in. The chat line Login 1 on this core since it started and the [Forge-login_counter]: log line are the same as before, and logs/syserr has nothing new. If the core refuses to start and logs/syserr names ue.login_counter_pb, the Lua file from step 1 is not under share/locale/protobuf/ue/. The client shows nothing yet. The message arrived, no window listens for it, and it was dropped without a word. Keep that in mind for step 4.
documents.s: Step 2: send it from the forge

documents.t: The client does not route by itself. A window says "send me login_counter messages with the header count" by calling luna.RegisterHandler with its own window handle, the namespace, the header and a callback. When a message arrives, the engine looks for callbacks registered for exactly that namespace and header and calls them with the payload. Createroot/uilogincounter.py Create root/uilogincounter.py with exactly this content. Four things carry the lesson: FORGE_NAME and HEADER must equal the forge name and the header in send_client, character for character. The handle comes from self.GetWindowHandle(), which exists only after the base __init__ has run. Register after it. The callback is wrapped in ui.__mem_func__. The engine holds the callable you register; wrapped, it holds a weak reference to the window, so the window can still be freed. A raw bound method keeps the window alive forever and __del__ never runs. The window unregisters in Destroy and in __del__, then calls the base __del__. luna.UnregisterHandler(handle) removes every registration that handle made. The handler gets the payload as a string. utils.Deserialize parses it into a GCLoginCount and returns None on a bad payload, so the handler returns early. Now create the window when the interface is built. In root/interfacemodule.py, make five small edits: Import it with the other windows: import uilogincounter as uiLoginCounter. Set self.wndLoginCounter = None in __Initialize. Create it in __MakeWindows: self.wndLoginCounter = uiLoginCounter.LoginCounterWindow(). In Close, call self.wndLoginCounter.Destroy() when it is set. At the end of Close, run del self.wndLoginCounter with the other windows. Repack the client with your packing tool and restart it. The packed root is read at startup. Check. Log in. A small board titled Login counter appears with Login 1, online 1 (online is every player on the core, so expect a higher number if others are logged in). Log out and in again: Login 2, online 1, because the forge keeps the count until the core stops. The server log line still reads login 2, online 1.
documents.s: Step 3: a window that registers its handler

documents.t: Registration is an exact string match on namespace and header. Change one letter and the window never hears from the server again. This version registers the header counts, while the forge sends count. Updateroot/uilogincounter.py Change HEADER in root/uilogincounter.py to "counts", repack the client and log in. Check. The board does not appear. The server log shows its normal line, logs/syserr on the server and syserr.txt on the client are empty, and no window complains. This is the whole rule of delivery: A push from the server carries no target window (handler 0). It reaches every window registered for that namespace and header, not just one. If no callback ran, the message falls back to the game window's BINARY_LunaMessage. That function has no branch for login_counter, so the message is dropped silently. Put it back: press the button below, which restores HEADER = "count", repack, restart and log in. The board returns. Updateroot/uilogincounter.py
documents.s: Step 4: break the match on purpose

documents.t: The loop after every change: Proto change: run sh protoc.sh, then repack the client and recompile the forge. Forge change: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/login_counter.forge, then restart the game cores. Window change: repack the client with your packing tool and restart it. When all three files agree, a login shows the board with Login N, online M, and the server log shows [Forge-login_counter]: <name> login N, online M. The client logs nothing on a successful delivery. When something is off, find the symptom here: What you see Cause Nothing, no error anywhere Namespace or header differs between send_client and RegisterHandler, the window is not registered, or it was destroyed without unregistering. The board shows Login 0 The field numbers in the two compiled .proto copies differ, for example a client that was not repacked after a number changed. The protobuf decoder keeps the unknown number aside and reads the known field as 0. ImportError: No module named login_counter_pb2 The generated Python was not packed into the client. Luna protobuf Deserialization error: ... in syserr.txt, then AttributeError The payload does not parse as the class you passed to utils.Deserialize. ForgeGame::SendClientPacket called from a non-forge script send_client was called from the when login block instead of a forge method. Core does not start, ue.login_counter_pb in logs/syserr The generated Lua file is missing from share/locale/protobuf/ue/.

The namespace is the forge name. The proto package, the file name and the environment name (game) are all wrong guesses, and all of them fail silently. Field numbers are the contract, not field names or declaration order. Change one side and the other side shows 0 or swapped values without an error. Regenerate and repack both sides together. The generator rebuilds every proto and empties its output folders. Never keep hand-written files in them. A window that dies without unregistering still counts as having handled the message. The dead callback returns without doing anything, the game window fallback is skipped, and the message is swallowed. Unregister in Destroy and in __del__. Registering the same window, namespace and header twice is harmless: the second call replaces the first. Two different windows registered for the same pair both receive every push. An exception inside the callback prints a traceback to syserr.txt and nothing else happens. The fallback does not run. luna.ClearHandlers() runs when the interface is torn down, so every registration is gone after you return to character select. A window built on the next login registers again.

Forge API reference: send_client, calling context and errors. How messages travel: the packet, the namespace and the handler id. How the client receives them: registration, the lifetime of handlers and the game window fallback. Your first Forge module: the module this one extends. Previous Your first Forge module Next Write a battle arbiter rule

You give the warrior skill 2, Vortice della spada, a Lua damage handler. When the victim faces the same way you do, the hit counts as a back hit and the attack before defence is multiplied by 1.3. You write one new file and add one line to the skill's own file. No forge, no quest compiler, no client file. On a test server you read the effect in the chat: the engine prints the breakdown of every skill hit, and pure jumps by 30% on exactly the hits your handler announces.
documents.s: A back hit that lands 30% harder

documents.t: The skill extension reference open beside you, and Beyond the formula for why a skill's damage can be shaped from Lua. This page uses both without repeating them. The skill file reference explains the keys of the YAML file. A test server, where server.type.test_server is set in the core config. The breakdown line in step 2 exists only there. On a test server every character is a GM implementor, so /setskill works for anyone. Verification stays on a test server: the line sits in the live damage path behind that flag. A warrior with skill 2 and a sword or a two-handed weapon, the weapons the skill allows. Set the level with /setskill 2 <level> if the character does not have it. Two or more ordinary monsters of one kind standing near each other. Not bosses or metin stones. Switch off other bonuses while you measure: a trait buff, a stealth effect or a potion moves the numbers between casts. Access to the skill files of the server. You edit them in the repository folder Locale/conf/skill/. The restart loop of Your first Forge module: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files. The client reads its own copy of the skill file from the pack, but it never reads the handler: key. Nothing in this tutorial needs a pack to be staged again or the client to restart.

A handler is a Lua file named after the skill vnum, <vnum>.lua, next to the skill's <vnum>.ucskill.yaml. The file returns a table. Each key of the table is the name of a handler, and a DAMAGE node of the skill picks one with handler: <name>. There is no registration call: the name in the YAML and the key in the Lua are the whole binding. Skill 31, Tranello, ships with one. Its file and the line that binds it: OpenLocale/conf/skill/31.lua damage_intent runs for each target of a cast, after the formula and the splash factor and before the target's defence is subtracted. It gets one intent and writes the result back into intent.attack. It does not return anything: the engine reads the fields, not the return value. intent:is_back_hit(35) is true when the caster's facing and the victim's facing differ by less than 35 degrees. Skill 2 has one DAMAGE node, id: dmg, and no handler. OpenLocale/conf/skill/2.ucskill.yaml Before you edit anything, cast skill 2 once at two monsters of the same kind. Check. The chat prints one breakdown line per monster, and both carry the same pure value, the attack before defence. Write it down as P. Skill damage: pure -> <n> | base (after def) -> <n> | % bonus <n> | 2nd type modifiers -> <n> pure is the attack the handler hands back, before defence. base (after def) is pure minus the defence of the victim. The last two numbers add the percentage modifiers and the closing modifier.
documents.s: Step 1: read the model and take a baseline

documents.t: Create Locale/conf/skill/2.lua. The key is palbang, the name of the skill's icon, as in 31.lua where it is amseop. The condition is the same is_back_hit(35). The factor is 1.3 for the back hit and nothing for any other hit. This file has no dagger term because skill 2 is not a dagger skill, so the factor is exactly 1.3. Copy 31's dagger term onto a dagger skill and the terms add: 1.0 plus 0.3 plus 0.5 reads as 1.8 against 1.5 in front, a ratio of 1.2. CreateLocale/conf/skill/2.lua Then bind it. Add handler: palbang to the DAMAGE node of Locale/conf/skill/2.ucskill.yaml, right after ability_scaling, indented as a key of the node, at the level of damageType. UpdateLocale/conf/skill/2.ucskill.yaml Restart the game cores. Check. The file loaded if logs/syserr has no line that starts with skill 2 . logs/syslog has the table line: Skill Prototype loaded from YAML: <n> skills, <n> policy variants over <n> policies Nothing else confirms the handler at boot. The proof comes in the next step.
documents.s: Step 2: write the handler and bind it

documents.t:
The log says the file loaded. It does not say the function runs. Make it talk: one chat line to the caster on every back hit, with the value before and after. is_test_server() keeps the line off a live server, where the handler still does its job. forge is read inside the function, at hit time, never at the top of the file. UpdateLocale/conf/skill/2.lua Replace the file's content, restart the game cores and cast skill 2 at two monsters, one of them facing away from you. A monster that has just been hit usually turns to face you, so use one that is idle or walking away. Check. The monster that faces away gives a line before its breakdown, and the breakdown has the raised pure: back hit on :

-> Skill damage: pure -> | base (after def) -> | % bonus | 2nd type modifiers -> The other monster has no back-hit line, and its breakdown still reads pure ->

.

Cast several times and compare each pure with the P you wrote down. Every back-hit line pairs with a pure that is 1.3 times P, rounded down, and every hit without a back-hit line keeps P. base (after def) rises by the same absolute amount as pure: the defence is subtracted after the handler, so the bonus is not eaten by it. Now delete the handler: line from 2.ucskill.yaml and restart. The back-hit lines are gone and pure is P on every target. You wrote nothing that takes the 30% away. The handler only changed one hit while it was worked out. Check. Three readings agree: the back-hit line appears only on a target that faces your way, pure is 1.3 times P on exactly those hits, and both disappear without the handler: line. To undo for good, also delete 2.lua.

The loop is the same after every change to the handler or the skill file: Edit Locale/conf/skill/2.lua or 2.ucskill.yaml. Restart the game cores: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. Read logs/syserr for lines that start with skill 2 , then cast the skill. No compile step exists. The restart is the loop: the skill table is read when the core starts, and a running core does not read an edited handler file again. The game core does not start if the YAML is broken, for example if the new line is indented wrong: Skill YAML: cannot parse file 2.ucskill.yaml: <yaml error> cannot initialize skill table from YAML Every fault in the Lua side is gentler. The core boots, one line goes to logs/syserr, and the node runs without the handler: Line in logs/syserr Cause skill 2 handler 'palbang' not found in 2.lua the handler: value and the key of the returned table differ skill 2 declares a handler but conf/skill/2.lua is missing the file is named or placed wrong skill 2 2.lua must return a table of handlers the file has no return M skill 2 extension load error: <message> a Lua syntax error in the file skill 2 handler 'palbang' implements none of gate, damage_intent or applied the slot name is misspelled skill 2 damage_intent error: <message> a runtime error inside the function; logged on every hit

A 2.lua without the handler: line is never read. No error, no effect. Write intent.attack. A handler that returns the new value instead changes nothing and logs nothing. Call methods with a colon: intent.caster:chat_packet(...). With a dot, the call raises and the hit goes on with whatever intent.attack held at that moment. Write it last. is_back_hit compares facings, not positions. A monster that faces your way counts wherever it stands, and a monster that turns to face you never counts. The angles are folded to the range of -180 to 180 and subtracted, so facings of 170 and -170 degrees give a difference of 340 and do not count. Edit a handler and the restart is the only loop. /reload p re-reads the skill table, so it picks up a new handler: line, but it keeps the functions already loaded from a 2.lua and your edit does not run. Without collect.scalePoly on the node, every victim of one cast gets the same attack before the handler, so two lines that differ differ only by the handler. A node with a scale poly breaks that comparison.

Skill extension reference: the three slots, gate, damage_intent and applied, and every field of the intent. Beyond the formula: why this hook sits before defence and where the old vnum branches went. A bonus that only counts when: the same test-server readout habit, for a trait. Previous A bonus that only counts when Next A map-wide empire skill

You draw a filled disc with a bright rim whose width pulses, inside a plain client window. The picture comes from one pixel shader. A Python class places the window and sends the shader a clock, so the rim breathes once a second or so. Two files make it: a shader in the client pack and a test window that you keep loose beside the client. The shipped aura shader on the right is the model; read it first.

A debug client built with the remote debugger flag. Its test board loads a loose Python file by name and shows it, which is how you iterate on a window without repacking Python. Your client's pack step for the root folder (pack-client-files). Shaders are read from the pack, so a new shader needs a repack and a client restart. The ui.ShaderQuad reference open beside you.

A shader quad is an ordinary window whose rectangle a pixel shader paints. The shader gets 16 floats from Python in a constant buffer at b13. The aura shader names the first six: red, green, blue, fill alpha, rim alpha and rim width in screen pixels. Openpack/root/shaders/ui/aura_ps.hlsl The window is told to span texture coordinates (-1, -1) to (1, 1), so length(input.TexCoord) is exactly 1 on the edge of the disc whatever the window size. The rim is measured in screen pixels through fwidth, so it stays one readable line at every size. Check. You can name the six floats and which of them is a width in pixels.

The aura has no clock, and a shader has no time input: the only way a value reaches it is the 16 floats. You add a seventh one, g_Time, and let it widen and narrow the rim. The file lives next to the model, under shaders/ui/ in the client files root folder. Createpack/root/shaders/ui/pulse_ps.hlsl The cbuffer keeps its 16-float shape: the new float takes the place of the first padding float. Check. g_Time sits seventh in the cbuffer, so Python must send it as the seventh value.

The test board loads a module named uiTest and builds its TestWindow class. The class makes a ui.ShaderQuad, parents it to itself, sets the shader and the disc-space UV, and in OnUpdate sends all 16 floats, with the time since the window opened in the seventh. SetParams fills what you leave out with zeros, so always send the whole tuple. The picking flag keeps the decorative quad from swallowing clicks. Creategame/uiTest.py The board calls Destroy before it replaces a test window, so the class releases its quad there. Check. The shader path is shaders/ui/pulse_ps.hlsl, exactly the file you created, and the UV is -1, -1, 1, 1.
documents.s: Step 2: a window that sends the clock

documents.t: Repack the root folder and start the debug client. Log in, open the test board (the window with the "uiTest" line), and press F10 or click Load. A window appears at 300, 200: a blue disc, faint inside, with a bright rim that grows and shrinks. If nothing appears, the shader failed and the quad draws nothing; Python raises no error. Look in the client log: PrimitiveRenderer2D: Failed to load shaders/ui/pulse_ps.hlsl DX11 shader compilation failed for 'shaders/ui/pulse_ps.hlsl': <compiler diagnostic> The first line with no compiler line means the file is not in the pack under that path. A compiler line carries the HLSL error. Fix the file, repack and restart the client: a failed pipeline stays cached under its path for the whole session, so Load alone never retries it. If the disc is a thin line or a square, the UV is still the default (0, 0, 1, 1). If the rim does not move, the seventh float is not the clock.
ui.ShaderQuad: textures, the shader contract and every trap. The render pipeline: how the quad's draw reaches the device. Previous A live dungeon panel Next A colour gradient on a particle

You build a Forge module named visible_buff. It defines one affect type, 3900, and a GM command /vbuff on adds it to you for 5 minutes. A second player standing nearby sees a green particle on you and, after targeting you, a target board icon with a countdown. The buff survives your death and "restart here", and it is gone after a warp. The server half is configuration: a name for the type and three flags. The engine does the rest. The client half is three edits in the client pack, because the server only ever sends the number 3900 and no client knows what to draw for it.
documents.s: A buff other players can see

documents.t: The finished module of Your first Forge module, and the loop you use there to compile, register and restart. This module uses the same loop. The affects reference open beside you, and Affects for why the engine keeps a type's look, its save rule and its death rule as flags outside the code that adds it. This page uses both without repeating them. Two clients on a test server, where every character can use GM commands. Call the characters A and B. B needs /kill. On a server that is not a test server, /vbuff needs the low wizard GM level and /kill the high wizard level. Put them on an ordinary map, close together. A client whose pack you can edit and rebuild. Three files change in it, and the client reads the pack at startup, so you rebuild once and restart both clients. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files. It highlights .lua, .forge, .quest, .py, .yml and .json, so the .mse particle file shows as plain text there.

An affect type is a number. The server does not need a name for it, but affect.add_name_definition gives it one, so affect.name_map.TUTORIAL_VISIBLE_BUFF can stand in for 3900 in your Lua. Three more calls flag the type: affect.add_broadcastable sends every add and remove of this type to everyone who can see the character, not only to its owner. Without it only the owner knows. affect.add_no_save keeps the type out of the character's saved affects. affect.add_no_clear_on_death keeps it when the character dies. The calls run once, when the core boots. Openshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/visible_buff.forge 3900 is clear of the types other modules use. Below 400 are skill affects and 1000 and up are quest affects. From 10000 up, the engine never clears a type on death and never saves it, so a test with such an id would prove nothing. The module returns a table, because a forge that returns nothing fails to load, and then the game core does not start. Create share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/visible_buff.forge with exactly this content, then register it. Add one line to share/locale/italy/quest/qc/quest_list: ../system/tutorial/visible_buff.forge Compile it alone, from the runtime root: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/visible_buff.forge Check. The compiler prints no error, and share/locale/italy/quest/forge/visible_buff.game exists. There is no state block, so nothing is created under object/. Restart the game cores and search the log: grep visible_buff logs/syslog You should see this line: [Forge-visible_buff]: loaded, affect 3900 logs/syserr says nothing about visible_buff.

Something has to add the affect. A command lets you do it at will, and keeps the buff out of login, where a re-add would hide the save test later. ch:add_affect(type, point, value, flag, duration, sp_cost, override) takes the type, the attribute point the affect changes, its value, a flag, a duration in seconds, an SP cost and whether to replace an existing one. This call adds 20 to the movement speed point for 300 seconds, so you feel the buff as well as see it. Keep flag at 0: a non-zero flag also sets a status bit, and a bit that has its own client particle would draw the character twice. Calling ch:remove_affect first, then add_affect, restarts the timer when you run the command twice and shows nearby players a remove followed by an add. (override set to true would also replace the affect in place.) /vbuff is a router, with on and off as its routes. new_low_wizard_route takes the usage text, the list of parameters (none here) and the callback. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/visible_buff.forge Replace the file's content with this version, compile again and restart the game cores. Check. The log has the router line next to the module line: [OK] cmd.register_router : [vbuff] [Forge-visible_buff]: loaded, affect 3900 On A, type /vbuff on. The chat says visible buff on for 300 seconds. Then list the affects of A: /affect_remove A The list has a row that starts with 3900, and its duration is close to 300. Nothing shows on screen yet, and that is expected: the server sent the element, and no client knows what to do with the number 3900. Run /vbuff off and list again: the row is gone.
documents.s: Step 2: add and remove the buff with a command

documents.t: A particle is a file the client draws on the character. Your effect is the first particle group of the GM mark, which sits in the client pack in locale/universal/effect/gm.mse, with the color changed to green so you can tell the two apart. Createlocale/universal/effect/visible_buff.mse Create locale/universal/effect/visible_buff.mse in the client pack, in the same folder as gm.mse, with exactly this content. It is a particle script: one emitter 124 units above the character, and the three lists TimeEventColorRed, TimeEventColorGreen and TimeEventColorBlue that set its color. The texture universalled.dds is the one gm.mse uses. Now tell the client which type owns it. The registration is one line in the Broadcastable-affect particles block of __main__ in root/introloading.py. The key is playerLoad.EFFECT_BROADCAST_AFFECT + 3900. The bone is "", the character's origin, like the battle royale beacons. A bone name such as "Bip01" would hang the particle on the skeleton. Createroot/introloading.py The excerpt shows only a few of the block's lines. Add its last line to the block in the real file, after the entries that are already there. The number must be the same as the server's, and nothing checks it. Rebuild the client pack and restart both clients. Check. On A, type /vbuff on. A green particle appears above A on both screens. B sees it without targeting A. Now target A on B: the target board shows no icon for the buff. The particle and the icon are two separate registrations, and you have made the first one. If the particle is missing on both, read the client's error log. A wrong .mse path logs RegisterEffect - LoadScript(<path>) Error and the affect then shows with no particle.

The target board lists a type only if the type has an entry in AFFECT_DATA_DICT in root/uiaffectshower.py. An entry is a tuple: a title, an icon file, a resize flag, a description or None, and whether the player may cancel it by hand. This entry reuses the icon of the bleeding affect and has no description. Createroot/uiaffectshower.py The excerpt shows only a few of the dictionary's entries. Add the 3900 line to AFFECT_DATA_DICT in the real file. The same dictionary draws the affect bar of the owner, so A gets the icon too. Rebuild the client pack and restart both clients. Check. On A, type /vbuff on. A's own affect bar shows the icon with a countdown. On B, target A: the target board shows the same icon and nearly the same countdown. Walk B away until A is out of sight, walk back and target A again: the particle is on A and the icon is on the target board, because the server replays the broadcast affects to a character that comes into view.

Run /vbuff on on A if the 5 minutes have passed. On B, type /kill A. A dies. On A, press "Restart here". The death clear skips every type in the no-clear-on-death set, and "restart here" is not a warp. So the buff is still there. Check. On A, the icon is still in the affect bar. /affect_remove A still lists 3900. On B, the target board of A still shows the icon. The particle is back on A on both screens. On a server that is not a test server, "restart here" works ten seconds after the death on an ordinary map.

Run /vbuff on on A again, let B kill A with /kill A, and press "Restart in town". A warp is a reconnect, and the character loads again from its saved affects. The no-save flag keeps the type out of the saved set, so the buff does not come back. Check. After the town loads, /affect_remove A has no 3900 row and A's affect bar has no icon. Log out and in with the buff on as another check: the result is the same.
documents.s: Step 6: lose the buff with a warp

documents.t: The loop is the same after every server change: Compile: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/visible_buff.forge. Restart the game cores: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. Read logs/syslog for the [Forge-visible_buff] line and logs/syserr for errors. Every client change needs a pack rebuild and a client restart. If you misspell a name, for example affect.name_map.TUTORIAL_VISIBLE_BUF, BUFF is nil and each flag call logs one line, and none of the flags is set: affect_add_no_clear_on_death wrong argument: int type The same line exists for affect_add_no_save and affect_add_broadcastable. In this module the next line, "loaded, affect " .. BUFF, then fails on the nil, the forge does not load and the game core does not start. A module that only passes the name on would load, and its buff would behave as if you had left the calls out.

Leave add_broadcastable out and nothing complains. A still has the affect and sees the icon on its own bar, but there is no particle on anyone and B's target board is empty. No log says why. The icon and the particle are separate. A particle needs a RegisterEffect line, an icon needs an AFFECT_DATA_DICT entry, and a missing one is silent. The client does not know which types are broadcast. A client entry for a type the server does not flag shows nothing to anyone. The number must match in the forge, introloading.py and uiaffectshower.py. The server never sends the name. A duration of 0 becomes 1 second and writes a line to logs/syserr. The three flags are also lists in share/locale/italy/affect_config.yaml: NO_SAVE_AFFECTS, NO_CLEAR_ON_DEATH_AFFECTS and BROADCASTABLE_AFFECTS. The two registrations merge. The doors fail in opposite directions: an unknown name in the YAML stops the core, and an unknown name in Lua is one log line. A broadcast reaches the characters in view when the affect is added or removed, and a character that comes into view later gets a replay. There is no periodic resend. The flags have no remove call, so taking a flag away needs a core restart. A registration on the client is first-wins: a second line for the same type is ignored.

Affects reference: the registration calls, add_affect in full, and the flags. Affects: how the engine keeps these rules outside the code that adds an affect. Send a message from the server to a client window: another client pack edit, a Python window that receives a server message. Previous Lift the party rules on one map Next A bonus that only counts when

You build a Forge module named open_party. On the map you choose, any two players can form a party, whatever their empires and whatever the gap between their levels. On every other map the stock rules hold. The rule is one party join policy: a guard that says which pairs it cares about, and a verdict that says which stock rules to drop. You check it in game with three characters, then break it twice on purpose, once with a missing return and once with a misspelled key, and read what the server does.
documents.s: Lift the party rules on one map

documents.t: The finished module of Your first Forge module, and the loop you use there to compile, register and restart. This module uses the same loop. The party join policy reference open beside you, and Policies for why the engine asks a policy instead of hard-coding the rule. This page uses both without repeating them. Three test characters on a test server, where every character can use GM commands. Two are of the same empire, call them A and B, with A at least 31 levels above B. The third, C, is of another empire. /level <n> sets a level, and it also clears the character's skills, so use throwaway characters. All three on one map, standing close together. Type /state and read the number after MapIndex. You need it in step 1. A text editor. The workbench on the right only shows the files; you create the real one in share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/. Why three characters: the stock client hides "Invite to party" ("Invito Gruppo") on a player of another empire, and the server cannot change that. A direct invite therefore shows the level rule, and the empire rule needs the other route, a join request from C to a leader who already has a party. Do not test with the party finder: it applies only part of the verdict.

A party join policy is a (name, guard, policy) triple. forge.sys.game.party_join_policy.register takes the three and returns a handle, a number greater than 0. Every time someone invites, asks to join or accepts, the engine walks the registered policies in order. The first one whose guard returns true gives the verdict, and the stock rules are applied with that verdict's values. This guard matches when the leader and the guest both stand on your map. The verdict is a table of only the fields you want to change: same_empire = false drops the empire rule, and level_window = 0 drops the level window. Every field you leave out keeps its stock value. Openshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/open_party.forge MAP_INDEX is a placeholder. Set it to the number /state printed. The module returns a table, because a forge that returns nothing fails to load, and then the game core does not start. Create share/locale/italy/system/tutorial/open_party.forge with exactly this content, then register it. Add one line to share/locale/italy/quest/qc/quest_list: ../system/tutorial/open_party.forge Compile it alone, from the runtime root: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/open_party.forge Check. The compiler prints no error, and share/locale/italy/quest/forge/open_party.game exists. There is no state block, so nothing is created under object/. Restart the game cores and search the log: grep open_party logs/syslog You should see these two lines. The handle varies: another policy registered earlier takes a lower number. [OK] party_join_policy [open_party]: handle=<n> [Forge-open_party]: loaded, policy <n> on map <map_index> logs/syserr says nothing about open_party.

Leave the map. Go to any other map with A and B, close together, and have A target B and press "Invito Gruppo". Check. A reads the level refusal in chat, <Gruppo> Possono essere invitati solo giocatori il cui livello differisce al massimo di 30., and B sees nothing. Your guard did not match, so the stock rules held.
documents.s: Step 2: see the stock rules first

documents.t: Go back to your map with A and B, stand close, and have A invite B again. Stay within a few steps: the client turns an accept into a refusal when the leader is more than 5000 units away. Check. B gets a dialog that asks whether to join A's group, and it stays for 10 seconds. B accepts. Both now have a party. The log shows one create line and two join lines: PARTY: Create <leader> pid <pid> PARTY: Join <name> pid <pid> leader <leader pid> PARTY: Join <name> pid <pid> leader <leader pid> The level gap did not matter. The policy gave this pair level_window = 0.
documents.s: Step 3: the level rule is gone

documents.t: A is now the leader of a party. Bring C next to A and target A. "Invito Gruppo" is not there, because C is of another empire. "Entra nel gruppo" is, because A is in a party. Press it. The request goes through the same policy: the verdict is resolved for the leader of the party and the guest, and the empire rule is judged with it. Check. A gets a dialog, <name> desidera entrare nel gruppo, with Accept and Deny. A accepts. A reads <Gruppo> <name> si è unito al tuo Gruppo. and C reads <Gruppo> <name> è entrato nel Gruppo. Try the same on another map first if you want to see the refusal it replaces: <Gruppo> Non puoi creare un gruppo con giocatori di altri regni.
documents.s: Step 4: the empire rule is gone

documents.t: A policy must return a table. This version builds the table and forgets to return it. It compiles, it loads, and it does nothing. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/open_party.forge Compile, restart, make sure no one is in a party, and repeat step 3 on your map. Check. The level refusal is back, as if the policy did not exist. A policy that fails does not block anyone: the engine logs the error and falls back to the stock rules. logs/syserr gets these two lines every time the policy is reached: Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation wrong return: expected [table], got nothing [party_join_policy open_party] lua callback error A policy that returns a boolean gives got [boolean] in the first line. A Lua runtime error gives Bridge::ValidateProcessorInvocation lua error: <message>. A guard fails the other way: an error or a non-boolean return counts as false, so the policy never applies, and the log pair carries open_party guard. Put the return back with the next button.
documents.s: Step 5: break the policy with a missing return

documents.t: This version spells the empire key sameEmpire. Nothing complains about it. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/open_party.forge Compile, restart, make sure no one is in a party, and repeat steps 3 and 4. Check. Step 3 still works, because level_window is spelled right. In step 4, C gets the empire refusal. logs/syserr is empty and logs/syslog shows nothing out of the ordinary. The engine reads only the keys it knows, and an unknown key, or a known key of the wrong type such as same_empire = "false", is ignored silently and the stock value stays. The only check is to play it. Restore the clean version with the last button: open_party-1.forge is also what the Solve view shows. Updateshare/locale/italy/system/tutorial/open_party.forge
documents.s: Step 6: break the policy with a misspelled key

documents.t: The loop is the same after every change: Compile: ./qc.sh --f ../system/tutorial/open_party.forge. Restart the game cores: sh shutdown.sh, then sh run.sh. Read logs/syslog for the party_join_policy and [Forge-open_party] lines, and logs/syserr for the errors above. If you pass something that is not a function to register, it throws party_join_policy.register: guard is not callable (or policy is not callable) into your forge.

The policy lifts the two rules you named. It does not touch these, and the invite or request fails with the stock message: the leader is in a dungeon, or the guest is in observer mode; the guest is already in a party, or the party already has 8 members; either character is in a team session, and the two are not in the same session as allies: <Gruppo> Non puoi invitare un nemico.; the character who invites, or who asks to join, is in a PvP arena, which is refused before the policy is asked; the guest blocked party invites, or the leader blocked requests; the party switch of the server is off.

The level refusal always says 30. Its text is fixed, so it stays 30 if you set a window of 10. A misspelled key is ignored without a log line. Check the spelling against the reference. A broken policy brings the stock rules back, and a broken guard skips your rule. Both fail safe, and both look like "my rule does nothing". The first matching guard wins, in registration order. Two guards that match the same pair hide the later one. The verdict is resolved again when an invite is accepted, so the guest must still be on your map at that moment. The policy judges admission only. Nothing removes a member who later walks off the map. The client decides what it shows. The server would admit C to a direct invite, but the stock client offers no button for it. Keep the guard cheap. It runs on every invite, request and accept on the core. A forge has no unload hook, so the policy lives until the core stops. To change MAP_INDEX, edit, compile and restart. unregister takes the handle you kept, as in Write a battle arbiter rule. The policy is per core. Both characters must be on the core that hosts your map.

Party join policy reference: every verdict field, including the ones that cap the party size and refuse with your own message. Policies: why these decisions are registered instead of written into the engine. Write a battle arbiter rule: the same guard and verdict shape on the combat side. Previous Write a battle arbiter rule Next A buff other players can see
A binding exposes a C++ function or object to Forge Lua. Register it on the core that needs it; the two cores are separate binaries.

Core Root table Registration game forge.sys.game ForgeGame::instance().GetEnvSysTable() db forge.sys.db ForgeDB::instance().GetEnvSysTable() Registration code runs once when its core starts. A binding exists only on the core that registers it; game bindings do not exist on db. Quest-side libraries such as pc and npc use older registration and are out of scope.
documents.s: What a binding is and where it lives

documents.t: Term Meaning Binding C++ registration exposing a function or type to Lua. Usertype A C++ type exposed as a Lua object. Namespace table A Lua table grouping bindings for an area. Stub Generated Lua declarations for editors and docs. Marshalling Converting arguments and returns between Lua and C++.

Write void luna::Register<Area>Bindings(), declare it extern in the game's Forge declarations, and add one call in game Forge initialization after the built-in forge.sys.game.send_* functions. Db areas use the same shape and are called at the end of db Forge initialization. Some registration functions take luna::Bridge* for event-bus or hook access. extern void RegisterActivityLockBindings(); RegisterActivityLockBindings(); The first line is the declaration, the second the call in the flat list of area registrations. Inside the function, obtain the root table and use create_named("activity_lock") to make forge.sys.game.activity_lock. A new area needs the function, declaration, and call; registration is not automatic.

Use table.set_function("name", lambda). A pure binding can take only its real parameters. Macro Lambda parameters Use LUNA_FORGE_BIND_NO_ARGS() sol::this_state ts, sol::this_environment te Access state or environment without real arguments. LUNA_FORGE_BIND_WITH_ARGS(args...) sol::this_state ts, args..., sol::this_environment te Access them with real arguments; environment is last. Use ts to build Lua tables. Use te to identify the calling forge, as send and registration functions do when they reject calls without a forge environment.

Direction Supported values Arguments Integers, floats, bool, std::string, const char*, sol::optional<T> for nil or absent arguments, sol::table, sol::object, sol::protected_function, and registered usertype pointers. Returns Scalars, strings, sol::table, usertype pointers, sol::object, or nothing. Use sol::nil for nil. Build a return table with sol::state_view lua(ts) and lua.create_table(). The db core uses CPeer* and has no character types.

Operation Form Object lua.new_usertype<T>("LPNAME", "field", sol::readonly(&T::member), "method", &T::Method) Enum table.new_enum("NAME", "KEY", VALUE) exposes forge.sys.game.<ns>.NAME.KEY. Use sol::readonly for fields scripts must not write.
Choose snake_case Lua names in set_function; they are not derived from C++ names. The namespace table groups an area.

Place a documentation comment above each set_function or new_usertype. It starts with /*! and an escaped ---@luadoc <namespace> line; the namespace selects the stub file, and the global namespace must exist. Use EmmyLua description, @param, @return, and @lua lines; classes use @class, @field, and an @lua NAME = {} declaration, and enums use @class ns.ENUM and @field KEY number. Escape each dash and at sign in the triple-dash directive, and escape Markdown characters in the block: at signs, stars, backticks, underscores, double dashes, and angle brackets. Re-run the docs generator from the Server folder after changing a comment; add a source to the Doxygen filter if needed. The resulting ---@meta stubs serve the Lua language server and docs, not the running server; an undocumented binding works but is invisible to editors.

A C++ exception or sol2 argument conversion failure becomes a Lua error logged with its message; the server keeps running. Validate input in the binding and use sys_err plus false or nil for invalid values. Usertype pointers are raw engine pointers: check for nil and do not keep them.

The smallest complete area in the engine is a lock registry with three functions: a namespace table, one doc comment and one lambda per function. void RegisterActivityLockBindings() { auto& env_sys_table = ForgeGame::instance().GetEnvSysTable(); auto reg = env_sys_table.create_named("activity_lock"); /*! \---\@luadoc forge.sys.game.activity_lock * * \---Sets or removes a process-local activity lock by player id. * \---\@param pid number * \---\@param locked boolean * \---\@lua function forge.sys.game.activity_lock.set(pid, locked) end */ reg.set_function("set", [](uint32_t dwPID, bool bLocked) { CActivityLock::instance().Set(dwPID, bLocked); }); /*! \---\@luadoc forge.sys.game.activity_lock * * \---Checks whether a player id is explicitly locked. * \---\@param pid number * \---\@return boolean * \---\@lua function forge.sys.game.activity_lock.is_set(pid) end */ reg.set_function("is_set", [](uint32_t dwPID) { return CActivityLock::instance().IsSet(dwPID); }); /*! \---\@luadoc forge.sys.game.activity_lock * * \---Clears every explicit activity lock. * \---\@lua function forge.sys.game.activity_lock.clear() end */ reg.set_function("clear", []() { CActivityLock::instance().Clear(); }); } Reading it: create_named("activity_lock") makes forge.sys.game.activity_lock; the Lua names are the strings given to set_function. uint32_t and bool parameters marshal from a Lua number and boolean. is_set returns the bool as a Lua boolean; the other two return nothing. Each comment names the stub file in its luadoc line and gives the Lua declaration in its lua line, so the editor shows forge.sys.game.activity_lock.set(pid, locked). The function is declared extern in the game Forge declarations and called once in the flat registration list, as shown above. From a forge on the game core: forge.sys.game.activity_lock.set(1001, true) sys_log(0, "locked: " .. tostring(forge.sys.game.activity_lock.is_set(1001))) forge.sys.game.activity_lock.clear()

A usertype hands Lua a pointer to an engine object. The map registry does this for a sectree map: RegisterSectreeMapBindings makes a sectree_map namespace and declares LPSECTREE_MAP with one method. lua.new_usertype<SECTREE_MAP>("LPSECTREE_MAP", sol::constructors<>(), /*! \---\@luadoc sectree_map * * \---Retrieves the settings of the map. * \---\@return sectree_map.MAP_SETTINGS * \---\@lua function LPSECTREE_MAP:get_settings() end */ "get_settings", [](LUNA_FORGE_BIND_WITH_ARGS(SECTREE_MAP& map)) -> sol::table { sol::state_view lua(ts); sol::table t = lua.create_table(); t["index"] = map.m_setting.iIndex; t["width"] = map.m_setting.iWidth; return t; }); lua is the global state, so the type name is global; the area table only holds functions that return the pointer. sol::constructors<>() forbids creating the object from Lua. Scripts only receive pointers produced by C++, here forge.sys.game.sectree_manager.get_map(map_index), which returns nil for an unknown map. The first parameter of a method is the object itself, taken by reference. The macro still appends the environment; Lua calls map:get_settings() with the colon. The returned table is built per call; nothing keeps a reference to the engine object. Check it from a forge on the game core: local map = forge.sys.game.sectree_manager.get_map(1) if map then sys_log(0, "width: " .. map:get_settings().width) end The binding is loaded when this logs a width and the core prints no registration error at start. After regenerating the stubs, the editor should also offer get_settings on LPSECTREE_MAP values. Nothing here needs an engine tool: build and restart the core as for any C++ change.
